1.heading: Insight
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why I do not teach "the ten principles of economics"
Most introductory textbooks open with a list of ten or so "principles" — like "people respond to incentives," "trade can make everyone better off," and "markets are usually a good way to organize economic activity." These principles are not wrong, exactly, but they are misleading as a framework. They present a stylized version of economics where the rough edges have been smoothed off and the central debates have been resolved in favor of one particular vision (broadly: markets work, government usually does not, prices are good signals). The actual discipline is more contested than the principles framework suggests, the historical record is messier than the textbook stories admit, and the empirical evidence is more nuanced than the bullet-point principles imply.

1.heading: Insight
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The framework I will use instead is six recurring themes rather than principles. Themes are questions and patterns the discipline keeps returning to, not settled conclusions. Each theme has a stylized story one will find in most textbooks, and each has a more complicated empirical reality that working economists actually engage with. If one finishes this book understanding both the stylized version and why it is a simplification, one will have done what an introductory course can deliver. Pretending the simplifications are the truth would be presenting something we know is wrong.
— A.S.

1.heading: Theme One: Scarcity Forces Choice — Including Choices About Choice
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📘 Principles Level — Scarcity as the starting point
The classical starting point of economics is scarcity: human wants exceed available resources, so choices must be made about what to produce, who gets to consume, when to consume vs. save, what to invest in. Every economic system — capitalist, socialist, hunter-gatherer, feudal — has to answer these questions. The differences across systems are largely about how they answer them: through markets, through central planning, through tradition, through political negotiation, through some mix.
Scarcity is real. In any given afternoon one cannot both go to the gym and finish reading a book. Two minutes spent here cannot also be spent there. Money spent on rent cannot also be spent on food. Hours of public sector spending on K-12 education cannot also be spent on Medicare. The recognition that all choices involve foregone alternatives — the opportunity cost of the path taken — is one of the truly portable concepts in economics. It applies to the decision about which course to take this semester, to a firm's decision about which project to fund, to a country's decision about its defense vs. social spending mix.

1.heading: Theme One: Scarcity Forces Choice — Including Choices About Choice
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "We do not have the resources for that"
One will hear politicians, commentators, and ordinary people say "we cannot afford that" about specific government programs. This is sometimes correct as a budget statement, but it is almost never correct as an economic claim. The U.S. produces approximately $28 trillion of goods and services per year. The question is not whether resources exist; the question is whether using resources for purpose X means giving up purpose Y. "We cannot afford universal pre-K" usually means "we choose not to reallocate from other uses." That is a legitimate choice, but it is a choice, not a constraint.
The economic question — and the more interesting one — is the trade-off, not the affordability. If universal pre-K requires raising taxes by 0.5% of GDP and produces a benefit of (let's say) 1.5% of GDP in higher long-run productivity, then it passes a cost-benefit test even though it requires reallocating resources. The "cannot afford it" framing obscures the actual decision being made. Whenever one hears "we cannot afford it," substitute "we choose other priorities" and see if the argument still feels the same. Often it does not.

1.body:
1939-1945
United States
Wartime Reallocation
How the U.S. Found 40% of GDP for Defense
In 1939, U.S. defense spending was about 1% of GDP. By 1944 it was 38% of GDP — a 37-percentage-point shift in a five-year period. To accomplish this, the U.S. instituted rationing of consumer goods (sugar, gasoline, tires, butter), price controls, capacity reallocation from automobiles to aircraft, civilian draft of millions of workers into military service, and massive borrowing financed by patriotic war bonds. Real consumer spending per capita actually fell during the war — Americans had higher nominal income but were not allowed to spend it on the goods they wanted, because those goods were not being produced.

1.heading: Theme One: Scarcity Forces Choice — Including Choices About Choice
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The interesting question for our purposes is this: in 1939, could a U.S. politician have said "we cannot afford a war that takes 38% of GDP"? They might have, but they would have been wrong. The resources existed; what was required was reallocation. Once the political consensus changed in late 1941, the reallocation happened with extraordinary speed. This case illustrates the difference between budget arithmetic ("we do not have the money allocated") and economic possibility ("the resources do not exist"). The latter is much rarer than the former. When next encountering a claim about a hypothetical government program, ask: is this really an affordability problem, or is it a priorities problem?
Figure 1.1 The production possibilities frontier. Point A is efficient: no additional consumption good can be produced without giving up a capital good. Point B is attainable but wasteful, and point C cannot be reached with current resources and technology. The slope of the frontier at any point is the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other, and the outward bow reflects resources that are not equally suited to both activities.

Accumulating capital, enlarging the labor force, or improving technology moves the whole frontier outward, and the combination that was impossible becomes feasible. Growth does not abolish scarcity: on the new frontier every additional consumption good still costs capital goods forgone.

1.heading: Theme Two: Incentives Matter — And Often Backfire
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📘 Principles Level — The textbook story
People — individuals, firms, governments — respond to incentives. Raise the price of gasoline through a tax, and people drive less, buy more efficient cars, or move closer to work. Subsidize solar panels, and more get installed. Increase fines for speeding, and more people slow down. The mechanism is straightforward: incentives change the relative attractiveness of different choices, and people shift toward more attractive options.
This is one of the most empirically supported propositions in economics. Hundreds of studies confirm that demand curves slope downward (people buy less of a good when its price rises) and supply curves slope upward (firms produce more when they are paid more). When economists predict the consequences of policy, they are applying this framework: a higher minimum wage will tend to reduce employment (firms substitute away from labor); a tax credit for solar installation will tend to increase solar installation; a tax on cigarettes will tend to reduce smoking. The empirical regularity is robust.
📗 Intermediate Level — Why incentives produce unintended consequences

1.heading: Theme Two: Incentives Matter — And Often Backfire
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The complication is that the incentive working as intended is only one of many incentives a policy creates. Policies create direct incentives (the intended response) and indirect incentives (responses one did not anticipate). The history of economic policy is largely the history of indirect incentives turning out to matter more than direct ones. Consider some examples that one will see again throughout this book:
Rent control reduces rents for current tenants (intended) but reduces the supply of rental housing over time as landlords convert to other uses (unintended), reducing total housing availability.
Cobra bounties in colonial India were intended to reduce cobra populations by paying for dead cobras. People started breeding cobras to collect the bounty. When the program ended, the breeders released their cobras, increasing the population. This is now called the "cobra effect."
Pay-for-performance in schools intended to raise math scores often does — by inducing teachers to teach to the test, reducing time on subjects not on the test, and sometimes leading to outright cheating on standardized tests.

1.heading: Theme Two: Incentives Matter — And Often Backfire
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
Stricter mortgage underwriting rules intended to prevent another 2008 crisis make it harder for first-time buyers to get mortgages, reducing homeownership among the young.
The principles framework would say "people respond to incentives." The fuller principle is: people respond to all the incentives a policy creates, and the unintended responses often turn out to be larger or more important than the intended ones. Designing policies that work well requires anticipating these indirect responses, not just the direct ones.

1.heading: Theme Two: Incentives Matter — And Often Backfire
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why economic policymaking is hard
The principle "people respond to incentives" combined with the corollary "responses go in many directions, including ones one did not anticipate" is most of why economic policy is genuinely difficult. Almost any policy that produces a desired direct effect also produces indirect effects that may partially or fully offset it. This is not an argument for never doing anything — that conclusion ignores the direct benefits. It is an argument for taking the indirect responses seriously when designing policy and not being surprised when they show up.

1.heading: Theme Two: Incentives Matter — And Often Backfire
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The economists who do the best policy analysis are not the ones who can identify the intended effect (anyone can do that). They are the ones who can identify the full set of incentive responses and estimate their relative magnitudes. This is also why economists often disagree about policy effects: they can have similar models of incentives but different estimates of which incentive responses will dominate empirically. When one reads economic policy commentary, ask: what are the direct effects the policy intends? What indirect effects might it also produce? Which is likely to matter more? Most policy debates can be productively reframed in those terms.
— A.S.

Figure 1.3 Marginal analysis. An activity should be expanded while the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost and contracted when it does not; the optimum, \(Q^*\), is where the two are equal. Decisions at the margin, rather than comparisons of totals, are the characteristic method of economic reasoning.
Figure 1.4 An incentive and the response it was not designed to produce. The colonial bounty on cobras in Delhi was intended to draw down the wild population, which is the flatter schedule. It also made cobra breeding profitable, and the response actually observed was the steeper one. The general lesson is that a policy creates a direct incentive and a set of indirect ones, and that the indirect responses are frequently the larger.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📘 Principles Level — The standard story
When two parties trade voluntarily, both expect to gain — otherwise they would not trade. This basic insight, applied at scale, explains why economic specialization and trade increase aggregate wealth. A farmer who is good at growing wheat can specialize in wheat and trade with a baker who is good at baking bread; both end up with more wheat and more bread than if each tried to do both. Apply this to nations: countries with different endowments (Saudi Arabia's oil, Germany's manufacturing capacity, Bangladesh's labor force) can specialize and trade and end up with more of everything than if each tried to be self-sufficient. David Ricardo showed in 1817 that this works even when one party is absolutely better at everything — comparative advantage means trade benefits both sides as long as relative costs differ.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
This is one of the most robust empirical findings in economics. Countries that opened to international trade in the second half of the 20th century — South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, China after 1978, Vietnam after 1986, India after 1991 — generally experienced large gains in measured GDP per capita. Cross-country regressions consistently find a positive correlation between trade openness and income levels.
📗 Intermediate Level — The distribution of gains
The complication: trade increases aggregate wealth, but the gains and losses are distributed unevenly. When a country imports manufactured goods more cheaply from abroad, consumers gain (lower prices) but domestic manufacturing workers lose (lower wages, fewer jobs, sometimes closed factories). The aggregate gain is positive, but the gains and losses go to different people.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
Economists have known this in theory for a century — the Stolper-Samuelson theorem from 1941 formalized when trade hurts which groups. The empirical evidence on the magnitude of the distributional effects has grown dramatically since the early 2000s. The work of Autor, Dorn, and Hanson on the "China Shock" showed that U.S. manufacturing communities exposed to Chinese import competition experienced large and lasting employment declines, reduced earnings, and increased participation in disability insurance programs. The aggregate U.S. welfare gain from trade with China is meaningful — Caliendo and Parro (2015) estimate roughly 3.4% over the 1995-2011 period — while the local losses in specific manufacturing communities were also large and concentrated. The textbook claim "trade benefits both sides" is true at the country level and false at the community level.

United States
The China Shock
The Empirical Case That Reshaped How Economists Think About Trade

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
From 2001 (China's WTO accession) to roughly 2007, the U.S. experienced a unique import surge from China. Manufacturing employment in the U.S. fell from approximately 17 million workers in 2000 to a low of about 11.5 million in early 2010 — roughly a one-third reduction. Autor, Dorn, and Hanson's series of papers (2013, 2016, 2021) used cross-county variation in exposure to Chinese imports to identify the employment, wage, and social effects. Their findings transformed trade economics.
The numbers: in counties heavily exposed to Chinese import competition, manufacturing employment fell roughly twice as fast as in less-exposed counties. Median earnings in exposed communities fell about 5-10% over a decade. Participation in federal disability programs rose meaningfully. Marriage rates fell. Mortality rates rose (the "deaths of despair" literature finds connections with trade exposure). Net new manufacturing job creation outside the affected sectors took roughly 10 years to materialize, and the new jobs were rarely in the same communities.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body: What this evidence did to economic thinking: most economists in 2001 expected trade with China to produce textbook gains (lower consumer prices, expansion of comparative advantage sectors, modest adjustment costs). The aggregate price benefits did materialize — consumer prices for goods affected by Chinese competition fell substantially. But the adjustment costs in affected communities were larger and more persistent than the textbook framework predicted, and the political consequences (rising opposition to trade liberalization across both parties) followed. The China Shock did not refute the "gains from trade" framework — it showed that distribution matters more than aggregate measures suggested. Modern trade policy debates take this much more seriously than they did 25 years ago.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — How to think about trade after the China Shock
The pre-2001 textbook treatment of trade focused almost entirely on aggregate efficiency gains and treated distributional effects as a footnote. The post-2013 treatment takes distribution as a central consideration. Both extremes can be wrong. "Trade is good" is too simple — it ignores serious adjustment costs that fall heavily on specific people. "Trade is bad" is also too simple — it ignores real and substantial benefits to consumers and to comparative-advantage industries. The honest answer: trade produces aggregate gains that are real but often modest in magnitude, and concentrated losses that are real and often large for affected groups. The interesting policy questions are about how to capture the gains while compensating the losers — questions that political systems have proven bad at answering.

1.heading: Theme Three: Trade and Specialization Create Wealth — But Not for Everyone
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The U.S. has a Trade Adjustment Assistance program that nominally helps workers displaced by trade. Empirical evaluation finds it has weak effects on long-run outcomes. European countries with stronger labor protections and more aggressive active labor market policies (training, relocation assistance, job placement) have handled trade adjustment somewhat better, though not perfectly. The key insight: the political backlash against trade liberalization that we have seen across developed democracies since 2016 is not irrational ignorance of the gains from trade. It is a reasonable response by people whose communities bore concentrated costs while the gains went to others. Understanding this is part of understanding modern trade policy.
— A.S.

1.heading: Theme Four: Markets Are Powerful — And Have Predictable Failure Modes
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📘 Principles Level — What markets do well
Markets — decentralized systems where buyers and sellers transact at prices that emerge from their interactions — accomplish something genuinely remarkable. They aggregate information from millions of individual decisions into prices that signal scarcity and value. They coordinate production across geographically dispersed actors who do not know each other. They incentivize innovation. They allow specialization to flourish. Hayek's classic 1945 essay "The Use of Knowledge in Society" articulated this as the central insight of market economics: no central planner can possibly have the dispersed local information that prices aggregate automatically. The implication is that for many problems — what shoes to make, what crops to plant, what restaurants to open — market processes produce better outcomes than top-down planning.

1.heading: Theme Four: Markets Are Powerful — And Have Predictable Failure Modes
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
The empirical evidence supports this for a wide class of problems. The Soviet Union's central planning of consumer goods produced chronic shortages and surpluses that markets handled effortlessly. China's reforms after 1978, which gradually allowed markets to operate in agriculture and manufacturing, produced the largest poverty reduction in human history. Countries with stronger property rights and more functional markets are systematically richer than countries without these institutions.
📗 Intermediate Level — When markets fail
The complication: there is a recognized class of problems where markets predictably fail to produce socially optimal outcomes. Economists call these market failures, and the catalog of them — refined over a century of theoretical and empirical work — is one of the discipline's most important contributions. The major categories:
Externalities: when a transaction affects parties who are not involved in it. Pollution is the canonical example: a factory imposes costs on people downwind who are not part of the buying-and-selling. The market fails because the factory does not pay these costs.

1.heading: Theme Four: Markets Are Powerful — And Have Predictable Failure Modes
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
Public goods: goods that, once provided, can be used by anyone without diminishing availability (national defense, basic research, GPS). Markets undersupply these because the producer cannot charge users.
Information asymmetries: when one party knows more than the other. The used-car market is the classic example (sellers know defects buyers do not see); insurance is another (buyers know health information that affects their costs to the insurer).
Monopoly and concentrated market power: when one firm dominates a market, it can charge prices above efficient levels. Competition fails to constrain pricing.
Coordination failures: when multiple equilibria exist and the economy settles on an inferior one. Standards adoption (QWERTY keyboard, gas vs electric vehicles for a century) often involves this.
Behavioral failures: when people do not behave rationally enough to make markets work as theorized. Addiction, present bias, loss aversion, framing effects — Kahneman, Thaler, and others document systematic deviations from rational choice that affect market outcomes.

1.heading: Theme Four: Markets Are Powerful — And Have Predictable Failure Modes
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Markets work" vs "Markets fail"
Do not reason from "markets fail for problem X" to "government should do X" without checking whether government can do better. Markets fail in identifiable ways, but governments also have their own characteristic failures: bureaucratic inertia, regulatory capture, electoral short-termism, principal-agent problems between politicians and voters, lobbying influence, knowledge limitations. The right question is rarely "does the market fail?" — for many problems the answer is yes. The right question is "does the market fail badly enough that the available government interventions improve outcomes?" Sometimes yes (national defense, basic research, environmental regulation, infrastructure), sometimes no (most consumer goods, food production), and sometimes the answer depends heavily on the specifics of how government intervention is designed (housing markets are an instructive example where poorly designed government intervention has made things worse and good intervention could help).

1.heading: Theme Four: Markets Are Powerful — And Have Predictable Failure Modes
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body: Both extremes get this wrong. The libertarian extreme says markets always work and government intervention always makes things worse. The opposite extreme says markets always fail and government should run everything. The empirical evidence supports neither extreme. Markets work superbly for some problems and badly for others. Government works well for some problems and badly for others. Most interesting policy debates are about specific problems where the answer is genuinely contested, not about which side of an ideological binary one is on.

1.heading: Theme Five: Macro Is Not Just Aggregated Micro
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Emergence and aggregation
One of the deepest themes in economics, and one of the most counterintuitive, is that the behavior of the whole economy is not simply the sum of the behavior of individual agents. Things happen at the aggregate level that do not happen at the individual level. This has its own name in economics: the fallacy of composition.
The classic example is saving. For an individual household, saving more is generally good — it builds wealth, provides for emergencies, funds retirement. From the individual perspective, more saving is unambiguously a virtue. But if all households suddenly decide to save more simultaneously, the resulting fall in aggregate consumption can trigger a recession, reducing everyone's income and therefore reducing total saving. This is the "paradox of thrift" — what is wise for one household becomes destructive when adopted by all. Keynes's General Theory built much of its argument on insights of this kind.

1.heading: Theme Five: Macro Is Not Just Aggregated Micro
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body: Other examples: an individual firm cutting costs is good for that firm; all firms cutting costs simultaneously reduces aggregate demand and can deepen a recession. An individual exporter benefits from a weaker currency; all countries simultaneously trying to depreciate their currencies (competitive devaluation) makes everyone worse off. An individual investor selling stocks during a downturn limits their losses; all investors selling simultaneously turns a price decline into a crash.

1.heading: Theme Five: Macro Is Not Just Aggregated Micro
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why this theme is so hard to grasp
The fallacy of composition is conceptually difficult because the human brain is wired for thinking about individual cases and not for thinking about aggregation. We learn lessons from our own experience and apply them to general claims. This works fine for almost everything in life except macroeconomics. The reasoning processes that serve well in personal finance, in firm management, in community organizing — they often produce the wrong answers when applied to whole-economy questions.
This is why macroeconomic policy debate is so contested. The intuitive arguments — "the government should balance its budget like a household," "if we just cut taxes everyone will work harder," "if we just raised the minimum wage poverty would end" — apply individual-level reasoning to aggregate-level questions. Sometimes the answers are similar, but often they are not. One of the most important things one will learn in macroeconomics (later in this book) is to recognize when individual-level intuition is misleading about aggregate outcomes. The theme of aggregation and emergence runs through this whole textbook.
— A.S.

1.heading: Theme Five: Macro Is Not Just Aggregated Micro
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body: Figure 1.6 The fallacy of composition, in the form in which it matters most for macroeconomics. What is true of one household taken in isolation — that saving more raises its wealth without affecting its income — is false of all households together, because one household's spending is another's income. This is why aggregate outcomes require their own theory rather than the summation of individual reasoning.

1.heading: Theme Six: Institutions Are Where Economics and Politics Meet
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why institutions matter
The sixth theme is the one most underemphasized in standard introductory textbooks: that economic outcomes depend heavily on the institutions within which economic activity takes place. Institutions are the formal and informal rules that structure interactions — property rights, contract enforcement, judicial systems, regulatory frameworks, central banks, voting systems, social norms.
Why this matters: two countries with similar resources, similar populations, similar geography can have very different economic outcomes if their institutions differ. North Korea and South Korea share a peninsula, a history, an ethnic background, a climate. South Korea is 25-30x wealthier than North Korea. The difference is institutional: South Korea has property rights, functional courts, competitive elections, regulatory frameworks that allow markets to operate. North Korea has none of these. The institutional difference explains nearly all of the income gap.

1.heading: Theme Six: Institutions Are Where Economics and Politics Meet
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson's research program — for which they shared the 2024 Nobel Prize — argues that institutional quality is the deepest determinant of long-run prosperity. Their key claim: "inclusive" institutions that distribute power broadly and allow innovation produce sustained growth; "extractive" institutions that concentrate power among elites and discourage broad participation produce stagnation. The argument has been refined and debated for two decades, but the central insight — institutions matter more than resources — has become mainstream.

1.heading: Theme Six: Institutions Are Where Economics and Politics Meet
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body: When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Eastern European countries faced a near-simultaneous transition from central planning to market institutions. The outcomes varied dramatically depending on institutional choices. Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovenia chose rapid liberalization with strong rule-of-law reforms; they recovered from initial transition recessions and joined the European Union by 2004. By 2024 their GDP per capita had converged substantially with Western European levels. Russia and Ukraine pursued slower and less complete reforms, with weaker rule-of-law institutions; their growth has been much more volatile and less sustained.

1.body: The lesson for the institutional theme: institutions can change, but the rate of change and the quality of new institutions matter enormously for outcomes. Poland's institutions did not become functional in a year — they were built over a decade through deliberate construction of judicial systems, regulatory bodies, property rights frameworks. The countries that moved faster on institutional construction (despite often slower on price liberalization) generally fared better than those that liberalized prices without building the supporting institutions. Markets need institutions; without them, "market reform" can just be a license for connected elites to capture assets, as happened in much of post-Soviet Russia in the 1990s. Institutions are not just background conditions — they are the operating system on which economic activity runs.

1.heading: Worked Examples
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📐 Worked Example 1.1 — Opportunity Cost in Personal and Public Decisions
A college student is considering whether to spend an additional semester at college earning a master's degree. Tuition is $20,000. The student would also forgo $40,000 in income from working full-time during that semester. (a) What is the opportunity cost of the master's? (b) The student's lifetime earnings would rise by an estimated $200,000 (present value) with the master's. Is the decision economically defensible? (c) How does this analysis change if the student already has a job that requires a master's degree to keep?
1
(a) Opportunity cost: the full economic cost of the decision is tuition ($20,000) plus foregone income ($40,000) = $60,000. The "out of pocket" cost is $20,000, but ignoring foregone earnings is a common analytical mistake.
2
(b) Cost-benefit: expected lifetime gain ($200,000) far exceeds total opportunity cost ($60,000). Net expected value of about +$140,000. The decision passes the cost-benefit test. Even discounting the $200,000 for risk and uncertainty about the actual earnings premium, the decision looks defensible.
3

1.body:
(c) Changed circumstances: if the master's is required to keep the existing job, then the foregone option is much worse — losing the entire career path, not just a year of income. The opportunity cost framing now includes the entire foregone career, not just one year. The decision becomes even more defensible, as the alternative (not getting the master's) involves much larger losses.
The portable insight: opportunity cost includes everything one gives up — direct costs (tuition) plus foregone alternatives (lost wages, career path, time). Most "expensive" decisions in life are not expensive because of the dollars out of pocket; they are expensive because of what one does not do. This same framework applies to government decisions: spending money on Program X means not spending it on Program Y. The opportunity cost is whatever Y would have produced, not the dollar figure of X alone.

1.heading: Worked Examples
1.title: Chapter 1, What Economics Actually Studies Six recurring themes that organize the discipline — scarcity and choice, incentives and unintended consequences, trade and specialization, markets and their failures, aggregation and emergence, and the role of institutions — and why each is more contested i
1.body:
📐 Worked Example 1.2 — Unintended Consequences of a Subsidy
A government wants to encourage homeownership. It introduces a $10,000 first-time homebuyer tax credit. (a) What is the intended direct effect? (b) Identify at least three indirect or unintended consequences. (c) Predict what happens to median home prices in the short run.
1
(a) Direct effect: the credit reduces the effective cost of homeownership for eligible buyers, increasing the demand for owner-occupied housing among first-time buyers.
2
(b) Indirect consequences include: (i) Some of the credit gets capitalized into home prices, raising prices for buyers who do not receive the credit. (ii) Renters delay buying decisions to qualify as "first-time" buyers, distorting the timing of purchases. (iii) Sellers of homes for under (some threshold) tighten their negotiations, knowing buyers have additional resources. (iv) The credit may pull forward demand from future years, reducing demand later when the program ends.
3

(c) Short-run price effect: the increased demand pushes prices up. Empirical evidence from past first-time homebuyer credits (e.g., U.S. 2008-2010) suggests roughly 30-60% of the credit gets captured by sellers in higher home prices. The actual benefit to buyers is therefore much smaller than the nominal $10,000.
The deeper lesson: a policy intended to help first-time buyers can largely benefit sellers if the supply of housing is inelastic (which it typically is in the short run). This is one of the most important results in housing economics: housing subsidies tend to get capitalized into prices, with much of the benefit accruing to existing homeowners and sellers rather than to the intended beneficiaries. The general lesson: when designing a policy intended to help one group, ask who else is affected by the resulting price changes, and check whether the indirect effects might dominate the direct ones.

2.heading: Insight
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — What changed in the 1990s and why it matters
If one took an undergraduate economics course in 1985 and another in 2025, one would notice a substantial shift in how empirical claims are made and defended. The 1985 course would feature theoretical models with parameters often pulled from "calibration" exercises rather than statistical estimation; cross-country regressions that we now recognize as poorly identified; and empirical claims that were closer to illustrative exercises. The 2025 course would feature randomized controlled trials, difference-in-differences designs from natural experiments, regression discontinuity designs exploiting threshold effects in policies, and instrumental variables with explicit defenses of identification assumptions. This is not a stylistic difference — it represents a genuine improvement in what economists know and how confidently we can claim it.

2.heading: Insight
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Why does this matter for an introductory course? Two reasons. First, the empirical foundation for what we teach has changed. Many "facts" that introductory textbooks reported confidently 30 years ago are now contested or known to be wrong, and many "controversial" claims have moved toward consensus. Second, knowing how the methods work supports critical reading of economic claims critically. When someone says "study X shows that policy Y has effect Z," one should know how to ask: how did the study identify the causal effect? What is the counterfactual? Are there reasons to think the result generalizes? These questions are not optional — they are the difference between economic reasoning and just-so storytelling.
— A.S.

2.heading: What Economists Actually Do
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two complementary modes of reasoning
Economic reasoning takes two complementary forms: theoretical reasoning (constructing models that predict what should happen in stylized situations) and empirical reasoning (testing what actually happens in real-world data). Both modes have evolved enormously since the discipline became modern in the late 19th century, but the basic distinction has been stable: theories generate predictions, empirics test them.
Theoretical economics has its own internal disagreements — about which assumptions are reasonable, which models are most useful, which mathematical techniques are appropriate. But the major theoretical frameworks (consumer choice theory, firm production theory, general equilibrium, game theory, growth theory, business cycle theory) are reasonably well-established. They produce predictions that can be tested.

2.heading: What Economists Actually Do
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body: Empirical economics is where most of the real action has been in the past 30 years. The challenge is fundamental: most economic phenomena cannot be directly experimented on. We cannot randomly assign half the country to receive a tax cut and the other half not. We cannot randomly give one set of workers a higher minimum wage and another set the same wage. How, then, are causal effects established? This is the central methodological problem of empirical economics, and the answer has evolved substantially.

2.heading: The Correlation-Causation Problem and Why It Matters
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why correlation is not causation
The single most important distinction in empirical work is between correlation (two variables move together) and causation (one variable produces changes in another). They are not the same thing. Two variables can be correlated without one causing the other for at least three reasons:
Reverse causation: what looks like X causing Y might actually be Y causing X. The classic example: higher police presence is correlated with higher crime rates, but it is not the police causing the crime; cities deploy more police where there is more crime.
Confounding (omitted variable bias): a third variable Z affects both X and Y. Higher SAT scores are correlated with higher lifetime earnings, but this could be because both SAT scores and earnings are caused by family income, talent, or schooling quality — variables that affect both.

2.heading: The Correlation-Causation Problem and Why It Matters
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Selection effects: the people who choose to do X are not random, so the difference between X-doers and non-X-doers reflects the choice as much as the effect of X. Students who attend Ivy League schools earn more than students who do not — but they also had different characteristics (motivation, family resources, ability) when they applied.
Naive empirical work that ignores these problems produces correlations that look like causal effects but are not. Most pre-1990 empirical economics, and most popular discussions of economic data today, fail to take these problems seriously enough.

2.heading: The Correlation-Causation Problem and Why It Matters
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Studies show that..."
One will see news articles that say "studies show that X causes Y." Treat this with skepticism. Most studies establish correlations, not causal effects. Before believing a causal claim from a study, ask: (1) Could the relationship be reversed? Is it possible Y is causing X, or that there is mutual causation? (2) What is the counterfactual? If we had not observed X, what would have happened? (3) Could there be a third variable? What unmeasured factor might be producing both X and Y? (4) Is the sample representative? Does this generalize beyond the specific group studied? (5) Is the effect size meaningful? A statistically significant effect can still be too small to matter practically.

2.heading: The Correlation-Causation Problem and Why It Matters
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body: The credibility revolution in economics was, in essence, about taking these questions seriously. The pre-1990 norm was "we ran some regressions and found that X correlates with Y, here are the coefficients." The post-1990 norm is "we found an identification strategy that lets us isolate causal effects of X on Y, and here is why we believe the strategy works." This is a much higher methodological bar. Empirical economics has become considerably more credible. The corollary is that many older "established findings" have not survived the higher bar — including some that introductory textbooks still report confidently.

2.heading: The Correlation-Causation Problem and Why It Matters
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Figure 2.1 Why a pooled correlation is not a causal effect. Pooling the three groups produces the steep fitted line: coffee appears strongly associated with the outcome. Within each group the relationship is close to flat. Smoking drives both coffee consumption and the outcome, and a comparison that ignores it attributes the confounder's effect to coffee. Every credible empirical design in the next section is a device for removing variation of exactly this kind.
Figure 2.2 Why correlation does not establish causation. A third variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome generates an association between them even when the treatment has no effect. Empirical work therefore seeks variation in the treatment that is unrelated to the confounder: randomization, a natural experiment, an instrument, or a discontinuity in assignment.

2.heading: The Credibility Revolution: Four Methods That Changed Empirical Economics
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
The four canonical methods of the credibility revolution
MethodHow it worksExample application
1. Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)
Randomly assign participants to treatment vs control group. Compare outcomes. The gold standard because random assignment eliminates selection bias.
Banerjee-Duflo-Kremer: hundreds of RCTs of development interventions (mosquito nets, deworming, microfinance, conditional cash transfers).
2. Natural Experiments
Exploit situations where something close to random assignment happened naturally — a policy was introduced in one place but not another, a draft lottery, a sudden rule change, a geographic boundary.
Card-Krueger 1994: New Jersey raised minimum wage in 1992, Pennsylvania did not. Compared fast-food employment before/after in both states.
3. Regression Discontinuity
Compare outcomes just above and just below an arbitrary threshold (a test score cutoff, an income limit, a geographic line). Units just above and below are similar except for treatment status.
Angrist-Lavy 1999: Maimonides' rule limits class size at 40 in Israel. Compares classes just above (small) vs just below (large) the cutoff.
4. Instrumental Variables

2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Use a variable (the "instrument") that affects the treatment X but does not directly affect outcome Y. The instrument's effect on Y must work entirely through X.
Angrist 1990: Vietnam draft lottery as instrument for military service. Random lottery number → forced military service → effects on lifetime earnings.
1992-1994
New Jersey vs Pennsylvania
Natural Experiment
The Card-Krueger Minimum Wage Study That Changed a Field
In April 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 — an 18.8% increase. Pennsylvania, just across the river, did not. David Card and Alan Krueger had begun surveying fast-food restaurants in both states the previous February. They re-surveyed the same restaurants after the minimum wage increase. This was a textbook natural experiment: a policy change in one place but not in a nearly identical neighboring place.

2.heading: The Credibility Revolution: Four Methods That Changed Empirical Economics
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
The economics profession's predicted result, based on textbook supply-and-demand reasoning, was that fast-food employment in New Jersey should have fallen relative to Pennsylvania. The actual result: New Jersey employment rose by 13% while Pennsylvania employment fell by 1%. The minimum wage increase had not destroyed jobs as theory predicted; if anything, it had created them.
The reaction was intense. Some economists argued the data was flawed (different measurement methods produced different results). Some argued that this specific case was anomalous. Some argued that the standard textbook model was missing something important — perhaps fast-food labor markets were not competitive, perhaps firms had wage-setting power (monopsony), perhaps the higher wage attracted more workers and reduced turnover. The debate ran for years. But the methodological contribution was lasting: Card and Krueger had shown what serious empirical economics could look like — exploiting a natural experiment to identify a causal effect that contradicted standard theory.

2.heading: The Credibility Revolution: Four Methods That Changed Empirical Economics
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Subsequent decades of careful minimum-wage research, using similar designs across many states and time periods, has produced a much more nuanced picture than either the original textbook story or the Card-Krueger result alone. The current consensus: modest minimum wage increases (10-20%) typically produce small employment effects (perhaps -1% to +1%), with real wage gains for low-wage workers offsetting the small employment cost. Very large minimum wage increases (50%+) can produce larger employment losses. The Card-Krueger study earned David Card the 2021 Nobel Prize.
Figure 2.3 The logic of a randomized controlled trial. Because assignment is random, the treatment and control groups differ systematically in nothing except the program itself, so the difference in their later outcomes estimates the causal effect without any further assumption about who selects into treatment. The cost is that the estimate applies to the population that was randomized, which is rarely the whole economy.

2.heading: The Credibility Revolution: Four Methods That Changed Empirical Economics
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Figure 2.4 Difference-in-differences. The treated and control groups need not be alike in level, only in trend. The control group's post-policy path is used to construct the counterfactual for the treated group, and the estimated effect is the gap between the observed and counterfactual paths. The identifying assumption — parallel trends in the absence of the policy — is assessed, not proved, by inspecting the pre-policy period.
Figure 2.5 An event study, which is the form in which difference-in-differences evidence is usually presented. Each point is the estimated difference between treated and control units in that year, with its confidence interval. The years before the change carry the weight of the argument: if the estimates there are indistinguishable from zero, the parallel-trends assumption survives a test it could have failed, and the post-period estimates can be read as the effect of the policy.

2.heading: The Credibility Revolution: Four Methods That Changed Empirical Economics
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Figure 2.6 Instrumental variables in one diagram. The unobserved confounder \(U\) moves both the treatment and the outcome, so a direct comparison is contaminated. An instrument \(Z\) is useful when it moves the treatment (relevance) and affects the outcome through no other channel (the exclusion restriction). The second condition cannot be tested; it must be argued from institutional knowledge, which is why instruments are persuasive only when the story behind them is.
Figure 2.7 Regression discontinuity. Where a rule assigns treatment at a threshold of some continuous variable, units just below and just above the threshold are comparable in everything except treatment. The discontinuity in the outcome at the cut-off is therefore attributable to the treatment, at least for units near the threshold.

2.heading: Positive and Normative — But Less Cleanly Separated Than Is Commonly Supposed
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
📘 Principles Level — The standard distinction
Economics textbooks have traditionally distinguished between positive economics (descriptive — what is, or what would happen if X) and normative economics (prescriptive — what should be done). The distinction is supposed to be clean: positive claims are scientific, testable, and the proper domain of economic expertise; normative claims involve value judgments that economics has no special authority over. The canonical example: positive — "a $15 minimum wage will reduce employment in certain sectors by 2%"; normative — "we should raise the minimum wage to $15."
📗 Intermediate Level — Why the distinction is messier
The clean distinction is mostly a useful fiction. In practice, positive and normative reasoning bleed into each other constantly:
Choosing what to study is normative. Why do economists study minimum wages so much and rent control somewhat less? Because we collectively think the questions matter. The research agenda reflects values about what is important.

2.heading: Positive and Normative — But Less Cleanly Separated Than Is Commonly Supposed
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Defining variables involves normative choice. What counts as "unemployment"? The official U.S. rate excludes "discouraged workers" who have stopped looking. The choice of what to include reflects a view about what kind of joblessness "counts."
Welfare measurements embed assumptions. When economists evaluate policies by their effect on "consumer welfare," they are making assumptions about how to aggregate gains and losses across people, how much to discount future generations, what kind of inequality matters. These are normative choices dressed in positive language.
Trade-off recommendations cross the line. When economists say "the optimal policy is X," they are combining positive analysis with implicit normative weights on competing objectives.
This does not make economics useless or "just opinion." Empirical work that establishes causal effects of policies is still meaningful and important. But it means that economists' policy recommendations are not the pure result of scientific analysis. They incorporate value choices, often unstated. The honest economist makes those choices explicit; the less-honest economist pretends they do not exist.

2.heading: Positive and Normative — But Less Cleanly Separated Than Is Commonly Supposed
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — When economists pretend to be neutral
One pattern one will see throughout encounters with economic policy debate: economists sometimes claim to be making purely scientific recommendations when they are actually making value-laden ones. "The optimal policy is X" almost always combines empirical claims (here are the effects of X) with normative weights (how to value those effects against alternatives). When one reads a confident policy recommendation from an economist, ask: what value choices are implicit in this analysis? What objective is being maximized? Whose welfare is being weighted, and how?

2.heading: Positive and Normative — But Less Cleanly Separated Than Is Commonly Supposed
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
The best economists are transparent about their value choices. They say "if one values equality more, this policy is better; if one values growth more, that policy is better." They distinguish between empirical disagreement (about what would happen) and normative disagreement (about which outcome is preferred). The economists who pretend their recommendations are purely positive are either fooling themselves or trying to mislead the reader. Take their empirical work seriously, but treat their recommendations as containing both science and values — usually with the values understated.
— A.S.

2.heading: Why Economists Disagree
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Public commentary often portrays economists as in constant disagreement about everything, which is wrong. Economists agree about more than the public realizes — surveys of professional economists show consensus on many issues that are politically contested (e.g., that carbon taxes effectively reduce emissions, that free trade has aggregate benefits, that rent control reduces housing supply over time). But there is genuine disagreement, and understanding what generates it is important. Four main sources:
Sources of economic disagreement
SourceHow it generates disagreement
Empirical uncertaintyThe effect of any policy depends on parameters we cannot measure precisely. Different economists make different point estimates within reasonable uncertainty ranges. Example: the elasticity of taxable income (relevant for tax policy) ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 in the literature.
Model selectionDifferent models emphasize different mechanisms. Saltwater and freshwater macroeconomists model business cycles differently and reach different policy conclusions. Neither is "wrong"; they are focusing on different aspects of the same reality.

2.heading: Why Economists Disagree
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
Time horizonsShort-run and long-run effects of policies are often different, sometimes opposite. Economists who weight short-run more reach different conclusions than those who weight long-run more.
Normative valuesHow to weight competing objectives (growth vs equality, present vs future, individual freedom vs collective welfare) is genuinely a value choice. Economists with different value weights reach different policy conclusions even when they agree on the empirical facts.
Figure 2.8 Why economists disagree, drawn from the minimum-wage literature. Each bar counts studies reporting an employment elasticity in that range. The distribution is centered near zero and has genuine mass on both sides, so two economists can each cite well-identified work and reach opposite conclusions. Disagreement of this kind is empirical rather than ideological, and it is resolved by better designs rather than by stronger assertions.

2.heading: Interactive: Evaluating Empirical Claims

2.body:
🎛 Interactive — Reading Empirical Claims Critically
Each tab presents an empirical claim. Identify the credibility issues.
Each tab below shows an empirical claim one might see in popular discussion. The hidden analysis identifies the credibility issues — correlation vs causation, sample selection, omitted variables, generalizability. Try to identify the issues independently before reading.
Pick an empirical claim to evaluate:
The pattern: almost all real-world empirical claims face one or more credibility issues. The question is not whether the claim is "true" in some absolute sense — it is whether the available evidence supports a causal interpretation. Good empirical research takes these issues seriously; popular reporting usually does not.

2.heading: Worked Examples
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
📐 Worked Example 2.1 — Identifying the Counterfactual
A study finds that students who attend an after-school tutoring program score 0.3 standard deviations higher on math tests than students who do not attend. The study concludes the tutoring program raises math achievement. (a) What is the implicit counterfactual? (b) What selection effects might be at work? (c) How might a study be designed to identify the causal effect of tutoring more credibly?
1
(a) Implicit counterfactual: the study compares actual tutored students to actual non-tutored students. The implicit counterfactual is "what would the tutored students have scored without tutoring." Without random assignment, we do not observe this directly.
2
(b) Selection effects: students (and parents) who choose tutoring are different from those who do not in many ways: parental engagement, baseline ability, motivation, family resources, awareness of programs. These factors independently affect math scores. Some of the 0.3 SD difference is the tutoring effect; some is the selection effect of who chose to enroll.
3

2.heading: Worked Examples
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
(c) Better designs: (i) RCT: randomly assign students to tutoring vs control. The gold standard. (ii) Lottery: if the program is oversubscribed, compare students randomly selected via lottery vs not selected. (iii) Regression discontinuity: if eligibility is based on a test cutoff, compare students just below vs just above the cutoff. (iv) Difference-in-differences: compare tutored students' before-vs-after improvements to non-tutored students' improvements over the same period.
The general principle: for any causal claim about the effect of a policy or treatment, identify the counterfactual and ask how the data makes it possible to observe it. If the answer is "we cannot directly observe the counterfactual, but we compare similar groups," ask how the groups were selected. The more selection bias there is, the less the comparison reveals about the causal effect. This single question — "what is the counterfactual?" — has more analytical power than almost any other in empirical economics.

2.heading: Worked Examples
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
📐 Worked Example 2.2 — Designing a Natural Experiment
The objective is to estimate the effect of increased state spending on K-12 education on student achievement. Cross-state correlations are confounded (states with more spending also have higher incomes, different demographics, etc.). (a) What kind of natural experiment would help identify the causal effect? (b) Give two real examples of natural experiments in education economics. (c) What identification assumptions does the design require?
1
(a) Useful natural experiments: (i) State supreme court rulings forcing school finance reform that affected districts differently based on pre-existing wealth gaps. (ii) Sudden changes in formula-based funding that shifted resources unpredictably. (iii) Policy changes affecting specific cohorts but not others, allowing comparisons of "treated" and "untreated" cohorts.
2

2.heading: Worked Examples
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body:
(b) Real examples: (i) Jackson, Johnson, and Persico (2016) used the timing of court-mandated school finance reforms across states. They found 25% increases in per-pupil spending raised wages of affected cohorts by ~10% in adulthood. (ii) Lafortune, Rothstein, Schanzenbach (2018) used variation in state finance reforms to estimate the effects of $1,000 in additional per-pupil spending — found 0.1 SD improvement in test scores.
3
(c) Identification assumptions: (i) Parallel trends: in the absence of treatment, treated and untreated areas would have evolved similarly. Hard to test directly; usually justified by showing they were tracking similarly before treatment. (ii) No anticipation: districts did not change behavior before the policy was implemented in anticipation. (iii) No spillovers: untreated districts were not indirectly affected by the policy.

2.heading: Worked Examples
2.title: Chapter 2, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
2.body: Why this matters: education spending is one of the most-studied causal questions in economics. The early literature (pre-1990) reached pessimistic conclusions because it relied on naive cross-state correlations and got confounded estimates. The post-2000 literature using natural experiments has found that money matters — but the design is everything. If one reads "studies show that spending does not affect outcomes," that is largely from the pre-credibility-revolution literature. The credibly-identified post-2000 literature finds positive effects of well-spent money. This is exactly the kind of issue where knowing the methodology matters for knowing what to believe.

3.heading: Overview

3.body:
⚙ Conceptual Walkthrough — Difference-in-Differences
\[ \text{DiD} = \left(\bar Y^{\,\text{treated}}_{\text{after}} - \bar Y^{\,\text{treated}}_{\text{before}}\right) - \left(\bar Y^{\,\text{control}}_{\text{after}} - \bar Y^{\,\text{control}}_{\text{before}}\right) \]
Y_treated_after − Y_treated_before
How much the treated group's outcome changed after the policy.
Y_control_after − Y_control_before
How much the control group's outcome changed over the same time. Captures everything else happening in the world that is affecting both groups.
The difference
Subtracting the second from the first removes everything that affected both groups identically. What is left is (hopefully) the causal effect of the treatment on the treated group.
Key assumption
Parallel trends: in the absence of treatment, the two groups would have evolved similarly over time. Defended by showing they were on parallel pre-treatment paths.

3.heading: Overview
3.title: Chapter 3, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
3.body:
Why DiD is so widely used: it does not require random assignment, but uses comparison across two dimensions (time and group) to subtract out confounding factors. Card-Krueger 1994 was a DiD design: difference in (New Jersey - Pennsylvania) employment, before vs after minimum wage increase. Difference-in-differences is now the standard method of policy evaluation in economics — used for evaluating everything from healthcare reform to minimum wage to trade liberalization.
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Empirical Reasoning in the Engine

3.heading: Overview
3.title: Chapter 3, How Economists Argue From thought experiments to natural experiments to randomized trials — what counts as evidence in modern economics, why the discipline transformed during the "credibility revolution" of the past 30 years, and how to read empirical claims with appropriate skepticism In
3.body:
The MacroNations engine is deterministic — given the same inputs, one gets the same outputs. This is unlike real economies but useful pedagogically because it makes it possible to isolate causal effects of lever choices. In one tournament round, change only tax_rate by 5pp and observe the effects: GDP gap shifts via the engine's policy-gap multiplier (1.4 for spending, −1.1 for taxes); debt accumulates differently; Gini moves through the tax_rate_gini coefficient. The engine effectively performs a "perfect natural experiment" for each lever change: holding everything else constant, what does this change cause? Real-world empirical economics never has this luxury. The credibility revolution has been about getting closer to this kind of "ceteris paribus" identification in real-world settings. One useful exercise: run two rounds with identical settings except for one lever, and compute the difference. This is a difference-in-differences with perfect control, which is the methodological ideal of empirical economics.
