3.heading: Insight
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why I teach trade this way
Most introductory textbooks present comparative advantage as a clean and complete argument for free trade. The presentation is technically correct but pedagogically misleading because it omits the most contested part of the contemporary debate: how the gains and losses are distributed. An economics student who learns Ricardo's argument and stops has the analytical equipment of 1817 — they can derive the aggregate gains from trade, but they cannot explain why so many people in 2026 oppose trade liberalization despite the aggregate gains being real.

3.heading: Insight
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
The fuller story includes both the aggregate gains (Ricardo's contribution) and the distributional consequences (the Stolper-Samuelson theorem of 1941, the China Shock literature of 2013-2021, and the political-economy work showing that compensation rarely actually flows from winners to losers). If one can hold both parts of the story in mind simultaneously — the aggregate gains are real AND the distributional losses are real AND the losers do not typically get compensated — one understands modern trade economics. If one can only hold one part, one will be surprised by political developments one should have predicted.
— A.S.

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
📘 Principles Level — Building intuition
The simplest way to see comparative advantage is to start with a stylized two-country, two-good example. Imagine two countries: Avianna and Bovinia. Each can produce wheat or cars. Workers in each country have different productivity:
CountryWheat (bushels/worker)Cars (cars/worker)
Avianna10020
Bovinia6030
Avianna has absolute advantage in wheat (100 > 60). Bovinia has absolute advantage in cars (30 > 20). For each country, the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other is the key:
In Avianna, producing 1 car requires foregoing 100/20 = 5 bushels of wheat. So 1 Avianna car = 5 Avianna wheat bushels.
In Bovinia, producing 1 car requires foregoing 60/30 = 2 bushels of wheat. So 1 Bovinia car = 2 Bovinia wheat bushels.
Bovinia has comparative advantage in cars (its opportunity cost is lower — 2 instead of 5). Avianna has comparative advantage in wheat (its opportunity cost is lower — 1/5 of a car per wheat bushel, vs Bovinia's 1/2 a car per wheat bushel). Both countries can benefit from specializing in their comparative-advantage good and trading.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Computing the Gains from Trade

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
\[ \text{gain}_A = C_A^{\text{trade}} - C_A^{\text{autarky}} \]The world gain is the sum of the national gains, which is the outward expansion of joint production possibilities.
No-trade equilibrium
Each country produces and consumes according to its own resources. If Avianna has 10 workers and divides time 50/50 between wheat and cars, it produces 500 wheat and 100 cars, and that is what it consumes.
Specialization
Each country shifts production toward its comparative-advantage good. If Avianna fully specializes in wheat with 10 workers, it produces 1,000 wheat. Bovinia with 10 workers fully specializing in cars produces 300 cars.
Trade
At any trade ratio between the two countries' opportunity costs (1:2 to 1:5 wheat per car), both countries gain. Suppose 1 car = 3 bushels. Avianna sends 300 wheat, receives 100 cars. Bovinia sends 100 cars, receives 300 wheat.
Post-trade consumption
Avianna: 700 wheat + 100 cars (vs 500+100 without trade) — gain of 200 wheat. Bovinia: 300 wheat + 200 cars (vs the 60*5 + 30*5 = 300+150 from balanced production, so gain of 50 cars). Both countries strictly better off.

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body: The deeper insight: the gains from trade are not magic. They come from concentrating each country's labor on its higher-productivity activity. Avianna giving up 5 wheat to free a worker for car production is wasteful when that worker only produces 20 cars — but if it could trade for cars at 2 or 3 wheat each, Avianna effectively "produces" cars more efficiently through trade than through domestic production. Trade is a technology — it converts wheat into cars at a better rate than the actual production process would.

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Cheap labor" arguments against trade
A common argument against trade with developing countries: "Their wages are so low we cannot compete." This sounds intuitive but misunderstands comparative advantage. Wages reflect productivity, not just the cost of labor. A U.S. textile worker is paid more than a Bangladeshi textile worker because the U.S. worker uses more capital, technology, and supporting infrastructure. The U.S. worker is more productive per hour. Whether the U.S. should produce textiles depends on whether U.S. relative productivity in textiles (vs other goods) exceeds Bangladesh's relative productivity in textiles. If not, the U.S. has comparative disadvantage in textiles regardless of the wage differential.

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body: The "cheap labor" framing also gets the question backwards. Trade with low-wage countries can hurt specific U.S. workers in directly-competing industries (the China Shock literature is precisely about this). But the framing implies that the U.S. should somehow "compete" with Bangladeshi wages — which would require massive U.S. wage reductions and is economically nonsensical. The right framing is: which industries should the U.S. specialize in, and how do we manage the adjustment for workers in industries we should not specialize in? That is a much more useful question than "should we accept the wage differential," which presumes the answer.

3.heading: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
Figure 3.1 Comparative advantage with linear frontiers. The slope of each frontier is the domestic opportunity cost of cloth in terms of wine. Home forgoes two-thirds of a unit of wine per unit of cloth and Foreign forgoes one and a half units, so Home has the comparative advantage in cloth and Foreign in wine — irrespective of which country is more productive in absolute terms.
Figure 3.2 The gains from trade. Specialising in the good of comparative advantage and trading at world prices places the consumption possibility line outside the production frontier. Consumption bundles that were unattainable in autarky become feasible; this expansion, not any change in productive capacity, is the gain from trade.

3.body: Figure 3.3 Opening a market to trade. At the autarky price domestic supply equals domestic demand. Facing a world price below it, domestic buyers purchase the larger quantity on the demand curve and domestic producers supply the smaller quantity on the supply curve; the difference is imported. Consumers gain more than producers lose, and the shaded area is the net gain. The same figure shows why the losses are concentrated among domestic producers while the gains are spread thinly across buyers.

3.heading: The Sources of Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
Where does comparative advantage come from? Why is Avianna more relatively productive in wheat and Bovinia more relatively productive in cars? Economic theory identifies four major sources:
Four sources of comparative advantage
SourceMechanismExample
1. Factor endowmentsCountries with more capital relative to labor have comparative advantage in capital-intensive goods. Heckscher-Ohlin model (1933).Saudi Arabia's oil; the U.S.'s capital-intensive manufacturing; Bangladesh's labor-intensive garments.
2. TechnologyCountries that innovate in particular technologies have comparative advantage in goods using those technologies. Ricardian model emphasized this.Germany's machine tools; Switzerland's pharmaceuticals; U.S.'s software and biotech.
3. Scale economiesCountries that get an early start in an industry develop expertise, supply chains, and skilled workers that make them more productive. New Trade Theory (Krugman 1979).Detroit's auto industry; Silicon Valley's tech industry; Taiwan's semiconductors.

3.heading: The Sources of Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body: 4. InstitutionsCountries with effective property rights, contract enforcement, and labor markets are more productive across many industries. Acemoglu-Robinson.Most developed economies have advantage in high-trust, complex contracts (financial services, R&D).

3.heading: The Sources of Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why this matters for policy
The traditional textbook treats comparative advantage as exogenous — countries have what they have, and trade simply lets them specialize. The richer modern view recognizes that comparative advantage is partly endogenous: countries can build it through deliberate investment in technology, infrastructure, education, and institutions. Singapore in 1965 had no obvious comparative advantage in anything. By 2025 it has comparative advantage in financial services, pharmaceuticals, and high-tech manufacturing. This was not predetermined — it was built through 60 years of policy choices about education, infrastructure, and industrial development.

3.heading: The Sources of Comparative Advantage
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
This has policy implications. The pure "let comparative advantage emerge" view of trade implies that government should largely stay out of trade and industrial policy. The "comparative advantage can be built" view implies a more activist role — investing in capabilities that may pay off as future comparative advantages. Both views have empirical support. Pure laissez-faire has worked in some cases (Hong Kong); active industrial policy has worked in others (Korea, Singapore, Taiwan). The question of which approach works when is genuinely contested. The recent return of industrial policy in the U.S. (CHIPS Act, IRA) reflects renewed confidence that comparative advantage can be built. Whether that confidence is well-placed will become clear over the next decade.
— A.S.

3.heading: The Distributional Question: Who Wins and Who Loses
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Stolper-Samuelson
The Stolper-Samuelson theorem (1941) formalized when trade hurts which groups. The intuition: when a country opens to trade, the goods it produces with its abundant factor (capital in the U.S., labor in Bangladesh) gets exported, raising demand for that factor; the goods produced with the scarce factor (labor in the U.S., capital in Bangladesh) get imported, reducing demand for that factor. The owners of the scarce factor lose, even after accounting for the gains from lower import prices.
Applied to the U.S.: the U.S. is capital-abundant relative to most trade partners. Trade with labor-abundant countries (China, Mexico, Bangladesh) raises the relative return to U.S. capital and reduces the relative return to U.S. less-skilled labor. The Stolper-Samuelson theorem predicted, decades before the empirical evidence, that increasing U.S. trade with developing countries would reduce wages for less-skilled U.S. workers. The empirical evidence of the past 25 years has largely confirmed this prediction.
1994-2023
North America
NAFTA Aftermath
NAFTA: 30 Years of Empirical Evidence

3.heading: The Distributional Question: Who Wins and Who Loses
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
The North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in January 1994, eliminating most tariffs and trade barriers between the U.S., Canada, and Mexico over a phased period. Now 30+ years on, the empirical record allows us to evaluate what actually happened against the predictions made at the time.
Aggregate effects: trade between the three countries roughly tripled. North American supply chains became deeply integrated — by 2010, roughly 40% of imports from Mexico contained U.S. components, and roughly 25% of imports from Canada did. U.S. consumers saw real benefits from lower prices on automotive, agricultural, and manufactured goods. Mexico's per-capita GDP grew approximately 30% in real terms over the NAFTA era — a meaningful gain but well below the average growth rate of the rest of Latin America during the same period and far short of the rapid convergence with U.S. living standards that NAFTA's proponents had hoped for (Weisbrot et al. 2017), with the export sector being a major engine.

3.heading: The Distributional Question: Who Wins and Who Loses
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body: Distributional effects: U.S. manufacturing employment fell from about 17 million in 1994 to a low of 11.5 million in early 2010, recovering to about 12.6 million by end-2024. Specific Midwest manufacturing communities — Detroit, Cleveland, Buffalo, parts of Pennsylvania — experienced concentrated job losses. Real wages for U.S. workers without college degrees stagnated or fell over the NAFTA era, though distinguishing trade effects from technology effects is empirically difficult. Mexican agricultural workers, particularly small corn farmers, also experienced losses as cheaper U.S. corn flooded Mexican markets after tariff removal.

3.heading: The Distributional Question: Who Wins and Who Loses
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
The political consequences became clear by 2016. Both major U.S. presidential candidates that year campaigned against NAFTA. The Trump administration renegotiated NAFTA into the USMCA in 2018-2020, with marginal changes. The Biden and Trump administrations from 2021-2026 have maintained trade restrictions on China and largely abandoned new free trade agreements. The empirical record on NAFTA supports both the aggregate gains argument and the distributional losses argument — and the political economy of those losses has driven 30 years of U.S. trade policy in directions the original NAFTA architects would not have predicted.
Figure 3.4 The distributional arithmetic of trade liberalisation. The aggregate effect is positive, but it is the sum of a small proportional gain spread over a very large number of consumers and a large proportional loss concentrated on a small number of workers and communities. Compensation is feasible in principle, since the gains exceed the losses, and is rare in practice, which is the central fact of contemporary trade politics.

3.heading: Trade Policy Instruments
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
Governments have a variety of tools for affecting international trade. Each works through different mechanisms and has different effects on prices, quantities, and the distribution of gains and losses.
Trade policy instruments and their effects
InstrumentHow it worksDistribution of effects
TariffTax on imports. Raises domestic price of imported goods. Domestic producers compete against the artificially-higher import price. Government collects tariff revenue.Domestic producers and government win; domestic consumers and foreign exporters lose.
QuotaQuantitative limit on imports. Imports become scarce; domestic prices rise. Quota holders (importers) capture quota rents.Domestic producers and quota holders win; consumers lose.
Voluntary export restraint (VER)Exporting country "voluntarily" limits exports. Same effect as quota but rents accrue to foreign exporters.Domestic producers and foreign exporters win; domestic consumers lose. Worst form of protection for the importing country.
Export subsidyGovernment pays domestic producers to export. Raises domestic price and lowers foreign price.Domestic producers and foreign consumers win; domestic consumers and taxpayers lose.

3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30

Non-tariff barriersRegulatory requirements, certification, technical standards that impede imports. Often hidden protection.Effects vary; usually opaque.
Industrial subsidiesGovernment supports specific domestic industries (CHIPS Act for semiconductors, IRA for clean energy).Subsidized industries and their workers win; taxpayers and competing industries lose.

3.heading: Trade Policy Instruments
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — When tariffs make sense and when they do not
The standard economics textbook position on tariffs is hostile: tariffs reduce aggregate welfare in the importing country, distort prices, invite retaliation, and benefit specific producers at the expense of broader consumers. This is largely correct as an aggregate statement. But it is incomplete as a policy guide because it ignores three considerations: (1) the distributional question already discussed, (2) national security and strategic concerns (we may not want to depend on a hostile country for critical components), and (3) infant industry arguments (sometimes domestic industries need temporary protection to develop scale).

3.heading: Trade Policy Instruments
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
My read on tariffs: broad, indiscriminate tariffs (like 10% tariffs on all imports) are almost always net welfare-reducing. Targeted tariffs (like protection for industries with national security implications or in industries where domestic scale economies matter) sometimes pass cost-benefit. The current U.S. mix of tariffs is somewhere in between, with a clear shift toward more protection since 2018 across both administrations. The empirical question is whether the political economy of tariffs — once erected, they are hard to remove because protected industries lobby to keep them — outweighs the targeted benefits. Historical experience suggests the political stickiness usually dominates. Once one builds a tariff on steel for national security reasons, the steel industry will fight to keep it long after the security concern has faded.
— A.S.

Figure 3.5 A tariff in a small open economy. The domestic price rises from the world price to the world price plus the tariff. Domestic production expands, domestic consumption contracts, and imports fall. Government collects the rectangle of revenue; the two shaded triangles are the production and consumption distortions, which are losses to the economy that accrue to no one.
Figure 3.6 A quota reaches the same domestic price as a tariff by a different route. Restricting the imported quantity raises the domestic price until demand and the permitted quantity are reconciled. The consumer loss and the production distortion are the same as under the equivalent tariff; what differs is who receives the rectangle between the world price and the domestic price. Under a tariff it is government revenue, under a quota it accrues to whoever holds the import licence.

3.heading: Worked Examples
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
📐 Worked Example 3.1 — Computing Comparative Advantage
Country X produces 80 bushels of wheat or 40 cars per worker. Country Y produces 30 bushels of wheat or 20 cars per worker. (a) Compute each country's opportunity cost of producing one car (in wheat). (b) Which country has comparative advantage in cars? (c) At what trade ratio (wheat per car) would both countries gain from trade? (d) Suppose each country has 100 workers and currently produces both goods with workers split 50/50. Compute total world production. Then compute total world production if each country fully specializes in its comparative-advantage good. Show the world gains from trade.
1
(a) Opportunity costs: Country X: 1 car = 80/40 = 2 bushels of wheat. Country Y: 1 car = 30/20 = 1.5 bushels of wheat.
2
(b) Comparative advantage in cars: Country Y has lower opportunity cost (1.5 < 2), so Country Y has comparative advantage in cars. Country X has comparative advantage in wheat.
3

3.heading: Worked Examples
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
(c) Mutually beneficial trade ratio: any price between 1.5 and 2 wheat per car. Country Y's domestic ratio is 1.5, so it will not accept fewer than 1.5 wheat per car. Country X's domestic ratio is 2, so it will not pay more than 2 wheat per car. Trade ratio range: 1.5 < price < 2 wheat per car.
4
(d) No trade: Country X (50 wheat workers + 50 car workers) produces 50×80 = 4,000 wheat and 50×40 = 2,000 cars. Country Y produces 50×30 = 1,500 wheat and 50×20 = 1,000 cars. World total: 5,500 wheat, 3,000 cars.
5
(d) Full specialization: Country X fully specializes in wheat: 100×80 = 8,000 wheat, 0 cars. Country Y fully specializes in cars: 0 wheat, 100×20 = 2,000 cars. World total: 8,000 wheat, 2,000 cars. Compared to no trade: +2,500 wheat, −1,000 cars.

3.heading: Worked Examples
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body: The trade-off: full specialization gives the world 2,500 more wheat but 1,000 fewer cars compared to no trade. At any trade ratio in the [1.5, 2] range, both countries strictly prefer the trading outcome to autarky. Notice that "more of everything" is not guaranteed at full specialization — what is guaranteed is that the production possibility frontier of the world has expanded, and at the right trade ratio both countries can consume more of both goods than they could without trade. The gain is the expansion of production possibilities, not literally "more of each good produced". Partial specialization (each country produces some of both) often allows both countries to consume more of both goods.

3.heading: Worked Examples
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
📐 Worked Example 3.2 — Tariff Welfare Analysis
The U.S. imports steel from abroad. Without tariff, the world price is $700/ton; U.S. consumers buy 100M tons (60M from imports, 40M from domestic producers). The U.S. imposes a 20% tariff, raising the U.S. price to $840/ton. After the tariff: U.S. consumers buy 90M tons (40M from imports, 50M from domestic producers). (a) Compute the gain to U.S. domestic producers. (b) Compute the loss to U.S. consumers. (c) Compute tariff revenue. (d) What is the net welfare effect for the U.S.?
1
(a) Producer surplus gain: domestic producers were getting $700/ton on 40M tons. Now they get $840/ton on 50M tons. Gain ≈ ($840−$700) × (40M + 50M)/2 = $140 × 45M = $6.3 billion. (Trapezoid area on supply curve.)
2
(b) Consumer surplus loss: consumers were paying $700 on 100M tons. Now they pay $840 on 90M tons. Loss ≈ ($840−$700) × (100M + 90M)/2 = $140 × 95M = $13.3 billion. (Trapezoid area on demand curve.)
3
(c) Tariff revenue: tariff is $140/ton × 40M imported tons = $5.6 billion.
4

3.heading: Worked Examples
3.title: Chapter 3, Trade, Comparative Advantage, and the Distributional Question Why specialization produces gains, how Ricardo's comparative advantage works mathematically, why those gains are not distributed evenly, what trade policy instruments actually do, and what the empirical evidence of the past 30
3.body:
(d) Net U.S. welfare: Producer gain + tariff revenue − consumer loss = $6.3B + $5.6B − $13.3B = −$1.4 billion. The tariff is net welfare-reducing for the U.S. by about $1.4B per year — the deadweight loss.
What the textbook arithmetic shows: a tariff has well-defined winners (domestic producers, government) and losers (consumers). The aggregate welfare effect for the importing country is negative — there is deadweight loss. But the loss is small relative to the gross transfers. The political economy of tariffs lives in this gap: small aggregate losses, large gains for concentrated and politically-active producers, costs spread thinly across millions of consumers. The producers lobby for tariffs; consumers rarely lobby against them. This is why tariffs tend to persist even when economists can show they reduce aggregate welfare. The Trump tariffs on steel and aluminum (2018) cost U.S. consumers and downstream industries an estimated $1.5-3 billion per year, with gains to the protected industries of about $500-700 million — exactly this pattern.

4.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Trade in the Engine
The MacroNations engine implements trade through the trade_openness lever (range 0-100, default 65). Higher openness raises productivity (+0.6 per pp above 65 per round) but with diminishing returns above 80. Trade openness also affects the engine's currency dynamics: countries with high trade openness face larger currency moves when there are global shocks. There is no separate "tariff" lever — increases in trade_openness model trade liberalization; decreases model tariff erection. The engine does not separately track distributional effects of trade (no division of citizens into "trade winners" and "trade losers") — but the gini state variable rises modestly when trade_openness increases rapidly, reflecting the empirical evidence that rapid trade liberalization tends to widen inequality without compensating institutions. Tournament strategy: maintain trade_openness in the 65-85 band for steady productivity gains. Moving below 50 forfeits substantial productivity. Moving above 90 invites currency volatility without much additional productivity benefit.

4.heading: Insight
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — What the textbook treatment leaves out
The classical supply-and-demand framework is one of the most useful tools in economics. It explains an enormous range of phenomena — why gas prices rise after hurricanes, why concert tickets for popular artists sell out, why housing in productive cities is expensive, why agricultural commodities are volatile. Within the assumptions it makes, the framework is rigorous and predictive. The danger is treating it as more universal than it actually is. The framework assumes well-informed buyers and sellers, frictionless transactions, homogeneous products, no search costs, and prices that adjust to clear markets continuously. None of those assumptions holds perfectly anywhere; many of them fail badly in important real markets.

4.heading: Insight
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
The healthcare market does not look like the textbook market — patients cannot usually see prices, cannot comparison-shop, often do not know what treatment they need. The labor market does not clear like the textbook says it should — unemployment exists even at "equilibrium" because matching workers to jobs takes time and information. The housing market is partly speculative — prices reflect expected future appreciation, not just current supply and demand. The platform markets of the internet age have winner-take-all dynamics no 1890s economist could have imagined. The supply-and-demand framework is the foundation, not the whole structure. One will need it everywhere, but one will need extensions and exceptions for many of the markets that matter most in modern economies.
— A.S.

4.heading: What a Market Is and What It Is Not
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📘 Principles Level — Defining "market"
A market is any arrangement that brings together buyers and sellers of a good or service. Markets can be highly organized (the New York Stock Exchange) or completely informal (a neighborhood babysitting network). They can be physical (a farmers' market) or virtual (Amazon, eBay). They can be local (Manhattan rentals) or global (oil). What unites them is the basic structure: parties on the buying side, parties on the selling side, some mechanism for them to find each other and agree on terms.
A competitive market is one where many buyers and many sellers transact, no individual buyer or seller has significant influence over the price, and goods are sufficiently similar that they are treated as interchangeable. The classic example: wheat futures. There are thousands of buyers and sellers, no single farmer or trader sets the price, all wheat of a given grade is essentially identical. Most introductory textbook analysis assumes competitive markets because that is where supply-and-demand reasoning is most accurate. Many real markets are not perfectly competitive but are "competitive enough" that the framework gives useful predictions.

4.body: Figure 4.1 Where the competitive model applies. A market is any arrangement through which buyers and sellers transact, and the supply-and-demand apparatus assumes that no single participant can move the price. That assumption is close to exact at the left of this spectrum and progressively less accurate toward the right, where firms choose prices rather than accept them.

4.heading: Demand: How Quantity Demanded Varies with Price
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📘 Principles Level — The demand curve
The quantity demanded at a given price is the amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price. The general empirical pattern, well-established across thousands of studies and centuries of observation: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls. This is the law of demand. The relationship plotted with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis gives a downward-sloping demand curve.
Why does demand slope downward? Two mechanisms reinforce each other. First, the substitution effect: when a good becomes more expensive relative to alternatives, buyers substitute toward those alternatives. When beef gets expensive, more people eat chicken. Second, the income effect: a higher price reduces buyers' real purchasing power, so they buy less of all goods including the one whose price rose. Combined, these effects produce the downward slope.

4.heading: Demand: How Quantity Demanded Varies with Price
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
Movements along the demand curve happen when the good's own price changes. Shifts of the entire demand curve happen when other factors change — income (higher income generally shifts demand right for "normal" goods), prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), preferences, expectations about future prices, the number of buyers in the market.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Linear Demand
\[ Q_d = a - bP + cY + dP_r \]\(Q_d\) is quantity demanded, \(P\) the price of the good itself, \(Y\) income, and \(P_r\) the price of a related good.
a
Choke price intercept — the quantity demanded if price is zero and other factors are at baseline.
−b·P
Own-price effect. b > 0 for normal goods. Higher b means demand is more responsive to price changes (more elastic).
+c·Y
Income effect. c > 0 for normal goods, c < 0 for inferior goods (instant noodles get bought less as income rises).
\(\pm d \cdot P_{related}\)
d > 0 if substitute (higher coffee price → more tea demanded). d < 0 if complement (higher car prices → less gasoline demanded).

4.heading: Demand: How Quantity Demanded Varies with Price
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
How econometricians actually estimate these: the challenge is that price and quantity are both determined endogenously by the market — they move together as supply and demand both shift. To estimate the demand curve specifically, one needs exogenous variation in supply (so price moves while demand does not) and exogenous variation in demand (so quantity moves while supply does not). This is one of the oldest identification problems in econometrics, solved (partially) by instrumental variables that shift one curve without shifting the other.
Figure 4.2 The demand curve. A reduction in the rent from \(P_1\) to \(P_2\) produces a movement along the curve from point A to point B, raising quantity demanded from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_2\). The curve itself does not move, because only the price of the good has changed.
Figure 4.3 A shift of the demand curve. A change in any determinant of demand other than the price of the good itself moves the entire curve. Here demand increases: at every price, buyers wish to purchase a larger quantity, and \(D\) shifts to \(D'\).

4.heading: Supply: How Quantity Supplied Varies with Price
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📘 Principles Level — The supply curve
The quantity supplied at a given price is the amount of a good that sellers are willing and able to produce and offer at that price. The general empirical pattern: as price rises, quantity supplied rises. This is the law of supply. Plotted as price vs quantity, the relationship gives an upward-sloping supply curve.
Why does supply slope upward? Because producing more units typically requires higher costs — using less efficient resources, paying overtime wages, working with lower-quality inputs. Producers need a higher price to make additional units worthwhile. At very low prices only the most efficient producers will operate; as price rises, less efficient producers find it profitable to enter, expanding total supply.
Like demand, supply curves shift in response to factors other than the good's own price. Production costs (input prices, wages, energy costs), technology, regulations, the number of sellers, and expectations all shift the supply curve. A drop in fuel prices reduces airline operating costs and shifts the airline supply curve rightward — more flights at any given ticket price.

4.heading: Supply: How Quantity Supplied Varies with Price
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: Figure 4.4 The supply curve and a shift of supply. The curve slopes upward because the marginal cost of production rises with output. A fall in input costs or an improvement in technology shifts the curve rightward from \(S\) to \(S'\), so that a larger quantity is offered at every price. The determinants that move the curve are input prices, technology, taxes and regulation, expectations, and the number of sellers.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
The intersection of supply and demand defines the market equilibrium — the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At this price, every buyer willing to pay finds a seller; every seller willing to produce finds a buyer. There is no shortage and no surplus.
Mechanically: if the actual price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — a surplus develops, and sellers compete by lowering prices to clear their inventory. If the actual price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds supplied — a shortage develops, and buyers compete by bidding prices up. In both cases, price adjusts toward equilibrium. This dynamic is what gives markets their self-organizing character. No one consciously sets the equilibrium price; it emerges from the interactions of decentralized actors trying to make their best individual decisions.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: In normal times, used car prices in the U.S. decline gently as new cars accumulate miles and wear. The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, which tracks wholesale used car prices, declined about 1-2% per year from 2010 to 2019. Then the pandemic hit. New car production collapsed in 2020-21 because of semiconductor shortages — auto manufacturers could not get the chips needed to complete vehicles. Rental car companies, expecting depressed travel demand, sold off about 700,000 vehicles into the used car market in early 2020. Then travel demand recovered faster than expected, and rental companies needed to rebuild fleets at the exact moment new car supply was constrained.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: The result: the Manheim index rose roughly 80% from January 2020 to its January 2022 peak — the largest two-year increase since the index began. A three-year-old Toyota Camry that would have sold for $18,000 in January 2020 was selling for $27,000 by early 2022. This was the supply-and-demand framework doing exactly what the textbook predicts: a supply shock (constrained new car production) combined with a demand shock (rental companies rebuilding) pushed prices up dramatically until quantity supplied equaled quantity demanded. By 2024, as new car production normalized, used car prices had retreated about 20% from their peak. By late 2025, they were still about 35% above pre-pandemic levels, reflecting the lasting effect of the 2020-21 supply disruption on the age distribution of the U.S. vehicle fleet.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: The lesson: supply-and-demand reasoning predicted the direction of the move (prices up) immediately when the shocks were identified. The magnitude was harder to predict because elasticities are difficult to measure precisely. But the qualitative framework worked. This is what the supply-and-demand framework gets right — directional predictions are reliable; precise magnitude predictions usually are not.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Confusing movements along curves with shifts of curves
Suppose the price of beef rises 20% and quantity demanded of beef falls 8%. Did the demand curve shift? No — this is a movement along the demand curve. The demand curve has not changed; we just moved to a different point on the same curve as price changed. A shift of the demand curve would require a change in something other than beef's own price — say, a change in income, in chicken prices, in consumer preferences, in expectations about future beef prices.
This distinction matters because it determines what we call the cause. If beef demand fell because of a beef recall (consumer preferences changed), that is a leftward shift of the demand curve, and equilibrium price would fall. If beef demand fell because beef prices rose, that is a movement along an unchanged demand curve, and the price increase was caused by something else (perhaps a supply contraction). The general principle: changes in own-price cause movements along the curve. Changes in other factors cause shifts of the curve. Confusing the two leads to circular reasoning where the explanation for a price change is the price change itself.

4.heading: Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
Figure 4.5 Market equilibrium. At the price \(P^*\) the quantity buyers wish to purchase equals the quantity sellers wish to sell, \(Q^*\). No participant has an incentive to alter behavior, and the market clears.
Figure 4.6 Disequilibrium and the adjustment process. Above \(P^*\) the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, and the resulting surplus drives the price down; below \(P^*\) the shortage drives it up. The equilibrium is therefore stable, in the sense that departures from it generate the pressure that removes them.
Figure 4.7 Comparative statics: an increase in demand with supply unchanged. The equilibrium moves from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\) along the supply curve, so price and quantity both rise. An increase in supply with demand unchanged produces the opposite signature — quantity rises while price falls — which is how the two cases are distinguished in data.

4.heading: Information Failures: Where the Textbook Model Breaks Down
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Asymmetric information
The classical supply-and-demand model assumes both sides of the market have full information about the goods being traded. In many real markets, this assumption fails badly — one side knows substantially more than the other. The economic consequences can be dramatic.
The canonical example is George Akerlof's 1970 "Market for Lemons" paper, which earned him a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize. Consider a used car market where sellers know whether their car is a high-quality "peach" or a low-quality "lemon" but buyers cannot tell the difference. Buyers will pay a price reflecting the average quality. But at the average price, sellers of peaches are unwilling to sell (they would be selling for less than their car is worth), while sellers of lemons are eager to sell. So peaches leave the market, the remaining cars are disproportionately lemons, the average quality falls, buyers adjust their offers downward, and the cycle continues. In the extreme, the market can collapse entirely — what Akerlof called adverse selection.

4.heading: Information Failures: Where the Textbook Model Breaks Down
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: The same logic applies to insurance markets (high-risk individuals are most eager to buy insurance, raising premiums and driving out low-risk buyers), labor markets (workers know their own productivity better than employers), credit markets (borrowers know their own repayment intentions), and many others. Asymmetric information is one of the most pervasive market failures, and most actual markets have institutional responses to it — warranties, certifications, reputations, regulation.

4.heading: Information Failures: Where the Textbook Model Breaks Down
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why information matters more than the textbook admits
Most introductory textbooks mention asymmetric information but treat it as a special case. I would argue it is closer to the rule than the exception. Healthcare: patients cannot evaluate medical advice; doctors know much more. Financial services: customers cannot evaluate the quality of investment products; brokers know much more. Used housing: sellers know about hidden problems; buyers do not. Job markets: workers know their own work habits; employers do not. Insurance: customers know their own risk; insurers must estimate. The textbook competitive market assumes away the most important friction in many of the markets that matter most to people's lives.

4.heading: Information Failures: Where the Textbook Model Breaks Down
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
This is one reason economic policy debate about regulation is so contested. The libertarian instinct is "leave markets alone — they will figure it out." Sometimes they do (used car warranties, AirBnB reviews, eBay ratings). Sometimes they do not (financial advice quality, medical care prices, online platform manipulation). The case for regulation is strongest precisely where information asymmetries are most severe and self-correcting institutions are weakest. The case against regulation is strongest where information is symmetric or where market-driven institutions handle the problem well. Reasonable people can disagree about specific cases; the analytical frame should be about whether market institutions are addressing the information problem, not whether information problems exist at all.
— A.S.

4.heading: Information Failures: Where the Textbook Model Breaks Down
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: Figure 4.8 Adverse selection in a market for used cars. Sellers know the quality of their own car and buyers do not, so buyers will pay only what the average car is worth. That price is below the value of the better cars, whose owners withdraw; the average quality of what remains falls, the price buyers will pay falls with it, and the process repeats. Equilibrium is reached where the expected quality is consistent with the price, which can be far below the level at which mutually profitable trades existed.

4.heading: Search Frictions: When Finding Counterparties is Costly
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Markets where matching takes time
In the textbook market, buyers and sellers meet instantly and frictionlessly. In many real markets, finding a counterparty is the central activity — and the framework needs modification. The 2010 Nobel Prize was awarded to Diamond, Mortensen, and Pissarides precisely for work on markets where search is the central feature: labor markets, housing markets, marriage markets (yes, economists analyze these too).
The defining feature: at any moment, there are jobs unfilled and workers looking, houses for sale and buyers searching, suitable partners who have not yet met. The matching process takes time and resources. Even when supply and demand are "balanced" in aggregate, there can be persistent unemployment, vacancies, and time-on-market because the matching is not instant. The U.S. unemployment rate has been positive for every year since data collection began — not because the labor market is constantly out of equilibrium in the textbook sense, but because matching workers to jobs takes time even when both sides exist.

4.heading: Search Frictions: When Finding Counterparties is Costly
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
Search frictions imply several things the textbook model misses. (1) Prices are dispersed: the same good can sell for different prices depending on search effort. (2) Information about prices is itself valuable: the comparison-shopping industry exists because consumers cannot costlessly know all prices. (3) Markets can have multiple equilibria: low-search-effort equilibria (high prices, less competition) and high-search-effort equilibria (low prices, more competition) can both exist for the same market.
Figure 4.9 Why a single price does not emerge when search is costly. Each additional seller sampled yields a smaller expected improvement, while the cost of sampling one more is roughly constant. The buyer stops where the two are equal, which is before the best available price has been found. Identical goods therefore trade at different prices at the same moment, and the dispersion is an equilibrium outcome rather than evidence of irrationality.

4.heading: Expectations: When the Future Drives the Present
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Forward-looking markets
In some markets, current prices depend heavily on expectations about future prices. The clearest examples are asset markets — stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities held as stores of value. A stock is not just a claim on current earnings; it is a claim on the entire stream of future earnings, discounted to the present. Its current price depends on what buyers and sellers expect future earnings and discount rates to be.
This produces dynamics the basic supply-demand framework cannot easily capture. When expectations shift — when investors become more optimistic about future earnings, or more pessimistic about future interest rates — current prices change without any change in current supply or current demand for the underlying real activity. Asset prices can deviate from fundamentals for extended periods, driven by self-reinforcing expectation cycles. The housing market in 2003-2007 is a canonical example: prices rose far above what supply-and-demand fundamentals could support, sustained by expectations that prices would continue rising, until the expectation cycle broke and prices collapsed.

4.heading: Expectations: When the Future Drives the Present
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
Expectations also matter in labor markets (workers and firms enter contracts based on expected future productivity and prices), in education (students invest in skills based on expected future returns), in business investment (firms build factories based on expected future demand). Most introductory economics teaches supply and demand in the present tense; many of the most important markets operate substantially in the future tense.
2003-2012
United States
Housing Bubble & Bust
When Expectations Detached Prices from Fundamentals
From 2003 to 2006, U.S. home prices rose roughly 50% in real terms — an unprecedented surge for a national housing market. The Case-Shiller index showed cities like Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Miami rising 80-100% in this short period. Supply-and-demand fundamentals could not account for the rise: population growth, income growth, and housing construction were all reasonably normal. What had changed was expectations: buyers, sellers, lenders, and rating agencies had all come to believe that home prices would continue rising indefinitely.

4.heading: Expectations: When the Future Drives the Present
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
The expectation became self-fulfilling for a while. Buyers willing to pay high prices today (because they expected to sell higher tomorrow) bid prices up. Lenders willing to issue mortgages with little documentation (because they expected the underlying collateral to appreciate) extended credit broadly. Investors purchased mortgage-backed securities at prices that only made sense if expected default rates stayed low (because they expected home prices to keep rising). The whole system rested on the expectation.
When the expectation broke in 2007-2008, the unwinding was rapid and brutal. Home prices fell 30% nationally and 50%+ in the bubble cities. Mortgage defaults rose. Mortgage-backed securities became "toxic assets." The financial system nearly collapsed (Ch22 covers the financial crisis mechanics). U.S. home prices took until 2017 to recover their 2006 peaks in nominal terms; in real terms they remained below the peak for over a decade.

4.heading: Expectations: When the Future Drives the Present
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
The deeper lesson for markets: when current prices depend heavily on expected future prices, the basic supply-demand framework needs to be supplemented with analysis of expectations dynamics. Most asset price collapses follow this pattern — a long period when expectations diverge from fundamentals, then a sudden adjustment when the divergence becomes unsustainable. Understanding markets with expectational dynamics requires holding two frames simultaneously: the current supply-demand equilibrium AND the expectations underlying it. Either alone is insufficient.
Figure 4.10 A price that reflects expectations rather than current fundamentals. Through the housing episode of the 2000s, prices rose far faster than rents and incomes, the variables that measure what a house is worth to live in. A buyer paying those prices was not valuing shelter but anticipating resale. Supply and demand still describe the market, but the demand curve is being shifted by beliefs about the future, which can reverse quickly.

4.heading: Interactive: Market Equilibrium Simulator
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
🎛 Interactive — Market Equilibrium with Shifts
Set demand and supply parameters; see equilibrium price and quantity, then shift the curves
Sliders set the slope and intercept of each curve. Demand: \(Q_{d} = a - b \cdot P\). Supply: \(Q_{s} = - c + d \cdot P\). The interactive computes the equilibrium and shows what happens when curves shift.
Demand intercept a (choke quantity): 100
Demand slope b (price sensitivity): 2
Supply intercept c (entry threshold): 10
Supply slope d (responsiveness): 1.5
Notice the elasticity effects: in the inelastic preset (steep curves), small shifts produce large price changes. In the elastic preset (flat curves), the same shifts produce small price changes but larger quantity changes. This is why housing prices move so much in response to demand changes — housing supply is highly inelastic in the short run.

4.heading: Worked Examples
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📐 Worked Example 4.1 — Solving for Equilibrium
A market has demand \(Q_{d} = 100 - 2P\) and supply \(Q_{s} = - 10 + 3P\). (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) If a sudden demand increase shifts demand to \(Q_{d} = 150 - 2P\), find the new equilibrium. (c) Compute the percentage change in price and quantity.
1
(a) Equilibrium: set \(Q_{d} = Q_{s}\): 100 − 2P = −10 + 3P → 110 = 5P → P* = $22. Quantity: Q* = 100 − 2(22) = 56 units.
2
(b) Demand shifts: \(Q_{d} = 150 - 2P\). New equilibrium: 150 − 2P = −10 + 3P → 160 = 5P → P* = $32. Quantity: Q* = 150 − 2(32) = 86 units.
3
(c) Percentage changes: ΔP/P = (32 − 22)/22 = +45%. ΔQ/Q = (86 − 56)/56 = +54%. Both price and quantity rose substantially because both supply and demand are moderately elastic.

4.heading: Worked Examples
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body: What the example shows: a demand shock raises both price and quantity. The relative sizes of the price and quantity adjustments depend on the elasticity of the supply curve. If supply were perfectly inelastic (vertical), all the adjustment would be in price; if supply were perfectly elastic (horizontal), all the adjustment would be in quantity. Real markets are between these extremes, and the ratio of price-change to quantity-change is informative about supply elasticity. This is also how empirical economists "back out" elasticity estimates from natural experiments — observe price and quantity responses to a shock, infer the underlying elasticities.

4.heading: Worked Examples
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
📐 Worked Example 4.2 — Identifying Demand vs Supply Shocks
In each scenario, determine whether the price and quantity changes are consistent with (a) a demand shift, (b) a supply shift, or (c) both. (i) U.S. egg prices double in a year; egg production falls 15%. (ii) Tesla prices fell 20% in 2024 while quantities sold rose 10%. (iii) Used car prices rose 50% in 2020-21 while quantities sold fell 5%. (iv) GPU prices spiked 200% in 2018 while quantities sold rose 30%.
1
(i) Eggs: Price ↑, Quantity ↓. This is the signature of a supply shift (leftward) — H5N1 avian flu in 2024-25 killed millions of laying hens, reducing supply. Price rose, quantity fell. Demand was approximately unchanged.
2
(ii) Tesla: Price ↓, Quantity ↑. This is the signature of a supply shift (rightward) — Tesla cut prices to expand market share, effectively shifting their supply curve down. Customers responded with more purchases. Demand approximately unchanged.
3

4.heading: Worked Examples
4.title: Chapter 4, Markets: Where Prices Come From How supply and demand interact to produce prices, why prices aggregate dispersed information in ways no central planner could match, and where the standard model misses important features — particularly information asymmetries, search frictions, and the rol
4.body:
(iii) Used cars 2020-21: Price ↑, Quantity ↓. Like eggs — looks like a leftward supply shift. Supply was constrained by reduced new car production (which kept used cars circulating longer). Some demand-side increase too (people avoiding public transport during pandemic), but the dominant effect was supply.
4
(iv) GPUs 2018: Price ↑, Quantity ↑. This is the signature of a demand shift (rightward) — the 2018 crypto mining boom caused demand for GPUs to surge. With somewhat elastic supply, both price and quantity rose substantially.
The diagnostic principle: when price and quantity move in the same direction, it is primarily a demand shift. When they move in opposite directions, it is primarily a supply shift. This simple test makes it possible to identify what is driving observed price changes — extremely useful for both real-world analysis and exam questions. The complication arises when both curves shift simultaneously (which often happens during major shocks); then one needs additional information to decompose the change.

5.heading: Overview

5.body:
The MacroNations engine does not model individual markets — it operates at the aggregate level (whole-economy GDP, price level, unemployment). But the same supply-and-demand intuitions apply to aggregate markets. The aggregate demand curve (Ch15 covers this) represents total spending across all sectors; the aggregate supply curve represents total production. Equilibrium produces aggregate output and the price level. The 10 levers in MacroNations operate by shifting these aggregate curves: fiscal stimulus (gov_spending up or tax_rate down) shifts AD right, raising both output and prices. Supply-side policies (rd_investment, infrastructure, green_energy) shift AS right over time, raising output without raising prices. Monetary tightening (interest_rate_target up) shifts AD left, lowering both. The same diagnostic principle from Worked Example 4.2 applies at the aggregate level: if output and price level move in the same direction, one is seeing demand effects; if they move opposite, one is seeing supply effects. Use this to debug a tournament strategy — if inflation is rising while output is falling, one has triggered a supply contraction, not a demand expansion.

5.heading: Insight
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why elasticity is the most underrated concept in intro economics
Of all the concepts in introductory economics, elasticity is probably the most underrated. Students learn it as a formula and move on. But elasticity is what determines the answer to nearly every applied question in economic policy. Who bears the burden of a tax? Whoever is more inelastic on their side of the market. Why do agricultural prices crash when there is a bumper crop? Because demand for food is inelastic, so a quantity increase requires a large price decrease. Why do gasoline taxes affect demand modestly in the short run but substantially in the long run? Because gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run (one has the current car and commute) but elastic over time (one can buy a fuel-efficient car or change where one lives).

5.heading: Insight
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
If one understands elasticity well, one can predict the qualitative effects of most policies and shocks immediately. Most poorly-designed economic policy fails because the designers did not think hard enough about elasticities. The luxury tax on yachts in the U.S. in 1991 collected almost no revenue and devastated the yacht industry because the demand for luxury yachts is highly elastic (buyers can postpone purchases or buy abroad). The COVID-era student loan payment pause was justified partly by "helping borrowers"; the actual benefit went disproportionately to high-income borrowers because their loan balances are higher — a classic elasticity-design mismatch. Whenever one hears an economic claim about who benefits or loses from a policy, ask: what are the relevant elasticities? The answer usually rewrites the political story.
— A.S.

5.heading: Price Elasticity of Demand
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📘 Principles Level — Definition and computation
The price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to changes in price. Formally:
\[ \varepsilon_d = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q_d}{\%\,\Delta P} \]
Because \(Q_{d}\) falls when P rises, the elasticity is technically negative. By convention, economists usually report the absolute value and call demand "elastic" or "inelastic" based on whether \(|\varepsilon_{d}|\) is greater or less than 1.
Elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| > 1)\): quantity changes proportionally more than price. A 10% price increase produces > 10% quantity decrease. Demand is responsive.
Inelastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| < 1)\): quantity changes proportionally less than price. A 10% price increase produces < 10% quantity decrease. Demand is unresponsive.
Unit elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| = 1)\): proportional response. A 10% price increase produces 10% quantity decrease.
Perfectly elastic (\(\varepsilon_{d}\) = −∞): any price increase eliminates all demand. The demand curve is horizontal.
Perfectly inelastic \((\varepsilon_{d} = 0)\): quantity demanded does not change at all with price. The demand curve is vertical.

⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Midpoint Formula
\[ \varepsilon_d = \frac{(Q_2 - Q_1) \,/\, \tfrac{1}{2}(Q_1 + Q_2)}{(P_2 - P_1) \,/\, \tfrac{1}{2}(P_1 + P_2)} \]The midpoint form divides by the average of the two values, so the elasticity is the same whether the price rises or falls.
Why use midpoints?

5.heading: Price Elasticity of Demand
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
The "simple" percentage formula gives different elasticities depending on whether one computes "P went from 10 to 12" (20% rise) or "P went from 12 to 10" (16.7% fall). The midpoint formula uses the average of the two prices/quantities, giving a consistent number regardless of direction.
Example
Q falls from 100 to 80; P rises from $10 to $12. ΔQ/avg(Q) = −20/90 = −22.2%. ΔP/avg(P) = 2/11 = 18.2%. Elasticity = −22.2%/18.2% = −1.22. \(|\varepsilon_{d}| > 1\), so demand is elastic.
Interpretation
\(|\varepsilon_{d}| = 1.22\) means a 1% price increase causes 1.22% quantity decrease. The 18% price increase caused a 22% quantity decrease — proportionally larger than the price change.
Why this matters for revenue
When demand is elastic, raising price reduces total revenue (the percentage quantity drop exceeds the percentage price gain). When inelastic, raising price increases total revenue. This is the relationship between elasticity and revenue maximization.

5.heading: Price Elasticity of Demand
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
Figure 5.1 Two demand curves through a common point. Facing an identical increase in price from \(P_1\) to \(P_2\), quantity demanded along the flatter curve falls from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_{\text{el}}\), while along the steeper curve it is almost unchanged. Elasticity measures this responsiveness as a ratio of percentage changes, which makes it independent of the units in which price and quantity happen to be recorded.
Figure 5.2 The limiting cases. A vertical demand curve describes a quantity that does not respond to price (\(\varepsilon = 0\)); a horizontal curve describes buyers who will purchase any quantity at the prevailing price and none above it (\(\varepsilon = \infty\)). Real demand curves lie between these bounds, and the analytically useful question is where.
Figure 5.3 Elasticity along a straight-line demand curve. The slope is identical at every point, but elasticity declines steadily from the upper left to the lower right and equals one at the midpoint. Slope and elasticity are therefore distinct concepts: a curve cannot be described as elastic or inelastic without reference to the point under consideration. The slope is constant along the curve; the elasticity is not.
