Luxury Tax Failure
The Yacht Tax: A Lesson in Demand Elasticity

5.heading: The Determinants of Elasticity
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
In November 1990, the U.S. Congress passed a 10% luxury tax on yachts costing more than $100,000, alongside taxes on private aircraft, luxury cars, jewelry, and furs. The tax was projected to raise $31 million per year and was justified as making the wealthy pay their "fair share." The actual result was a near-collapse of the U.S. yacht industry.
Within two years of the tax, sales of U.S.-made yachts above the threshold collapsed. The Joint Economic Committee's official 1991 analysis attributed direct losses of about 7,600 jobs to the boating industry, with additional losses in jewelry (~330 jobs) and aircraft (~1,470 jobs); industry groups including the National Marine Manufacturers Association argued the total combined direct and indirect losses (including supplier industries) ran much higher, into the tens of thousands. Wealthy buyers either postponed purchases, bought slightly cheaper boats below the threshold, or — most damaging — bought yachts in Mexico or Europe to avoid the tax.

5.heading: The Determinants of Elasticity
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
By 1993, the tax was repealed. What had gone wrong? The Congressional analysis had implicitly assumed that demand for luxury yachts was inelastic — that buyers would simply absorb the tax. The reality was that demand was highly elastic. Luxury purchases can be postponed, downscaled, or shifted to foreign suppliers. The tax made U.S.-built yachts uncompetitive relative to alternatives, and demand collapsed. The 1991 revenue yield was about $16.6 million against the original $31 million projection, and once associated unemployment costs were netted out, the JEC estimated the tax was a net fiscal loss in fiscal 1991.
The deeper lesson: taxes generate revenue most effectively when demand for the taxed good is inelastic, and they generate deadweight loss most severely when demand is elastic. The yacht tax was the worst possible combination — small revenue, large efficiency loss, concentrated job losses for non-wealthy workers. The wealthy were largely unaffected; the people who built the yachts bore the brunt. This is now one of the standard cautionary tales in tax policy, taught in every public finance course.

5.heading: The Determinants of Elasticity
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body: Figure 5.4 Estimated price elasticities for familiar goods. Reading from left to right, the pattern is the one the determinants predict: a good with no substitute and a trivial budget share is almost perfectly inelastic, a necessity with distant substitutes is inelastic in the short run and considerably more elastic once the stock of equipment can be replaced, and a single brand within a category — the narrowest definition of a market — is highly elastic because the next brand is a close substitute.

5.heading: Elasticity and Total Revenue
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — The revenue relationship
Total revenue is price times quantity: TR = P × Q. When price changes, both P and Q change (in opposite directions, given downward-sloping demand). What happens to total revenue depends on which effect dominates — and that is determined by elasticity.
If demand is elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| > 1)\): the quantity effect dominates. Raising price reduces total revenue; lowering price increases revenue.
If demand is inelastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| < 1)\): the price effect dominates. Raising price increases total revenue; lowering price decreases revenue.
If demand is unit elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| = 1)\): the two effects exactly cancel. Total revenue is constant as price changes.

5.heading: Elasticity and Total Revenue
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body: This relationship explains many real-world pricing patterns. Tobacco companies historically raised prices because cigarette demand is inelastic — higher price meant higher revenue. Airlines run elaborate yield-management systems precisely because flight demand is elastic at the marginal traveler — a different price for different seats can extract more revenue than uniform pricing. Streaming services raise subscription prices steadily because they have found subscription demand is inelastic in the short run (people resist canceling).

5.heading: Elasticity and Total Revenue
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Confusing "elastic" with "high quantity response"
Sometimes students learn that "elastic" means "large quantity response" and stop there. The full definition matters: elastic means quantity response is proportionally larger than the price change. A 10% price change causing 5% quantity change is inelastic, even though 5% is "substantial." A 10% price change causing 15% quantity change is elastic, even if 15% feels modest.
This matters because the elasticity threshold \((|\varepsilon_{d}| = 1)\) determines the revenue effect. Even a "large" quantity response is inelastic if it is smaller in percentage terms than the price change — and in that case, the price rise produces revenue gains, not losses. Always compute the ratio carefully. Elasticity is about proportionality, not absolute magnitude.

5.heading: Tax Incidence: Who Really Pays
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Statutory vs economic incidence
One of the most important applications of elasticity is determining the incidence of a tax — who ultimately bears the burden. The statutory incidence is determined by law (who legally writes the check). The economic incidence is determined by elasticity (who ends up paying through price changes). These can be wildly different.
The basic principle: the more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden. If demand is more inelastic than supply, consumers bear most of the tax (they cannot easily reduce their purchases, so they absorb the higher prices). If supply is more inelastic than demand, producers bear most of the tax (they cannot easily reduce production, so they absorb the lower net prices). The fraction of a tax borne by buyers vs sellers is approximately \(\varepsilon_{s} / (\varepsilon_{s} + |\varepsilon_{d}|)\).

5.heading: Tax Incidence: Who Really Pays
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body: Why this matters: politicians often claim that "we are taxing corporations" or "we are taxing the wealthy." Whether those statements are correct in economic terms depends on the elasticities. A corporate tax may be largely paid by consumers through higher prices (if product demand is inelastic) or by workers through lower wages (if labor markets are imperfectly competitive). A tax legally collected from sellers can be largely paid by buyers, and vice versa. Statutory incidence is a political/legal fact; economic incidence is determined by markets.

5.heading: Tax Incidence: Who Really Pays
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — The most important tax incidence example to understand
Consider a tax on cigarettes. The statutory incidence is on the seller (the retailer or wholesaler writes the check). The economic incidence: cigarette demand is inelastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| \approx 0.4)\), and cigarette supply is more elastic. So consumers bear the substantial majority of the tax — typically 70-80% of cigarette taxes show up as higher consumer prices, with the rest absorbed by sellers (and a small fraction lost as deadweight loss from foregone transactions). Cigarette taxes are effective tools for both raising revenue AND reducing smoking precisely because demand is inelastic enough to maintain revenue while elastic enough that some smokers do quit.

5.heading: Tax Incidence: Who Really Pays
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
Now consider a tax on luxury cars. Statutory incidence: typically on the buyer (sales tax). Economic incidence: luxury car demand is highly elastic. Buyers substitute toward non-luxury cars, buy used, postpone purchases, or buy abroad. The tax barely changes consumer prices because consumers can easily avoid it; the burden falls largely on workers in luxury car manufacturing. This is the same pattern as the 1991 yacht tax. The lesson: design taxes on inelastic goods if one wants revenue with limited distortion; on elastic goods, the same tax produces less revenue and more harm to workers in affected industries. Cigarettes work; yachts do not. The principle is general — economists evaluate proposed taxes substantially through the lens of expected incidence.
— A.S.

5.heading: Supply Elasticity
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📘 Principles Level — Definition
The price elasticity of supply measures how responsive quantity supplied is to price changes. Same formula structure as demand elasticity:
\[ \varepsilon_s = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q_s}{\%\,\Delta P} \]
Supply elasticity is positive (higher prices → more quantity supplied). The classifications mirror demand: elastic \((\varepsilon_{s} > 1)\), inelastic \((\varepsilon_{s} < 1)\), unit elastic \((\varepsilon_{s} = 1)\), perfectly elastic (horizontal), perfectly inelastic (vertical).
What determines supply elasticity? Primarily the ease of changing production. Industries that can rapidly add capacity (manufacturing with available labor and capital) have elastic supply. Industries with long capacity-building lead times (semiconductor fabs, oil refineries, housing) have inelastic short-run supply. Industries with absolutely fixed quantities (land in a specific location, vintage art, the Bordeaux 2003 wine vintage) have nearly perfectly inelastic supply.

5.body: The policy implications were also dictated by elasticities. For semiconductors, the inelastic supply led to the CHIPS Act — government subsidies for domestic fabs that would expand U.S. supply over the medium term. Tax cuts or other demand-side policies would have been useless because demand was not the problem. For baby formula, the FDA accelerated approval of imports — a supply-side response targeting the inelastic supply problem. For toilet paper, no policy was needed because supply caught up within weeks naturally. Each policy choice was effectively shaped by the underlying elasticities. A policy designer who does not understand elasticities cannot correctly diagnose what intervention will help.

Commodity markets are the standard illustration, and the pattern explains why a shock that produces a spectacular price spike often leaves little trace two years later.

5.heading: Cross-Price and Income Elasticities
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Other elasticities that matter
Two other elasticities matter for understanding markets:
Cross-price elasticity of demand: how much demand for good X changes when the price of good Y changes:
\[ \varepsilon_{xy} = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q_x}{\%\,\Delta P_y} \]
If \(\varepsilon_{xy} > 0, X\) and Y are substitutes — when Y's price rises, people switch to X. Coke and Pepsi are substitutes; cross-elasticity is positive. If \(\varepsilon_{xy} < 0, X\) and Y are complements — when Y's price rises, people buy less of both. Cars and gasoline are complements; cross-elasticity is negative.
Income elasticity of demand: how much demand changes with income:
\[ \varepsilon_I = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q}{\%\,\Delta Y} \]
If \(\varepsilon_{I} > 0\), the good is normal (more demand at higher income). If \(\varepsilon_{I} > 1\), the good is a luxury (demand grows proportionally more than income — vacation travel, fine dining). If \(0 < \varepsilon_{I} < 1\), the good is a necessity (demand grows less than proportionally with income — food, basic clothing). If \(\varepsilon_{I} < 0\), the good is inferior (demand falls as income rises — instant noodles, used clothing).

5.heading: Cross-Price and Income Elasticities
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body: Figure 5.7 Two further elasticities, classified by sign. The cross-price elasticity is positive when a rise in the price of the other good raises demand for this one, which is what makes the two substitutes, and negative when they are consumed together. The income elasticity is positive for a normal good and negative for an inferior one. The signs are not permanent attributes of a product: the same good can be normal at one income level and inferior at another.

5.heading: Worked Examples
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📐 Worked Example 5.1 — Computing Elasticity and Revenue
A coffee shop sells lattes at $4.00, selling 200 per day. They raise the price to $4.50. Sales fall to 180 per day. (a) Compute the price elasticity of demand using the midpoint formula. (b) Compute total revenue at each price. (c) Is demand elastic or inelastic? Was the price increase a good business decision in revenue terms?
1
(a) Elasticity: ΔQ = −20, avg Q = 190. ΔQ/avgQ = −20/190 = −10.5%. ΔP = $0.50, avgP = $4.25. ΔP/avgP = 0.50/4.25 = +11.8%. Elasticity = −10.5%/11.8% = −0.89.
2
(b) Revenue: Old: 200 × $4.00 = $800/day. New: 180 × $4.50 = $810/day. Revenue rose $10/day.
3
(c) Verdict: \(|\varepsilon_{d}| = 0.89 < 1\), so demand is inelastic (just barely). With inelastic demand, raising the price increases revenue. The decision raised revenue by 1.25% — modest but positive. If demand had been elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| > 1)\), the same price increase would have reduced revenue.

5.heading: Worked Examples
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body: What the example shows: elasticity directly determines the revenue effect of a price change. For a near-unit-elastic good like coffee, small price changes produce small revenue changes — the business is operating near the revenue-maximizing point. Most chains experiment to find this sweet spot. Starbucks's "value tier" (drip coffee) is priced inelastically — slow price growth, stable demand. Their premium drinks (cold brew, frappuccinos) operate with more elastic demand because alternatives are more plentiful. The elasticity is what determines the optimal pricing strategy.

5.heading: Worked Examples
5.title: Chapter 5, Elasticity: When the Slope Matters A single concept — the responsiveness of one variable to another — that determines who pays a tax, why pandemic shortages produced wildly different price effects across categories, why some farmers face perpetual price volatility, and why pharmaceutical
5.body:
📐 Worked Example 5.2 — Tax Incidence Calculation
A market has demand elasticity \(|\varepsilon_{d}| = 0.5\) and supply elasticity \(\varepsilon_{s} = 2.0\). The government imposes a $1.00 per-unit tax. (a) What fraction of the tax is borne by buyers vs sellers? (b) How much will consumer price rise? (c) How much will seller's net price fall? (d) Compare to a case where demand is elastic \((|\varepsilon_{d}| = 2.0)\) and supply is inelastic \((\varepsilon_{s} = 0.5)\).
1
(a) First case: buyer share = \(\varepsilon_{s} / (\varepsilon_{s} + |\varepsilon_{d}|) = 2.0 / (2.0 + 0.5) = 2.0/2.5\) = 80%. Seller share = 20%. The more inelastic side (buyers, with low \(|\varepsilon_{d}|\)) bears more of the tax.
2
(b) Consumer price rise: 80% × $1.00 = +$0.80.
3
(c) Seller's net price fall: 20% × $1.00 = −$0.20. (Seller receives $0.80 from buyer instead of original $1.00 equivalent.)
4
(d) Reversed case: buyer share = 0.5 / (0.5 + 2.0) = 0.5/2.5 = 20%. Seller share = 80%. Now the more inelastic side is sellers, who bear the brunt. Consumer price rises only $0.20; sellers' net price falls $0.80.

5.heading: Worked Examples

5.body: What this shows: the same statutory tax produces dramatically different real-world burdens depending on elasticities. In the first case, the tax functions like a sales tax on consumers (80% of burden). In the second case, it functions like an income tax on producers (80% of burden). The political rhetoric about "taxing X" is often misleading because the legal liability and the economic burden can diverge enormously. The general principle: the more inelastic side bears more of the tax. This applies to income taxes (labor vs capital), payroll taxes (workers vs employers), tariffs (consumers vs foreign producers), and every other tax. Whenever one sees a tax debate, ask about elasticities.

6.heading: Overview

6.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Elasticity in the Engine
The MacroNations engine does not expose elasticities explicitly as parameters, but they are baked into the coefficient structure of every policy lever. The tax-rate-to-GDP coefficient (−1.1) embeds the elasticity of taxable income — empirical work suggests ETI ≈ 0.25, which means raising tax rates produces a 0.25% income response per percentage point of rate. The government-spending-to-GDP multiplier (1.4) embeds the elasticity of aggregate demand response to fiscal stimulus — empirically around 1.0-1.5 depending on slack. The Laffer-style drag at high tax_rate reflects an elasticity that becomes steeper as rates rise — the engine becomes "more elastic" near 70%+ rates, capturing the empirical evidence that taxable income responses are nonlinear. For tournament strategy: think of the engine as a stylized economy with empirical elasticities at typical OECD magnitudes. Pushing levers gently produces predictable effects; pushing them sharply hits nonlinearities where elasticities become extreme.

6.heading: Insight
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Beyond "markets vs government"
The textbook framing of "markets vs government" makes for clean exposition but bad analysis. Real economies are mixed economies, and have been for centuries. Even libertarian utopias would require government for property rights enforcement, contract enforcement, currency stability, defense, and protection from fraud. Even socialist economies use market-like mechanisms for many decisions (one does not centrally plan which restaurant a family will eat at tonight). The interesting question is not "markets or government?" — both, always — but "for each specific problem, what mix of market mechanisms and government institutions produces the best outcomes?"

6.heading: Insight
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The empirical answer varies dramatically by problem. Consumer goods (food, clothing, electronics): mostly market, with some regulation against fraud and unsafe products. Healthcare: every developed country has heavy government involvement because pure market provision fails badly. Education: mixed everywhere, with debate about the right mix. Infrastructure: mostly government because of public good characteristics. National defense: entirely government because no private actor can provide it. The right question is always specific: "for this particular problem, what is the best mix?" Not "is government good or bad?" — which is an ideologically loaded question that has no useful general answer.
— A.S.

6.heading: Price Ceilings: Rent Control as the Textbook Case
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📘 Principles Level — The mechanics
A price ceiling is a legal maximum price for a good. If the ceiling is set above the market equilibrium, it has no effect — the equilibrium price was already below the ceiling. If it is set below equilibrium, it becomes a binding price ceiling. At the ceiling price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied — a shortage develops.
The classic example is rent control: a legal maximum on rents in a particular city or neighborhood. The intent is to make housing affordable for current tenants. The standard textbook analysis identifies multiple consequences: (1) a shortage emerges as more renters want housing at the controlled price than landlords are willing to provide; (2) landlords let buildings deteriorate because they cannot recoup maintenance costs through higher rents; (3) landlords convert rental units to condominiums or commercial use; (4) new construction of rental housing declines; (5) the existing housing stock becomes less efficiently allocated as tenants stay in below-market units they would not otherwise occupy.
📗 Intermediate Level — What the empirical evidence shows

6.heading: Price Ceilings: Rent Control as the Textbook Case
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: Most of the textbook predictions are empirically supported. Diamond, McQuade, and Qian (2019) studied San Francisco rent control's effects using a difference-in-differences design after a 1995 expansion of the policy. They found: rent control reduced housing supply in affected buildings by about 15% as landlords converted to ownership or redeveloped. Tenants in controlled units stayed about 19% longer than similar tenants in uncontrolled units. The supply contraction drove a citywide rent increase of 5.1% as displaced demand pushed up rents in the uncontrolled portion of the market. The refined welfare accounting in the published version: rent control delivered $2.9 billion in present discounted benefits to covered tenants (averaging $2,300–$6,600 per affected person per year), but imposed $2.9 billion in present discounted costs on other tenants through the 5.1% citywide rent increase — a near-perfect transfer with substantial deadweight loss from misallocation. Roughly 42% of the costs fell on future SF residents and 58% on incumbents in uncovered units.

6.heading: Price Ceilings: Rent Control as the Textbook Case
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The pattern is consistent across multiple studies of rent control in different cities and time periods. Sims (2007) found similar patterns for Massachusetts rent control. Autor, Palmer, and Pathak (2014) studied the elimination of Cambridge MA rent control and found property values rose 15-20% — implying the policy had been suppressing housing values substantially. The consensus in housing economics: rent control benefits current tenants in covered units but worsens housing affordability overall and reduces total welfare. This is one of the clearest cases where the textbook framework's predictions hold up empirically.

6.heading: Price Ceilings: Rent Control as the Textbook Case
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why rent control persists despite the evidence
If the evidence against rent control is so strong, why do major cities keep adopting or extending it? Several reasons. First, the benefits to current tenants are visible and concentrated; the costs are diffuse and delayed — one can identify the tenant who benefits, but one cannot identify the future tenant who could not find an apartment because of suppressed construction. Second, the political constituency of current tenants is strong and locally organized; the constituency of future tenants does not yet exist in the political system. Third, the alternative policies (zoning reform, public housing investment, housing vouchers) are slower to deliver visible benefits and harder to enact.

6.heading: Price Ceilings: Rent Control as the Textbook Case
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The economic critique of rent control is one of the most empirically settled positions in microeconomics. The political popularity of rent control is one of the clearest examples of how political incentives can persistently produce policies that economic analysis identifies as harmful. The honest economic position: rent control is a poor policy for achieving its stated goals; better alternatives exist (housing vouchers, zoning reform that allows more supply, public housing investment, anti-displacement protections). The political position can be different: rent control may be politically achievable in places where better alternatives are not. Reasonable people can disagree about whether to support second-best policies when first-best ones are politically infeasible. But the empirical claim — rent control's harms substantially outweigh its benefits — is solid.
— A.S.

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📘 Principles Level — The mechanics
A price floor is a legal minimum price for a good. If the floor is set below equilibrium, it has no effect. If above equilibrium, it becomes binding: at the floor price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — a surplus develops. The minimum wage is a price floor on labor. The basic textbook prediction: if set above equilibrium, the minimum wage creates a surplus of labor (unemployment).
For decades the textbook story was simple: minimum wages cause unemployment. This was an empirical claim that turned out to be more contested than the simple textbook reasoning suggested. The Card-Krueger 1994 study (covered in Ch2) found that a New Jersey minimum wage increase produced essentially no employment loss — and possibly slight employment gains. This finding contradicted the simple textbook model and launched 30 years of careful empirical work that has substantially modified our understanding.
📗 Intermediate Level — The modern empirical consensus
The current empirical consensus on minimum wage effects, after Cengiz, Dube, Lindner, and Zipperer (2019) and many other carefully-identified studies:

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
Modest minimum wage increases (10-20%) produce small employment effects, typically in the range of −1% to +1% of low-wage employment. Often statistically indistinguishable from zero.
Real wage gains for low-wage workers are clear and substantial — affected workers see large wage increases that more than offset the small employment effects.
Wage spillover effects extend up the wage distribution — workers earning slightly above the new minimum also see wage gains as employers maintain pay differentials.
Very large minimum wage increases (50%+ or pushing to substantially above local median wage) can produce larger employment losses, though the threshold is not precisely identified.
The traditional textbook model assumed perfect labor market competition; the modern finding is consistent with labor markets having monopsony power (employers as wage-setters), allowing some redistribution from employer profits to wages without employment loss.

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The traditional framework — "minimum wage causes unemployment" — was too simple. The empirical evidence supports a more nuanced view: modest increases work as intended (raising worker pay with minimal employment effect), while extreme increases bear larger costs. The interesting policy debate has shifted from "should we have a minimum wage" to "how high should it be set in particular labor markets".
2014-2025
Seattle
$15 Minimum Wage
Seattle's $15 Wage: A Decade of Evidence
In June 2014, Seattle passed a law raising its minimum wage to $15/hour, phased in over 3-7 years depending on employer size. At the time, this was the highest minimum wage in the U.S. — about 60% above the federal minimum of $7.25 and roughly equal to the local median wage of $15-16. Economists predicted varying outcomes; the experiment became one of the most-studied minimum wage cases ever.

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The empirical findings have evolved as more data has become available. Early studies (Jardim et al., 2018) using University of Washington data suggested significant negative effects on hours worked — workers earning $13-15/hour saw modest hourly raises but reduced hours, leaving net pay flat or down. A separate Berkeley study using different data found primarily positive effects with little employment loss. The methodology debate that followed clarified that effects depend heavily on whether one measures jobs lost vs hours reduced, whether one can distinguish causal vs trend effects, and which subgroups one studies.

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: By the mid-2020s, with a decade of data, the empirical literature on Seattle has narrowed though not fully converged. The UW research (Jardim et al. and follow-ups) continues to find disemployment effects measured primarily in reduced hours; the Berkeley studies (Reich et al.) continue to find essentially no employment effects in food services. What is clearer across both camps: Seattle's $15 minimum wage did not produce the apocalyptic job losses some predicted, and substantial real wage gains for low-wage workers materialized. There were modest disemployment effects at the margin — some jobs eliminated, some hours reduced, some entry-level positions filled with more experienced workers. But the overall outcome was net positive for low-wage workers as a group, with manageable adjustment costs.

6.heading: Price Floors: The Minimum Wage Debate
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The deeper lesson: predictions based on simple textbook models often overestimate the disemployment effects of minimum wages. Real labor markets have monopsony elements, search frictions, and matching dynamics that absorb modest wage shocks. Whether this extends to higher minimum wages ($20? $25?) remains uncertain. But the simple "minimum wages cause unemployment" story has been substantially modified by 30 years of careful empirical work.
Figure 6.2 A binding price floor in the labor market. At a wage above the market-clearing level \(w^*\), the quantity of labor supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, and the difference appears as unemployment. Whether a given statutory minimum is in fact binding, and how large the employment response is, is an empirical question taken up later in the chapter.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why all taxes have costs but not all costs are equal
Any tax that changes behavior produces some deadweight loss. This is unavoidable. But it is wrong to conclude that all taxes are therefore equally undesirable. The smart question is: among the tools available to raise needed revenue, which produces the most revenue with the least efficiency cost? Different taxes vary enormously in this dimension.
The principles that economists have developed for "good" tax design:
Tax inelastic goods. Taxes on inelastic demand or supply produce less deadweight loss per dollar of revenue. This is why economists favor consumption taxes on broad categories (VAT, sales taxes) over taxes on specific elastic categories.
Tax negative externalities. Taxes on goods with negative externalities (carbon emissions, congestion, alcohol, tobacco) can produce welfare gains rather than losses — because the underlying activity was producing too much of itself relative to the social optimum.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
Use broad bases with lower rates. A 5% tax on all consumption produces less deadweight loss than a 50% tax on one specific good (because deadweight loss scales with the square of the tax rate). This is the case for VAT-style broad consumption taxes over targeted excise taxes.
Avoid taxes that change form rather than reduce activity. Some taxes drive activity underground or into less productive forms without reducing it. High income taxes can drive earners to offshore tax shelters; high cigarette taxes can drive smuggling; high estate taxes can drive complex avoidance schemes. The actual revenue gain from these taxes is much less than the nominal rate suggests.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Thinking taxes can have zero efficiency cost
It is tempting to assume that taxes on "the rich" or "corporations" have no efficiency cost because the targets can afford it. This conflates incidence with cost. The right framework: even if the rich bear the burden of a tax, the tax causes some behavioral response (less effort, less investment, less entrepreneurship, asset reallocation) that creates deadweight loss. The question is the magnitude. Empirical evidence on taxable income elasticity suggests it is roughly 0.2-0.4 for typical U.S. high-income taxpayers — meaning a 1% increase in the marginal rate reduces taxable income by 0.2-0.4%. This translates to deadweight loss of perhaps $0.30-$0.50 per dollar of additional revenue at typical marginal rates.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: So taxes on the rich are not free, but they are not catastrophic either. The interesting policy question is whether the social value of the revenue (e.g., funding education, healthcare, infrastructure) exceeds the deadweight loss. Often it does; sometimes it does not. The simple stories that "we can tax X without consequences" and "any tax destroys the economy" are both wrong. The actual analytics involve careful estimation of elasticities and comparison to alternative uses of resources.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss

6.body:
Figure 6.3 Consumer and producer surplus at the competitive equilibrium. Consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the price — the difference between what buyers were willing to pay and what they paid. Producer surplus is the area between the price and the supply curve. Their sum, total surplus, is the standard measure of the gains from trade in this market and the benchmark against which policy is evaluated.
Figure 6.4 The effect of a per-unit tax. The wedge between the price buyers pay, \(P_b\), and the price sellers receive, \(P_s\), equals the tax. Quantity traded falls from \(Q^*\) to \(Q_{\text{tax}}\). The shaded rectangle is revenue collected, \(t \cdot Q_{\text{tax}}\); the shaded triangle is the deadweight loss — the surplus from mutually beneficial trades that no longer occur.

6.heading: Taxes: Beyond Pure Deadweight Loss
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: Figure 6.5 Statutory and economic incidence differ. The side of the market that is less responsive to price — here buyers, whose demand is close to vertical — absorbs the larger share of the tax, irrespective of which side the legislature requires to remit it. The legal assignment of a tax therefore carries almost no information about who ultimately bears its burden. The division is governed by relative elasticities alone.

6.heading: Subsidies: When the Government Wants More of Something
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📘 Principles Level — How subsidies work
A subsidy is a government payment that reduces the effective price of a good. Subsidies can be paid to consumers (lowering their out-of-pocket cost), to producers (lowering their cost of production), or in mixed forms. Mechanically, a subsidy shifts the relevant curve: a consumer subsidy shifts demand up by the subsidy amount; a producer subsidy shifts supply down by the subsidy amount. Either way, the equilibrium quantity rises and the gap between buyer and seller prices opens up (in the opposite direction from a tax).
Like a tax, the incidence of a subsidy depends on elasticities. The more inelastic side captures more of the benefit. A subsidy for first-time homebuyers in a market with inelastic housing supply (most U.S. cities) primarily benefits home sellers through higher prices, not buyers — as Ch1 Worked Example 1.2 showed. A subsidy for crop insurance in agriculture (inelastic demand for insurance, more elastic supply) benefits farmers more than insurance companies. A subsidy for solar panel installation goes partly to homeowners (lower out-of-pocket costs) and partly to installers and panel manufacturers (higher prices).

6.heading: Subsidies: When the Government Wants More of Something
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — When subsidies are good policy
The textbook treatment of subsidies often emphasizes deadweight loss — the resources allocated to the subsidized activity that would not have been allocated absent the subsidy represent inefficient over-production. This is correct for subsidies of ordinary goods with no externalities. But subsidies for goods with positive externalities can produce net welfare gains — the activity was producing too little relative to the social optimum, and the subsidy moves output toward the optimal level.

6.heading: Subsidies: When the Government Wants More of Something
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The clearest examples: subsidies for basic research (positive externalities to all of society from new knowledge), vaccinations (positive externalities to others from herd immunity), education (positive externalities to society from a more capable workforce), clean energy (positive externalities from reduced carbon emissions). For each of these, the unregulated market produces less than the socially optimal amount because individual decision-makers do not capture the full benefit of their actions. Subsidies can correct this. The requirement is that the subsidy be well designed: targeted at activities with real externalities, sized appropriately, and not captured by interests that would have done the activity anyway.

6.heading: Subsidies: When the Government Wants More of Something
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The U.S. CHIPS Act (2022) and IRA (2022) both involve large subsidies. The CHIPS Act subsidizes semiconductor manufacturing for national security and supply chain reasons; the IRA subsidizes clean energy for climate and industrial policy reasons. Whether these are good policies depends on whether the targeted activities actually have the externalities claimed, whether the subsidies are sized appropriately, and whether they get captured by lobby interests or actually drive the intended behavior. The empirical verdict will be clear over the next 5-10 years.
— A.S.

6.heading: Subsidies: When the Government Wants More of Something
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: Figure 6.6 A per-unit subsidy. The payment drives a wedge between the price the buyer pays and the price the seller receives, in the opposite direction to a tax, and quantity rises above the competitive level. The division of the benefit follows the same elasticity rule as tax incidence: the more inelastic side captures the larger share, whichever side the check is written to. The cost to the treasury is the subsidy multiplied by the new quantity, which exceeds the gain in total surplus unless the subsidy is correcting an external benefit.

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Correcting market failures
The most economically defensible category of government intervention is correcting externalities — situations where market transactions affect third parties not party to the transaction. Negative externalities (pollution, congestion, secondhand smoke) cause markets to produce too much of an activity from the social perspective; positive externalities (vaccination, education, basic research) cause markets to produce too little.
The classical solution, developed by Arthur Pigou in the 1920s, is the Pigouvian tax: a tax on the activity producing the negative externality, set equal to the marginal external cost. The tax raises the private cost to match the social cost, causing producers and consumers to internalize the externality. The equilibrium output then equals the socially optimal output.

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The carbon tax is the contemporary canonical example. Carbon emissions impose costs on others (climate change effects on future generations and other countries) that are not reflected in the private cost of fossil fuel use. A carbon tax of, say, $50/ton of CO₂ raises the price of fossil fuels by an amount approximating the social damage, leading users to economize on emissions and producers to shift toward lower-carbon alternatives. The carbon tax is the most economically efficient policy for addressing climate change — preferred by nearly all economists across the ideological spectrum, including most conservative economists. Political adoption has been more limited because climate change is contested and the political coalition for explicit carbon pricing has been weaker than for less efficient regulatory approaches.
2008-2025
British Columbia
Carbon Tax: Rise and Repeal
What 17 Years of British Columbia's Carbon Tax Taught Us — Before It Was Repealed

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
In July 2008, British Columbia became one of the first jurisdictions in North America to implement a comprehensive carbon tax. The tax started at C$10/ton of CO₂ and rose gradually to C$80/ton by 2024. Revenue was initially used on a revenue-neutral basis to reduce personal income taxes and corporate taxes — though this revenue-neutrality commitment was loosened over the years, with revenue increasingly funding climate programs and household rebates. On April 1, 2025, the BC government repealed the consumer carbon tax in response to political pressure and the broader Canadian federal climate policy shift. The 17-year run nevertheless constitutes one of the cleanest natural experiments in carbon policy, and remains highly informative even though the policy itself is no longer in force.
The empirical evidence from 2008-2024:

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
BC's emissions trajectory diverged from the rest of Canada. Studies estimate the tax reduced BC's greenhouse gas emissions by 5-15% relative to counterfactual (Murray & Rivers 2015 review of multiple methodologies), with a frequently-cited University of Ottawa estimate finding a 19% per-capita reduction in fossil fuel consumption between 2008 and 2013. The carbon tax appears to have caused real emission reductions.
BC's economy grew at approximately the same rate as the rest of Canada. The carbon tax did not cause measurable economic harm relative to non-taxing provinces — at least in aggregate. Some emissions-intensive sectors faced specific challenges.
The revenue-neutral design (carbon tax offsetting cuts in income taxes) helped maintain political support initially. But as the tax rate rose to C$80/ton and revenue use drifted away from strict revenue-neutrality, the political coalition supporting the tax eroded.
Behavioral changes were broad: people drove slightly less, bought somewhat more efficient cars over time, improved home insulation. No single dramatic response, but many small ones across the economy.

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The 2025 repeal is itself a data point about political-economy sustainability. Even a well-designed Pigouvian tax with measured environmental benefits and modest economic costs proved difficult to sustain politically at higher rates and over long time horizons.

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The BC experience supports the Pigouvian framework in important ways while also revealing its political limits: a well-designed carbon tax can produce real emission reductions without major economic damage. But the political sustainability of carbon pricing depends heavily on transparent revenue recycling, public messaging, and the broader political context — and even seemingly successful programs can be reversed. The U.S. has not adopted a federal carbon tax, partly because of political opposition and partly because climate policy has shifted toward subsidies (IRA) rather than taxes — an approach economists generally consider less efficient per ton of CO₂ reduced but more politically achievable. The contrast between the economically optimal policy (carbon tax) and the politically feasible policy (subsidies + regulation) — and BC's eventual choice of neither — is a useful illustration of how economic analysis, political feasibility, and policy durability interact.

6.heading: Externalities and Pigouvian Taxes
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: Figure 6.7 Setting a price on an external cost. The efficient quantity of emissions is where the marginal damage of one more ton equals the marginal cost of abating it, not zero: eliminating the last ton costs more than the harm it does. A tax at that rate, or a permit market that clears at that price, induces exactly this quantity while leaving each firm free to abate or to pay. That is the respect in which a price instrument outperforms a uniform technical standard.

6.heading: When Government Helps and When It Hurts: A Summary Framework
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — The honest framework
The honest economic answer to "should the government do X?" is almost never a categorical yes or no. It is: here are the empirical considerations, here are the relevant elasticities, here is what is worked elsewhere, here are the political-economy risks, here is how to design the intervention if one does it, here is what the failure modes look like. The libertarian answer ("no, let markets work") and the statist answer ("yes, let government solve it") are both rhetorical shortcuts that skip the actual analysis.

6.heading: When Government Helps and When It Hurts: A Summary Framework
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
The most analytically defensible interventions — Pigouvian taxes on negative externalities, well-designed antitrust, basic infrastructure provision, public goods funding — are not particularly partisan in economic terms. They have broad support across the ideological spectrum among economists, even if politicians dispute them. The contested interventions tend to involve harder empirical questions (what is the right minimum wage? how aggressive should antitrust be?) where reasonable economists disagree. The mark of serious policy thinking is engaging the empirical questions, not retreating to ideological priors. That is the standard this textbook tries to model throughout.
— A.S.

6.heading: When Government Helps and When It Hurts: A Summary Framework

6.body: Figure 6.8 A summary framework for the question the chapter has been circling. The case for intervention depends on two things at once: how large the market failure is, and whether the administrative capacity exists to address it without introducing a larger distortion. A serious failure in a state that cannot implement the remedy is not an argument for the remedy, and a negligible failure in a capable state is not an argument for using the capacity.

6.heading: Interactive: Policy Instrument Comparison
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
🎛 Interactive — Comparing Policy Instruments for a Single Goal
Different instruments achieve the same outcome (e.g., reducing emissions) with different efficiency costs
Pick a policy goal; the chart compares the welfare cost of achieving the same outcome via different instruments. The pattern illustrates why economists usually prefer price-based instruments (taxes/subsidies) to quantity-based instruments (mandates/quotas) for most goals.
Policy goal:
The general pattern: for most goals, well-designed price-based instruments (Pigouvian taxes, EITC-style transfers, R&D tax credits) achieve the goal with lower welfare cost than command-and-control alternatives. This is why economists across the political spectrum tend to favor carbon taxes over emission mandates, vouchers over public provision in many cases, and the EITC over minimum wage. The political feasibility often runs the other direction — voters prefer visible mandates and benefits over abstract price changes — which is why economic-optimum and political-feasible policies often diverge.

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📐 Worked Example 6.1 — Pigouvian Tax for a Negative Externality
A coal-fired power plant produces electricity. The private marginal cost is $30/MWh. The marginal external cost (air pollution health damages plus climate damages) is estimated at $40/MWh. Market demand sets the equilibrium at 1000 MWh/day at a price of $30/MWh. (a) What is the socially optimal output? (b) What Pigouvian tax achieves it? (c) Compute the welfare gain from imposing the tax compared to no intervention. Assume demand has elasticity \(|\varepsilon_{d}| = 0.8\) at the equilibrium.
1
(a) Socially optimal output: the social marginal cost is private MC + external MC = $30 + $40 = $70/MWh. Optimal output is where social MC = demand. With \(|\varepsilon_{d}| = 0.8\) at the original equilibrium, a price change from $30 to $70 (a ~76% midpoint increase) implies a quantity change of about −60%. So Q* ≈ 1000 × 0.4 = 400 MWh/day.
2
(b) Pigouvian tax: set equal to marginal external cost: $40/MWh. This raises the effective marginal cost facing producers to $70/MWh, which matches the social MC. Output falls to Q*, internalizing the externality.
3

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: (c) Welfare gain: the original equilibrium produced 600 "excessive" MWh (from 400 to 1000) each imposing $40 external cost not captured in private decisions. Triangle area = 0.5 × 600 × $40 = $12,000/day in external costs eliminated. Some efficiency loss from reduced beneficial production of electricity, but this is smaller than the avoided external damage. Net welfare gain: positive (the "Harberger triangle" of avoided externality exceeds the consumer/producer surplus loss).

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The deeper insight: Pigouvian taxes produce net welfare gains — unlike most taxes which only produce deadweight loss in exchange for revenue. This is because the underlying activity was producing too much from the social perspective; the tax moves output toward the optimum. The revenue collected is an additional benefit, available for other public uses or for offsetting other distortionary taxes. This is why economists nearly unanimously favor carbon taxes over regulatory mandates for climate policy: not because they are hostile to climate action but because they are the most efficient way to achieve a given level of emission reduction. The political opposition to carbon taxes has been about politics (visible price increases, distributional concerns) rather than economics.

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
📐 Worked Example 6.2 — Evaluating Two Minimum Wage Proposals
A state currently has a $10/hour minimum wage. Two proposals: Proposal A raises it to $12 (20% increase); Proposal B raises it to $18 (80% increase). Median local wage is $20/hour. (a) Based on the empirical literature, what employment effects would one expect from each? (b) What is the political-economy challenge for each? (c) Which would one support and why?
1
(a) Expected employment effects: Proposal A is a modest increase well below the local median wage. Based on Cengiz et al. (2019) and the Card-Krueger tradition, expect employment effects in the −1% to +1% range for affected workers — essentially statistically zero. Substantial wage gains for low-wage workers with minimal adjustment costs. Proposal B is much larger; the ratio to median wage is 90%, higher than typically studied. Expect more disemployment effects, perhaps in the 5-10% range for the most affected sub-groups. The exact magnitude is uncertain because few labor markets have minimum wages this high relative to median.
2

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body:
(b) Political economy: Proposal A is politically easier — modest impact, predictable effects, supported by most empirical research. Proposal B is politically harder — bigger immediate visible gain for workers (which builds support) but bigger risk of business closures and adjustment problems (which builds opposition). Larger proposals also face more business lobbying and adverse media attention.
3
(c) My recommendation: support Proposal A with a clear plan to study its effects and consider further increases in 3-5 years. The empirical research strongly supports modest increases as net beneficial; Proposal B is in territory where the evidence is thinner and the risks are larger. Phased implementation lets us learn whether the larger increases (Seattle-style) are workable in this specific labor market before committing.

6.heading: Worked Examples
6.title: Chapter 6, Government and Markets When markets fail, when governments fail, what the actual choices look like — price controls, minimum wages, taxes, subsidies, and externality corrections — and how to think about each beyond the pure deadweight-loss framing that dominates introductory textbooks The
6.body: The general principle: minimum wage debates often get framed as "for or against," but the empirical reality is "in what range." Modest increases (20-30% of current minimum, kept below ~60% of local median) are well-supported by evidence as net positive. Very large increases enter empirically uncertain territory where the effects might still be net positive but the risks are larger. The serious policy debate is about magnitude and pacing, not about whether to have a minimum wage at all. Pretending otherwise — claiming either "any minimum wage destroys jobs" or "any minimum wage is helpful" — gets the empirical reality wrong.

7.body: The MacroNations engine implements government intervention through several levers. The regulation lever (0-100, optimum 50) embodies the chapter's central insight: both excessive and insufficient regulation hurt fin_health. Moving regulation from 50 to 80 produces a fin_health drag; moving from 50 to 20 also produces a fin_health drag. The engine has no "perfect deregulation" equilibrium — competitive markets need institutional support to function well. The tax_rate lever implements the Laffer-style nonlinearity: rates above 40% trigger an efficiency drag (capturing the empirical reality that high marginal rates produce larger elasticity responses), but rates below 12% produce a "underfunding" penalty as the state cannot provide basic functions. The welfare_spending lever rewards redistribution with HDI gains and Gini improvements, but with diminishing returns (eventually the marginal HDI gain falls below the marginal cost). The infrastructure and rd_investment levers are essentially public-good provision (positive externality goods); each produces productivity gains over multiple rounds.

7.body:
Tournament strategy: think of the engine as embodying the "mixed economy" framework of this chapter. Pure laissez-faire (regulation at 0, welfare at 0, tax at 5%) underperforms substantially; heavy intervention (regulation at 100, welfare at 30, tax at 60%) also underperforms. The winning strategies cluster in the "moderate intervention" range — around 50 regulation, 15-20% welfare, 25-35% tax_rate — exactly matching the cross-country empirical evidence on what produces sustained prosperity.

7.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
GDP is the most consequential single number ever invented by an economist. It decides whether incumbent governments win re-election, whether central banks cut rates, whether the IMF declares an emergency. And yet — as Kuznets himself warned Congress in 1934 — "the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income."
This chapter presents GDP the way most textbooks do. Then it presents GDP the way actual macroeconomists at the BEA, the IMF, and central banks use it: as a flawed but indispensable instrument that one must understand precisely so one knows when to trust it and when to look behind it.
— A.S.

7.heading: What "GDP" Actually Means: Six Words That Each Matter
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
📘 Principles Level — Reading the definition slowly
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specified period. Every textbook offers this sentence. What is worth doing carefully is unpacking what each phrase is actually doing in it.
Let's go word by word — because the meaning of GDP, and the reasons GDP statistics are sometimes misleading, all live in this definition.
📚 Key Terms — defined here, used throughout the chapter
Market value
The price at which a good or service trades in the marketplace. We use prices as weights so we can add up apples + cars + haircuts in a common unit (dollars). A $30,000 car contributes 1,000 times more to GDP than a $30 textbook because that is what their relative market values say.
Final good
A good purchased by its end user — the household, business, or government that will actually use it (not resell it or use it as an input to make something else). A loaf of bread one eats is a final good. Counted in GDP.
Intermediate good

7.heading: What "GDP" Actually Means: Six Words That Each Matter
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
A good used up in the production of another good in the same period. The flour and yeast that bakeries buy to make bread are intermediate goods. Not separately counted in GDP — their value is already embedded in the final loaf's price.
Goods vs. services
Goods are tangible (cars, smartphones, food). Services are intangible activities one pays for (haircuts, healthcare, software subscriptions, banking). GDP counts both equally — services are about 80% of the U.S. economy today.
Within borders
GDP measures what is produced inside a country's geographic territory, regardless of who owns the firm. A Toyota factory in Kentucky producing Camrys contributes to U.S. GDP. A Ford factory in Mexico contributes to Mexican GDP.
In a given period
GDP is a flow measured per unit of time — usually per quarter (3 months) or per year. It is not a stock of accumulated wealth; it is the rate at which new production happens. Asking "what is the U.S. GDP?" without a time period is like asking "what is the speed?" without saying "miles per hour."
📘 Principles Level — Why "intermediate" goods are excluded (the double-counting problem)

7.heading: What "GDP" Actually Means: Six Words That Each Matter
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
Imagine a wheat farmer sells $100 of wheat to a flour mill. The mill grinds it and sells $200 of flour to a bakery. The bakery bakes bread and sells $500 of bread to consumers. Total spending across all stages: $100 + $200 + $500 = $800. But the actual final output of this little economy was only $500 of bread.
If we counted every transaction, we would count the wheat (in the flour) and the flour (in the bread) more than once. To avoid this double counting, GDP counts only the value of the bread — the final good. The wheat and flour show up implicitly, embedded in the bread's price.
An equivalent (and equally valid) way: count the value added at each stage. The farmer adds $100. The mill adds $200 − $100 = $100. The bakery adds $500 − $200 = $300. Total value added = $100 + $100 + $300 = $500. Same answer as the final-goods approach. This is not a coincidence — it is an accounting identity.

In practice the statistical agencies compute them from different sources and publish a discrepancy, which is a useful indicator of how much confidence any single quarter's figure can bear.

7.heading: The National Income Identity: One Number, Three Faces
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
📘 Principles Level
GDP is the same number measured three different ways, all of which give the same answer:
Expenditure approach: add up everything everyone spent on final output (households, businesses, governments, foreigners net of imports).
Income approach: add up everything everyone earned from producing that output (wages, profits, rents, interest).
Production (value-added) approach: add up the value created at every stage of production in every firm, summed across all sectors.
The crucial fact: the three sums are equal by accounting identity, not approximation. Every dollar that someone spent on output is a dollar that someone else received as income for producing it. The expenditure approach is what most textbooks teach because it gives the most familiar formula.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The National Income Identity (Expenditure Approach)
\[ Y = C + I + G + NX \]
Y
GDP — total market value of final goods and services produced in the country in the period. The single number one will see on every news ticker. The variable name "Y" comes from "yield" (or just because Y was an unused letter in the alphabet of economic notation).
C

7.heading: The National Income Identity: One Number, Three Faces
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
Consumption — household spending on final goods and services. About 68% of U.S. GDP. Three subcategories: durable goods (cars, appliances, things lasting more than 3 years), nondurable goods (food, clothing, gasoline — used up quickly), and services (healthcare, haircuts, streaming subscriptions — the fastest-growing category).
I
Investment — business spending on new capital, residential construction, and inventory change. About 18% of U.S. GDP. See the Pitfall box below: this is NOT the same as "investment" in everyday English. Subcategories: nonresidential fixed investment (factories, machines, software), residential investment (new homes), and inventory investment (goods produced but not yet sold).
G
Government purchases of goods and services — military equipment, teachers' salaries, road construction. About 17% of U.S. GDP. Critically, this excludes Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Those are transfer payments, not purchases of current output (see definition below).
NX

7.heading: The National Income Identity: One Number, Three Faces
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was. President Roosevelt's economic advisors wer
7.body:
Net exports = Exports − Imports. About −3% of U.S. GDP (a persistent trade deficit since the early 1980s). Why subtract imports? Because imports are already counted in C, I, and G but represent foreign production, not domestic. Subtracting them removes the foreign component.
📚 More Key Terms (used above)
Transfer payment
A payment from the government (or one party to another) for which no good or service is produced in return. Social Security checks, unemployment insurance, food stamps, disability benefits — all transfers. The recipient did not produce anything new this year; the government is just moving money from one citizen to another. Transfers are excluded from GDP because GDP counts new production.
Imputed value
An estimated dollar value the BEA assigns to a non-market activity to keep GDP comparable across countries. The most important example: the BEA estimates how much rent owner-occupied homes would command if rented out, and counts that "imputed rent" in GDP. Without this, a country where everyone owns their home would appear poorer than one where everyone rents the same houses.

7.heading: The National Income Identity: One Number, Three Faces
7.title: Chapter 7, Measuring National Income Why GDP — a single number invented in 1934 to count Depression-era output — quietly governs presidencies, central bank decisions, and the team's MacroNations score In 1932, no one knew how bad the Depression really was.
