9.body:
The annual growth rate expressed as a percentage. Important: use the rate as a percent (3, not 0.03). At growth = 0%, the formula gives infinity (consistent with: things never double if they do not grow).
How to use it: A country growing 2% per year doubles in 70/2 = 35 years. A country growing 7% per year doubles in 70/7 = 10 years. South Korea sustained an average growth rate of about 7% for forty years — meaning its real GDP doubled four times over that span (2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16x). The rule of 70 is the back-of-envelope tool every macroeconomist uses to translate growth rates into decades of progress.

9.heading: Why Growth Matters: The Tyranny of Compounding
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📐 Worked Example 9.1 — Two paths over 50 years
Country A and Country B both start with GDP per capita of $20,000 in 2024. A grows at 1% per year; B grows at 3% per year. Compute their GDP per capita in 2074, 50 years later. By how much does each grow?
1
Country A formula: Y₅₀ = $20,000 × (1.01)^50
2
(1.01)^50 ≈ 1.6446, so Y₅₀ ≈ $32,892 for Country A.
3
Country B formula: Y₅₀ = $20,000 × (1.03)^50
4
(1.03)^50 ≈ 4.3839, so Y₅₀ ≈ $87,679 for Country B.
5
Multiplication factor: Country A grew 1.64×; Country B grew 4.38× — about 2.7 times further over the same 50-year period.
6
Rule-of-70 sanity check: A doubles in 70/1 = 70 years; B doubles in 70/3 ≈ 23 years. So in 50 years, A has not even doubled yet (consistent with our 1.64×), while B has doubled twice (50 ÷ 23 ≈ 2.17 doubling cycles, giving a multiplier near 4.5×). ✓
A 2-percentage-point difference in growth, sustained over a generation, produces a $54,000 gap in per-capita income. This is why economists obsess over a country's trend growth rate, not just its current output level. The trend is destiny.

9.heading: Why Growth Matters: The Tyranny of Compounding
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
✏ Try This — China's three doublings
Between 1990 and 2020, China's real GDP per capita grew at an average annual rate of about 8.5%. How many times did it double over that 30-year span?
▸ Reveal answer
Doubling time ≈ 70 / 8.5 ≈ 8.2 years. Over 30 years, that is about 30 / 8.2 ≈ 3.66 doubling periods. So real GDP per capita rose by a factor of roughly 2^3.66 ≈ 12.6. China's real per-capita output increased by roughly 13× in 30 years. This is why the Chinese transformation was, in absolute terms, the largest reduction in poverty in human history. From 1990 to 2020, more than 800 million Chinese moved out of extreme poverty — more than the entire population of Europe.
Figure 9.1 Why small differences in the growth rate dominate everything else. Each line is income per head starting from the same level and growing at a constant rate. After seventy years, two percent leaves income four times its starting value and five percent leaves it more than twenty times. No redistribution within a country can produce a change of that order, which is why growth rates receive the attention they do.

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📘 Principles Level — A simple framework for thinking about output
Where does GDP come from? At the broadest level, every dollar of output is produced by combining three things: capital (the tools and machines workers use), labor (people working hours), and productivity (everything that determines how effectively those people and tools translate into actual output — technology, organization, institutions, ideas).
Macroeconomists summarize this in a production function: a mathematical statement that output is a function of inputs. The most common form was first written down by Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas in 1928 and remains the standard specification in the field.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Cobb-Douglas Production Function
\[ Y = A\,K^{\alpha} L^{\,1-\alpha} \]
Y
Output (real GDP). The thing we are trying to explain.
A
Total Factor Productivity (TFP) — the technology / institutions / management efficiency multiplier. If two countries have identical K and L but A differs, the country with higher A produces more output. This is the dominant source of cross-country income differences.
K

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
Capital stock — the value of all factories, machines, equipment, infrastructure, software in use. A higher K means workers have better tools.
L
Labor input — total hours worked, often with quality adjustments for education and skills (sometimes refined to "effective labor" hL where h is human capital per worker).
α
The Greek letter "alpha". Capital's share of output, typically estimated at α ≈ 0.33 in advanced economies. Means: when the capital stock rises 1%, output rises about 0.33% (holding A and L fixed).
1−α
Labor's share of output, typically about 0.67. The exponents on K and L sum to 1, which gives the function the property of constant returns to scale — doubling both inputs doubles output. Empirically, this fits well at the country level.
Reading it in plain language: Output equals productivity times a weighted geometric average of capital and labor, where the weights are the income shares earned by each factor. If one knows A, K, L, and α, one can compute Y. Equivalently, if one observes Y, K, L, and α, one can solve for A — which is how we measure productivity (more on this in section 9.4: growth accounting).

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body: An important property: diminishing returns to capital. Because α < 1, doubling K alone (with L fixed) does not double output — it raises output by a factor of \(2^{α}\) ≈ 1.26 if α = 0.33. The first machine in a workshop is enormously productive; the tenth machine adds much less. This single mathematical property drives the Solow model's central prediction (next section).

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📐 Worked Example 9.2 — Computing output and the marginal product of capital
An economy has A = 1.5, K = 100, L = 100, and α = 0.33. (a) Compute output Y. (b) If capital rises by 10% to K = 110, what is the new Y? (c) If instead labor rises by 10% to L = 110 (with K fixed at 100), what is the new Y? Explain the difference.
1
(a) Initial Y: Y = 1.5 × 100^0.33 × 100^0.67 = 1.5 × 100 = 150 (since 100^0.33 × 100^0.67 = 100^(0.33+0.67) = 100^1 = 100)
2
(b) Capital rises 10%: Y = 1.5 × 110^0.33 × 100^0.67. Now 110^0.33 ≈ 4.756 and 100^0.67 ≈ 21.04. So Y ≈ 1.5 × 4.756 × 21.04 ≈ 150.1 × 1.0327 ≈ 154.9 — that is a 3.27% rise.
3
(c) Labor rises 10%: Y = 1.5 × 100^0.33 × 110^0.67 ≈ 1.5 × 100 × (110/100)^0.67 ≈ 150 × 1.0664 ≈ 159.96 — that is a 6.64% rise.
4
The relationship: A 1% increase in K raises Y by about 0.33% (= α). A 1% increase in L raises Y by about 0.67% (= 1-α). These exponents are exactly the elasticities of output with respect to each input — and exactly each factor's share of GDP.

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body: The capital share α is not just an exponent; it is a measurable economic quantity. Capital owners (shareholders, landlords, lenders) earn about 33% of national income; workers earn about 67%. This is why a 10% capital boost gives 3.3% more output and a 10% labor boost gives 6.7% more. The Cobb-Douglas function has this beautiful unifying property — its mathematics aligns precisely with how income gets distributed in a competitive economy.

9.heading: The Production Function: How Inputs Become Output
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body: Figure 9.2 Diminishing returns to capital. Output per worker rises with capital per worker, but each additional unit of capital adds less than the one before, so the function flattens. This single property drives the central prediction of the Solow model: accumulation alone cannot sustain growth indefinitely.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📘 Principles Level — Capital accumulation and the steady state
Robert Solow won the 1987 Nobel Prize for a deceptively simple model published in 1956. The model has three moving parts:
Output is produced by capital and labor through a Cobb-Douglas-style production function with diminishing returns to capital.
Households save a fraction s of their income, and this saving funds new capital investment.
Capital depreciates at a rate δ (delta) — old machines wear out.
From these three building blocks, Solow derived a remarkable result: every economy converges to a long-run steady state where capital per worker, output per worker, and consumption per worker all stop growing (in the absence of technological progress). The level of the steady state depends on the savings rate, depreciation rate, and population growth — not on where the economy started.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
The intuition is diminishing returns. When an economy is poor, capital is scarce, so each new machine raises output substantially. Most of the new output gets saved and invested, so capital grows fast, output grows fast. As the economy gets richer, capital becomes plentiful — each new machine adds less. Eventually, the marginal output from new investment just barely covers the cost of replacing depreciated old capital. Net capital accumulation stops. The economy reaches its steady state.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Capital Accumulation
\[ \Delta K = sY - \delta K \]
ΔK
"Delta K" — the change in the capital stock over one period. Positive ΔK means the economy is accumulating capital; negative ΔK means it is running down.
s
Savings rate — the fraction of output that households save (and that gets invested). Typical values: 15-25% in developed economies, 30-45% in fast-growing East Asian economies.
Y
Total output (real GDP). sY is therefore the gross investment in new capital each year.
δ
"Delta" — the depreciation rate. Typical value: about 5-7% per year. If δ = 0.05, then 5% of the existing capital stock wears out each year.
δK

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
The dollar amount of capital that depreciates this year. Subtracted from new investment to get net capital growth.
Reading it in plain language: Capital this period equals the new investment from saving (sY) minus the wear-and-tear that destroys old capital (δK). When sY > δK, the capital stock grows. When sY = δK, it stays constant — the steady state. When sY < δK, it shrinks (rare but possible during wars or natural disasters).
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Steady-State Capital Stock
\[ k^{*} = \left(\frac{sA}{\delta}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}} \]
k*
The steady-state level of capital per worker. The asterisk denotes "long-run equilibrium." Once the economy reaches k*, capital per worker stops changing.
s
Savings rate (same as before). Higher s → higher k* — more saving means more capital accumulation, all else equal.
A
Productivity (TFP). Higher A → higher k* — more productive economies sustain higher capital stocks.
δ
Depreciation rate. Higher δ → lower k* — when capital wears out faster, less of it accumulates.
α
Capital's share parameter (~0.33). Determines how steeply diminishing returns set in.
1/(1−α)

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
A multiplier that magnifies the effect of changes in s, A, or δ. With α = 0.33, this exponent is 1/0.67 ≈ 1.49 — meaning a 10% rise in the savings rate produces about a 15% rise in steady-state capital per worker.
Where this comes from: at the steady state, ΔK = 0, so sY = δK. Substituting \(Y = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\), dividing by L, and rearranging gives the formula above. The full derivation is more involved, but the implication is what matters: countries with higher savings rates, higher productivity, and slower depreciation reach higher steady-state capital and output per worker.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "More saving = faster growth forever"
A common student mistake is to think that a country can permanently raise its growth rate by raising its savings rate. The Solow model says this is wrong. A higher savings rate raises the steady-state level of GDP per worker — but it does not raise the long-run growth rate, which (in the basic model with no technological progress) is zero per worker.
More saving leads to a richer destination. Once one arrives, growth stops (per worker). To grow forever, one needs technological progress — i.e., a continually rising A. This is the Solow model's most subtle and most important insight. Capital accumulation alone cannot sustain growth indefinitely. Only ideas can.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
1960–2024
South Korea
Convergence
The Miracle on the Han River: Convergence in Action
In 1960, South Korea had GDP per capita of about $158 (current dollars), placing it among the poorest countries in the world — roughly on par with Ghana and many other newly-independent nations. (Real GDP per capita in constant 2015 dollars was around $1,028, providing a more comparable measure across decades.) The U.S. figure that year was $3,007 — about 19 times higher in nominal terms. South Korea was, by every available measure, a desperately poor country recovering from war.
Over the next six decades, South Korea's real GDP per capita grew at an average rate of about 6-7% per year — among the highest sustained growth rates in human history. By 2024, GDP per capita had reached approximately $36,238 in current US dollars, or about $55,071 in purchasing power parity terms. The U.S. figure that year was about $82,769 — still ahead, but the ratio had shrunk dramatically from roughly 19× in 1960 to about 2.3× in nominal terms (and about 1.5× in PPP terms). Korea did not just get richer — it caught up.
What did Korea do that Solow's model anticipated? Three things stand out:

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
Extraordinarily high savings rates. South Korean households and firms saved 25-40% of GDP for decades — roughly twice the U.S. rate. Solow's prediction: high s → high steady-state capital per worker. Confirmed.
Heavy investment in human capital. Massive public spending on universal primary education, then secondary, then world-class universities. South Korea today has the highest tertiary-education rate among OECD countries. Higher human capital effectively raises A in the production function.
Aggressive adoption of foreign technology. South Korea licensed, copied, reverse-engineered, and eventually invented technologies originally developed in the U.S., Japan, and Europe. Catching up on the global technology frontier raises A faster than inventing from scratch.
What did Korea do that Solow's model does NOT explain? The institutional foundation: the Park Chung-hee government's industrial policy, the "chaebol" conglomerates, the export-led development strategy, the rule of law, the stable bureaucracy. The Solow model treats institutions as part of A — productivity. But it does not tell us how to build good institutions. That is the central unsolved problem in development economics.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
Stop and reflect: If one were appointed economic advisor to a country with GDP per capita of $1,500 — say, where Bangladesh was in the early 2000s — and one wanted to follow the Korea recipe, what would one's first three policies be? Now ask: what could go wrong with each? The Korea miracle is replicable in principle but has been replicated only a few times in practice. Why?
Figure 9.3 The Solow diagram. Saving per worker, \(s f(k)\), is concave; the investment required to maintain capital per worker, \((\delta + n)k\), is linear. Where they cross, capital per worker is constant at \(k^*\). Below \(k^*\) the capital stock deepens and the economy grows; above it, depreciation and population growth dominate. The arrows show the direction of adjustment: the steady state is stable, and long-run growth in output per worker must come from technology rather than from accumulation.

9.heading: The Solow Growth Model: Why Convergence Is Predicted but Not Always Observed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body: Figure 9.4 An increase in the saving rate. The steady state is where investment per worker just covers depreciation and the equipment required by new workers. Raising the saving rate lifts the investment schedule and moves the economy to a higher capital stock and a higher level of output per head. It does not raise the long-run growth rate: once the new steady state is reached, output per worker is constant again. Only technological progress produces sustained growth in this model.

9.heading: Growth Accounting: Decomposing GDP Growth Into Capital, Labor, and TFP
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Where does growth actually come from?
Once one has a production function, one can ask a deeply important empirical question: of any country's actual measured GDP growth, how much came from accumulating more capital, how much from adding more labor, and how much from rising productivity (TFP)?
Robert Solow worked out the answer for the United States in 1957. He found something startling: roughly 87% of long-run U.S. growth in output per worker between 1909 and 1949 was attributable to TFP — to "technical progress" — not to capital deepening. Modern updates put the share lower (more like 50-65%), but the basic insight stands: most growth, in the long run, comes from getting smarter, not from getting more equipment.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Growth Accounting Decomposition
\[ \%\Delta Y = \%\Delta A + \alpha\,\%\Delta K + (1-\alpha)\,\%\Delta L \]
%ΔY
Percentage growth rate of output. The total observed GDP growth — what we are trying to decompose.
%ΔA
Percentage growth in TFP — the "Solow residual." What is left over after we account for K and L. Cannot be observed directly; computed by subtraction.
α · %ΔK

9.heading: Growth Accounting: Decomposing GDP Growth Into Capital, Labor, and TFP
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
Capital's contribution to growth: capital growth weighted by capital's share of income. If K grew 4% and α = 0.33, capital contributed 0.33 × 4 = 1.32 percentage points to output growth.
(1−α) · %ΔL
Labor's contribution to growth: labor growth weighted by labor's share of income.
How this is used: An economist gets data on Y, K, L, and α from national accounts, computes growth rates, and reads off the contribution of each factor. The leftover — the part of output growth that cannot be explained by K or L — is attributed to TFP. This residual approach gives TFP its other name: the "Solow residual" or "measure of our ignorance."

9.heading: Growth Accounting: Decomposing GDP Growth Into Capital, Labor, and TFP
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📐 Worked Example 9.3 — Growth accounting for a hypothetical economy
A country's real GDP grew 4% last year. Its capital stock grew 5%. Labor input (hours worked, quality-adjusted) grew 1.5%. Capital's share is α = 0.33. (a) Compute the contribution of capital and labor to output growth. (b) What was TFP growth? (c) What share of total growth is attributable to TFP?
1
(a) Capital contribution: α · %ΔK = 0.33 × 5% = 1.65 percentage points
2
Labor contribution: (1−α) · %ΔL = 0.67 × 1.5% = 1.01 percentage points
3
(b) TFP growth (the residual): %ΔA = %ΔY − α·%ΔK − (1−α)·%ΔL = 4% − 1.65% − 1.01% = 1.34 percentage points
4
(c) TFP share of total growth: 1.34 / 4.0 = 33.5% of growth came from TFP — the "ideas" residual.
Roughly one-third of this country's growth was unexplained by simple input accumulation. That is TFP — the contribution of better technology, smarter management, improved institutions, and ideas in general. Notice that even though capital grew faster than labor (5% vs. 1.5%), labor's contribution to growth is comparable because labor has a much larger income share (0.67 vs. 0.33). Always weight by share, not by raw growth.

The episodes shown differ not only in their total but in their composition: the American post-war boom and the information-technology decade were productivity-led, while the East Asian records were driven to an unusual degree by factor accumulation — which is precisely why the question of whether they could be sustained was contested at the time.

📘 Principles Level — The deep determinants of TFP
The Solow model tells us that countries with high savings rates and high productivity (TFP) become rich. But it does not tell us why some countries have higher savings rates and higher productivity. To answer that, we need to look beyond the production function at what economists call the "deep determinants" of growth — the underlying conditions that shape an economy's capacity to accumulate capital and adopt technology.
Three categories of explanations dominate the modern growth-economics literature:
Three theories of why TFP differs across countries
TheoryCore claimKey evidence
Institutions
Property rights, rule of law, contract enforcement, control of corruption, and inclusive political institutions are the deep cause of long-run prosperity.
Acemoglu, Johnson, & Robinson (2001) showed that European colonies where settlers established secure property rights (e.g., U.S., Australia) became rich, while those where they set up extractive institutions (e.g., much of Latin America, Africa) stayed poor — even centuries after colonial rule ended.
Geography

9.heading: Why Are Some Countries Rich? Institutions, Geography, and the Limits of Theory
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
Climate, disease environment, access to coastlines, and natural-resource endowments shape long-run development.
Tropical countries are systematically poorer than temperate ones (Sachs & collaborators). Landlocked countries grow slower than coastal ones. Malaria-endemic regions struggle with productivity for biological reasons.
Culture / Human Capital
Religious norms, social trust, work ethic, and accumulated human capital (education, skills, scientific knowledge) drive productivity differences.
Putnam's work on social trust correlates with growth; Mokyr's work on the "Republic of Letters" links the Scientific Revolution and Industrial Revolution; education levels in 1900 strongly predict GDP per capita today.

9.heading: Why Are Some Countries Rich? Institutions, Geography, and the Limits of Theory

9.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why this matters more than the model
The Solow model is a tool. Like all tools, it has a domain of applicability. It explains a great deal about how capital and labor combine to produce output, given a fixed level of A. It tells us almost nothing about what determines A. And A — productivity — is responsible for most of the cross-country variation in income.
This is humbling. The thing we most need to explain (why some countries are 50× richer than others) is the thing our central model handles least well. The ongoing argument among Daron Acemoglu, Jeffrey Sachs, Joel Mokyr, Dani Rodrik, and others over what really drives long-run growth is one of the most important debates in social science. None of them claims to have a complete answer.
What I tell my students: learn the Solow model thoroughly because it provides a vocabulary and a framework. But do not mistake the framework for an explanation. When someone indicates "we just need to invest more in infrastructure" or "we just need lower taxes" — one will know that real growth depends on a much deeper layer of institutional, cultural, and historical factors that no single policy lever can move.
— A.S.

9.heading: Convergence: A Prediction That Mostly Failed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
📘 Principles Level
Solow's model has a striking prediction: poor countries should grow faster than rich ones, and over time the gap should narrow. The intuition is diminishing returns. A poor country has little capital, so each new machine raises output substantially. A rich country has abundant capital, so each new machine adds little. With higher returns to capital, the poor country attracts investment, accumulates capital faster, and catches up. This is called the convergence hypothesis.
It is the most famous prediction of the Solow model. And it is mostly wrong.
If one plots every country's growth rate from 1960-2024 against its 1960 GDP per capita, one does not see a clean negative relationship. One sees a scatter cloud. Some poor countries grew very fast (South Korea, China, Singapore, Taiwan, Botswana, Ireland). Others stagnated or even fell (much of sub-Saharan Africa, Argentina, Venezuela). Some rich countries continued to grow well (the U.S., Australia); others have struggled (Italy, Japan).

9.heading: Convergence: A Prediction That Mostly Failed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body: What the data does show is conditional convergence: countries that have similar institutions, savings rates, and human capital do converge to similar income levels. Within the OECD, Western European countries did catch up to U.S. living standards from 1950-1980. East Asian countries with similar policies converged to each other. But unconditional convergence — poor countries automatically catching up to rich ones — is not what we observe. The world has not flattened.

9.heading: Convergence: A Prediction That Mostly Failed
9.title: Chapter 9, Production and Growth Why some nations are 100 times richer than others, why the gap can close in a single generation, and why the most important number in economics is not GDP but the rate at which GDP grows In 1960, South Korea was poorer than Ghana. The Korean War had ended just seven
9.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Globalization will make all countries equally rich"
A simple read of Solow predicts unconditional convergence: open economies + capital flows + technology transfer should equalize incomes. The 1990s "end of history" optimism partly rested on this view. The reality from 1990-2024 has been mixed. China and a handful of East Asian and East European economies have converged dramatically. Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East have not. The developed-country/developing-country gap has narrowed for some countries and widened for others.
The lesson: openness, capital flows, and technology access are necessary for catch-up but not sufficient. Without strong institutions and human capital, an economy cannot absorb the technologies on offer. A country with no engineers cannot run a semiconductor plant. A country with no contract law cannot host foreign investment. The world looks more like an exclusive club than an inflating tide.

🎮 MacroNations Connection — The Innovation Pillar (200 points)
The Innovation pillar in MacroNations is built from prod_pts (100 of 200, reading the productivity index 0.5–5.0), inn_hdi (60 of 200, reading HDI 0.30–0.99), and inn_fin (40 of 200, reading fin_health). The dominant lever for productivity is rd_investment (range 0–10% of GDP, default 2%): each 1pp above 2% adds 0.048 per round to the productivity index, compounding to roughly +0.5 over 10 rounds — enough to take productivity from 1.5 to 2.0 by tournament end. The infrastructure lever (range 0–20%, default 5%) contributes 0.025/round per pp above 5%. The green_energy lever (range 0–100%, default 30%) adds 0.002/round per pp above 30%. Innovation also rewards HDI, which is driven principally by welfare_spending (coefficient 0.35) — so high welfare spending pulls Innovation up too. There is no separate "education spending" lever in the engine; human capital effects come through R&D, infrastructure, and welfare-driven HDI.

10.heading: Insight
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Most introductory students view "Wall Street" with some combination of suspicion, confusion, and indifference. The financial system seems to operate by rules separate from the real economy — driven by greed, gambling, and elite manipulation. There is some truth in that view. But it is incomplete and ultimately misleading.
The financial system has one fundamental economic job: channel saving from those who have spare income into investment by those who can productively use it. When this channel works well, it is one of the great wealth-creating institutions in human history. When it breaks (1929, 2008, 2023 banking stress), entire economies seize up. This chapter presents what the financial system is supposed to do, the machinery that makes it work, and why deep functioning capital markets are roughly as important to long-run growth as having a working road network or postal service.
— A.S.

10.heading: The Two Sides of the Financial System
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — Savers and Borrowers
At any moment in any economy, there are two kinds of people. There are savers — households whose income exceeds their current spending, who set aside the surplus for future use. And there are borrowers — firms that want to expand a factory, families that want to buy a house, governments that want to fund a deficit, students who want to invest in their education. The financial system is the meeting place between these two groups.
If saving and borrowing happened person-to-person, an entrepreneur with an idea for a new factory would have to wander door-to-door, knocking on the houses of strangers, hoping to find a household with $5 million in spare savings willing to lend it for a 7-year term at a fair rate of interest. This would be hopelessly inefficient, expensive, and risky. So societies invent financial institutions: banks, bond markets, stock exchanges, mutual funds, pension funds. Each of these is a different mechanism for solving the same problem — pooling many savers' contributions and channeling them to many borrowers, with the institution managing the contracts, the risk assessment, and the matching.

10.heading: The Two Sides of the Financial System
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📚 Key Terms — defined here, used throughout the chapter
Saving
Income not spent on current consumption. For households: the part of disposable income left over after expenditures. For nations: total income minus total consumption (private + government).
Investment (in macro)
Real capital formation — businesses buying machinery, building factories, residential construction, software development. Per chapter 7, this is NOT the same as buying stocks or bonds.
Financial market
An institution where savers and borrowers meet directly. Examples: the bond market and the stock market. The saver lends or invests directly in a firm; no intermediary is needed (though brokers and exchanges may facilitate).
Financial intermediary
An institution that stands between savers and borrowers. The saver lends to the intermediary; the intermediary lends to the borrower. Examples: banks, mutual funds, pension funds, insurance companies. The intermediary takes on the risk-assessment and matching role.
Asset / Liability

10.heading: The Two Sides of the Financial System
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
An asset is something of value that one owns (a house, a savings account, shares of stock). A liability is something one owes (a mortgage, a credit-card balance). One person's asset is often another person's liability — a bank deposit is one's asset and the bank's liability.
Interest rate
The price of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the principal per year. Per chapter 8, the real interest rate is what matters for economic decisions; the nominal rate is what is quoted.
Loanable funds market
A simplified macroeconomic model in which all savers and all borrowers meet in a single hypothetical market. The "supply of loanable funds" is total saving; the "demand for loanable funds" is total investment desire. The interest rate is the price that clears this market.

10.heading: The Two Sides of the Financial System
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body: Figure 10.1 The two routes from saving to investment. Direct finance passes through markets, where the saver holds a claim on the borrower and bears the risk directly. Indirect finance passes through an intermediary, which holds the claim, bears the risk, and issues the saver a safer and more liquid liability in return. The entire apparatus exists to reconcile what savers want — safety, liquidity, small denominations — with what borrowers need, which is usually the opposite.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two ways to raise money
Suppose Apple wants to build a new chip-design facility costing $5 billion. Apple has two basic ways to raise the money in the financial markets, each with very different consequences for who controls the firm and how the money gets paid back.
Apple can borrow by issuing bonds. A bond is an IOU: Apple promises to pay back the principal on a specific date and to make interest payments along the way. Bondholders are creditors — they have no ownership stake or voting rights, but they have a strong claim to repayment that takes priority over shareholders if things go badly. Apple's existing shareholders keep all the upside of the new facility.
Or Apple can sell ownership by issuing new shares of stock. A share is a fractional ownership claim on the firm. Shareholders are owners — they vote for directors and receive dividends if the firm chooses to pay them, and their wealth rises and falls with the firm's market value. New shareholders dilute existing ones, but Apple has no obligation to repay them anything.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks

10.body:
Most large firms use both. The choice between debt and equity — and the resulting capital structure — is one of the central decisions in corporate finance.
Bonds vs. Stocks — two fundamentally different financial instruments

Holder is a...Creditor / lenderOwner / shareholder
Voting rights?NoneYes (one share = one vote, typically)
Claim on profits?Fixed interest payments onlyResidual: whatever's left after debts
MaturityFixed (e.g., 10-year bond)None — held indefinitely

⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Bond Yield Basics
\[ \text{YTM} \approx \frac{C + (F - P)/n}{(F + P)/2} \]\(C\) is the annual coupon, \(F\) the face value, \(P\) the price, and \(n\) the years to maturity.
Yield to Maturity (YTM)
The total annualized return an investor earns if they buy a bond at its current market price and hold it until maturity. The single most important number for bond investors.
Annual Coupon

10.body:
The fixed dollar interest payment the bond pays each year. A 5% coupon on a $1,000 face-value bond pays $50/year.
Face value
The amount the bond will pay at maturity (also called par value). Typically $1,000 for U.S. corporate bonds.
Price
The current market price one would pay to buy the bond. Bonds trade above face ("at a premium") when interest rates have fallen since issuance, below face ("at a discount") when rates have risen.
n
Number of years until the bond matures.
Reading it in plain language: The numerator captures all the income the bond produces — coupon payments plus the difference between what one will receive at maturity (face) and what one paid (price), spread over n years. The denominator averages the price one paid and the face one will receive. The result is an approximate annualized return. The exact YTM requires solving a polynomial, but this approximation is within ~0.1 percentage points for most bonds.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body: Critical inverse relationship: when bond prices rise, bond yields fall. When prices fall, yields rise. This is mathematical, not behavioral: the coupon is fixed; the only variable is the price one paid. This is why headlines saying "bond yields rose today" mean exactly the same thing as "bond prices fell today" — they are two ways of describing one event.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Higher interest rates are good for bondholders"
It seems intuitive: higher rates mean better returns, right? For existing bondholders, the opposite is true. If one bought a 10-year bond at a 3% yield in 2020, and rates rise to 6% in 2024, one's bond becomes less valuable — anyone could now buy a freshly-issued bond yielding 6% instead. To make one's old 3% bond competitive, its market price has to fall enough that someone buying at the lower price would also earn an effective 6%. One experiences an immediate loss of market value, even though the bond's coupon has not changed.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body: This dynamic was a major contributor to the March 2023 banking stress when Silicon Valley Bank failed. SVB held billions of dollars of long-dated Treasury and mortgage-backed bonds purchased during the 2020-2021 era of low rates. When the Fed raised rates aggressively in 2022, the market value of SVB's bonds dropped sharply — though the bonds were still "money good" (would pay face value if held to maturity), the bank's depositors panicked when they realized SVB's bond portfolio had unrealized losses. Higher interest rates can make a healthy bank look insolvent on paper, even when its bonds will eventually pay in full.

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📐 Worked Example 10.1 — Computing a bond's yield
A 10-year corporate bond has a face value of $1,000 and a 4% coupon (so it pays $40/year). It currently trades at $920. (a) What is its approximate yield to maturity? (b) What does the discount price indicate about how interest rates have moved since the bond was issued?
1
Identify the inputs. Coupon = $40/year; Face = $1,000; Price = $920; n = 10 years.
2
Apply the approximate-YTM formula. YTM ≈ ($40 + ($1,000 − $920)/10) / (($1,000 + $920)/2)
3
Compute numerator: $40 + $80/10 = $40 + $8 = $48. The investor gets $40 in annual coupon plus an effective $8/year in price appreciation (recovering the $80 discount over 10 years).
4
Compute denominator: ($1,000 + $920)/2 = $960. Average of price and face.
5
YTM: $48 / $960 = 5.0%

10.heading: Financial Markets: Bonds and Stocks
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body: (a) The bond's yield to maturity is approximately 5.0%, even though its coupon rate is only 4%. The bond is selling below par (at $920 instead of $1,000) precisely because investors require a higher return — likely because (b) market interest rates have risen since the bond was issued. The price had to fall enough that even a 4% coupon could deliver a 5% effective return. If rates had fallen instead, the bond would be priced above $1,000 and its YTM would be below 4%.

10.body: Figure 10.2 Bond prices and yields move inversely. The coupon payments of an existing bond are fixed in money terms, so a purchaser who pays a higher price receives a lower return. Statements that 'bond markets fell' and 'yields rose' therefore describe the same event, and the relationship is arithmetic rather than behavioral.

10.heading: Financial Intermediaries: Banks and Mutual Funds
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — When direct markets do not work
Bond and stock markets work well for large, well-established firms — Apple, Toyota, the U.S. Treasury. But what about a small business that wants to borrow $300,000 to buy a new oven for its bakery? Issuing a bond is impractical: the costs of registering, marketing, and trading it would dwarf the loan itself. The savers willing to lend $300,000 do not even know the bakery exists.
This is where financial intermediaries come in. A bank takes deposits from millions of households (each one a saver), pools them, and uses the pool to make loans to thousands of borrowers (the bakeries, the homeowners, the small manufacturers). The bank does the credit assessment. The bank diversifies the risk across many loans. The bank handles the contracts. Savers do not need to find borrowers — they just deposit at the bank, and trust the bank to make sensible loans on their behalf.
The economic value the bank creates is real. Without it, most small loans would never happen, and most small savings would sit idle.
Major financial intermediaries — what they pool, what they fund
IntermediaryWhat it poolsWhat it funds
Commercial bank

10.heading: Financial Intermediaries: Banks and Mutual Funds
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why mutual funds matter more than people realize
Vanguard founder John Bogle, who introduced the first index mutual fund in 1976, may have done more for ordinary American savers than any financial-policy reform of the 20th century. Before low-cost index funds, a typical saver who wanted exposure to U.S. stocks paid 1-2% per year in fund-management fees plus loads (sales commissions). Over 40 years of compounding, this fee drag could consume roughly half of an investor's lifetime returns.
By offering a mutual fund that simply held the entire S&P 500 at near-zero fees, Bogle effectively gave every saver access to professional-quality diversification at almost no cost. Today the largest U.S. index funds charge as little as 0.03% per year. The cumulative wealth transfer to ordinary savers — taken from financial-industry middlemen — runs into the trillions of dollars. Most students who will graduate from college will retire wealthier than they otherwise would because of this single financial innovation.
— A.S.

The bank borrows short and liquid and lends long and illiquid, which is the service it provides and the risk it runs. Capital — the difference between what it owns and what it owes — is the cushion that absorbs loan losses before depositors are touched. A bank with eight percent capital is insolvent once its assets fall in value by more than eight percent, which is a smaller shock than it sounds.

10.heading: The National Accounts: Why Saving Equals Investment
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — An accounting identity, not a behavioral claim
This is one of the most-used and most-misunderstood results in macroeconomics. In a closed economy (no foreign trade), total saving equals total investment. This is not a coincidence and it is not an empirical regularity — it is a mathematical consequence of how the national income accounts are constructed. Let's see why.
From chapter 7, GDP in a closed economy is:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Deriving the Saving = Investment Identity
\[ Y = C + I + G \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S = I \]
Y
Total income / output (GDP) in a closed economy. Foreign trade is omitted to keep the algebra clean; with trade, S also includes net exports.
C
Household consumption.
I
Investment (real capital formation, per chapter 7).
G
Government purchases of goods and services.
T
Net taxes — taxes paid to the government minus transfer payments (Social Security, etc.) received from the government. T is the net flow of resources from households to government.
Y − T − C
Private saving \((S_{private})\): household income minus taxes minus consumption — the surplus households do not spend.
T − G

10.heading: The National Accounts: Why Saving Equals Investment
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
Public saving \((S_{public})\): government tax revenue minus government spending. Positive when there is a budget surplus; negative when there is a deficit.
S = I
Total national saving (private + public) equals total investment, by accounting identity. Always. In a closed economy, the only way the country can finance investment is through its own saving.
How the algebra works: Start with Y = C + I + G. Subtract C and G from both sides to get Y − C − G = I. Now add and subtract T on the left side (which does not change the equation): (Y − T − C) + (T − G) = I. The first parenthesis is private saving; the second is public saving; their sum is national saving S. So S = I.
What it means in plain English: Every dollar invested in new factories and equipment is also a dollar that someone — a household, the government, or the two combined — saved instead of consuming. There is no other way to finance investment. If the country wants more investment, total saving must rise to make room for it.

10.heading: The National Accounts: Why Saving Equals Investment
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "S = I means saving causes investment"
The identity S = I does not say that saving causes investment, only that they are equal at every moment by accounting necessity. Whether saving and investment are both high or both low is a separate question — one determined by households' consumption decisions, firms' investment plans, the government's fiscal stance, and the interest rate that brings them all into balance.
An economy can be stuck in a "low-saving, low-investment" equilibrium (where both are 15% of GDP) or a "high-saving, high-investment" one (where both are 35% of GDP). South Korea moved from the first to the second over the course of two generations. Whether the managed economy can make that shift depends on policy, culture, and institutions — not on accounting identities.

10.heading: The Loanable Funds Market
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — Supply, demand, and the interest rate
The simplest macroeconomic model of the financial system imagines a single market — the market for loanable funds — where all the savers and all the borrowers in the economy meet. The price in this market is the real interest rate (per chapter 8). The supply curve is national saving (which rises with the interest rate, as savers respond to higher returns by saving more). The demand curve is investment (which falls with the interest rate, as fewer projects look profitable when borrowing costs rise). Where they cross is the equilibrium real interest rate and the equilibrium amount of saving and investment.
This stylized model abstracts away an enormous amount of real-world complexity (different debt instruments, different credit risks, money creation by banks, foreign capital flows). But it captures the central economic logic: the interest rate is a price that adjusts to make the supply of saving equal the demand for investment.

Drag the sliders; watch the supply and demand curves shift in real time

If the government allows pre-tax saving (401(k), IRA), the after-tax return rises at every interest rate. Saving supply curve shifts right. Result: lower equilibrium interest rate, higher equilibrium investment.
Investment tax credits
If the government subsidizes business investment, firms find more projects profitable at every interest rate. Investment demand curve shifts right. Result: higher equilibrium interest rate, higher equilibrium investment.
Government deficit
When G > T (deficit), public saving is negative; total national saving falls. Saving supply curve shifts left. Result: higher equilibrium interest rate, lower private investment. This is crowding out.

10.heading: The Loanable Funds Market
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📐 Worked Example 10.2 — A tax incentive for saving
An economy is in equilibrium with national saving and investment both at $2 trillion and the real interest rate at 4%. The government enacts a new IRA-style tax incentive that increases the after-tax return on saving, shifting the saving supply curve to the right by $200 billion at every interest rate. (a) What happens to the equilibrium interest rate? (b) What happens to investment? (c) What share of the new saving translates into actual new investment vs. just lower rates? (Hint: depends on the slope of the investment demand curve.)
1
(a) Direction of effects. A rightward shift of supply lowers the equilibrium price (interest rate) and raises the equilibrium quantity (saving = investment).
2
(b) The new equilibrium. Suppose the investment demand curve has a slope such that a 1 percentage-point fall in the interest rate raises investment by $100 billion. If the saving curve shifts right by $200B, the new equilibrium falls roughly halfway between the two extremes: rate falls by ~1 percentage point to 3%, and investment rises by ~$100B to $2.1T.
3

10.heading: The Loanable Funds Market
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
(c) Pass-through. Of the $200B increase in saving offered at the original 4% rate, only $100B becomes actual new investment; the other $100B is "absorbed" by the rate falling to 3%, which discourages some saving and lets the market clear at a lower volume than the maximum supply offered.
The pass-through from "extra saving" to "extra investment" depends on how responsive both sides of the market are to interest rates. If investment demand were perfectly inelastic (vertical), no extra investment would happen — all the saving incentive would be absorbed in lower rates. If investment demand were perfectly elastic (horizontal), all the extra saving would become extra investment with no rate change. Empirically the elasticities are between these extremes, so a fraction of any saving boost translates into real capital accumulation.

10.body: Figure 10.4 The market for loanable funds. The real interest rate is the price that equates desired national saving with desired investment. Anything that raises saving at a given interest rate shifts the supply curve to the right and lowers the rate; anything that raises desired investment shifts demand to the right and raises it.

10.heading: The Norway Sovereign Wealth Fund: National Saving as Policy
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
1990–present
Norway
Sovereign saving
How a Country of 5 Million Built the World's Largest Investment Fund
Most resource-rich countries fall victim to what economists call the "resource curse": a windfall of oil, gas, or minerals briefly enriches the country, but the foreign-exchange inflows distort the currency, the political process is captured by extractive interests, the non-resource economy withers, and when the resource runs out, the country is left poorer than it started. The list of victims is long: Nigeria, Venezuela, Algeria, Iraq, Iran, much of post-Soviet Central Asia.

10.heading: The Norway Sovereign Wealth Fund: National Saving as Policy
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
Norway, when it discovered oil in the North Sea in 1969, deliberately chose a different path. The Norwegian Parliament's logic, codified into law over the following decades, was simple: oil is a one-time gift from the past, but the population it should benefit includes generations not yet born. To honor that obligation, the country would not consume oil revenues directly. Instead, every krone of oil income would be transferred to a sovereign wealth fund — the Government Pension Fund Global — which would invest the money in foreign stocks and bonds (to avoid distorting the domestic economy). The government would be allowed to spend, in any given year, only an amount equivalent to the fund's expected long-run real return — about 3% of fund assets. The principal would be preserved forever.
The numbers, three decades on, are remarkable:
$2.08 trillion in assets at end of 2024, growing to roughly $2.2 trillion by end-2025
Equivalent to $385,000 per Norwegian citizen
Owns approximately 1.5% of every publicly traded company in the world
Portfolio: 70% global equities, 27% fixed income, 3% real estate and renewables

10.heading: The Norway Sovereign Wealth Fund: National Saving as Policy
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
2024 return: 13%, generating a profit of $222 billion — roughly equivalent to the entire GDP of Greece
Strict ethical exclusions: 180+ companies blocked from the portfolio for involvement in tobacco, coal, weapons of mass destruction, severe environmental damage, or human rights violations
What makes the Norway case especially valuable as a teaching example is what it tells us about saving. National saving does not have to be "private households setting money aside." It can be a deliberate policy — a country choosing to defer current consumption so that future generations inherit financial wealth as well as natural resources. Norway's experience shows that the link between saving, investment, and future welfare that this chapter has been describing is not abstract. A country can choose to save more — and the consequences for living standards over decades are vast.

10.heading: The Norway Sovereign Wealth Fund: National Saving as Policy

What are the political-economy constraints in the U.S. that Norway did not face? If one were designing a fund modeled on Norway's for the United States, what should it invest in, who should manage it, and how should withdrawals be governed?

10.heading: Government Deficits and Crowding Out
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why deficits raise interest rates
When a government runs a budget deficit (spends more than it taxes), it must borrow the difference. Where does the money come from? In our loanable funds framework, the government competes with private firms for the same pool of national savings. To attract savers' funds away from corporate bonds and into Treasury bonds, the government must offer a competitive yield. The increased demand for borrowing pushes interest rates up. At the higher rate, fewer private investment projects are profitable. Some private investment that would have happened gets "crowded out" by government borrowing.
This effect is the central reason why economists worry about persistent fiscal deficits: not the absolute size of the debt, but the cost in terms of foregone private capital formation, which in turn slows long-run growth (per chapter 9).
⚙ Public saving and the deficit
\[ S_{\text{public}} = T - G, \qquad \text{deficit} = G - T = -\,S_{\text{public}} \]
\(S_{public}\) > 0
Budget surplus. Government takes in more taxes than it spends, contributing positively to national saving.
\(S_{public}\) = 0

10.heading: Government Deficits and Crowding Out
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
Balanced budget. Neither adds to nor subtracts from national saving.
\(S_{public}\) < 0
Budget deficit. Government spends more than it taxes; it must borrow to fund the gap. Deficit absorbs national saving that would otherwise have funded private investment.
The fundamental tradeoff: a $1 trillion deficit subtracts $1 trillion from public saving and therefore from total national saving. In a closed economy, this is a $1 trillion absorption of private saving away from private investment. The economy's total stock of capital grows more slowly than it would have. Through the long-run growth channel, GDP per capita is permanently lower.
What about open economies? The picture is modified when foreign capital can flow in. If foreigners are willing to lend at the prevailing world interest rate, the deficit can be financed without raising domestic rates as much — but the country accumulates external debt instead. The U.S., as the world's reserve-currency issuer, has historically been able to attract enormous foreign capital flows, which is why its deficits have not raised interest rates as much as a closed-economy model would predict. This will not necessarily continue forever.

10.heading: Government Deficits and Crowding Out
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Government borrowing always crowds out private investment"
The textbook crowding-out story assumes the economy is at full employment, with all available resources already being used. When the economy is in a recession with idle capital and unemployed workers, the story can flip. Government borrowing during a recession may not crowd out private investment because the resources were not being used anyway. In fact, government spending can crowd in private investment by raising aggregate demand and giving firms the confidence that demand will exist for their output.
This is why the textbook crowding-out framework belongs to the chapter on the long run (this one), and why the short-run effect of fiscal policy is treated very differently in chapters on aggregate demand and stabilization (chapters 19–22). Both stories can be true — they apply to different time horizons and starting conditions. The 2008-09 stimulus did not crowd out private investment, because there was massive slack. A deficit of similar size at full employment would.

10.heading: Government Deficits and Crowding Out
10.title: Chapter 10, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
10.body: Figure 10.5 Crowding out. A government deficit absorbs private saving, shifting the supply of loanable funds available to private borrowers to the left. The real interest rate rises from \(r_1\) to \(r_2\) and private investment falls. How much is displaced depends on the interest sensitivity of investment and on whether the economy has idle resources — which is why the effect is weak at the zero lower bound and strong at full employment.

11.heading: Overview
11.title: Chapter 11, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — Connecting back to chapter 9
Recall from chapter 9 that capital accumulation and TFP growth are the two sources of long-run output growth. This chapter has been fundamentally about where the capital comes from — how saving turns into productive investment via the financial system.
Empirically, countries with deeper, better-functioning financial systems grow faster. Studies that compare countries on financial-development measures (banking-sector depth, stock-market capitalization, contract-enforcement quality) find that a one-standard-deviation improvement in financial development is associated with roughly 1 additional percentage point of GDP growth per year (King & Levine, 1993; many subsequent studies). Over four decades, that is a doubling of per-capita income.
Why? A good financial system performs five distinct functions, each economically valuable:
Mobilizes saving — pools small individual savings into investable scale.
Allocates capital — directs funds toward the highest-productivity investments via interest rates and credit screening.

11.heading: Overview
11.title: Chapter 11, Saving, Investment & the Financial System How the financial system turns ordinary household saving into the capital that drives long-run growth — and why a country that fails to save fails to grow In December 1969, Phillips Petroleum announced that an exploratory drill in the North Sea h
11.body:
Monitors managers — disciplines firms after capital has been advanced (through dividend rules, debt covenants, shareholder votes).
Diversifies risk — allows individuals to spread risk across many projects through mutual funds, insurance, and derivatives.
Eases trade — reduces the friction of buying and selling assets, making capital more "liquid" and therefore more useful.
Countries that lack one or more of these functions — say, weak property rights so banks cannot enforce loan contracts, or shallow stock markets so firms cannot raise equity — accumulate capital more slowly and less productively, even when their saving rates are similar to richer countries. This is one of the deep reasons why the institutional framework discussed in chapter 9 matters: institutions determine whether the financial system actually performs its function.
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Capital, Debt, and Sustainability

11.body: MacroNations does not expose a separate "saving rate" lever — instead, national saving is implicit in one's fiscal stance: budget_balance = tax_revenue − gov_spending. A balanced budget plus household saving funds private investment; a chronic deficit absorbs saving and raises debt. The engine does not have an explicit Financial Development lever either, but the regulation lever (range 0–100, optimum at 50) governs financial system stability — regulation away from 50% (either too light or too heavy) damages fin_health. The Sustainability pillar reads sust_debt_pts (80 of 200, with a tighter threshold than Stability — full marks at debt ≤ 30%, zero at 150%), plus HDI (70) and potential GDP (50). Debt is therefore penalized in two pillars simultaneously (Stability and Sustainability) — letting debt rise past 100% can cost roughly 50-70 points across both.
