11.heading: Insight
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Money is the most magical institution in economics, and almost every student arrives in this chapter with a wrong intuition about what it is. Most people believe that money is "backed" by something — gold reserves, government promises, the productive capacity of the economy. None of this is quite right. The U.S. dollar is not backed by gold (it has not been since 1971). It is not backed by an explicit government promise to do anything specific. The Federal Reserve does not promise to redeem dollars for any particular good or service.

11.heading: Insight
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
What backs the dollar is something subtler and more powerful: everyone else's willingness to accept it in exchange for goods and services. As long as I can use a $20 bill to buy lunch tomorrow, the bill is worth $20 to me today. If everyone simultaneously decided dollars were worthless, dollars would be worthless. This sounds tautological. It almost is. But this circularity — money's value resting on a self-fulfilling expectation — is the most consequential coordination problem in human society. Most of the time it works beautifully. When it breaks (Weimar Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008, Brazil 1993, Venezuela 2018), it breaks catastrophically.
— A.S.

11.heading: What Money Does: Three Functions
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — Define money by what it does, not what it is
Economists do not define money by its physical form (coins, paper, deposits) — too narrow, since over the centuries money has taken hundreds of forms. They define it by what it does. Anything that performs all three of the following functions in an economy is, by economists' definition, money:
📚 The Three Functions of Money
Medium of exchange
A thing that sellers will routinely accept in exchange for goods or services. This is what eliminates the need for barter (the dreaded "double coincidence of wants" problem — finding someone who has what one wants AND wants what one has). When everyone agrees to accept dollars, transactions become enormously easier.
Unit of account
A standard measure of value used to quote prices and record debts. When one asks "how much does this cost?", the answer is in a unit of account. Without a stable unit of account, businesses cannot compare options, write multi-year contracts, or do basic accounting. This was the function Brazil's URV was designed to restore.
Store of value

11.heading: What Money Does: Three Functions
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: A thing that holds purchasing power over time. If one earns money today and want to spend it next month, one needs a store of value to hold the wealth in the meantime. Money fails as a store of value during high inflation (the value erodes), which is why during hyperinflations people switch to dollars, gold, or real estate.

11.heading: What Money Does: Three Functions
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why hyperinflation happens "all at once"
Notice the relationship between the three functions. As long as something stays a usable medium of exchange and unit of account, modest losses in store-of-value function (a few percent inflation) are tolerable. But once high inflation erodes the store-of-value role enough that businesses lose faith in the local currency as a stable measure, they begin quoting prices in a foreign stable currency — typically U.S. dollars in Latin America, euros in Eastern Europe — even though the actual transaction is still settled in the local currency. At that point the unit-of-account function has collapsed: the local currency is no longer trusted as a yardstick of value, even though it is still being used to pay. With unit-of-account gone, contracts become impossible, planning falls apart, and people refuse to accept the local currency for transactions — destroying the medium-of-exchange function. The three functions are stable individually but mutually reinforcing. Once one starts to fail, the others follow within months. This is why high inflation rarely stays modest — it tips into crisis once a threshold is crossed.

11.heading: What Money Does: Three Functions
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The genius of the Brazilian Real Plan was recognizing this dynamic and engineering a controlled separation of the functions. The URV took over the unit-of-account role while the cruzeiro continued to handle medium-of-exchange. By stabilizing the unit-of-account function first, Brazil broke the inflation-inertia cycle without forcing an immediate currency replacement. Then, once everyone had been thinking in URV for four months, the conversion to the real currency was almost a formality.
— A.S.

11.heading: Kinds of Money: From Cowrie Shells to Cryptocurrency
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level
Money has taken bewilderingly diverse forms over human history: cattle in ancient India, cowrie shells in West Africa and East Asia, copper rings in West Africa, large carved stones in Yap, salt blocks in Ethiopia, tobacco leaves in colonial Virginia, beaver pelts in colonial Canada, gold coins in classical Greece and Rome, paper notes in Tang-dynasty China, electronic balances today. What all of these have had in common is that society agreed on them as media of exchange. What distinguishes them is whether their physical form had value beyond the monetary function.
Kinds of money — distinguished by where their value comes from
TypeWhat it isExamples
Commodity money
An object with intrinsic value used as money — has worth even if not used as currency
Gold/silver coins, salt blocks, tobacco leaves, cattle. The commodity could always be melted down or consumed.
Commodity-backed money
Tokens (paper, coins) that have no intrinsic value but are convertible on demand into a commodity
Pre-1971 U.S. dollars (convertible to gold via central banks); 19th-century banknotes redeemable in silver.
Fiat money

11.heading: Kinds of Money: From Cowrie Shells to Cryptocurrency
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Tokens with no intrinsic value, no convertibility — value comes purely from social acceptance and government decree
Modern U.S. dollars, euros, yen, pounds. "Fiat" is Latin for "let it be done" — government declares the token to be money.
Cryptocurrency
Decentralized digital tokens whose supply is governed by software protocol; no central issuer, no intrinsic value
Bitcoin, Ethereum. Mostly used as speculative store of value rather than medium of exchange. El Salvador adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 (results so far: limited everyday use).

11.heading: Kinds of Money: From Cowrie Shells to Cryptocurrency
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Fiat money is worthless without backing"
A common claim from gold-standard advocates and cryptocurrency enthusiasts is that fiat money is "worthless" because it is not backed by anything physical. This is a misunderstanding of what backing means. Fiat money IS backed — but by something more powerful than gold reserves: by the credibility of the issuing institution and the network effect of universal acceptance.
Consider: throughout history, governments on the gold standard have repeatedly devalued their currencies by changing the gold conversion ratio whenever it suited them. Britain abandoned gold in 1931. The U.S. devalued gold backing in 1934 (forcing private gold turn-in at $20.67/oz, then revaluing to $35) and abandoned the link entirely in 1971. Pure commodity backing did not prevent debasement — it just made the politics of debasement noisier.

11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: Meanwhile, the U.S. dollar has held its value reasonably well over the past 50 years (modest inflation averaging ~3-4% per year) because the Federal Reserve has, on the whole, defended its mandate. The "backing" is the Fed's institutional credibility, the Constitution's structure, and Americans' continued willingness to accept dollars. That backing turned out to be more durable than the metallic kind.

11.heading: Measuring the Money Supply: M1 and M2
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — How much money exists?
Once we agree that "money" is whatever serves the three functions, an obvious question follows: how much of it is in the economy at any given time? The answer turns out to be surprisingly contested, because the line between "money" and "highly liquid asset that is almost as good as money" is fuzzy. The Federal Reserve publishes two main measures, each drawing the line in a different place.
📚 The U.S. Money Supply Aggregates
Currency
Physical bills and coins in circulation outside banks. About $2.4 trillion in early 2026 — roughly $7,000 per American on paper, although a substantial portion is held abroad as a store of value or in the underground economy.
Demand deposits
Checking-account balances available on demand for spending. About $5 trillion in early 2026.
M1
The narrow money supply. Currency + demand deposits + other liquid checkable deposits. About $18.5 trillion as of early 2026. This is "money" in the most usable sense — what one can spend immediately without converting anything.
M2

11.heading: Measuring the Money Supply: M1 and M2
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The broader money supply. M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits (under $100,000) + retail money-market mutual funds. About $22.4 trillion as of January 2026. This includes "near-money" — slightly less liquid balances that can be converted to spending money quickly.
Monetary base (M0 or "high-powered money")
Currency in circulation + reserves held by banks at the Federal Reserve. Around $5.6 trillion currently. This is the money the Fed directly creates and controls — the foundation upon which the banking system builds the broader M1 and M2.

11.heading: Measuring the Money Supply: M1 and M2
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why M2 has been the Fed's preferred measure
For decades, the Fed paid close attention to M2 as a leading indicator of inflation. The intuition came from the quantity theory of money (chapter 12): if M grows much faster than real output, prices should rise. From the late 1980s through the early 2000s, this relationship was reasonably reliable, and many central banks targeted M2 growth ranges directly.
Then around 2010, the relationship broke down. Following the Global Financial Crisis, the Fed expanded its balance sheet from about $900 billion to over $4 trillion through quantitative easing. The monetary base exploded. Yet inflation remained below target for most of the next decade. The reason is that the new reserves the Fed created mostly stayed parked at the Fed (banks held them as excess reserves earning interest from the Fed) rather than being multiplied into M2 through new loans. The transmission mechanism between the monetary base and the broader money supply broke down.

11.heading: Measuring the Money Supply: M1 and M2
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The Fed has subsequently de-emphasized M2 in favor of direct interest-rate policy and inflation targeting. But the M2 indicator did warn of trouble in 2021: M2 grew over 25% year-over-year due to the combination of QE and pandemic stimulus payments. Two years later, U.S. inflation peaked at 9.1%. The relationship is imprecise, but it has not disappeared.
— A.S.

11.heading: Measuring the Money Supply: M1 and M2
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: Figure 11.1 The monetary aggregates are nested definitions, ordered by how readily the asset can be spent. M1 is currency and the deposits that can be drawn on directly. M2 adds savings balances, small time deposits and retail money funds, which are close substitutes but require a step before they can be used. Neither is the quantity of money in any deep sense; both are conventions, and the boundary has been redrawn whenever the payment system has changed.

11.heading: Banks and the Creation of Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — How a deposit becomes more deposits
Here is the most counterintuitive fact in introductory macroeconomics: banks create money. Not in the literal sense of printing bills (only the central bank can do that), but in the sense that the M1 and M2 money supply rises whenever a bank makes a new loan. The mechanism is so subtle that most people who use banks every day do not realize it is happening.
Consider a deposit of $1,000 in cash into a checking account at First National Bank. From one's perspective, one still has $1,000 — it is in one's checking account, available on demand. But the bank does not keep one's $1,000 sitting in its vault. It keeps a small fraction (say 10%) as a reserve against possible withdrawals, and lends the other 90% — $900 — to a borrower. The borrower now has $900 to spend. One still has one's $1,000 in the bank. The total spending power in the economy has just risen from $1,000 to $1,900.

11.heading: Banks and the Creation of Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The borrower then spends the $900 on, say, restaurant supplies. The restaurant deposits the $900 in its bank, which keeps $90 as reserve and lends out $810. Now there is $1,000 + $900 + $810 = $2,710 in spending power. The cycle continues. With a 10% reserve ratio, the eventual total of money created from one's initial $1,000 deposit is approximately $10,000.
📚 Key Banking Terms
Reserve
The portion of deposits a bank keeps available rather than lending out. Held either as vault cash or as balances at the Federal Reserve.
Reserve ratio
The fraction of deposits a bank keeps as reserves. Historically set by the Fed (the required reserve ratio) but reduced to 0% in 2020. Today, banks hold reserves voluntarily, based on risk management and the interest the Fed pays on reserves.
Fractional reserve banking
The system in which banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest. The basis of essentially all modern banking. Without it, banks could not perform their economic function of channeling saving into investment.
Bank run

11.heading: Banks and the Creation of Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
A situation where many depositors simultaneously demand their money back. Because the bank keeps only fractional reserves, if too many depositors withdraw at once, the bank cannot meet demand — even if it is fundamentally solvent. Bank runs ended dozens of U.S. banks every year before 1933 and contributed enormously to the Great Depression. Mostly stopped after FDIC deposit insurance was created in 1933.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Money Multiplier
\[ m = \frac{1}{R} \]A deposit of one dollar supports \(1/R\) dollars of deposits in total when banks hold the fraction \(R\) in reserve and the public holds no currency.
m
The money multiplier. Indicates how many dollars of M1 are created in the banking system from one new dollar of monetary base.
R
The reserve ratio — fraction of deposits that banks keep as reserves rather than lending out. R is between 0 and 1.
1 / R
The reciprocal of R. Comes from the geometric series: 1 + (1−R) + (1−R)² + ... = 1/R, which sums up the new deposits created at each round of lending.

11.heading: Banks and the Creation of Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Reading it in plain language: If banks keep 10% of deposits as reserves (R = 0.10), then each $1 of new monetary base eventually expands the M1 money supply by $10. If banks keep 20% (R = 0.20), the multiplier is $5. The smaller the reserve ratio, the more aggressive the expansion. The basic insight is that the same dollar can be the basis of many separate transactions, as long as not everyone tries to withdraw at once.
Why the simple formula understates the reality: the formula assumes (1) banks lend out exactly what they do not keep as reserves, (2) all loaned money is redeposited, (3) reserves come only from required-reserve regulation. In modern banking, banks may hold excess reserves beyond what is required, people may hold cash (which does not get redeposited), and banks may face other constraints. The actual money multiplier in the U.S. today is closer to 3-4 rather than the textbook's hypothetical 10, mainly because banks hold large excess reserves.

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📐 Worked Example 11.1 — Tracing money creation
A central bank creates $100 of new monetary base by buying a Treasury bond from a private seller, who deposits the proceeds at Bank A. Banks, all of them, maintain a 10% reserve ratio and lend out the rest. Trace the first three rounds of deposit creation, then estimate the total final M1 expansion.
1
Round 1. Bank A receives $100 deposit. Reserves = $10, loan = $90. M1 expanded so far: $100 (the original deposit) + $90 (the new loan, which the borrower can spend) = $190
2
Round 2. The $90 loan is spent and redeposited at Bank B. Reserves = $9, new loan = $81. M1 now: $100 + $90 + $81 = $271
3
Round 3. The $81 loan is redeposited at Bank C. Reserves = $8.10, new loan = $72.90. M1 now: $100 + $90 + $81 + $72.90 = $343.90
4
Pattern. Each round adds 0.9 times the previous round's loan. The geometric series sums to: $100 × (1 / 0.10) = $1,000 total deposits created.

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The original $100 of monetary base ultimately supports $1,000 of M1 deposits. The monetary base rose by $100, but the broader money supply rose by approximately 10 times that. This is the textbook money multiplier in action. Important caveat: in practice, banks hold excess reserves and people hold cash, so the realized multiplier is much smaller than the simple formula predicts.
✏ Try This — A bank run reverses the process
Suppose in the same economy, depositors panic and withdraw $100 of cash from Bank A. Reserves at Bank A fall by $100. To restore its 10% reserve ratio, what must Bank A do? Estimate the total contraction of M1.
▸ Reveal answer

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Bank A must call in $900 of loans to restore its reserve ratio (because losing $100 of reserves means it cannot support $1,000 of deposits at 10% — it can only support $0). Those borrowers, when forced to repay, withdraw money from their banks, which then must call in their own loans, and so on. The total contraction is approximately $1,000 of M1 destroyed from a $100 cash withdrawal — the multiplier works in reverse. This is exactly what happened thousands of times during the 1929-33 banking panics, when about a third of U.S. banks failed and the M1 money supply contracted by approximately 25% — a major contributor to the Depression's severity.
Figure 11.2 Deposit expansion with a ten percent reserve ratio. Each deposit supports a loan of ninety percent of its value, which returns to the banking system as a new deposit. The series sums to \(1000 \times \frac{1}{0.10} = 10{,}000\). The simple multiplier is an upper bound: currency held outside banks and reserves held in excess of the requirement both reduce it, which is why the identity failed to predict broad money after 2008.
11.5 The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — The most powerful institution in the U.S. economy
The Federal Reserve System (informally "the Fed") is the central bank of the United States. Created by Congress in 1913 in response to repeated banking panics, it has three core responsibilities:
Conduct monetary policy — set short-term interest rates and influence the money supply to pursue the dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability (defined since 2012 as 2% PCE inflation).
Supervise and regulate banks — set capital requirements, conduct stress tests, intervene in failing banks. After 2008, this role expanded significantly under the Dodd-Frank Act.
Provide liquidity in crises — act as lender of last resort when banks face panic, lending against good collateral to prevent solvent banks from failing due to temporary cash shortages. This was the role for which central banks were originally invented.
The Fed has five tools to affect the money supply. The table below lists them in roughly the order they are used today — from primary daily tools at the top to deprecated or crisis-only tools at the bottom:
The Fed's monetary policy toolkit, listed by current importance
ToolHow it worksWhen used

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Open-market operations
The Fed buys (or sells) government securities in the open market. Buying creates new reserves; selling absorbs reserves.
The primary, daily tool. The Fed uses it to keep the federal funds rate (the rate banks charge each other for overnight reserves) at its target.
Interest on reserves
Since 2008, the Fed pays banks interest on the reserves they hold at the Fed. Raising this rate makes banks willing to hold more reserves rather than lending them out.
The main lever for setting the floor on short-term rates in the modern (post-2008) "ample reserves" regime.
Discount window
The Fed lends directly to banks at a stated rate, accepting collateral. Originally the main lender-of-last-resort mechanism.
Less central today; used in crises (2008-09, March 2020, March 2023) to provide emergency liquidity to specific banks.
Reserve requirements
Historically set by the Fed; banks had to hold a minimum fraction of deposits as reserves (10% on transaction accounts). Reduced to 0% in March 2020 and not restored.
Largely deprecated as an active tool; banks today hold reserves based on their own risk management.
Quantitative easing (QE)

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Large-scale asset purchases beyond short-term Treasuries — including long-term bonds and mortgage-backed securities. Floods the banking system with reserves.
Used in major crises when the federal funds rate is already at or near zero. Deployed in 2008-2014, 2020-2022.
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Money printing causes inflation immediately"
A widely repeated claim is that "central bank money printing always causes inflation." This is half-right and dangerously oversimplified. Money creation causes inflation only when the new money flows into actual spending. If new reserves sit at the Fed (as they did 2008-2019, when banks held trillions in excess reserves), they do not cause inflation because they are not being spent on goods and services.
The Fed's balance sheet expanded from $900B to $4.5T between 2008 and 2014. CPI inflation over that period averaged 1.6% per year — below the Fed's 2% target. By contrast, the Fed's balance sheet plus pandemic fiscal stimulus from 2020-2021 caused M2 to surge over 25% YoY, AND the stimulus checks were spent rather than saved, AND supply chains were disrupted. Two years later, inflation peaked at 9.1%.

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: The lesson: money creation is necessary but not sufficient for inflation. What matters is whether the new money translates into spending on real goods and services. This insight will be formalized in chapter 12 (the quantity theory of money) and is critical for understanding modern monetary policy.

11.heading: The Federal Reserve: How Central Banks Control Money
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Figure 11.3 The money market. The central bank sets the quantity of base money, drawn here as vertical because it does not depend on the interest rate; the demand for money slopes downward because interest is the opportunity cost of holding it. An open-market purchase shifts supply to the right and lowers the equilibrium nominal rate from \(i_1\) to \(i_2\).
Figure 11.4 The Federal Reserve's balance sheet since 2007. In the conventional regime the central bank held a small portfolio and steered a scarce quantity of reserves. Two episodes of large-scale asset purchases replaced that with an abundant-reserve system an order of magnitude larger. The important consequence is operational: with reserves abundant, the policy rate is set by the rate paid on reserves rather than by rationing their quantity.

11.heading: The Real Plan: How Brazil Defeated 5,000% Inflation Without Printing Less
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
1993–1994
Brazil
Currency stabilization
The Most Successful Currency Stabilization in Modern History
By 1993, Brazil's monthly inflation rate routinely exceeded 40%. Annual inflation that year passed 5,000%. Brazilians shopping in supermarkets watched price-tag stickers being changed by store employees who walked the aisles all day with pricing guns. Salaries had to be paid weekly — even daily — because by month's end, monthly wages had lost half their purchasing power. Multiple previous stabilization plans — Cruzado (1986), Bresser (1987), Verão (1989), Collor (1990), Collor II (1991) — had all failed, often catastrophically. Brazil had earned the unwanted distinction of being the textbook case for chronic inflation that no government could break.

11.heading: The Real Plan: How Brazil Defeated 5,000% Inflation Without Printing Less
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
What broke the cycle was a remarkable insight from a small group of economists at PUC-Rio (Persio Arida, André Lara Resende, Edmar Bacha, and others). They diagnosed Brazilian inflation as having two distinct causes: (1) ongoing fiscal deficits and money creation (the standard story), but also (2) inflation inertia — the self-reinforcing dynamic where every economic agent raised prices preemptively because they expected everyone else to raise prices. Even if the government fixed the underlying fiscal problem, inertia would keep inflation going.
Their solution was to attack the unit-of-account function of money directly. On March 1, 1994, the government introduced the Unidade Real de Valor (URV) — Real Unit of Value — a non-monetary index whose value was pegged to roughly $1 USD. Crucially, the URV was a unit of account only: prices, wages, and contracts were quoted in URV, but actual payments were still made in old cruzeiros reais. The exchange rate between URV and cruzeiros was recalculated daily and published by the central bank.

11.heading: The Real Plan: How Brazil Defeated 5,000% Inflation Without Printing Less
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
For four months — March, April, May, June 1994 — Brazilians lived in a strange transitional economy. They saw prices in URV (stable), saw the same prices in cruzeiros (rising daily), and did all their thinking and contracting in URV. By the time most prices were quoted in URV, inflation expectations had effectively been re-anchored. Then, on July 1, 1994, the government simply made the URV the new currency, called the real (R$). Bank balances, contracts, and prices converted at the day's URV-cruzeiro rate. The old hyperinflated cruzeiro disappeared overnight.
The result was extraordinary. Annual inflation fell from over 5,000% in 1993 to about 22% in 1995, then to single digits within a few more years. The architects of the plan, Persio Arida and his colleagues, became national heroes. Finance Minister Fernando Henrique Cardoso, who had championed the plan, won the 1994 presidential election largely on its strength. Brazil has had its share of problems since — fiscal stress, recessions, political turmoil — but it has not returned to chronic inflation in the 30+ years since the plan.

11.heading: The Real Plan: How Brazil Defeated 5,000% Inflation Without Printing Less
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
What makes this case so important pedagogically: the Real Plan worked not by changing the monetary base or money creation rules, but by repairing the unit-of-account function of money. It is the cleanest real-world demonstration that money's value is fundamentally about expectations and credibility, not about the physical quantity of bills in circulation.
Stop and reflect: If money is fundamentally about expectations, what does that imply about the role of central bank credibility? Why do central banks fight so hard to maintain their independence from political pressure? What might happen to the U.S. dollar if markets came to believe the Fed was no longer committed to price stability? The Brazilian case suggests the answer should worry policymakers: once credibility goes, restoring it is enormously costly and uncertain.

Watch how a single deposit cascades through the banking system

What is being observed: the bars show the new deposits created at each round of bank lending. The first round is one's initial deposit; each subsequent round is the previous round multiplied by (1 − reserve ratio). The total of all rounds is the M1 expansion.

The figure describes a limit rather than a prediction. Banks that hold excess reserves, and households that keep part of the new money as currency, both reduce the realized multiple, which since 2008 has been far below the ratio this curve implies.

11.heading: Why Central Bank Independence Matters
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📘 Principles Level — The temptation to print money
Money creation is enormously tempting for governments. Politicians who control the printing press can fund wars, finance pet projects, redistribute wealth, or buy electoral support without raising taxes. The cost — inflation — falls on the broader public over time, often after the politicians have left office. This temporal mismatch is the classic time-inconsistency problem in monetary policy: governments that promise low inflation often find it irresistible to break the promise once the public has accepted the promise as credible.
The institutional response, developed throughout the 20th century, is central bank independence: structurally insulating the monetary authority from short-term political pressure. The Fed's chair serves a 4-year term that does not align with the presidential election cycle. The Fed's governors serve 14-year terms (one of the longest tenures in U.S. government). The Fed's budget comes from interest income on its own balance sheet, not from congressional appropriation. The European Central Bank goes further: any direct lending to governments is explicitly prohibited by treaty.

The empirical evidence is striking. Cross-country studies (Alesina & Summers, 1993; many followups) show a clear inverse relationship: countries with more independent central banks have lower average inflation, with no apparent cost in growth or unemployment. The U.S., Germany, Switzerland, and other countries with strong central bank independence have mostly avoided the inflationary spirals that have plagued Argentina, Turkey, Venezuela, and Zimbabwe — countries where the central bank ultimately answered to the political leadership.

Instead it uses the modern IS-MP convention: one sets the interest_rate_target lever, and the engine handles money-supply mechanics internally. The relationship in the engine is: rate above the 4.0% neutral level subtracts 0.4pp from inflation per pp; rate below neutral adds inflation pressure. Combined with the 50% adaptive / 50% anchored expectations (anchor at 2%), this implements the long-run "neutrality of money" idea operationally: hold rates at 4% steady-state, and inflation stabilizes at the 2% target. There is no separate "Central Bank Independence" parameter — credibility in this engine is implicit in one's willingness to hold rate paths stable round to round. Erratic rate changes do not activate a hidden penalty, but they fail to deliver the inflation control that consistent policy would.

The Fed's monetary policy toolkit
ToolHow it worksWhen used

11.heading: The Fed's Toolkit: Conventional and Unconventional
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Before 2008, the Fed's balance sheet was approximately $900 billion — small enough that the federal funds rate could be controlled by tiny daily open market operations. The 2008 financial crisis changed everything. In response to the crisis, the Fed launched three rounds of quantitative easing between 2008 and 2014, growing the balance sheet to $4.5 trillion by 2014. The Fed began modest tightening (QT) in 2017, reducing the balance sheet to about $3.8 trillion by mid-2019, but had to reverse course in late 2019 as repo market stress signaled reserves had become too scarce.
The COVID response in 2020-21 was even more dramatic. The Fed announced unlimited Treasury and MBS purchases on March 15, 2020. By April 2022 the balance sheet peaked at $8.95 trillion — roughly 10x its pre-2008 size. The Fed then began a second QT cycle in June 2022, allowing approximately $95 billion of securities to roll off monthly. By the end of 2025, the balance sheet had been reduced to approximately $6.5 trillion, with QT concluding in December 2025 as the Fed announced it would begin reinvesting maturing securities into new Treasuries to maintain balance sheet size proportional to economic growth.

11.body: The new normal: a permanently large central bank balance sheet operating in an "ample reserves" regime where the federal funds rate is controlled primarily through IORB and reverse repo rates rather than through scarcity of reserves. This is a structural shift from pre-2008 monetary plumbing. It also means QE and QT have become standard tools available even when not at the zero lower bound — though their usefulness in non-ZLB conditions remains debated.

11.heading: The Money Multiplier and the Quantity Theory
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Money Multiplier
\[ m = \frac{1}{rr + cr\,(1 - rr)} = \frac{M}{MB} \]\(rr\) is the reserve ratio, \(cr\) the currency-to-deposit ratio, and \(MB\) the monetary base.
rr
Reserve ratio: fraction of deposits banks hold as reserves rather than lending out. Higher reserve requirements reduce the multiplier.
cr
Currency-to-deposit ratio: how much money the public chooses to hold as currency rather than as deposits. Higher cr reduces the multiplier (currency does not circulate as deposits to be re-lent).
Empirical values
Pre-2008 U.S.: rr ≈ 10% (required) + 0% (excess), cr ≈ 0.4, multiplier ≈ 2.5. Post-2008 with massive excess reserves: effective rr much higher (banks chose to hold many reserves voluntarily), multiplier collapsed to roughly 1.0. The money multiplier as a useful concept is largely obsolete in the ample reserves regime — but understanding the mechanics helps explain pre-2008 monetary policy.

11.heading: The Money Multiplier and the Quantity Theory
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
Why the multiplier matters for understanding history: the 1930s saw the U.S. money multiplier collapse from about 5 to 2.5 as banks panicked and hoarded reserves while households hoarded currency. The Fed did not expand the monetary base aggressively enough to offset this collapse, and total money supply contracted by about a third — the central monetary failure of the Great Depression. Friedman and Schwartz's A Monetary History of the United States made this argument the cornerstone of post-1960s monetary economics.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Quantity Theory of Money
\[ M \times V = P \times Y \]The money stock multiplied by velocity equals the price level multiplied by real output.
M
Money supply (typically M2).
V
Velocity of money: how many times each dollar gets spent per year. Equal to PY/M by definition.
P × Y
Nominal GDP (price level × real output).
In growth rates
Δ%M + Δ%V = Δ%P + Δ%Y, or rearranged: Δ%P = Δ%M + Δ%V − Δ%Y. If V is stable, inflation equals money growth minus real growth. This was Milton Friedman's "inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon" — but it requires V to be stable.

11.heading: The Money Multiplier and the Quantity Theory
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The empirical problem: velocity has not been stable post-1980. M2 velocity in the U.S. fell from about 2.0 in 1980 to roughly 1.1 by 2020 — a sustained 50% decline as financial innovation, declining inflation, and changing payment patterns altered how often dollars get spent. The quantity theory still holds as an identity, but its predictive power has weakened because V is too variable to use M growth as a reliable inflation indicator. This is why modern central banks target interest rates rather than monetary aggregates — money supply targeting (briefly tried under Volcker in 1979-82) was abandoned because velocity changes made the relationship between M and inflation too noisy.
1979-1982

11.heading: The Money Multiplier and the Quantity Theory
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: When Paul Volcker became Fed Chair in August 1979, U.S. inflation was running at 11.5% and accelerating. Volcker had to break the back of inflation expectations. He made a strategic choice that is worth understanding: rather than targeting interest rates directly, Volcker announced the Fed would target M1 growth, letting interest rates rise to whatever level was needed to slow money growth. The political logic was crucial — by appearing to target a "technical" variable (M1), the Fed could deflect blame for the unprecedented interest rate spike that resulted. The federal funds rate rose from 11% to a peak of 20% in 1981.

11.heading: The Money Multiplier and the Quantity Theory
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
The strategy succeeded in breaking inflation: CPI fell from 14.8% in March 1980 to 3.8% by 1982. But it failed as a monetary technique. M1 became extremely volatile — partly because the very high interest rates and the introduction of NOW accounts (interest-bearing checking) made depositors shift between M1 and M2 components rapidly. Velocity, which had been relatively stable through the 1970s, became erratic. By 1982, the Fed effectively abandoned strict M1 targeting and returned to a more discretionary interest rate framework. The Volcker era proved both the power of monetary policy to control inflation and the limits of mechanical money-aggregate targeting.
The deeper lesson: the quantity theory holds in the long run, but in the short to medium term, velocity is not stable enough to use as a policy guide. Modern central banks target interest rates and use money aggregates as one of many information variables — not as the operating target. This is the right conclusion from the Volcker experiment: monetarism's policy prescription failed even though its diagnostic framework worked.

11.heading: Worked Examples
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📐 Worked Example 11.1 — Computing the Money Multiplier
In an economy: reserve ratio rr = 10%, currency-to-deposit ratio cr = 40%, monetary base MB = $1 trillion. (a) Compute the money multiplier. (b) Compute total money supply M. (c) If the Fed increases MB by $200 billion via open market operations, how does M change? (d) If during a crisis banks raise their voluntary reserve ratio to 30%, what happens to M (holding MB constant)?
1
(a) Multiplier: m = 1 / (rr + cr × (1 − rr)) = 1 / (0.10 + 0.40 × 0.90) = 1 / (0.10 + 0.36) = 1 / 0.46 ≈ 2.17.
2
(b) M: M = m × MB = 2.17 × $1T = $2.17 trillion.
3
(c) +$200B MB: ΔM = m × ΔMB = 2.17 × $200B = +$434B. New M = $2.6T.
4
(d) Crisis with rr = 30%: new m = 1 / (0.30 + 0.40 × 0.70) = 1 / (0.30 + 0.28) = 1 / 0.58 ≈ 1.72. New M = 1.72 × $1T = $1.72T — a drop of $450B even with constant MB.

11.heading: Worked Examples
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: The Great Depression lesson: when banks hoard reserves (raising rr) and households hoard currency (raising cr), the money multiplier collapses even if the Fed keeps the monetary base constant. This is exactly what happened in 1929-1933: M2 fell by ~30% despite no change in MB. The Fed should have aggressively expanded MB to offset the collapse in m — the Friedman-Schwartz critique of 1930s Fed policy. The post-2008 Fed knew this history and pumped MB through QE to maintain M during the financial crisis, with much better results.

11.heading: Worked Examples
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body:
📐 Worked Example 11.2 — Applying the Quantity Theory
An economy has nominal GDP of $25T and money supply M2 of $22T. (a) Compute velocity. (b) If M2 grows at 6% per year and real output grows at 2%, what does the quantity theory predict for inflation (assuming constant V)? (c) Compare to actual U.S. experience 2020-2024: M2 grew about 25% in 2020 alone but inflation was only mildly elevated for a year. What does this tell us about velocity?
1
(a) Velocity: V = PY/M = $25T / $22T = 1.14. Each dollar circulates about 1.14 times per year.
2
(b) Quantity-theory inflation: Δ%P = Δ%M + Δ%V − Δ%Y = 6% + 0% − 2% = 4% inflation.
3
(c) 2020 anomaly: if M2 grew 25% in 2020 and Y growth was about −3% (recession), then with constant V the quantity theory predicted inflation of +28%. Actual inflation in 2021 was about 7% (a year later). The difference must have come from V: velocity collapsed by roughly 20% in 2020 as households hoarded cash rather than spending it.

11.heading: Worked Examples
11.title: Chapter 11, The Monetary System What money actually is, how banks conjure it into existence, and why central banks hold the most concentrated economic power on the planet On the morning of July 1, 1994, Brazilians woke up to a new currency. The day before, every price in the country was quoted in tw
11.body: The implication: the quantity theory is an identity that must hold by definition, but it is useless as a policy guide if V is volatile. The 2020-22 inflation episode came not from monetary expansion alone but from monetary expansion combined with eventual velocity recovery as households resumed spending. The Fed's massive M2 expansion in 2020 was largely absorbed by falling velocity — exactly what should happen when households are saving rather than spending. The inflation came later, when velocity normalized and the supply side could not keep up. Pure monetarist reasoning would have predicted catastrophic inflation in 2020; what actually happened required understanding velocity dynamics as well.

12.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Milton Friedman's most famous claim — "inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon" — is one of the most-cited and most-abused propositions in economics. Cited because the long-run cross-country and historical record overwhelmingly supports it: every hyperinflation in history has been accompanied by rapid money creation, and no country has ever had high inflation while keeping its money supply growth disciplined. Abused because the relationship is not mechanical, not instant, and not visible in every short-run episode.
The 2008-2014 quantitative easing expanded the Fed's balance sheet from $900B to $4.5T and produced average inflation below the 2% target. The 2020-2021 expansion of M2 by 26.8% YoY, two years later, produced 9.1% inflation. The difference was not the size of the central bank's balance sheet — it was whether the new money flowed into actual spending. This chapter presents why the simple version of the theory works in the long run, why it sometimes seems to fail in the short run, and how to read monetary data the way an actual macroeconomist does.
— A.S.

12.heading: The Classical Dichotomy: Real vs. Nominal Variables
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two kinds of variables, two different stories
To understand the relationship between money and prices, we first need to draw a fundamental distinction that 18th-century economists called the classical dichotomy: economic variables come in two kinds, real and nominal, and money affects them differently in the long run.
📚 Real vs. Nominal — the most consequential distinction in macroeconomics
Nominal variables
Variables measured in current dollar (or other currency) units. Examples: nominal GDP, nominal wages, nominal interest rates, the price of a hamburger in dollars. These all change when the price level changes.
Real variables
Variables measured in physical units or in inflation-adjusted "constant" dollars. Examples: real GDP (output of actual goods and services), real wages (purchasing power of labor income), real interest rates, the relative price of a hamburger in terms of haircuts. These are not directly affected by changes in the price level alone.
Classical dichotomy

12.heading: The Classical Dichotomy: Real vs. Nominal Variables
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
The principle that, in the long run, real variables are determined by real factors (technology, preferences, capital, labor, institutions — the topics of Part IV) and nominal variables are determined by the money supply. The two stories run on independent tracks in the long run.
Monetary neutrality
A direct consequence of the classical dichotomy. In the long run, changes in the money supply have no effect on real variables. Doubling the money supply doubles all prices and nominal wages, leaving relative prices, real output, and real wages unchanged. Often summarized as: "money is a veil over the real economy."

12.heading: The Classical Dichotomy: Real vs. Nominal Variables
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Monetary neutrality means money does not matter"
A frequent student misreading. Monetary neutrality applies to the long run only. In the short run, money very much affects real variables: monetary policy can fight recessions, lower unemployment, and accelerate growth (chapters 19-22). But these short-run real effects fade. Over a horizon of, say, ten years, an economy with 10% money growth will have roughly 10% higher prices than an economy with 0% money growth, but the same real output (assuming everything else is held constant).
Why does the long run differ from the short run? In the short run, prices and wages are sticky — they do not adjust instantly to monetary changes. So monetary expansion temporarily raises real spending, employment, and output. But over time, prices and wages adjust upward to match the larger money supply, and the real-economy effects unwind. By the time everyone has adjusted, only the price level has permanently changed. This is why this chapter is in the "long run" part of the textbook: we are tracing the destination, not the path.

12.body: Figure 12.1 The classical dichotomy. In the long run the real side of the economy is determined by real forces and the nominal side by the quantity of money, so that doubling the money stock doubles prices and leaves output, employment and relative prices unchanged. The proposition is close to exact over decades and plainly false over quarters, and almost every disagreement in monetary economics is about how long the short run lasts.

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📘 Principles Level — A 400-year-old theory that still works
The relationship between money and prices was first articulated clearly in the 16th century, when European economies experienced sustained inflation following the influx of silver and gold from the New World. The Spanish economist Martín de Azpilcueta noted in 1556 that the prices of goods rose roughly in proportion to the money supply. Over the following four centuries, the relationship was refined, formalized, and tested by John Locke, David Hume, Irving Fisher, and most influentially Milton Friedman. The mathematical statement of the theory has remained essentially unchanged since Fisher's The Purchasing Power of Money (1911).
The core idea is captured in the equation of exchange:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Equation of Exchange
\[ M V = P Y \]
M
Money supply — typically M2 in modern usage. The total stock of money in the economy at a point in time.
V
Velocity of money — the average number of times each dollar is spent on final goods and services per year. Computed as V = (P × Y) / M. Velocity reflects how rapidly money circulates: the higher V, the more transactions a given money stock can support.
P

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
Price level — typically the GDP deflator or CPI. The economy-wide average price of goods and services.
Y
Real GDP — total output of goods and services in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The same Y from chapter 7.
P × Y
Nominal GDP — the total dollar value of all final goods and services produced. The right-hand side of the equation is total spending on output.
Reading it in plain language: the total stock of money (M) multiplied by how often each dollar gets spent (V) must equal the total dollar value of all transactions on final output (P × Y). This is an identity — it must hold by definition because V is constructed to make it hold. It becomes a theory only when we add an assumption about V.
The U.S. velocity, by way of context: if 2024 nominal GDP was about $29 trillion and M2 was about $21 trillion, then V ≈ 29/21 ≈ 1.4. Each dollar of M2 was spent about 1.4 times that year on final goods and services. Historically, U.S. M2 velocity ran around 1.7–2.1 from the 1960s through 2000, then fell sharply during and after the 2008 GFC, dropping further to about 1.13 in mid-2020 during the pandemic.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — From Identity to Theory

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
\[ \%\Delta M + \%\Delta V = \%\Delta P + \%\Delta Y \]
%ΔM
Percentage growth rate of the money supply.
%ΔV
Percentage growth rate of velocity.
%ΔP
Percentage growth rate of the price level — i.e., the inflation rate (π).
%ΔY
Percentage growth rate of real output (real GDP growth).
How we go from identity to theory: the equation MV = PY mathematically implies that the growth rates also add up — taking logs and differentiating gives %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔY. This is still an identity. It becomes the quantity theory of money when we make two specific assumptions:
Velocity is approximately stable in the long run: %ΔV ≈ 0. People's habits about how often they spend their money cash holdings change slowly, mostly due to the development of credit cards, electronic payments, and similar institutional innovations.
Real output growth is determined by real factors (technology, capital, labor — chapter 9), not by money. So in the long run, %ΔY is given exogenously.

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: With these assumptions, the equation simplifies to: π ≈ %ΔM − %ΔY. Inflation equals money growth minus real GDP growth. If money grows 8% per year and real output grows 2%, prices rise about 6% per year. This is the central prediction of the quantity theory.

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📐 Worked Example 12.1 — Predicting inflation from money growth
An economy has nominal GDP of $20 trillion, M2 of $14 trillion, and real GDP growth of 2.5% per year. The central bank announces it will increase M2 by 9% over the next year. (a) Compute current velocity. (b) Assuming velocity stays constant, what will the inflation rate be? (c) What money growth rate would the central bank need to hit a 2% inflation target?
1
(a) Velocity: V = (P × Y) / M = $20T / $14T ≈ 1.43. Each dollar of M2 supports about $1.43 of nominal GDP per year.
2
(b) Inflation prediction: using the simplified quantity theory, π ≈ %ΔM − %ΔY = 9% − 2.5% = 6.5% — well above target.
3
(c) Required money growth for 2% inflation: %ΔM = π + %ΔY = 2% + 2.5% = 4.5%
To hit a 2% inflation target with 2.5% real growth, the central bank needs to grow M2 at about 4.5% per year — not zero, because some money growth is needed to support the rising real volume of transactions. This is approximately the benchmark the Federal Reserve uses internally, though the Fed's official inflation target is operationalized through interest rates and the PCE price index, not through M2 targets directly.

12.heading: The Quantity Theory of Money
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. 12.body:
✏ Try This — A failure of the simple theory
Between 2008 and 2014, the Fed's monetary base (M0) rose roughly fivefold, from about $900 billion to $4.5 trillion. According to the simplest version of the quantity theory, this should have caused massive inflation. CPI inflation over that period averaged about 1.6% — well below target. What does this tell us about the assumptions underlying the quantity theory?
▸ Reveal answer
The 5× expansion was in the monetary base (M0), not in M2 or M1 — the new reserves stayed parked at the Fed and were not lent out into the broader economy. M2 over the same period rose only about 60% (about 8% per year), and velocity fell sharply, so total nominal spending did not surge. The lesson: the quantity theory requires (a) the right monetary aggregate (M2 or broader, not M0), and (b) reasonably stable velocity. Both assumptions failed in 2008-2014. The 2020-2022 episode was different in both respects: M2 grew at record rates AND the new money was actively spent (via fiscal stimulus), so velocity did not drop enough to absorb it. Inflation followed within 18 months, exactly as a careful quantity theorist would have predicted.

The relationship is close to proportional over long horizons and high inflation rates, which is the empirical content of the quantity theory. Over short horizons and at low inflation rates the association is much weaker, because velocity and output are not constant.

12.heading: Hungary 1946: The Worst Hyperinflation Ever Recorded

12.body:
1945–1946
Hungary
Hyperinflation record
Prices Doubling Every 15 Hours: The Pengő Crisis
By the end of World War II, Hungary's economy lay in ruins. Roughly 40% of the country's capital stock had been destroyed in the fighting between Nazi German forces and the advancing Soviet Red Army. The country had been on the losing side of the war and was required to pay $300 million in reparations and to cover the living costs of a 700,000-strong Soviet occupying force. The new coalition government inherited devastated industry, depleted foreign reserves, and an exhausted population that needed immediate relief.

12.heading: Hungary 1946: The Worst Hyperinflation Ever Recorded
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: Faced with overwhelming financial obligations and few good options, the postwar Hungarian government chose the path that has destroyed many currencies: it ordered the central bank to print money. Initially, the goal was modest — fund reconstruction, pay wages, cover the reparations. But once it became clear that the printing press was the path of least political resistance, money creation accelerated. The monthly inflation rate rose from a high but manageable 50% in late 1945 to 207% per day at the peak in July 1946. At that rate, prices doubled approximately every 15 hours. Workers were paid two and three times daily because the morning's wages had lost half their value by evening.

12.heading: Hungary 1946: The Worst Hyperinflation Ever Recorded
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: The denominations of pengő banknotes tell the story most vividly. Before 1945, the largest banknote in Hungary was 1,000 pengő. By the end of 1945, it was 10 million pengő. By the middle of 1946, the central bank issued the 100 quintillion (\(10^{20}\)) pengő note — the largest-denomination banknote ever printed by any government in history. A separate "tax pengő" was introduced as a parallel index for tax payments. People stopped using the currency for any transaction that could be conducted in barter; cigarettes and gold became informal media of exchange.

12.heading: Hungary 1946: The Worst Hyperinflation Ever Recorded
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: The crisis ended only when the government finally committed to a credible stabilization. On August 1, 1946, a new currency — the forint — was introduced at a conversion rate of 4 × \(10^{29}\) (400 octillion) pengő to 1 forint. Crucially, the new currency was paired with strict commitments to stop printing money for budget financing and to back the forint with tangible reserves. Industry had partially recovered by then, the Soviet occupation forces had stabilized, and credibility could be restored. Within a few months, prices in forint terms were stable. They remained reasonably stable for the next two decades. The pengő itself ceased to exist on July 31, 1946, as one of the most worthless currencies ever printed.

12.heading: Hungary 1946: The Worst Hyperinflation Ever Recorded
