The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: What this case illustrates with force: the quantity theory's central prediction works at extreme amplitudes. When money supply growth rates run into the millions of percent per month, every other economic factor becomes irrelevant. Velocity, real output, supply chains — all are dwarfed by the avalanche of new currency. The hyperinflation episode is not a disproof of the quantity theory; it is the most extreme confirmation imaginable. What no theory can address is the political dynamic that allows a government to keep printing money long enough to reach this point.

12.heading: The U.S. 2020–2022 Episode: A Modern Test of the Theory
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
2020–2022
United States
Modern monetary test
Did Friedman's Theory Hold? The "Transitory" Debate Settled
When COVID-19 struck the United States in March 2020, the policy response was on a scale not seen since World War II. The Federal Reserve cut rates to zero, launched a massive asset purchase program, and expanded its balance sheet from $4.2 trillion to over $9 trillion within two years. Simultaneously, Congress passed three major fiscal stimulus packages totaling about $5 trillion — direct cash payments to households, expanded unemployment insurance, and small-business support. Between the two, the U.S. M2 money supply grew at 26.8% year-over-year by February 2021, the fastest peacetime money growth in U.S. history since the Fed was established in 1913.

12.heading: The U.S. 2020–2022 Episode: A Modern Test of the Theory
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: What happened next is now a textbook case in the validity (and limits) of the quantity theory. Throughout 2021, U.S. inflation began to rise — first in goods prices affected by supply-chain disruptions, then more broadly. Most policymakers and forecasters, including the Federal Reserve, characterized the inflation as "transitory": a temporary product of supply-chain bottlenecks and shifted demand patterns that would resolve as the economy normalized. By mid-2021, with CPI inflation already at 5.4%, the Fed continued to expect inflation to fall back below 3% within a year.

12.heading: The U.S. 2020–2022 Episode: A Modern Test of the Theory
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
A small group of economists, working from a Friedmanite quantity-theory framework, predicted otherwise. They argued that 26% M2 growth, combined with massive fiscal stimulus that put new money into spending hands rather than into bank vaults, would inevitably raise prices — but with the "long and variable lag" Friedman had described, typically 18-24 months. Their prediction: CPI inflation would peak around 9% in mid-2022. CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, almost exactly 18 months after the M2 growth peak. The "transitory" framing was abandoned; Fed Chair Jerome Powell formally retired the word in November 2021.
Two important caveats prevent us from declaring complete victory for the quantity theory:
Other factors mattered. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 spiked oil and food prices through commodity-market channels independent of monetary growth. Supply-chain disruptions raised goods prices. These contributed perhaps 2-3 percentage points to peak inflation.

12.heading: The U.S. 2020–2022 Episode: A Modern Test of the Theory
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
Velocity was not stable. M2 velocity had collapsed during the pandemic from 1.4 to 1.1, then partially rebounded as spending normalized. The simple quantity-theory formula assumes constant velocity, which clearly did not hold.
Even with these caveats, the modern Hungarian-style test was a clean win for monetarist analysis. After the 2008 QE, money supply growth (M2) was modest, velocity collapsed, and inflation stayed low — consistent with the theory. After the 2020 stimulus, money supply growth was extreme, velocity did not fully absorb it, and inflation surged with an 18-month lag — also consistent with the theory. "Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon" still appears to hold, provided we use the right monetary aggregate, allow for long lags, and account for non-monetary shocks.

12.heading: The U.S. 2020–2022 Episode: A Modern Test of the Theory
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why "transitory" was the wrong mental model
The Fed's "transitory" framing in 2021 was not, strictly speaking, wrong about the supply-side disruptions. Bottlenecks really were resolving; shifted demand really was normalizing. The error was treating the 2020-2021 monetary expansion as if it had no consequences for medium-term inflation. The Fed had become accustomed, over the 2008-2019 period, to a world in which large monetary expansions did not produce much inflation — because banks held excess reserves and velocity was falling. They projected this experience onto the 2020-2021 episode without recognizing that the difference was crucial: this time, the new money was put into spending hands via direct fiscal payments, not into bank reserves via Treasury purchases.
The lesson: institutional memory and recent experience are dangerous guides during structural breaks. Macroeconomics requires constantly checking whether the assumptions behind one's favorite theory are holding. The quantity theory framework is one of the field's oldest and most durable; abandoning it because it did not fit 2008-2014 was a mistake the Fed admitted in retrospect.
— A.S.

12.heading: Inflation as a Tax: The Quiet Wealth Transfer
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why governments love inflation in private
When a government creates money to fund spending, the resulting inflation transfers real resources from holders of money and government bonds to the government itself. This transfer is called the inflation tax (or "seigniorage" when applied to currency creation). It is one of the oldest forms of public finance — used by Roman emperors, medieval monarchs, and modern democratic governments alike.
The mechanism is simple. Suppose one holds $10,000 in cash or in a non-interest-bearing checking account. If inflation runs at 5% per year, the real value of the money falls by $500 per year — 5% of $10,000. That $500 of lost purchasing power does not disappear; it accrues to whoever issued the new money that drove the inflation. In modern economies, that means the government, which receives the resources by issuing new currency or by having the central bank buy government bonds with newly created reserves.
The inflation tax has three properties that make it politically attractive:
It requires no legislation. No congressional vote, no public debate, no electoral accountability.

12.heading: Inflation as a Tax: The Quiet Wealth Transfer
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
It is invisible. Most people do not realize they are paying it — they blame "the cost of living going up" rather than recognizing the government is the beneficiary.
It is regressive. Wealthy households hold most of their wealth in inflation-protected assets (real estate, stocks, indexed bonds). Poor households disproportionately hold cash and have wages that do not immediately adjust. The inflation tax falls hardest on the financially least sophisticated.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Inflation Tax Revenue
\[ \text{inflation tax revenue} = \pi \times \frac{M}{P} \]
π
The inflation rate. The annual rate at which the price level rises.
M / P
Real money balances — the inflation-adjusted value of the money supply. Equal to the total purchasing power that the public is currently holding in monetary form.
π × (M/P)
The total real wealth that holders of money lose each year to inflation. This is exactly the real resources the government receives from creating new money.
Intuition: if the public holds $20 trillion in real money balances and inflation is 5%, then $1 trillion of real purchasing power is transferred from the public to the money issuer each year. That is the inflation tax.

12.heading: Inflation as a Tax: The Quiet Wealth Transfer

The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: The Laffer-curve aspect: raising the inflation rate does not proportionally raise inflation tax revenue, because at higher inflation rates people hold less real money (they switch to alternative stores of value, foreign currency, or barter). At very high inflation, real money balances collapse — the tax base shrinks faster than the rate rises. This is one reason hyperinflations are economically self-defeating even for the government that started them.

12.heading: Inflation as a Tax: The Quiet Wealth Transfer

12.body:
📐 Worked Example 12.2 — Computing the inflation tax
A country has M2 of $4 trillion (in real terms). The government plans to fund a $200 billion deficit next year through new money creation. (a) What inflation rate would this require, assuming people continue to hold the same real money balances? (b) Why is this assumption optimistic — what would actually happen?
1
(a) Required inflation: we need π × $4T = $200B, so π = $200B / $4,000B = 5%. The government would need 5% inflation to extract $200B in real resources from money holders.
2
(b) Why the assumption fails: if 5% inflation persists, people respond by holding less real money — shifting to inflation-protected assets, foreign currency, or simply spending faster. Real money balances M/P fall. To maintain $200B in real revenue, the government needs to inflate faster than 5%. This raises real money balances even less, requiring still faster inflation. The dynamic feedback is exactly what generates hyperinflation: governments keep raising the inflation tax rate, but the tax base keeps collapsing, until the currency loses its function entirely. Hungary 1946 is the limit case.

12.heading: Inflation as a Tax: The Quiet Wealth Transfer
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body: The inflation tax is bounded by the public's willingness to hold money. A government targeting modest amounts of inflation tax revenue (say, 1-2% of GDP at low inflation rates) can do so quietly and persistently — this is roughly what happens in countries with chronic 5-10% inflation. A government trying to extract larger amounts triggers the feedback loop and slides into crisis. This is the central theoretical insight that explains why hyperinflations always start with fiscal desperation and only end with credible commitments to fiscal discipline.

12.body: Figure 12.3 The inflation tax. Seigniorage is the product of money growth and the real money balances the public is willing to hold. Because expected inflation reduces those balances, revenue rises, peaks and then declines. A government that responds to the decline by printing faster enters the spiral that defines a hyperinflation.

12.heading: The Fisher Effect: Inflation and Nominal Interest Rates
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why bond yields jump when inflation rises
From chapter 8 one already knows that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus the inflation rate: r = i − π. The Fisher effect (named after Irving Fisher, who articulated it in 1930) takes this one step further: in the long run, nominal interest rates adjust one-for-one with inflation expectations.
The intuition is straightforward. Lenders care about real returns — what their money will actually buy when repaid. If lenders expect 5% inflation, they will demand a nominal rate that gives them their target real return plus 5% to compensate for the lost purchasing power. Borrowers, expecting their nominal income to rise with inflation, are willing to pay the higher nominal rate. So when expected inflation rises by 1 percentage point, nominal rates rise by 1 percentage point.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Fisher Effect
\[ i = r + \pi^{e} \]Over long horizons, with a stable real rate, the nominal rate moves one-for-one with expected inflation.
i
Nominal interest rate — what the bond actually pays.
r

12.heading: The Fisher Effect: Inflation and Nominal Interest Rates
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
Real interest rate — determined in the long run by real factors (capital productivity, time preference, savings supply) per chapter 10's loanable funds model. In the U.S. historically, this has averaged about 1-2%.
\(π^{e}\)
Expected inflation rate. Critically, what matters for the nominal rate is what people expect inflation to be — not necessarily what it turns out to be.
Reading the relationship: if the real rate is 2% and expected inflation is 3%, the nominal rate should be about 5%. If expected inflation rises to 8%, the nominal rate should rise to 10% — the same real rate plus higher inflation compensation.
The Volcker disinflation as a Fisher effect demonstration: in the late 1970s, U.S. inflation expectations were running at 10-13%, and 10-year Treasury yields rose above 15%. As Paul Volcker's Fed crushed inflation between 1980 and 1983, expectations gradually came down, and 10-year yields fell — though with a lag, since lenders required time to be convinced that low inflation would persist. By the late 1990s, with expectations anchored at 2-3%, 10-year yields had fallen to 5-6%. The relationship has been visible in U.S. data for 40+ years.

12.heading: The Fisher Effect: Inflation and Nominal Interest Rates
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "The Fed sets interest rates, so the Fisher effect does not apply"
A common student confusion. The Federal Reserve sets the federal funds rate, a very short-term overnight rate. The Fisher effect concerns longer-term nominal interest rates determined by markets — 10-year Treasury yields, mortgage rates, corporate bond yields. The Fed has only indirect influence on long rates, primarily through its effect on inflation expectations.
If markets believe the Fed will keep inflation near 2%, long-term rates will stay relatively low even when the Fed raises short-term rates. If markets lose faith and expect 8% inflation, long-term rates will jump above where the Fed wants them — and the Fed will be unable to lower them without creating yet more inflation. This is why central bank credibility is so valuable: a credible central bank can set short rates without losing control of the long end of the yield curve. A non-credible one cannot.

12.heading: The Costs of Inflation
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why moderate inflation matters less than people think, and considerably more than economists once thought
If inflation simply raises all prices and wages proportionally, why do people complain so much about it? In a perfectly indexed economy with rational expectations, inflation should impose only minor costs. But real economies are far from perfectly indexed, and the costs are larger and more varied than a simple model suggests.
The seven main costs of inflation, ordered from smallest to largest
CostWhat it isMagnitude
Shoe-leather costs
The inconvenience of attempting to hold less cash and make more frequent trips to the bank — the literal "wearing out of shoe leather" from extra trips.
Trivial in modern economies with electronic banking. Significant only in hyperinflation.
Menu costs
The cost of changing prices in catalogs, menus, websites, contracts. Higher inflation means more frequent reprinting, renegotiation, recoding.
Modest in moderate inflation. Becomes severe at high inflation when prices change weekly or daily.
Misallocation from relative-price variability

12.heading: The Costs of Inflation
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
Different prices adjust at different speeds, so high inflation distorts relative prices. Producers and consumers make worse decisions because the price signals are noisy.
Important and underappreciated. Inflation above ~5% measurably impairs economic efficiency.
Tax distortions
The U.S. tax code is not fully indexed for inflation. Capital gains, interest income, and depreciation allowances are based on nominal values. Higher inflation → effectively higher real tax rates on capital.
Significant. Estimated at roughly 0.1-0.2 percentage points of real GDP per year per percentage point of inflation above target.
Confusion and cost of accounting
Businesses, households, and governments must constantly distinguish nominal from real changes. Decisions become harder; mistakes more frequent.
Moderate but persistent.
Arbitrary redistribution
Unexpected inflation transfers wealth from creditors to debtors, from workers with sticky wages to employers, from those on fixed nominal incomes (retirees) to those whose income adjusts.
Large in episodes of unexpected inflation. The 1970s inflation in the U.S. transferred trillions in real wealth from bondholders to borrowers.

12.heading: The Costs of Inflation

The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
Loss of price stability and central bank credibility
Once inflation expectations become unanchored, regaining them requires deep recessions (per chapter 22). The Volcker disinflation cost the U.S. economy several years of high unemployment.
By far the largest cost. The disinflation of 1980-1983 cost roughly $1 trillion in lost output (in 2024 dollars).

12.heading: The Costs of Inflation
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why central banks fight even small inflation overshoots
The standard textbook treatment of inflation costs makes them look modest. Shoe leather, menu costs — these are minor inconveniences. So why does the Fed fight tooth and nail to keep inflation at 2% rather than letting it run at 4%? The answer lies in the bottom row of the table: credibility, once lost, is enormously expensive to regain.
Once inflation expectations come unmoored — once households and firms start writing higher inflation into their wage demands and price setting — pulling them back requires the central bank to demonstrate it will tolerate substantial economic pain to restore the anchor. The 1980-1983 Volcker disinflation pushed unemployment to 10.8% and caused the worst recession since the Great Depression to that point. The benefit was decades of low inflation. But the cost was real: roughly $1 trillion in lost output. Compared to that downside, fighting a brewing inflation early at the cost of a quarter-point overshoot is a bargain.

12.heading: The Costs of Inflation
12.title: Chapter 12, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
12.body:
This is why the 2021-2022 Fed delay in raising rates was so heavily criticized in retrospect. Once inflation broke 5% and started showing up in wage demands, the disinflation effort became dramatically more expensive than it would have been if the Fed had moved 6-12 months earlier. Modern monetary policy is partly about technical management, but mostly about preserving an institutional asset: credibility.
— A.S.

The serious costs lie further right: inflation obscures relative prices, interacts with a tax code written in nominal terms, redistributes arbitrarily between debtors and creditors, and at high enough rates destroys the usefulness of money as a unit of account altogether.

13.heading: Overview
13.title: Chapter 13, Money Growth and Inflation Why printing money causes prices to rise — usually, eventually, with long and variable lags. The theory that explains every hyperinflation in history, and one that almost called the 2022 U.S. inflation correctly In July 1946, Hungarians experienced the worst in
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — What 50 years of data look like
One way to test the quantity theory is to compare countries. If the theory is correct, countries with persistently higher money growth should have persistently higher inflation. The data overwhelmingly support this prediction at long time horizons.
Robert Barro and others have documented the relationship in dozens of empirical studies. Among countries averaging less than 10% annual money growth (most developed economies), the M-π relationship is noisy because velocity changes and other factors dominate. Among countries with sustained money growth above 20%, the relationship becomes nearly mechanical. Argentina, Turkey, Venezuela, Zimbabwe, Iran — all have experienced both rapid money growth and high inflation, in close numerical correspondence over multi-year averages.

The engine has a structural 2% anchor built in: inf_expectations = 0.5 × prev_inflation + 0.5 × 2.0. This means even if one lets inflation drift to 5%, the next round will see expectations at (0.5 × 5) + (0.5 × 2) = 3.5%, pulling inflation downward automatically — provided one does not keep pushing in the wrong direction. 13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
For decades, macroeconomics textbooks treated "open economy" topics as an afterthought — a chapter or two at the end, after the "real" material on growth, money, and business cycles. That treatment is wrong. Every country in the modern world is open in some meaningful sense. Capital flows globally. Goods cross borders. Currencies trade 24 hours a day with daily volumes exceeding $7.5 trillion — that is about $7.5 trillion per day, vastly larger than the underlying flow of goods trade and several times annual world GDP.
This chapter is short because the conceptual machinery is compact — half a dozen key concepts and one impossible-to-violate constraint (the trilemma). But the conceptual machinery is enormously powerful. Once one internalizes how trade flows, capital flows, and exchange rates fit together, one can analyze nearly any open-economy policy question — from EU adoption to dollarization to currency wars to capital controls. The Switzerland 2015 case lets us walk through almost every concept with one vivid example.
— A.S.

13.heading: The Three Core Concepts: Trade, Capital, and Exchange Rates
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — The three flows that define an open economy
An open economy interacts with the rest of the world along three dimensions. Goods and services cross borders (exports and imports). Capital crosses borders (foreigners buying domestic assets; residents buying foreign assets). And the exchange rate — the price at which one currency converts into another — adjusts to make all of this possible.
These three flows are tightly linked. When American consumers buy more Japanese cars, they ultimately pay in yen, which means somebody is selling dollars for yen, which puts downward pressure on the dollar relative to the yen. When foreign investors decide American Treasury bonds are safer than European ones, they sell euros for dollars, pushing the dollar up. The exchange rate is the price that makes all of these markets clear simultaneously.
📚 Key Terms — defined here, used throughout the chapter
Exports (X)
Goods and services produced domestically and sold to foreigners. A Boeing 737 sold to an Indian airline is a U.S. export. Includes both physical goods and services (consulting, software, tourism revenue from foreign visitors).
Imports (M)

13.heading: The Three Core Concepts: Trade, Capital, and Exchange Rates
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Goods and services produced abroad and bought by domestic residents. A Toyota Camry assembled in Japan and sold in the U.S. is a U.S. import.
Net exports (NX)
NX = X − M. The trade balance. Positive when a country exports more than it imports (trade surplus); negative when it imports more (trade deficit). The same NX from chapter 7's Y = C + I + G + NX.
Capital outflow (CO) / Net capital outflow (NCO)
The net amount of domestic residents buying foreign assets minus foreigners buying domestic assets. Positive when residents are net lenders to the world; negative when foreigners are net lenders to us. A country running a trade deficit must, by accounting identity, be a net capital importer.
Nominal exchange rate (e)
The rate at which one currency converts into another. If 1 USD = 1.10 CHF, then e = 1.10 CHF/USD. There are two equivalent ways to quote this (CHF per USD, or USD per CHF), and one must always check which one is being used.
Real exchange rate (ε)
The nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price levels: ε = e × P / P*, where P is the domestic price level and P* is the foreign price level. Measures the relative cost of goods across countries, not just currencies.

13.heading: The Three Core Concepts: Trade, Capital, and Exchange Rates
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Appreciation / Depreciation
A currency appreciates when it can buy more foreign currency (gets stronger). It depreciates when it can buy less (gets weaker). Important: if quoted as "foreign per domestic" (e.g., CHF per USD), an appreciation means the number gets bigger; if quoted as "domestic per foreign" (e.g., USD per CHF), an appreciation means the number gets smaller. Always check which way the rate is quoted.
Pegged / floating exchange rate
A pegged rate is fixed by the central bank at a target value (e.g., Saudi riyal = 3.75/USD since 1986). A floating rate is determined by supply and demand in foreign-exchange markets (e.g., USD/JPY). Many countries operate in between (managed float): they let the rate move but intervene at extremes.

13.heading: The Three Core Concepts: Trade, Capital, and Exchange Rates
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "A strong currency is always good"
Politicians often boast about a "strong dollar" or "strong yuan" as if currency appreciation were automatically beneficial. The reality is more nuanced. A strong currency:
Helps consumers and importers — foreign goods become cheaper.
Helps domestic residents traveling or buying foreign assets — their currency stretches further.
Hurts exporters — their products become more expensive abroad, reducing competitiveness.
Hurts domestic producers competing with imports — foreign rivals look relatively cheaper.
Reduces nominal GDP growth indirectly through lower NX.
Whether "strong" is good depends on which side of these trade-offs one's economy is on. Switzerland in 2015 illustrates the asymmetric pain: the franc spiked nearly 30% intraday and settled around 14-20% higher against the euro, immediately devastating exporters (Swatch, Nestle, Roche) and the tourism industry, but it also dramatically lowered the cost of imported goods for Swiss consumers. The CHF rise was both blessing and curse — but the political pain came from the exporters, not from the consumers who benefitted silently.

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — Every trade deficit is funded by a capital flow
One of the most elegant identities in macroeconomics says that, for any country, the trade balance must be offset by net capital flows. The intuition is straightforward. If Americans buy more goods from Japan than they sell to Japan, where do the extra yen come from? They come from selling dollar assets to Japanese investors (or borrowing from them). The country with a trade deficit is, by mathematical necessity, a country accumulating net liabilities to the rest of the world.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Trade Balance / Capital Account Identity
\[ NX = NCO \]The trade balance equals net capital outflow.
NX
Net exports (X − M). The current account balance (ignoring services and transfers, which we fold in here). Positive = trade surplus.
NCO
Net capital outflow: domestic purchases of foreign assets minus foreign purchases of domestic assets. Positive = country is lending abroad on net.
NX = NCO

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
An accounting identity. Not a behavioral claim. Forced by how the international accounts are constructed. A country running a trade surplus must be accumulating net foreign assets; a country running a trade deficit must be accumulating net foreign liabilities.
Reading it in plain language: goods flow one way; payment flows the other way. If Americans send fewer dollars worth of goods abroad than the dollar value of goods they receive (trade deficit), the difference is the value of American assets (Treasuries, stocks, real estate, debt) that foreigners are accumulating in exchange. The U.S. has run trade deficits for over 40 years, accumulating massive net foreign liabilities. This has been sustainable because the U.S. assets foreigners want to hold are large, deep, and trusted markets.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Saving, Investment, and the Trade Balance
\[ S - I = NX = NCO \]
S
National saving (per chapter 10). Total income not consumed.
I
Domestic investment (real capital formation).
S − I

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
The country's excess saving over domestic investment opportunities. When S > I, the country invests the excess abroad (running a current account surplus). When S < I, the country borrows from abroad to fund investment (current account deficit).
The identity links chapter 10's loanable funds market to international flows. In a closed economy, S = I always. In an open economy, S need not equal I — the gap is exactly what flows across borders. The U.S. has S < I and runs a persistent trade deficit (importing capital to fund excess investment over saving). Germany has S > I and runs a persistent trade surplus (exporting capital because domestic investment opportunities are saturated). Trade imbalances do not happen because of "unfair trade practices" — they happen because of saving-investment imbalances between countries.

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📐 Worked Example 13.1 — From saving-investment to the trade balance
An economy has the following: GDP = $25 trillion, C = $17T, I = $5T, G = $4.5T, T (net taxes) = $4T. (a) Compute private saving, public saving, and national saving. (b) Compute NX from the national accounts identity. (c) Verify that S − I = NX. (d) Comment on whether this country is a net borrower or lender to the rest of the world.
1
(a) Saving: Private = Y − T − C = 25 − 4 − 17 = $4T. Public = T − G = 4 − 4.5 = −$0.5T. National S = $4T + (−$0.5T) = $3.5T.
2
(b) NX from Y = C + I + G + NX: NX = Y − C − I − G = 25 − 17 − 5 − 4.5 = −$1.5T (trade deficit).
3
(c) Check S − I = NX: $3.5T − $5T = −$1.5T = NX ✓
4
(d) This country is a net borrower from the rest of the world. Domestic investment ($5T) exceeds national saving ($3.5T) by $1.5T; the gap is filled by net capital inflows from abroad. The trade deficit ($1.5T) is the goods-side mirror of the same capital flow.

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body: The U.S. has fit this pattern for over four decades. Persistent trade deficits ($1-1.5T per year recently) are funded by persistent net capital inflows — foreigners buying U.S. Treasuries, corporate bonds, stocks, and real estate. This is not inherently bad: the U.S. uses the imported capital to fund productive investment, and U.S. residents benefit from foreign products and foreign-owned investment domestically. But the situation does create vulnerabilities (chapter 22 explores these in depth).

13.heading: The Balance of Payments: An Accounting Identity
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body: Figure 13.1 The balance of payments is an identity. Every purchase of foreign goods must be paid for with foreign currency, and that currency is obtained either by selling goods abroad or by selling an asset. A current account deficit is therefore necessarily matched by a financial account surplus: the country is selling claims on itself. Whether that is benign depends entirely on what the borrowed funds are doing, a question the identity itself cannot answer.

13.heading: How Exchange Rates Are Determined
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — The forex market as supply and demand
In the long run, exchange rates are determined by the relative purchasing power of currencies — a doctrine called purchasing power parity (PPP). In the short run, exchange rates are determined by the supply of and demand for currencies in foreign-exchange markets, with capital flows mattering far more than trade flows on a day-to-day basis. Both stories matter, on different time horizons.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Purchasing Power Parity
\[ e = \frac{P}{P^{*}} \]In the long run the nominal exchange rate reflects the ratio of national price levels.
e
Nominal exchange rate, quoted as units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency.
P
Domestic price level — the cost of a representative basket of goods at home.
P*
Foreign price level — the cost of the same basket abroad, in foreign currency.

13.heading: How Exchange Rates Are Determined
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Reading it in plain language: if the same basket costs $100 in the U.S. and 12,000 yen in Japan, then PPP says the exchange rate should be 120 yen per dollar (otherwise it would be cheaper to ship the basket from one country to the other and arbitrage the difference). PPP works reasonably well at long horizons (decades) but fails substantially in the short run, because many goods cannot be cheaply arbitraged (haircuts, hospital stays, real estate), and because exchange rates are also driven by capital flows that have nothing to do with goods prices.
The Economist's Big Mac Index tests PPP using the simplest possible "basket": the price of a Big Mac in different countries. As of 2025, a Big Mac costs $5.79 in the U.S. and roughly 25 yuan in China. PPP would imply an exchange rate of about 4.3 yuan/USD. The actual market rate is around 7.2 yuan/USD — meaning the yuan trades about 40% below its PPP value. The Big Mac Index is whimsical but conceptually revealing: persistent deviations from PPP suggest persistent over- or undervaluation of currencies relative to their fundamentals.

Demand for the domestic currency comes from foreign purchases of domestic goods and assets; supply comes from domestic residents acquiring foreign goods and assets. The rate adjusts until the two are equal. An increase in demand for domestic assets appreciates the currency, which in turn widens the trade deficit — the two halves of the balance of payments are linked by the exchange rate.

13.heading: The Switzerland 2015 Case: Every Concept in One Event
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
2011–2015
Switzerland
Currency intervention
The Day the SNB Surrendered: 90 Seconds That Reshaped Forex Markets
Between 2010 and 2011, the European debt crisis sent terrified capital fleeing the Eurozone in search of safe havens. Switzerland — small, politically stable, with a long tradition of monetary discipline and bank secrecy — became the destination of choice for trillions of euros of nervous money. By August 2011, the Swiss franc had appreciated nearly 40% against the euro in just over a year, threatening to crush Swiss exporters and tourism. Watch makers, pharmaceutical companies, machinery exporters all complained that their products had become uncompetitive overnight. Deflation was looming. The Swiss National Bank had to act.

13.heading: The Switzerland 2015 Case: Every Concept in One Event
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
On September 6, 2011, the SNB announced an unprecedented commitment: it would buy foreign currency in unlimited quantities to prevent the franc from appreciating beyond 1.20 per euro. This was not a guideline or a target — it was a hard floor. The SNB pledged to print as many francs as necessary, swap them for euros at 1.20, and absorb the resulting balance-sheet expansion. For three and a half years, the policy worked. The franc stayed close to 1.20. Swiss exports recovered. Tourism stabilized.
But the policy had costs. To defend the floor, the SNB had to keep buying euros — and the inflows kept coming. By December 2014, the SNB held foreign currency reserves of roughly 500 billion CHF, equivalent to about 70% of Swiss GDP. To put that in perspective: imagine the Fed accumulating $20 trillion of foreign-currency reserves on its balance sheet, far exceeding U.S. annual output. The SNB's balance sheet had become a massive bet that the euro would not depreciate further. And then, in early January 2015, signals from the European Central Bank suggested that a massive new round of euro-weakening quantitative easing was imminent.

13.heading: The Switzerland 2015 Case: Every Concept in One Event
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
The SNB faced two options: (1) continue defending the floor and watch its balance sheet grow indefinitely as Mario Draghi's ECB flooded the market with euros, eventually owning much of the eurozone's outstanding government debt; or (2) abandon the floor and accept a one-time massive franc appreciation. They chose option 2. On January 15, 2015 at 9:30 GMT, the floor was removed. Within ninety seconds the franc was up 30% — briefly trading as high as 0.85 CHF per euro before settling around 1.04. Simultaneously, the SNB cut the deposit rate to −0.75%, the lowest in history, to discourage further capital inflows.
The damage was widespread. Several forex brokers, including FXCM, Alpari UK, and Excel Markets, became insolvent. Citibank, Deutsche Bank, and Barclays reported losses of $150-300 million each. Hedge funds with short-CHF positions were wiped out. Polish and Hungarian homeowners with Swiss-franc mortgages saw their effective debts jump 20-30% overnight. The Swiss stock market fell more than 10% in a single day. Swatch's CEO called it "a tsunami."

13.heading: The Switzerland 2015 Case: Every Concept in One Event
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
The longer-term consequences were more nuanced. Swiss exports did suffer initially (about 1-2% of GDP impact), but the country avoided the Japan-style stagnation many had feared. Swiss companies cut costs, became more efficient, and pivoted toward higher-value products. By 2018, the franc had retreated somewhat toward 1.15-1.18 EUR/CHF. The SNB's reserves stabilized around 95% of GDP — extraordinary, but no longer growing.
What this case teaches: A small open economy faced with massive capital inflows has only bad options. Intervention can defer the problem but accumulates fiscal risk (a giant central bank balance sheet bet against the home currency). Abandoning intervention triggers immediate trauma. There is no clean path. The single most important lesson is that currency intervention is profoundly asymmetric: easy to start, agonizing to stop, dangerous to maintain. This is exactly why most major central banks have moved away from explicit pegs and toward floating regimes with implicit guardrails.

13.heading: The Switzerland 2015 Case: Every Concept in One Event
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Stop and reflect: The SNB's three-and-a-half-year defense of the 1.20 floor accumulated foreign currency reserves equal to about 70% of Swiss GDP. If Swiss inflation had been low and ECB-style quantitative easing had not been expected, the SNB could have continued defending the floor indefinitely. Why this option did not remain feasible? Think about what happens when a central bank holds enormous foreign assets denominated in a currency the foreign country's own central bank is trying to weaken.
Figure 13.3 The Swiss franc before and after 15 January 2015. For three years the Swiss National Bank held the franc at a ceiling of 1.20 per euro by selling unlimited quantities of its own currency, accumulating reserves worth most of annual output. When the policy was abandoned without warning the exchange rate moved by around twenty percent within minutes. The episode is the cleanest available demonstration of the trilemma: the commitment could be maintained only by giving up control of the balance sheet.

13.heading: The Impossible Trinity (Trilemma): Three Things, Pick Two
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — The hardest constraint in international finance
Every open economy faces a fundamental constraint articulated by Robert Mundell in the 1960s. A country can pursue at most two of the following three desirable policies — never all three at once:
A fixed exchange rate — a peg that lets businesses plan and protects against currency volatility.
Free movement of capital — letting investment flow in and out without restrictions, which most modern economies value.
An independent monetary policy — being able to set interest rates to fight domestic recession or inflation.
This is the impossible trinity or trilemma. It is one of the most rigorously tested empirical regularities in macroeconomics, and it has shaped every major international monetary architecture from Bretton Woods (1944-1971) to the European Monetary Union to modern emerging-market debates over capital controls.

The colored side connecting two corners represents the policy combination a country chooses; the opposite corner is what gets sacrificed. There is no real-world economy that operates at the center — the trilemma forces a choice.
The trilemma in practice — how real countries make the trade-off

Eurozone members

13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Free capital flows + independent monetary policy
Floating exchange rate. The dollar, pound, yen, and euro all swing significantly in response to shocks.
Switzerland 2011–2015
Tried for all three! Floor on the franc + capital openness + ability to cut rates
The trilemma caught up with them. By 2015, defending the floor against ECB easing required printing infinite francs. They had to abandon either the floor (which they did) or capital openness (politically unacceptable).

13.heading: The Impossible Trinity (Trilemma): Three Things, Pick Two
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why the trilemma is the most useful tool one will learn in this chapter
The trilemma is what separates students who understand international macroeconomics from those who do not. Anyone can recite the equations of PPP and the balance of payments. The trilemma is harder because it forces the analyst to think about which constraint binds in a given situation.
When one reads a news article about a currency crisis, an emerging market in trouble, a central bank facing speculative pressure — always ask: "Which corner of the trilemma are they trying to live at? Why is it impossible to remain there? Which corner are they being forced toward?" Argentina in 2001, Mexico in 1994, Thailand in 1997, Britain in 1992, Russia in 1998, Switzerland in 2015 — every one of these crises was fundamentally a trilemma collision. Capital flows changed; the country could no longer simultaneously hold a peg, open capital markets, and an independent policy. Something had to give.

13.heading: The Impossible Trinity (Trilemma): Three Things, Pick Two
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
The trilemma also explains why the eurozone has been such a difficult experiment. Member countries gave up their independent monetary policy in exchange for the certainty of a fixed rate and open capital markets within the bloc. When asymmetric shocks hit (like the 2009-2012 sovereign debt crisis affecting Greece more than Germany), countries on the wrong end had no independent monetary policy to deploy. The solution had to come from fiscal transfers (which Germany resisted) or from the European Central Bank (which broke with its formal mandate to act). The trilemma was the deep constraint shaping every policy decision in that crisis.
— A.S.

13.body: Figure 13.4 The impossible trinity. A country may fix its exchange rate, permit free movement of capital, and set its own interest rate — but only two of the three at once. With open capital markets, holding the rate fixed requires the domestic interest rate to follow the anchor currency's; retaining monetary independence requires either a floating rate or capital controls.

13.heading: Exchange Rate Regimes: A Spectrum of Choices
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Exchange rate regimes from rigid to flexible
RegimeWhat it isExamples / costs
Dollarization / Currency Union
Country abandons its own currency entirely; adopts a foreign currency or shares one with neighbors.
Ecuador (USD since 2000), El Salvador (USD since 2001), Eurozone members. Permanent loss of monetary policy. Permanent gain of credibility.
Hard peg (currency board)
Domestic currency exists but is rigidly tied to a foreign anchor, with full reserve backing.
Hong Kong dollar (1983-present). Bulgaria's lev. Easier to abandon than dollarization but politically costly.
Soft peg / adjustable peg
Official target rate that can be changed in extremis. Central bank intervenes to defend it.
Pre-1971 Bretton Woods system. Modern: Saudi Arabia (riyal/USD), most Gulf states. Vulnerable to speculative attack when fundamentals diverge.
Managed float
Rate floats day-to-day but central bank intervenes at extremes or against destabilizing speculation.
China (post-2015), India, Brazil. The most common modern regime for emerging markets.
Free float
Exchange rate determined purely by markets. Central bank does not intervene.

13.body:
U.S., UK, Japan, Eurozone (vs. outside world), Australia, Canada. Volatility but maximum monetary independence.
Figure 13.5 Exchange-rate regimes form a continuum rather than a pair of options. Moving rightward buys monetary independence at the price of exchange-rate stability, which is the trilemma expressed as a menu. No point on the line is correct in general: the right choice depends on how exposed the economy is to trade, how credible its own monetary institutions are, and how severe the shocks it faces tend to be.

13.heading: Why Trade Deficits Are Mostly Misunderstood
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
📘 Principles Level — A trade deficit is not a national debt
"Trade deficit" is one of the most consistently misused terms in political discourse. Treated as a national scoreboard, it is invoked to justify tariffs, sanctions, and protectionist policy. Most of the rhetoric is wrong. A trade deficit is neither inherently bad nor inherently good — it depends on what is funding it and what the imported capital is being used for.
From section 13.2, recall: S − I = NX. A trade deficit (NX < 0) means national saving falls short of domestic investment by an amount equal to the deficit. This can happen for two very different reasons:
Investment is unusually high (productive capital formation outpacing domestic saving). Foreign capital flows in to fund profitable opportunities. Examples: U.S. in the 1990s tech boom; Korea during its industrialization push. This kind of trade deficit is healthy — the foreign capital pays for future productive capacity.

13.heading: Why Trade Deficits Are Mostly Misunderstood
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
Saving is unusually low (consumption outpacing income). Foreign capital flows in to fund current consumption. Examples: Greece pre-2010 (importing German Mercedes and Italian wine on credit); U.S. mortgage borrowing 2003-2007. This kind of trade deficit is problematic — debts accumulate without productive capacity to service them.
The trade deficit by itself does not indicate which case one is in. One needs to look at what investment is being funded and whether it has decent returns.

13.heading: Why Trade Deficits Are Mostly Misunderstood
13.title: Chapter 13, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
13.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Trade deficits transfer jobs abroad"
A widespread political claim. It contains a kernel of truth — when Americans buy Chinese goods instead of American ones, some specific U.S. workers (in textiles, manufacturing) lose jobs. But the aggregate-level claim is largely wrong. The U.S. trade deficit has fluctuated between 3% and 6% of GDP for forty years, while U.S. unemployment has ranged from 3.5% to 10% over the same period — the two have essentially no correlation. Aggregate U.S. employment is determined by domestic factors (Fed policy, fiscal stance, structural conditions), not by the trade balance.
This does not mean trade has no distributional effects: it does. Specific workers and regions lose; others gain. The mistake is treating the trade balance as the aggregate scoreboard rather than understanding it as a financial-flow consequence of saving and investment decisions. Tariffs that try to "reduce the trade deficit" almost always fail to do so, because they do not change underlying saving-investment imbalances; they just shift which goods get imported.

14.heading: Overview
14.title: Chapter 14, Open-Economy Macroeconomics Why the exchange rate is the most consequential price in any economy that trades, why countries cannot have everything they want in international finance, and how a single 4:30 AM announcement in Zurich erased $400 billion of value in 90 seconds At 4:30 AM Eas
14.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — The Trilemma in the Engine
The MacroNations engine does not expose an exchange-rate-regime lever or a separate capital-account lever. The trilemma operates indirectly through the interest_rate_target, trade_openness, and currency state variable. The engine uses uncovered interest parity (UIP) directly: each 1pp change in interest rate moves the currency by 1.5% (a 100bp hike strengthens the currency by 1.5 index points). Currency appreciation then feeds back through a trade penalty: currency_trade = −(Δcurrency / prev_currency) × 15 percentage points of GDP. So raising one's rate strengthens one's currency, which hurts one's trade balance. The engine does not permit a pure float vs. peg choice — every country is implicitly on a managed float where the trade-off between rate independence and currency stability is fully transmitted through these equations.
