14.heading: Insight
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Unemployment is the macroeconomic variable people feel most viscerally. Inflation eats away at savings slowly; GDP growth is an abstraction. But losing one's job is immediate, personal, and devastating. The labor market is also the macroeconomic arena where simple textbook models fail most spectacularly. The standard "wage equals marginal product of labor" framework predicts that minimum wages destroy jobs and that wages adjust quickly to clear markets. The empirical evidence on both points is, charitably, mixed — and on the minimum wage front, frequently contradictory to the standard prediction.

14.heading: Insight
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Why is this? Because labor markets are not like wheat markets. Workers and jobs are heterogeneous; matching is costly; firms care about morale and turnover; long-term relationships matter; and information about who is good at what is genuinely scarce. Modern labor economics — the kind that earned David Card his Nobel — treats these frictions as the first-order features, not the second-order corrections, of the labor market. This chapter is built around that newer view. If at the end of the chapter one can read a news article about the labor market and not be fooled by sloppy supply-and-demand reasoning, I will have done my job.
— A.S.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📘 Principles Level — The categories everyone in macroeconomics uses
Every month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) surveys about 60,000 U.S. households as part of the Current Population Survey. Based on what people answer, each adult (age 16+) gets placed into exactly one of three categories:
Employed: did any paid work in the past week, even one hour. Includes part-time and self-employed workers.
Unemployed: did no paid work but actively searched for a job in the past four weeks AND is available to start work.
Not in the labor force: not working and not searching — students, retirees, stay-at-home parents, discouraged workers who have given up, the disabled.
These three categories sum to the total adult population. The first two add up to the labor force — people either working or looking for work.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Standard Unemployment Rate (U-3)
\[ u = \frac{\text{unemployed}}{\text{labor force}} \times 100 \]
u
The unemployment rate, reported monthly as a percentage. This is the headline number one sees in the news. The BLS officially calls it U-3.
Unemployed

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
People without jobs who have actively searched in the past 4 weeks. People who have given up looking ("discouraged workers") are NOT counted as unemployed — they fall into "not in the labor force." This is a crucial measurement quirk.
Labor Force
Employed + Unemployed. Does NOT include people who are neither working nor looking.
In March 2026 (most recent month at writing): Labor force = 170.09 million. Unemployed = 7.24 million. u = 7.24 / 170.09 = 4.26%, which the BLS reports as 4.3%.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Two Other Important Measures
\[ \text{LFPR} = \frac{\text{labor force}}{\text{adult population}} \times 100, \qquad \frac{E}{P} = \frac{\text{employed}}{\text{adult population}} \times 100 \]
LFPR
Labor force participation rate. What share of adults are either working or looking? In the U.S. this was around 67% in 2000, fell to 63% after the Great Recession, dropped to 60.2% in April 2020 (lowest since the early 1970s), and as of early 2026 sits around 61.9%. This drop is consequential: about 5 million Americans have left the labor force since 2000 who would have been in it under prior trends.
E/P

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Employment-to-population ratio. Sidesteps the search-effort issue by just asking: what share of adults actually have jobs? In April 2023, when U-3 hit its 50-year low of 3.4%, E/P was 60.4% — meaning nearly 40% of working-age adults were not employed, even at "full employment." This is the gap LFPR tries to highlight.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "Unemployment fell, so the job market is great"
A widely-reported and widely-misunderstood phenomenon. The unemployment rate can fall for two very different reasons:
Good reason: people who were unemployed found jobs. Both employment and labor force participation rise.
Bad reason: people who were unemployed gave up looking. They drop out of the labor force entirely. Unemployment falls because the denominator shrinks, not because more people are working.
To distinguish these, always look at three numbers together: unemployment rate, labor force participation rate, AND employment-to-population ratio. In a healthy recovery, all three move in healthy directions. In a discouragement-driven decline, unemployment looks good but LFPR and E/P both deteriorate. This is why economists obsess over labor force participation — it strips away the measurement artifact.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📚 The Alternative Unemployment Rates — U-4, U-5, U-6
U-3
The headline rate. Unemployed who actively searched ÷ labor force. ~4.3% in March 2026.
U-4
U-3 plus discouraged workers (gave up looking because they think no jobs are available).
U-5
U-4 plus other marginally attached workers (would like a job but have not searched recently for various reasons).
U-6
U-5 plus part-time workers who want full-time work but cannot get it (involuntary part-time). The most comprehensive measure. ~8.0% in March 2026.
Why so many measures? Because "unemployed" is a fuzzy category. A laid-off engineer searching online every day is unemployed; a parent who wants to work but has stopped looking because childcare is impossible is "not in the labor force"; a barista working 15 hours a week who wants 40 is "employed." Each of these has different policy implications, so the BLS publishes a spectrum of measures. The gap between U-3 and U-6 indicates how much "hidden slack" there is in the labor market.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📐 Worked Example 14.1 — Reading a real labor market snapshot
In March 2026, the BLS reported: Adult population (16+) = 274.7 million. Labor force = 170.09 million. Employed = 162.85 million. Unemployed = 7.24 million. (a) Verify the unemployment rate. (b) Compute the labor force participation rate. (c) Compute the employment-to-population ratio. (d) If 5 million people who were "not in the labor force" all started looking for jobs tomorrow but did not find them, what would the unemployment rate become?
1
(a) Unemployment rate: u = 7.24 / 170.09 = 4.256% ≈ 4.3% ✓ matches the BLS report.
2
(b) LFPR: 170.09 / 274.7 = 61.92%. Two-thirds of a percentage point below the pre-COVID level of 63.4% in February 2020.
3
(c) E/P ratio: 162.85 / 274.7 = 59.28%. Even at low headline unemployment, fewer than 60% of adults have jobs.
4
(d) Counterfactual: labor force rises to 175.09 million, unemployed rises to 12.24 million. u = 12.24 / 175.09 = 6.99% ≈ 7%. The "true" slack in the economy depends heavily on how many discouraged workers re-enter the labor force as conditions improve.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: This is exactly what happens during recoveries. As job prospects improve, people who had given up start looking again. The headline unemployment rate can stay flat or even rise during a recovery's early months, because the inflow of returning workers temporarily exceeds the rate at which they find jobs. This is one of the main reasons why a falling unemployment rate during the early months of a recovery is sometimes a worse sign than a stable one — it can mean people are giving up, not that jobs are appearing.

14.heading: How We Measure Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.1 Stocks and flows in the labor market. The published unemployment rate is a ratio of two stocks, but it moves because of flows: separations, hires, entry and exit. Two very different labor markets can report the same rate, which is why the participation rate and the flows are read alongside it.

14.heading: The Three Types of Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why unemployment never goes to zero
Even in the best of economic times, the U.S. unemployment rate has never been below about 2.5%. Why it does not go to zero? Because some unemployment is structural to how labor markets work — it never disappears, even in booms. Economists divide unemployment into three categories based on what is causing it:
📚 The Three Types of Unemployment
Frictional
Short-term unemployment as workers move between jobs. A recent graduate looking for their first job; an engineer who quit to find a better fit; a parent re-entering the workforce after raising children. This is unavoidable in any economy where people move, change careers, or seek better matches. Roughly 1-2% of unemployment is frictional in good times.
Structural

14.heading: The Three Types of Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Long-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between worker skills/location and job requirements. A coal miner in West Virginia when coal jobs disappear; a steelworker in 1980s Ohio when domestic steel collapses; a journalist in 2010s when local newspapers fail. The skills and the locations do not match the new economy. Structural unemployment can persist for years; the unemployed worker may need retraining or relocation to find work.
Cyclical
Unemployment caused by recessions — insufficient overall demand for goods and services. When consumers stop spending, businesses lay off workers regardless of their skill or location. This is the kind of unemployment we will address with monetary and fiscal policy in Chapters 17-19. Cyclical unemployment can vanish quickly once demand recovers.
⚙ The Natural Rate of Unemployment
\[ u = u^{*} + u^{\text{cyclical}} \]\(u^{*}\) is the natural rate: frictional plus structural unemployment.
u*

14.heading: The Three Types of Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Natural rate of unemployment — the unemployment rate that prevails when the economy is at potential output. NOT zero. Reflects the unavoidable churn of frictional and structural unemployment. In the U.S. today, most estimates put u* somewhere between 3.5% and 4.5%.
u − u*
Cyclical unemployment — the gap between current and natural rates. Positive in recessions, negative in booms (when demand exceeds normal and the economy "overheats"). This is the part that monetary policy can affect.
Why u* is invisible: the natural rate is never directly observed; it must be estimated from data, often with substantial uncertainty. The CBO, Fed, and private forecasters publish estimates of u* that frequently differ by a percentage point or more. Knowing u* is essential for monetary policy — the Fed tightens when actual unemployment is below u* and loosens when above — but the uncertainty is exactly why monetary policy is so difficult.

14.heading: The Three Types of Unemployment
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.2 Three kinds of unemployment, with the horizon over which each persists and the instrument that addresses it. The distinction matters because the policy error in each direction is costly: treating structural unemployment as cyclical produces inflation without durable employment gains, and treating cyclical unemployment as structural leaves an output gap open that policy could have closed.

14.heading: The Beveridge Curve: The Most Important Diagram in Modern Labor Economics
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📘 Principles Level — Job openings versus unemployment
Imagine one plots two things over time. On the horizontal axis, the unemployment rate. On the vertical axis, the job openings rate — the number of unfilled jobs as a share of total employment plus openings. One would expect these to be negatively related: when unemployment is high, there are few openings (recessions), and when unemployment is low, openings are abundant (booms). And indeed, that is exactly what the data show.
This downward-sloping relationship is called the Beveridge curve, named after Lord William Beveridge, the British economist who first identified it in the 1940s. The Beveridge curve is the closest thing modern labor economics has to a fundamental diagram. Every recession traces a movement along the curve. But sometimes — and this is the interesting part — the entire curve shifts. When the curve shifts outward (up and to the right), it means the economy is getting less efficient at matching unemployed workers to job openings. When it shifts inward, matching is getting better.
⚙ The Beveridge Curve in Words

14.heading: The Beveridge Curve: The Most Important Diagram in Modern Labor Economics
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
\[ v = f(u), \qquad f'(u) < 0 \]The vacancy rate is a decreasing, convex function of the unemployment rate; its curvature reflects matching frictions.
v
Vacancy rate: job openings as a share of (employment + openings). U.S. averages about 4-5% in normal times; spiked to a record 7% in 2022.
u
Unemployment rate: as defined in §14.1.
Movements along
Cyclical changes in labor demand. Recession → up-right movement (high u, low v). Boom → down-left movement (low u, high v).
Shifts of
Changes in matching efficiency — how easily firms and workers find each other. Outward shift = bad matching (more u for any v). Inward shift = good matching.
Why this matters: the Beveridge curve gives policymakers a way to distinguish between cyclical unemployment (movements along the curve, fixable with monetary policy) and structural unemployment (shifts of the curve, requiring training, relocation help, or time). The Fed cares enormously about which one is dominant at any moment.

14.heading: The Beveridge Curve: The Most Important Diagram in Modern Labor Economics
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.3 The Beveridge curve. Vacancies and unemployment move in opposite directions along the curve as demand varies over the cycle. A shift of the whole curve outward is a different event: the same number of vacancies now coexists with more unemployment, which indicates that matching workers to jobs has become less efficient rather than that demand has fallen.

14.heading: The 2020-2024 U.S. Labor Market: Three Beveridge Curve Shifts in Four Years
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
2020–2024
United States
Labor market
The Most Violent Beveridge Curve Episode in U.S. History
The pre-COVID U.S. Beveridge curve, traced out over 2010-2019, was a well-behaved downward-sloping arc. Unemployment fell from 9.6% (2010) to 3.5% (Feb 2020); the vacancy rate rose from about 2% to 4.5%. The curve was reasonably stable, with mild inward improvement as the recovery matured. Then came the pandemic.
Phase 1 — March-April 2020: explosive outward shift. In two months, U.S. unemployment exploded from 3.5% to 14.8%. Twenty-two million jobs vanished. But job openings did not fall proportionally; many firms still had open postings they could not fill because of lockdowns. For the first time in modern data, the U.S. had simultaneously high unemployment AND not-low vacancies. The Beveridge curve had shifted dramatically outward — matching efficiency had collapsed.

14.heading: The 2020-2024 U.S. Labor Market: Three Beveridge Curve Shifts in Four Years
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Phase 2 — Summer 2020: partial reversal. As lockdowns eased, many of the workers laid off in March-April were recalled by their previous employers. This created an unusually high "matching efficiency" period — workers and jobs reconnected because they already had pre-existing relationships. Unemployment fell to 6.7% by November 2020 without a major rise in job openings. The Beveridge curve traced back partway toward its pre-pandemic position.
Phase 3 — 2021-2022: dramatic outward shift again. This is the most interesting and unusual part of the story. Starting in early 2021, job openings began climbing to unprecedented levels, eventually peaking at 12.0 million openings in March 2022 (a vacancy rate of ~7%). At the same time, unemployment came down only modestly — sitting at 3.6% by March 2022, similar to pre-pandemic levels but with the labor force still 2 million people smaller. The Beveridge curve had shifted dramatically outward and upward: there were 2 job openings for every unemployed worker, an all-time record.
Why did matching efficiency break down so severely? Three reasons economists generally point to:

14.heading: The 2020-2024 U.S. Labor Market: Three Beveridge Curve Shifts in Four Years
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
The Great Resignation — record-high quit rates as employed workers reevaluated careers, retired early, or switched industries. This made matching harder because firms were competing for workers who were themselves looking, not just for unemployed workers searching the same firms.
Geographic mismatch — jobs were in growing tech and logistics sectors; many unemployed had service-sector skills.
Demographic shifts — early retirement during the pandemic permanently removed millions from the labor force.
Phase 4 — 2023-2025: gradual normalization. By late 2023, job openings had eased to 8-9 million and the unemployment rate had drifted up from its 3.4% bottom toward 4%. The labor market was cooling without a recession. By early 2026, unemployment sat at 4.3% with vacancies around 7-8 million — still slightly above the pre-pandemic Beveridge curve but no longer in record-anomaly territory.

14.heading: The 2020-2024 U.S. Labor Market: Three Beveridge Curve Shifts in Four Years
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
The four-year journey is the most remarkable Beveridge-curve episode ever recorded. It illustrates that the labor market can break and re-form in unexpected ways, and that the relationship between unemployment and vacancies — far from being a fixed economic law — is itself an outcome of social, demographic, and structural dynamics.
🎛 Interactive — The Beveridge Curve
Trace the U.S. labor market through four years; see the shifts
What is being observed: the unemployment rate (X) and the job vacancy rate (Y), with each phase highlighted. The pre-COVID Beveridge curve (gray dots) represents normal labor market matching. When the curve shifts up-and-right, matching efficiency has worsened. The dramatic 2021-22 shift represents the Great Resignation period — record openings AND not-low unemployment, which violated everything textbooks taught.

14.heading: The 2020-2024 U.S. Labor Market: Three Beveridge Curve Shifts in Four Years
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.4 The American labor market from 2020 to 2024, drawn as a path rather than a scatter. The collapse moved the economy down and to the right in weeks. The reopening moved it up and to the left along a curve well outside the pre-pandemic relation, indicating worse matching. The final stretch is the unusual part: vacancies fell a long way with only a small rise in unemployment, which is the mechanical counterpart of the disinflation achieved without a recession.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why labor markets do not clear like wheat markets
The simple supply-and-demand model predicts that when unemployment rises, wages fall, which restores full employment. In practice, wages are remarkably sticky downward: they almost never fall in nominal terms even during severe recessions. During 2008-09, with unemployment reaching 10%, U.S. nominal wages continued rising at about 2% per year. Why do wages not adjust as price theory predicts?
Modern labor economics identifies four major reasons.
Why wages stay high in the face of unemployment — four theories
TheoryThe mechanismReal-world evidence
Minimum wages
Legal floors below which wages cannot fall. Binding mostly for low-skill workers.
U.S. federal minimum is $7.25/hour (unchanged since 2009), but many states are well above (CA $16+). About 1% of hourly workers earn at or below the federal floor.
Unions and collective bargaining
Workers organize and negotiate wages above the competitive level, with credible threats to strike.
U.S. union membership has fallen from ~33% in 1955 to ~10% in 2026, mostly in the public sector. In Europe, coverage is much higher (60%+ in Belgium, France, Italy).
Efficiency wages

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Firms pay above the market-clearing wage on purpose, because higher wages improve worker effort, reduce turnover, attract better candidates, and boost loyalty. (Henry Ford famously did this in 1914 with the $5/day wage.)
Strongly supported by empirical evidence. Studies show that firms paying above-market wages have lower turnover, higher productivity, and stronger applicant pools — often a net financial benefit.
Insider-outsider theory
Already-employed workers ("insiders") have bargaining power that the unemployed ("outsiders") lack. Insiders negotiate to protect their wages even when outsiders would gladly work for less.
Why a recession can persist: firms could lower wages and hire more, but insider workers resist, the unemployed cannot bid wages down, and the system stalls at high unemployment.
1992–2021
New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania
Card-Krueger
The Card-Krueger Minimum Wage Study That Broke the Standard Model

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
The standard textbook treatment of minimum wages is unambiguous. A minimum wage set above the market-clearing wage creates a surplus — quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — which means unemployment for low-wage workers. The diagram is the first thing taught in every introductory micro course. The empirical evidence used to back it up: aggregate statistical comparisons of teenage employment rates across states with different minimum wages.
In 1992, David Card and Alan Krueger of Princeton University set out to test the prediction directly using a quasi-experiment. New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour on April 1, 1992 — a 19% increase. Pennsylvania, just across the border, kept its minimum at $4.25. The two states had similar economies and similar fast-food industries. If the textbook model was right, New Jersey fast-food employment should fall relative to Pennsylvania's. The researchers surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants in both states before and after the increase.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
The result, published in the American Economic Review in 1994: fast-food employment in New Jersey rose by about 13% relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage increase. Stores that had been paying below the new minimum (those most affected by the law) actually increased employment more than stores paying above $5.00. The textbook prediction was decisively wrong, not just in magnitude but in sign.
What is the explanation? Several possibilities, each with some support in subsequent research:
Monopsony power. Many low-wage labor markets are dominated by a few employers (fast-food chains in a town, for example). A monopsonist already pays below the worker's marginal product. Raising the minimum wage can move closer to the competitive level — increasing employment, not decreasing it.
Efficiency wage effects. Higher wages reduce turnover and absenteeism, which firms find profitable. So a forced increase pays for itself.
Lower turnover means firms keep more workers, even if total hires do not change.
Modest pass-through to prices. Firms raise prices a little; consumers absorb the cost; nobody loses much.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
The Card-Krueger study sparked decades of follow-up research. Some critics (notably David Neumark and William Wascher in 2000) reanalyzed the data and found weaker positive employment effects but also no strong negative ones. The current consensus among labor economists, after thirty years of accumulated evidence: moderate minimum wage increases have small or even slightly positive effects on employment in most settings. Very large increases can create employment effects, but the threshold appears to be much higher than the standard textbook predicts. David Card was awarded the 2021 Nobel Prize in Economics for this and related work in labor economics, methodological work that established the "credibility revolution" in empirical economics.
The lesson for this textbook: when the simplest model predicts something dramatic, check whether real labor markets behave like the model assumes. Often they do not. The labor market is held together by frictions, relationships, and social norms that simple supply-and-demand diagrams omit entirely.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why the standard minimum wage diagram persists despite its failures
If the Card-Krueger evidence has held up for 30 years, why does every intro textbook still teach the standard "minimum wage destroys jobs" diagram first? Two reasons:
First, pedagogical clarity. The supply-and-demand model is easy to draw and easy to manipulate. Its predictions are sharp, even if often wrong. Students learn the diagram, learn how to shift the curves, and move on. Teaching the modern view requires acknowledging that labor markets are complex, evidence-based assessments are necessary, and there is not a single clean diagram that captures everything. That is pedagogically harder.
Second, political comfort. The standard prediction aligns with a particular political worldview: government intervention in markets is bad, prices should clear, and minimum wages hurt the people they are meant to help. Acknowledging that the prediction is empirically weak undercuts that political narrative, and so the textbook treatment lives on despite the evidence.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
My approach in this textbook: teach the standard model, but always note when the empirics disagree. On minimum wages specifically, the empirics disagree substantially with the textbook model for moderate increases. Take both seriously, weigh them, and form one's own view. That is what economics literacy actually requires.
— A.S.

14.heading: Why Wages Do not Fully Adjust: Four Theories
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.5 Wage rigidity and involuntary unemployment. If the real wage is held above the market-clearing level — by efficiency-wage considerations, contracts, insider bargaining power or a statutory minimum — the quantity of labor supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, and the difference is unemployment among workers who would accept work at the prevailing wage. The theories differ in why the wage does not fall, not in the geometry.

14.heading: Job Search Theory: A Simple Model
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why even rational job seekers stay unemployed for a while
Why an unemployed worker does not accept the first job offer received? Because not all jobs are equally good. Wages vary; benefits vary; locations vary; commutes vary; growth potential varies. A worker who accepts the first offer may end up in a worse job than one who waited somewhat longer for a better offer. Job search theory formalizes this trade-off: workers compare the expected gain from continued searching against the cost of remaining unemployed.
⚙ The Reservation Wage Rule
\[ \text{accept an offer if } w \ge w^{*} \]\(w^{*}\) is the reservation wage: the wage at which accepting and continuing to search are equally attractive.
w*
The reservation wage — the lowest wage at which the worker is just indifferent between accepting and continuing to search. Below w*, decline and keep searching. Above w*, accept.
w
The wage offered by a specific job.
What raises w* (makes workers pickier, increases unemployment duration):
More generous unemployment insurance (lower cost of staying unemployed)
Higher savings/wealth (worker can afford to wait)
Spousal income (household has another earner)

14.heading: Job Search Theory: A Simple Model
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
Belief that better offers will arrive soon (information about the market)
Higher skill (worker expects to be matched to a higher-paying job)
What lowers w* (makes workers less picky, shortens unemployment):
UI benefits expiring or reduced
Savings running out
Long unemployment spells (employers discount workers who have been jobless a long time)
Pessimism about labor market improvement

14.heading: Job Search Theory: A Simple Model
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
📐 Worked Example 14.2 — UI generosity and unemployment duration
An unemployed worker receives a job offer paying $22/hour. She estimates that if she keeps searching for another 4 weeks, she has a 50% chance of receiving a better offer paying $30/hour. Her unemployment insurance pays $15/hour-equivalent. (a) What is her expected value from waiting another 4 weeks? (b) Should she accept the $22 offer? (c) If her UI is cut to $8/hour-equivalent, does her decision change?
1
(a) Expected value of waiting 4 weeks: 50% chance of $30/hour offer, 50% chance of a $22/hour offer (or similar). Expected hourly wage if she waits: 0.5 × 30 + 0.5 × 22 = $26/hour. While she waits, she earns $15/hour-equivalent (UI). The wait period earnings: $15/hour × 160 hours = $2,400. Plus the expected wage gain over 1 year if she gets the $30 job: 0.5 × ($30 − $22) × 2,000 = $8,000.
2
(b) Decision: waiting yields about $10,400 in expected gain (UI received + expected wage premium). Cost of waiting: foregone wages of $22 × 160 = $3,520. Net gain from waiting: $10,400 − $3,520 ≈ $6,880. She should keep searching.
3

14.heading: Job Search Theory: A Simple Model
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body:
(c) UI cut to $8/hour: wait-period earnings drop to $8 × 160 = $1,280. Expected wage gain unchanged at $8,000. Net gain from waiting: $9,280 − $3,520 = $5,760. Still positive — she should still wait. But the gain has shrunk substantially. For workers with worse expected offers or shorter time horizons, a UI cut would flip the decision toward accepting now.
This is the canonical insight from search theory: generous unemployment insurance lengthens unemployment spells (workers wait for better offers) but also raises the quality of matches (workers find better-fitting jobs). The U.S. has historically had less generous UI than European countries, leading to shorter unemployment durations but lower-quality matches. The 2020-2021 pandemic UI expansion ($600/week federal supplement) was the largest U.S. labor-market natural experiment in decades, raising reservation wages dramatically and contributing to the matching difficulty firms experienced in 2021-2022.

14.heading: Job Search Theory: A Simple Model
14.title: Chapter 14, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
14.body: Figure 14.6 The job-search decision. A worker who expects better offers to arrive turns down an offer below a threshold wage, because accepting forecloses the option of continuing to search. Unemployment of this kind is voluntary in the narrow sense and efficient in a range: a good match found in six weeks is worth more than a poor one accepted immediately. It also explains why unemployment insurance raises measured unemployment somewhat while improving the quality of the eventual match.

15.heading: Overview
15.title: Chapter 15, Unemployment How we measure who is out of work, why some unemployment never disappears, why the 2020-2024 U.S. labor market broke many standard textbook models — and why the most important diagram in modern labor economics deserves more attention than it usually gets in introductory cour
15.body:
📘 Principles Level — The labor market is not one market
The headline unemployment rate hides enormous variation across groups. In April 2023, when overall U-3 was 3.4%, the unemployment rate for white workers was 3.1%, for Black workers 4.7%, for Hispanic workers 4.4%, for teenagers 9.2%, and for college graduates 1.9%. These gaps reflect deep structural differences in labor market access — discrimination, geographic mismatch, network effects, and educational disparities.
Demographics also matter for understanding the trend. The U.S. unemployment rate of the 1980s averaged 7.3%; the 2010s averaged 6.2%; the 2020s so far has averaged 5.4%. Part of this decline reflects an aging workforce (older workers have lower unemployment) and a more-educated workforce (educated workers have lower unemployment). The "natural rate" we discussed in §14.2 has likely fallen 1-1.5 percentage points over the past 40 years primarily because of these demographic shifts.

🎮 MacroNations Connection — Unemployment in the Engine
The engine tracks unemployment as a state variable derived from Okun's law: Δunemployment = −0.5 × (gdp_growth − potential). NAIRU is hardcoded at 4.5%. Unemployment feeds the Equality pillar's unemp_pts component (40 of 200, full marks at u ≤ 3%, zero at u = 15%), and contributes to Gini via unemp_gini = 0.5 × max(0, u − 4.5) — high unemployment raises inequality. Levers that lower unemployment in the engine: gov_spending_pct (via 1.4× multiplier raising gdp_growth, which Okun then translates to lower u with 1-round lag), interest_rate_target reductions (via the −0.5/pp monetary boost to gdp_growth), and slow-moving supply-side levers (rd_investment, infrastructure) that raise potential and thus permit higher growth without overheating. There is no separate "labor market flexibility" lever — the engine does not model structural reforms separately.
