15.heading: Insight
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
The AD-AS framework is the closest thing macroeconomics has to a unified short-run model. It connects every macro topic one has learned: GDP measurement (Chapter 7), money supply (Chapter 11), inflation (Chapter 12), unemployment (Chapter 14). Every Fed press conference uses its language, even if not explicitly. Every recession is explained through it. Learning to use it well is the single biggest payoff for any introductory macroeconomics student.
But the framework has real limits, and pretending otherwise does the reader a disservice. The standard textbook treatment makes three assumptions that frequently fail: that aggregate supply is well-behaved in the short run, that demand and supply shocks can be cleanly separated, and that the price level adjusts smoothly to clear markets. In the 2020-2024 episode, all three failed simultaneously. The framework still gave us most of the right intuitions about the 2022 inflation peak and the 2023 disinflation — but only if one knew how to bend the standard diagrams to fit unusual circumstances. That kind of bending is what real macroeconomists do every day.
— A.S.

15.heading: The Aggregate Demand Curve
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why total spending falls when the price level rises
The aggregate demand (AD) curve shows the relationship between the overall price level (P) and the total quantity of goods and services demanded in the economy (Y). It slopes downward: when the price level is higher, people demand less real output. This is superficially similar to a microeconomic demand curve, but the reasons are entirely different — and worth understanding precisely, because they shape policy thinking.
📚 Three reasons the AD curve slopes downward
Wealth effect
(Sometimes called the Pigou effect after A. C. Pigou.) When the price level rises, the real value of money holdings and other nominal assets falls. People feel poorer. They cut back on consumption. Quantitatively small in the modern U.S. economy because most household wealth is in inflation-protected forms like real estate and equity.
Interest rate effect

15.heading: The Aggregate Demand Curve
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
(Sometimes called the Keynes effect.) When the price level rises, households need more cash to make the same nominal transactions. This raises the demand for money, which pushes up the equilibrium interest rate. Higher rates reduce investment (firms) and durable-goods consumption (households). The largest of the three effects in modern economies.
Exchange-rate effect
(Sometimes called the Mundell-Fleming effect.) When the price level rises, domestic goods become more expensive relative to foreign goods (real exchange rate appreciates). Net exports fall. Important for small open economies; modest for the U.S.
Together, these three effects mean: a higher price level reduces the quantity of real output demanded. The AD curve slopes downward, but for fundamentally macroeconomic reasons — money, interest rates, exchange rates — not because of the simple substitution-and-income-effect logic of microeconomic demand curves.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — What shifts AD
\[ Y = C + I + G + NX \]
C
Consumption. Shifts AD when: consumer confidence changes, wealth changes (stock market booms or crashes), expected future income changes, taxes change.
I

15.heading: The Aggregate Demand Curve
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Investment. Shifts AD when: business confidence changes, interest rates change for non-price-level reasons (Fed policy), tax incentives for investment change, expected future demand changes.
G
Government purchases. Shifts AD when: Congress passes spending bills, military spending changes, infrastructure investment changes.
NX
Net exports. Shifts AD when: foreign GDP changes, exchange rates change for non-price-level reasons, trade policy changes.
Critical distinction: a change in the price level causes movement along the AD curve. A change in any of these other variables causes the AD curve to shift. Confusing the two is the most common student error in this chapter — and a frequent error in policy commentary too.

15.heading: The Aggregate Demand Curve
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Treating AD like a microeconomic demand curve
The AD curve looks like the demand curve from Chapter 4, but they describe completely different things. A microeconomic demand curve relates the price of one good to the quantity of that good demanded. The AD curve relates the overall price level (P, the average price of all goods) to total real output (Y).
When the price of apples rises, people substitute toward oranges — that is the microeconomic story. When the overall price level rises, there is nothing to substitute toward; all prices have gone up. The AD curve slopes down for entirely different reasons (wealth, interest rate, exchange rate effects). Do not import substitution logic from microeconomics; it does not apply.

15.heading: The Aggregate Demand Curve
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Figure 15.1 The aggregate demand curve. It slopes downward for reasons quite distinct from those behind an individual demand curve: a lower price level raises the real value of money-denominated wealth, lowers the interest rate consistent with a given money stock, and depreciates the real exchange rate. All three raise the quantity of output demanded.
Figure 15.2 What moves aggregate demand. The curve slopes downward because a lower price level raises real balances, lowers the interest rate and improves competitiveness abroad. Anything that raises desired spending at a given price level — monetary easing, fiscal expansion, stronger foreign demand, improved confidence — shifts the whole curve rightward. Distinguishing a movement along the curve from a shift of it is the single most common source of error in applying the model.

15.heading: The Aggregate Supply Curve: Two Time Horizons
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why the supply story splits in two
The aggregate supply (AS) curve shows the relationship between the price level and the total quantity of goods and services that firms in the economy produce. Unlike AD, the shape of the AS curve depends critically on the time horizon. In the long run, total output is determined entirely by real factors — technology, capital, labor, institutions (Chapter 9). The price level has no effect. The long-run aggregate supply curve (LRAS) is vertical at potential GDP.
In the short run, the price level matters. The short-run aggregate supply curve (SRAS) is upward-sloping: higher prices induce firms to produce more, at least temporarily. The economy can deviate from potential output for a while, but it always returns to LRAS in the long run.
📚 Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) — vertical at potential output
What determines its position
Real factors that drive long-run growth: capital stock, labor force, productivity, technology, natural resources, institutional quality. Not the price level. Not the money supply. Y* = potential output, the level of real GDP the economy can sustain at full employment.
What shifts LRAS rightward

15.heading: The Aggregate Supply Curve: Two Time Horizons
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
More capital (investment), more labor (immigration, higher participation), better technology, productivity improvements, better institutions, lower regulatory drag (when starting from heavy regulation). Anything from Chapter 9 that raises long-run growth shifts LRAS right.
What shifts LRAS leftward
Destruction of capital (war, natural disaster), shrinking labor force, technological regress (rare). Truly leftward shifts of LRAS are uncommon but devastating when they occur — for example, the COVID pandemic temporarily lowered LRAS in 2020 due to mass deaths, lost work hours, and disrupted productivity.
📚 Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS) — upward-sloping
Three theories of why SRAS slopes up
Sticky-wage theory: nominal wages are set in advance by contract or by social norm. When prices rise unexpectedly, real wages fall, making labor cheaper for firms. Firms hire more workers and produce more. (Chapter 14: wages are highly sticky downward; less sticky upward.)

15.heading: The Aggregate Supply Curve: Two Time Horizons
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Sticky-price theory: firms set nominal prices in advance and adjust them only periodically (menu costs, contracts, etc.). When the general price level rises and firms have not yet adjusted their own prices, their products look relatively cheap; demand for their goods rises; they produce more.
Misperception theory: producers see prices rising in their own market and mistakenly think this is a real price increase (a profit opportunity) rather than general inflation. They produce more in response. Once they realize the price rise is general, output returns to potential.
What shifts SRAS rightward
Anything that lowers production costs at every price level: falling input prices (lower oil, lower commodity prices, lower wages), favorable supply shocks (good weather for agriculture, technological breakthroughs), expectations of lower future inflation. Increases in productivity show up here in the short run.
What shifts SRAS leftward

15.heading: The Aggregate Supply Curve: Two Time Horizons
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Anything that raises production costs at every price level: rising input prices (oil shock, commodity price spike, wage spike), adverse supply shocks (drought, pandemic, supply-chain disruption), expectations of higher future inflation. This is what happened in 1973-74 with OPEC, and again — partly — in 2021-22 with the pandemic supply-chain disruptions.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Short-Run vs. Long-Run Output
\[ Y = Y^{*} + \alpha\,(P - P^{e}), \qquad \alpha > 0 \]
Y*
Potential output (LRAS).
P
Actual price level.
\(P^{e}\)
Expected price level (formed before the period begins). Key driver of how SRAS shifts over time.
α
A positive constant capturing how strongly output responds to price-level surprises. Larger α = flatter SRAS.
Reading this: output exceeds potential when actual prices exceed expected; output falls short of potential when actual prices fall short of expected. This is the formal expression of "demand surprises raise output in the short run, but only as long as the surprise persists." Once expectations adjust (\(P^{e}\) catches up to P), output returns to Y*.

15.heading: The Aggregate Supply Curve: Two Time Horizons
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body: Figure 15.3 Aggregate supply over two horizons. In the long run output is determined by technology, capital and labor, so the curve is vertical at potential output and the price level is determined by demand alone. In the short run, nominal wages and prices adjust slowly, so a higher price level raises output, and the curve slopes upward. Long-run equilibrium is where all three curves intersect.

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
📘 Principles Level — Four types of shocks, four outcomes
The economy is in equilibrium where AD intersects SRAS. In long-run equilibrium, that intersection also sits on LRAS at potential output Y*. Shocks move the economy away from long-run equilibrium temporarily. The standard framework identifies four pure cases.
The four pure types of macroeconomic shocks
ShockWhat movesEffect on PEffect on Y & unemployment
Positive demand shock
AD shifts right
Rises
Y rises, unemployment falls. Boom. Examples: fiscal stimulus, Fed easing, sudden surge in consumer confidence.
Negative demand shock
AD shifts left
Falls (or rises slowly)
Y falls, unemployment rises. Demand-driven recession. Examples: 2008-09 financial crisis, 2001 dot-com bust, sudden collapse in consumer or investment confidence.
Positive supply shock
SRAS shifts right
Falls
Y rises, unemployment falls. The dream scenario. Examples: technological breakthrough, falling oil prices, productivity surge, immigration of skilled workers.
Negative supply shock
SRAS shifts left
Rises

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body: Y falls, unemployment rises. Stagflation — the worst case. Examples: 1973 OPEC oil embargo, 2022 Russia-Ukraine energy shock, pandemic supply-chain disruptions, droughts.

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
⚠ Why stagflation is the policy nightmare
Demand shocks have a happy property: prices and output move in the same direction. A recession (Y down, P down) calls for Fed easing, which raises both. A boom (Y up, P up) calls for tightening, which lowers both. Monetary policy can stabilize both at once.
Supply shocks are the nightmare. They push prices and output in opposite directions. A negative supply shock raises P and lowers Y. If the Fed tightens to fight inflation, it lowers Y further. If the Fed eases to support output, it raises P further. There is no clean policy response. This is why the 1970s, with their repeated supply shocks, were so devastating for monetary policy — and why central bankers are particularly afraid of supply shocks even today.

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Long-Run Self-Correction
\[ \begin{aligned} Y > Y^{*} &\;\Rightarrow\; P^{e} \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; \text{SRAS shifts left} \;\Rightarrow\; Y \to Y^{*} \\ Y < Y^{*} &\;\Rightarrow\; P^{e} \downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; \text{SRAS shifts right} \;\Rightarrow\; Y \to Y^{*} \end{aligned} \]
Y > Y*
Economy is booming above potential. Tight labor markets push up wages. Firms raise prices. Workers and firms start expecting higher inflation (\(P^{e}\) rises). SRAS shifts left. Eventually Y returns to Y*, but at a permanently higher price level.
Y < Y*
Economy in recession below potential. High unemployment pushes down wage demands. Firms cut prices. Expectations of lower inflation set in. SRAS shifts right. Eventually Y returns to Y*. But this self-correction can be very slow if wages are sticky downward (Chapter 14), which is why recessions can persist for years.

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
The asymmetry matters: the upward adjustment (Y above Y* → SRAS left) tends to happen reasonably fast because wages and prices adjust upward easily. The downward adjustment (Y below Y* → SRAS right) is slow because wages are sticky downward. This asymmetry is one major reason Keynesian economists argue for active policy intervention during recessions: the natural correction mechanism works much faster going down (preventing booms) than going up (escaping recessions).
Figure 15.4 A contraction in aggregate demand. In the short run the economy moves from A to B: both output and the price level fall, and a recessionary gap opens between actual and potential output. The gap is closed either by policy that restores demand or, more slowly, by nominal wages and prices falling far enough to shift the short-run supply curve down — which is the adjustment the 1930s showed can take a very long time.

15.heading: Putting It Together: Equilibrium and Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Figure 15.5 An adverse supply shock. The short-run supply curve shifts up and to the left: the price level rises while output falls. This is stagflation, and it presents the central policy dilemma of the model — demand policy can offset the output loss or the price increase, but not both, because any movement along the demand curve improves one at the expense of the other.
Figure 15.6 How a boom ends without policy. An expansion moves the economy along the short-run supply curve from A to B, with output above potential. The tight labor market then raises nominal wages, the short-run supply curve shifts up, and the economy returns to potential output at C with a permanently higher price level. The adjustment is the mechanism behind the proposition that demand policy determines prices in the long run and output only in the short run.

15.heading: Case Studies: Two Defining Supply Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
1973–1975
United States
OPEC Oil Embargo
The Classic Negative Supply Shock
On October 17, 1973, the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) announced an oil embargo against the United States and several allies in response to U.S. support for Israel in the Yom Kippur War. Over the following five months, crude oil prices quadrupled — from about $3 per barrel in September 1973 to roughly $12 per barrel by March 1974. The shock was both sudden and economy-wide. Energy is an input to virtually every good and service produced in a modern economy. When energy prices spike, the cost of producing everything else rises in proportion.
In the AD-AS framework, this is a textbook negative supply shock: SRAS shifts left. The predicted result: higher prices, lower output, higher unemployment. The actual result fit the prediction almost perfectly:
Inflation jumped from 3.4% in 1972 to 12.3% in 1974 — the highest peacetime rate since 1947.
Real GDP contracted in five of the six quarters from late 1973 through early 1975. Output fell about 3% peak-to-trough.
Unemployment rose from 4.6% in October 1973 to 9.0% in May 1975, the highest since World War II.

15.heading: Case Studies: Two Defining Supply Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
The Fed faced a genuine policy dilemma. Inflation called for tightening. The recession called for easing. The Fed at first tried to do both — alternately tightening and loosening — and accomplished neither goal. The episode left inflation embedded in expectations for the rest of the 1970s, requiring the brutal Volcker disinflation of 1980-83 to root out. The 1973-75 episode is the canonical case study taught in nearly every macro textbook because it fits the AD-AS framework so cleanly. It is also why every modern central bank treats supply shocks with extreme caution.
2020–2024
United States
The combined-shock episode
The Pandemic: A Triple Shock That Broke Standard Models
The COVID-19 pandemic and its policy response was the most complex AD-AS episode in modern U.S. history. Unlike 1973, the 2020-2022 period involved multiple simultaneous shocks of different signs and types:

15.heading: Case Studies: Two Defining Supply Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Phase 1 — Spring 2020: a simultaneous demand AND supply collapse. Lockdowns shut down restaurants, gyms, travel, and in-person services — that is a demand collapse. Lockdowns also closed factories, broke supply chains, and removed workers from production — that is a supply collapse. AD shifted hard left, and SRAS shifted hard left at the same time. The result: GDP fell 9.1% in a single quarter (Q2 2020) — the largest quarterly drop ever recorded. But surprisingly, inflation initially fell. CPI rose only 0.6% in 2020. The demand collapse dominated, and the price level effects of the two shocks partially offset.
Phase 2 — 2021: massive positive demand shock collides with continuing supply problems. Federal stimulus payments, expanded unemployment insurance, and zero interest rates pushed AD sharply right. Supply chains were still snarled, semiconductor shortages persisted, and millions of workers had retired or dropped out (Chapter 14's outward Beveridge curve shift). AD up, SRAS still partly suppressed. Result: prices started rising fast, but the economy did not fully recover potential output until 2022. CPI inflation jumped from 1.4% in January 2021 to 7.0% by December 2021.

15.heading: Case Studies: Two Defining Supply Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Phase 3 — 2022: Russia invades Ukraine, oil and food prices spike. A pure negative supply shock layered on top of the existing demand-supply imbalance. SRAS shifted further left. Oil rose from $76 to $120 per barrel in three months. Wheat prices doubled. CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022 — the highest reading in 40 years. Unemployment, somehow, stayed at 3.6%. The Phillips curve relationship between unemployment and inflation appeared to vanish.
Phase 4 — 2023-2024: the "immaculate disinflation". The Fed raised rates from near zero to 5.25-5.50% over 18 months — the fastest tightening cycle in 40 years. Inflation fell sharply: from 9.1% (June 2022) to 3.1% (June 2023) to 2.4% (September 2024). But output kept growing. Unemployment barely budged from 3.5-4.0%. The standard textbook prediction was that this kind of disinflation should require a recession. It did not.

15.heading: Case Studies: Two Defining Supply Shocks
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
What this case teaches: the AD-AS framework correctly predicted the directions of most movements — demand-driven inflation in 2021-22, supply-side amplification in 2022. But the framework's standard treatment of the supply curve, and its prediction that disinflation requires recession, failed substantially in 2023-24. The most plausible explanation: the 2023 inflation decline came largely from the supply side normalizing (supply chains repaired, workers returning, energy markets stabilizing) — i.e., SRAS shifting right — combined with credible Fed commitment that kept inflation expectations from drifting up. Standard AD-AS accounts for most of the story; the unusual nature of the supply curve's behavior accounts for the rest.
Figure 15.7 Stagflation in the 1970s. Inflation and unemployment rose together while output fell, a combination that no shift of aggregate demand can generate: demand shocks move the two in opposite directions. An adverse supply shock does exactly this, which is why the decade is the standard case for the proposition that the source of a shock, and not only its size, determines what policy can achieve.

15.heading: Interactive: The AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
🎛 Interactive — AD-AS Equilibrium
Shift AD and SRAS; see prices, output, and unemployment respond
Aggregate Demand shift (AD): 0
Short-Run Aggregate Supply shift (SRAS): 0
What is being observed: the blue AD curve slopes down (price level on Y, output on X); the red SRAS curve slopes up; the gray LRAS is vertical at potential output Y*. The green dot is the short-run equilibrium. The dashed lines show the original (pre-shock) curves. Drag the sliders or click a preset to see each case.

15.heading: Interactive: The AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — When the standard diagram misleads
The standard AD-AS diagram assumes that aggregate demand and aggregate supply move independently. In 2020 they did not. Lockdowns simultaneously suppressed AD (people could not go out) and SRAS (factories could not operate). The standard "shift one curve at a time" exercise does not capture this kind of correlated shock. Real policymakers had to think about the two shocks together and decide which was dominant for inflation (in 2020: the demand collapse) and for output (in 2020: roughly equal).
The standard diagram also assumes a stable mapping from output to unemployment via Okun's Law. In 2020-2022 that relationship broke down. Unemployment fell to 3.4% in April 2023, the lowest since 1969, while output grew at a moderate pace and inflation cooled rapidly. The labor market and product market decoupled in ways the standard models would not have predicted.

15.heading: Interactive: The AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
The argument here is not that the AD-AS model should be discarded. The model is the most useful single framework in macroeconomics. But every model is a simplification. When the simplification fails, one needs to know which assumption broke and reason directly from first principles. The 2020-2024 episode was the most consequential test of macroeconomic models in our lifetimes, and the lesson is that frameworks must be applied with judgment, not memorized as catechism.
— A.S.

15.heading: Worked Examples: Reading the AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
📐 Worked Example 15.1 — Tracing a demand-driven recession
An economy starts in long-run equilibrium at Y = 100 and P = 100. The 2008 financial crisis hits: household wealth falls, consumer confidence collapses, and credit becomes scarce. Trace the short-run and long-run effects on Y, P, and unemployment, using the AD-AS framework.
1
Identify the shock: the wealth-and-confidence shock reduces consumption and investment. AD shifts left. No direct effect on production technology, so SRAS and LRAS are unchanged.
2
Short-run effects: at the new (lower) AD curve, the intersection with the unchanged SRAS occurs at lower Y and lower P. So Y < Y* and P < original P. Output falls, prices fall (or rise more slowly), and by Okun's Law, unemployment rises. This matches the 2008-09 data: GDP fell 4.3% peak-to-trough; CPI inflation collapsed from 5.6% (July 2008) to −2.1% (July 2009); unemployment rose from 5.0% to 10.0%.
3

15.heading: Worked Examples: Reading the AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
Long-run effects (if no policy response): the recession lowers wage demands, which gradually shifts SRAS rightward. Lower nominal wages reduce production costs at every price level. Over time, the SRAS shift restores Y to Y*, but at an even lower price level. Self-correction works, but slowly — wages are sticky downward (Chapter 14).
4
With monetary policy response: the Fed cuts rates to zero (Dec 2008) and undertakes quantitative easing. This shifts AD back rightward toward its original position. The recovery is faster than self-correction would have been, though still slow because of the depth of the shock and zero-lower-bound constraints.
The 2008-09 episode is the cleanest demand-shock case study in modern U.S. history. AD-AS gets the directions and rough magnitudes right. The persistence of the recovery (it took until 2014 for unemployment to fall below 6%) reflects the depth of the shock and the slow nature of self-correction — features the static diagram captures only in spirit, not in timing.

15.heading: Worked Examples: Reading the AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
📐 Worked Example 15.2 — A negative supply shock with fiscal response
An economy in long-run equilibrium suddenly faces a 100% increase in global oil prices (a la 1973 or 2022). The government considers fiscal stimulus to offset the recession. Trace the consequences and explain why the policy response is fraught.
1
The shock: oil is an input to nearly all production. Production costs rise at every price level. SRAS shifts left.
2
Short-run effects of the shock alone: with AD unchanged and SRAS shifted left, the new equilibrium has lower Y and higher P. Stagflation: recession plus inflation. This is the worst possible combination for policy.
3
Fiscal stimulus response: the government increases spending or cuts taxes to combat the recession. This shifts AD right. Result: Y rises back toward Y*, but P rises further. The recession is partially offset, but inflation gets worse.
4

15.heading: Worked Examples: Reading the AD-AS Diagram
15.title: Chapter 15, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
15.body:
The trade-off cannot be escaped. Fighting the recession (rightward AD shift) makes inflation worse. Fighting inflation (leftward AD shift, or central bank tightening) makes the recession worse. With pure supply shocks, monetary and fiscal policy face a no-win choice — they can pick between recession with stable prices, or growth with high inflation, but not both at once.
This is why supply shocks are uniquely difficult for policy. The 1973-1975 episode produced both a recession and double-digit inflation simultaneously, and U.S. policy lost credibility for nearly a decade trying to find a stable response. The 2022 episode could have repeated this disaster — but the Fed's quick and aggressive tightening, combined with the fact that the supply-chain disruption normalized in 2023, allowed for a much better outcome. The 1973-75 mistake was treating the supply shock with policies designed for demand shocks. The 2022-24 response, by contrast, was tightening even at the cost of growth — and it paid off.

16.heading: Overview
16.title: Chapter 16, Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply The most important framework in short-run macroeconomics — what it explains beautifully, where it visibly breaks, and the case study (2020-2024) that simultaneously confirms and complicates everything it predicts In early 2022, U.S. inflation was run
16.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — AD-AS in the Engine
The MacroNations engine implements AD-AS implicitly through its GDP and inflation equations. Aggregate demand shifts come from gov_spending_pct (1.4× multiplier), tax_rate (−1.1× multiplier), and interest_rate_target (−0.5/pp monetary impulse). Aggregate supply shifts come from rd_investment, infrastructure, and green_energy — these raise potential over 3-5 rounds, shifting LRAS rightward. Supply shocks are implemented as crisis shocks: a pandemic crisis subtracts 4pp from gdp_growth and adds 1.5pp to inflation simultaneously — exactly an SRAS leftward shift. The four-shock typology shows up in pillar scoring: demand booms raise GDP score short-term but cost Stability via inflation; supply shocks cost both pillars simultaneously; positive supply shocks (sustained R&D investment) raise GDP and Stability together by lifting potential without raising inflation. This is why patient R&D investment is uniquely valuable — it is the only lever that improves all five pillars simultaneously over time.

16.heading: Insight
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
IS-LM was developed in 1937 by John Hicks as a graphical interpretation of John Maynard Keynes's General Theory. For most of the next sixty years, it was THE framework macroeconomists used to think about short-run policy. Every macroeconomics PhD student learned it. Every Fed staff economist used it. Every undergrad textbook from Samuelson through the 1990s built on it. And then it stopped working. The 2008-2014 zero-lower-bound period exposed structural assumptions in the model that had been invisible during normal times. Modern central banks have largely moved on — they think in terms of interest rate rules and inflation targets, not money supplies and LM curves.

16.heading: Insight
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
But IS-LM still has enormous pedagogical value. It teaches the crucial insight that monetary and fiscal policy interact — that the effects of one depend on what the other is doing — in a way no other simple model captures. It teaches the concept of crowding out. It teaches why central bank independence matters. It teaches the liquidity trap — the situation where conventional monetary policy stops working because interest rates have hit their lower bound. The aim is that the reader leaves this chapter knowing the standard model AND knowing exactly when not to trust it. That dual literacy is what separates someone who has taken intro macro from someone who actually understands modern monetary policy.
— A.S.

16.heading: The Goods Market and the IS Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📘 Principles Level — Where output is determined when prices are fixed
The IS curve describes equilibrium in the goods market. In the short run, the framework assumes the overall price level is sticky (this is the same sticky-price assumption we used to derive the upward-sloping SRAS curve in Chapter 15). With prices fixed, output adjusts to clear the market: whatever quantity people want to buy at the current price level, firms will produce. The IS curve traces out the combinations of interest rate (r) and output (Y) that keep this goods-market equilibrium intact.
Why does it slope downward? Because lower interest rates encourage investment — businesses borrow more to build factories, households borrow more to buy cars and houses — which raises total spending and therefore output. Higher rates do the opposite. So lower r ↔ higher Y, which is a downward-sloping curve when r is on the vertical axis and Y is on the horizontal axis.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Deriving the IS Curve
\[ Y = C(Y - T) + I(r) + G + NX \]
Y
Real output (the variable on the horizontal axis of the IS-LM diagram).
C(Y − T)

16.heading: The Goods Market and the IS Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Consumption as a function of disposable income. As Y rises and T (taxes) is fixed, consumption rises by the marginal propensity to consume (MPC). This builds in the Keynesian spending multiplier.
I(r)
Investment as a function of the interest rate. Crucial: this is where r enters the IS curve. As r rises, I falls. As r falls, I rises. This is the linchpin of the entire IS-LM story.
G
Government spending. Exogenous — chosen by Congress, not by the model. Shifts the IS curve when changed.
NX
Net exports. Treated as exogenous in the simple closed-economy version of IS-LM. Generalizations (the Mundell-Fleming model) make NX depend on the exchange rate.
Reading the IS curve: as r falls, I rises, which raises Y through both the direct increase in I and the multiplier effect on C. So lower r → higher equilibrium Y. The IS curve slopes downward in (r, Y) space.
What shifts IS right: higher G (fiscal stimulus), lower T (tax cuts), surge in business confidence (autonomous I rises), surge in consumer confidence (autonomous C rises), favorable exchange rate movements (NX rises). What shifts IS left: the opposite of each.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Why "IS"? The Investment-Saving Identity

16.heading: The Goods Market and the IS Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
\[ I(r) = S(Y) + (T - G) - NX \]Investment equals saving: private, public and foreign.
I(r)
Desired investment at interest rate r.
S(Y)
Private saving as a function of output.
T − G
Public saving (government surplus). Negative if there is a deficit.
−NX
Foreign saving inflow (capital imports from the rest of the world).
The original Hicksian intuition for the "IS" label: at every point on the IS curve, planned investment equals planned saving. Below the curve, planned I exceeds planned S, causing output to expand. Above the curve, planned S exceeds planned I, causing output to contract. Either way, the economy gravitates toward the IS line. This is the same accounting identity from Chapter 13 (S − I = NX), rearranged for the closed-economy and short-run context.

16.heading: The Goods Market and the IS Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Confusing the IS curve with a demand curve
The IS curve looks like a downward-sloping demand curve, and students often confuse the two. They are entirely different objects.
A demand curve fixes income and traces out how quantity responds to price. The IS curve fixes the goods-market equilibrium condition (S = I) and traces out how the equilibrium quantity Y responds to the interest rate r. Income is not held constant on the IS curve — it varies along the curve, and the variation matters for the multiplier effect. The IS curve is an equilibrium locus, not a demand schedule. If one remembers nothing else from this section, remember: the IS curve answers "what combinations of r and Y are consistent with goods-market equilibrium?", not "how much do people want to buy at each price?"

16.heading: The Goods Market and the IS Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Figure 16.1 The IS curve. Each point is a combination of the interest rate and output at which planned spending equals output. A lower interest rate raises investment and, through the multiplier, raises the output consistent with goods-market equilibrium. The curve is flatter the more sensitive investment is to the interest rate and the larger the multiplier.
Figure 16.2 What moves the IS curve. Each point on the curve is a rate and an output level at which planned spending equals output, so anything that raises planned spending at a given interest rate — higher government purchases, lower taxes, stronger investment confidence, stronger exports — shifts it rightward by the change times the multiplier. The slope is a separate matter: it reflects how sensitive investment is to the interest rate, and a steep curve is one on which monetary policy has little traction.

16.heading: The Money Market and the LM Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📘 Principles Level — Where the interest rate is determined when money supply is fixed
The LM curve describes equilibrium in the money market. The central bank chooses the money supply M (or so the model assumes). The demand for money depends on two things: it rises with income Y (more transactions need more cash) and falls with the interest rate r (higher r is the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing money instead of bonds). The LM curve traces out the combinations of r and Y at which the demand for real money balances equals the supply.
Why does it slope upward? Because higher Y raises money demand. To keep the money market in equilibrium with a fixed supply, something has to fall — and that something is the willingness to hold money, which falls when r rises. So higher Y must be matched by higher r along the LM curve.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Deriving the LM Curve
\[ \frac{M}{P} = L(Y, r) \]
M / P
Real money supply. M is the nominal money stock (controlled by the central bank). P is the price level (assumed fixed in the short run). Their ratio is the real value of money in the economy.
L(Y, r)

16.heading: The Money Market and the LM Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Real money demand. Rises with Y (more income → more transactions → need more money). Falls with r (higher r → bigger opportunity cost of holding money).
Reading the LM curve: if Y rises, money demand rises, and r must rise to bring demand back down to the fixed supply. So higher Y ↔ higher r along the curve. LM slopes upward.
What shifts LM right (downward): the central bank raises the money supply (M ↑) — historically done through open market operations, in which the central bank buys bonds from private banks and pays for them with newly-created reserves, putting more money into the banking system. This means at any Y, equilibrium r is lower. What shifts LM left (upward): central bank cuts M, or P rises (which lowers M/P even with fixed M). The COVID-era M2 expansion (Chapter 12) was an enormous rightward LM shift.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Why "LM"? Liquidity Preference and Money
\[ L(Y, r) = \frac{M}{P} \]Liquidity preference equals the real money supply.
L

16.heading: The Money Market and the LM Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Liquidity preference — Keynes's terminology, introduced in his 1936 General Theory. It just means "the demand for money." Keynes called it "liquidity preference" because it captures the public's preference for holding their wealth in liquid form (cash, which is immediately spendable) rather than in less liquid forms (bonds, which earn interest but must be sold first to spend). The function L expresses how strong this preference is at any given combination of income and interest rate.
M
The money supply (controlled by the central bank).
The original Hicksian intuition: at every point on the LM curve, the public's desired holdings of money equal the actual supply. Off the curve, money markets clear by interest-rate adjustment — bond prices rise or fall until people willingly hold the supply of money the central bank has chosen.

16.heading: The Money Market and the LM Curve
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body: Figure 16.3 The LM curve. Each point is a combination of output and the interest rate at which the demand for money equals a given supply. Higher output raises the transactions demand for money; with the quantity fixed, the interest rate must rise to restore equilibrium. A central bank that instead targets the interest rate replaces this curve with a horizontal policy line, which is the modern reformulation discussed later in the chapter.

16.heading: IS-LM Equilibrium: Where the Two Markets Clear Simultaneously
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📘 Principles Level — Combining the two curves
The two curves give us two relationships between r and Y: the IS curve (goods-market equilibrium, downward-sloping) and the LM curve (money-market equilibrium, upward-sloping). Both must hold at the same time for the economy to be in short-run equilibrium. Graphically, that means the equilibrium point is the intersection of the two curves. Algebraically, it is the unique pair (r*, Y*) that satisfies both equations simultaneously.
The power of the framework is that it makes it possible to ask: what happens to r and Y when something changes? The answer always involves shifting one or both curves and finding the new intersection.
Figure 16.4 Equilibrium in the IS-LM model and a fiscal expansion. The intersection gives the interest rate and output at which both the goods market and the money market clear. An increase in government purchases shifts IS to the right; output rises, but so does the interest rate, and the induced fall in investment is the crowding-out that makes the final increase in output smaller than the simple multiplier implies.

16.heading: Fiscal and Monetary Policy in IS-LM
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two levers, two effects
The IS-LM framework lets us see clearly what each kind of macroeconomic policy does. Fiscal policy (changes in G or T) shifts the IS curve. Monetary policy (changes in M) shifts the LM curve. Each shift has a predictable effect on equilibrium r and Y.
The four basic IS-LM policy experiments

⚙ Crowding Out — Why Fiscal Stimulus is Smaller Than the Multiplier Suggests
\[ \Delta G \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta Y \;\Rightarrow\; r \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; I(r) \downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta Y \text{ is reduced} \]
Step 1
Government spends an additional dollar. Total demand rises by $1 directly.
Step 2

16.heading: Fiscal and Monetary Policy in IS-LM
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Households earn that dollar, spend MPC of it on consumption. Other households earn that, and so on. The direct multiplier takes effect. Naive prediction: ΔY = ΔG × 1/(1−MPC).
Step 3
Higher Y raises money demand. With the money supply fixed, the interest rate rises (we move along the LM curve).
Step 4
Higher interest rates reduce private investment I(r). Some of the demand created by government spending is offset by reduced private investment. This is crowding out.
In summary: the actual change in Y is smaller than the naive multiplier predicts. How much smaller depends on the slope of the LM curve (how interest-rate-sensitive money demand is) and the slope of the IS curve (how interest-rate-sensitive investment is). This is one of the most important practical insights from IS-LM: fiscal stimulus is real, but it does not deliver the full multiplier — some of it leaks into higher rates instead of higher output.

16.heading: Fiscal and Monetary Policy in IS-LM
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body: Exception: when monetary policy "accommodates" fiscal expansion by also expanding M (shifting LM right alongside IS), crowding out can be avoided. This is what happened during World War II: the Fed pegged interest rates and let the money supply expand to finance war spending without raising r. Output rose dramatically without crowding out.

16.heading: Fiscal and Monetary Policy in IS-LM
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Believing the IS-LM model gives THE answer about crowding out
Whether crowding out is large or small in any specific situation depends entirely on parameters the model does not pin down. The slope of LM depends on how sensitive money demand is to interest rates. The slope of IS depends on how sensitive investment is to interest rates. In severe recessions with high unemployment, real-world estimates suggest crowding out is small and the multiplier is large (fiscal stimulus works well). In booms with full employment, crowding out is large and the multiplier is small. The model frames the question correctly but does not answer it. Quantitative estimates require empirical work that goes far beyond the diagram.

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — When the LM curve goes flat
Suppose the central bank lowers its policy interest rate — the very short-term overnight rate the central bank directly controls (in the U.S. this is the federal funds rate; in the U.K. the Bank Rate; in the eurozone the deposit facility rate) — to zero. Can monetary policy push it lower? In principle, slightly — a few major economies (the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, Switzerland) have experimented with mildly negative policy rates. But there is a hard practical limit: if interest rates become sufficiently negative, people just hold paper cash, which yields exactly zero. So rates cannot go far below zero. This is the zero lower bound (ZLB) — sometimes called the effective lower bound (ELB) because the true floor is slightly below zero, not exactly at zero.

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
At the ZLB, monetary policy as conventionally understood is stuck. The central bank can flood the economy with money, but if rates cannot fall further, money demand is infinitely elastic at the ZLB — any extra money just sits as bank reserves earning the floor rate. The LM curve becomes horizontal at r = 0. In IS-LM terms, the economy is in a liquidity trap: shifts in the LM curve do nothing to r, and therefore nothing to Y.
This is exactly the prediction that Keynes had warned about in 1936, and what Hicks's IS-LM model formalized in 1937 — though for much of the postwar era many macroeconomists treated the zero-lower-bound case as a theoretical edge case that was unlikely to bind in practice. Then it happened, twice.
2008–2015
United States
Zero Lower Bound
Seven Years at the Zero Lower Bound — IS-LM's Most Famous Test

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
In December 2008, the Federal Reserve cut the federal funds rate to a target range of 0 to 0.25%, where it remained until December 2015. Seven years. During that period, the Fed expanded its balance sheet through three rounds of quantitative easing (QE1 in 2008-10, QE2 in 2010-11, QE3 in 2012-14), growing from $900 billion in 2008 to $4.5 trillion by 2015. In standard IS-LM terms, these were enormous rightward shifts of the LM curve. The standard model's prediction: with rates already at zero, these shifts should do nothing to output. The economy was in a liquidity trap.
The actual outcome was more nuanced. The QE rounds appear to have had some effect on long-term interest rates (which were not at zero) by changing the composition of the central bank's balance sheet, and may have affected inflation expectations. Most empirical studies find QE was modestly stimulative — far less powerful than conventional rate cuts would have been, but not literally zero as standard IS-LM predicted.

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Where IS-LM was clearly right: conventional monetary policy reached its limit. The Fed could not stimulate further by cutting rates; it had to invent new tools. And the recovery was painfully slow. Real GDP did not return to its pre-crisis trend until 2014. Unemployment took until late 2015 to fall below 5%. The 2008-09 episode is the strongest evidence in modern macroeconomic history that the liquidity trap is real, and that policymakers should be very cautious about letting nominal rates get close to zero.
This was also the period that effectively killed the conventional money-supply-based view of monetary policy embedded in LM. The Fed could not even define a single useful "money supply" anymore — broader aggregates like M2 grew dramatically, but most of the growth sat as bank reserves rather than circulating in the economy. Trying to track monetary policy through M became hopeless. Central banks shifted decisively to interest-rate-based frameworks.
2020–2022
United States
Pandemic-era ZLB
The COVID Lower-Bound Episode — Faster, Sharper, Different

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
The U.S. hit the ZLB a second time in March 2020. The Fed cut rates from 1.50-1.75% to 0-0.25% in two emergency moves over twelve days. This time, the ZLB period lasted only twenty-two months (until March 2022) rather than seven years. The Fed combined zero rates with another aggressive QE program, expanding its balance sheet from $4.3 trillion to $9 trillion. The recovery was also dramatically faster — unemployment fell from 14.8% (April 2020) to 6.7% (December 2020) to 3.9% (December 2021).
But the COVID ZLB period was different in one critical respect: it was paired with enormous fiscal stimulus. The CARES Act (March 2020), the December 2020 supplemental, and the American Rescue Plan (March 2021) together amounted to nearly $5 trillion of direct fiscal injection — roughly 25% of GDP across three packages. In IS-LM terms, this was an unprecedented rightward IS shift, made possible by the LM curve being flat at zero (no crowding out via interest rates since rates could not rise).

16.heading: The Liquidity Trap and the Zero Lower Bound
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
This is exactly the IS-LM prescription for a liquidity trap: monetary policy is impotent, so fiscal policy must do the heavy lifting, and the flat LM means no crowding out. The outcome — rapid output recovery, eventually accompanied by inflation — is precisely what the model would predict for that combination of policies. The 2020-2022 episode is in some ways the cleanest large-scale validation of the IS-LM logic about fiscal-monetary interaction at the ZLB that we have.
Figure 16.5 The liquidity trap. Where the nominal interest rate is already at its lower bound the LM curve is effectively horizontal: additional money is absorbed into balances rather than pushing the rate lower, so monetary expansion alone does little. Fiscal expansion, by contrast, raises output with no offsetting rise in the interest rate, which is why the estimated fiscal multiplier is larger at the bound than away from it.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why central banks no longer think in terms of LM
If one walks into any major central bank today — the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan — and ask the staff economists how they think about monetary policy, one will not hear them talk about LM curves or money supplies. One will hear them talk about interest rate rules: the central bank sets the short-term policy rate based on a reaction function that responds to inflation and output. The money supply is whatever it has to be to implement the chosen rate; it is not itself a policy instrument.
This shift in thinking — from "central bank chooses M, the LM curve determines r" to "central bank chooses r directly, M adjusts passively" — has been formalized in what is sometimes called the IS-MP model. The MP curve replaces LM. It traces out the interest rate the central bank will set as a function of output (and inflation, though that is typically suppressed in the simple version). It is usually drawn as a flat or slightly upward-sloping horizontal line at the central bank's chosen rate.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
In the IS-MP version, the policy story becomes simpler: fiscal expansion shifts IS right, and unless the central bank "accommodates" by holding rates fixed (flat MP) or raises rates (upward MP shift), output rises until inflation pressure builds, at which point the central bank tightens. There is no LM curve to worry about, no money supply to track, no shift in M that might or might not transmit to rates.
⚙ A Taylor-Style MP Rule
The most influential reaction function in modern monetary policy is the Taylor rule, proposed by Stanford economist John B. Taylor in 1993. The rule says the central bank should respond to two things: how far inflation is from its target, and how far output is from potential. Taylor showed that a simple formula along these lines actually fit how the Fed had behaved from 1987 to 1992 — making it both a recommendation for what central banks should do and a reasonable description of what they actually were doing.
\[ r = r^{*} + \phi_{\pi}\,(\pi - \pi^{*}) + \phi_{Y}\,\frac{Y - Y^{*}}{Y^{*}} \]
r*
The "neutral" or "equilibrium" real interest rate the central bank would set when inflation is at target and output equals potential.
π − π*

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
Inflation gap. Positive when inflation exceeds target.
Y − Y*
Output gap. Positive when output exceeds potential.
φ values
Reaction coefficients. Taylor (1993) suggested \(\phi_{\pi } = 1.5\) and \(\phi_{Y} = 0.5\) as reasonable values matching Fed behavior 1987-1992. The Taylor principle — a foundational requirement for stable monetary policy — says that \(\phi_{\pi }\) must be greater than 1. Translation: when inflation rises by 1 percentage point, the central bank must raise nominal rates by more than 1 percentage point, so that the real rate (nominal minus inflation) actually rises. If the central bank raises nominal rates by less than the inflation increase, real rates fall, which stimulates demand and pushes inflation higher — a self-reinforcing spiral. The 1970s great inflation is often blamed partly on Fed violations of this principle.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body: This is the modern monetary policy framework. It quietly replaces LM. The "money market" in LM is gone — replaced by an explicit policy reaction function. The 2022-2024 Fed tightening cycle was a textbook implementation: inflation rose from 2% to 9%, so the Fed raised rates by 525 basis points to bring real rates from deeply negative to positive. That is the \(\phi_{\pi }\) term doing its job, exactly as Taylor's rule prescribes.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — On teaching a model that central banks no longer use
One might reasonably ask: if real central banks have abandoned LM and use Taylor-style rules instead, why are we still teaching IS-LM at all? Three reasons:
First, pedagogical foundations matter. IS-LM presents the connection between the goods market and the money market, the concept of crowding out, and the central insight that fiscal and monetary policy interact. These ideas survive in IS-MP — one cannot really understand the modern framework without first understanding the older one.
Second, IS-LM at the zero lower bound is exactly the right framework. When the central bank cannot adjust rates because they are stuck at zero, the LM curve is horizontal — and the IS-LM story for fiscal policy is much sharper than the IS-MP story (which assumes the central bank is choosing rates actively). The 2008-2015 and 2020-2022 episodes are best understood through IS-LM.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
There is also a closely-related tool worth naming here: forward guidance — the practice of central banks telling markets what they plan to do in the future, in order to influence current behavior. After 2008, when the policy rate could not be cut further, the Fed leaned heavily on forward guidance ("we expect to keep rates exceptionally low at least through mid-2013," for example, in its August 2011 statement). The idea: even if today's short rate is stuck at zero, a credible commitment to keep rates low for years lowers long-term rates immediately, because long rates are essentially averages of expected future short rates. Forward guidance is now a standard part of every major central bank's toolkit.
Third — and this is the most important point — every Fed staff memo, every Brookings paper, every Congressional Budget Office study still cites IS-LM-style reasoning when discussing fiscal-monetary interaction. It is the lingua franca of policy discussion. One needs to know it to read what economists are actually writing about. Even economists who do not believe in LM as a literal description of the money market still use IS-LM diagrams to communicate.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
So: learn IS-LM. Use it well. Know its limits. And remember that when one reads modern central bank speeches, the framework is closer to IS-MP than IS-LM — but the basic intuitions about fiscal-monetary interaction are unchanged.
— A.S.

16.heading: The Modern Reformulation: From LM to MP
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body: Figure 16.6 The modern replacement for the LM curve. A central bank that targets an interest rate rather than a monetary aggregate faces a horizontal monetary policy line at the rate it has chosen, and supplies whatever quantity of reserves that rate requires. Policy easing lowers the line and moves equilibrium along IS. The substantive content of IS-LM survives — fiscal and monetary policy interact, and crowding out still operates through the rate — but the money-market mechanism that generated the upward slope has been replaced by a decision.
