16.heading: Worked Examples
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📐 Worked Example 16.1 — Tracing a fiscal expansion
An economy is in IS-LM equilibrium at Y = $20 trillion and r = 3%. Congress passes a $500 billion increase in government spending. The marginal propensity to consume is 0.7. The interest sensitivity of investment is such that each 1 percentage point rise in r reduces investment by $80 billion. Trace the effects on r and Y, and compute the crowding-out effect.
1
Naive multiplier effect (ignoring r): multiplier = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.33. So ΔY without crowding out would be 3.33 × $500B = $1.67 trillion.
2
IS curve shifts right. At unchanged r = 3%, equilibrium Y would rise by $1.67T. But this raises money demand, pulling us up the LM curve.
3
New equilibrium: the actual change in (r, Y) depends on both curves' slopes. Suppose LM is moderately steep — let r rise by 0.8 percentage points to 3.8%. Crowding-out check: the higher r reduces I by 0.8 × $80B = $64B.
4
Actual ΔY: the $64B reduction in I, multiplied through, gives $64B × 3.33 ≈ $213B reduction from the naive effect. So actual ΔY ≈ $1.67T − $213B ≈ $1.46 trillion. Effective multiplier ≈ 1.46 / 0.5 ≈ 2.9, lower than the naive 3.33.

16.heading: Worked Examples
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body: The fiscal expansion did most of what was intended — but about 13% of the effect was crowded out by higher interest rates reducing private investment. The size of the crowding-out effect depends critically on the LM slope. In a deep recession with low interest sensitivity of money demand (LM nearly flat), crowding out is minimal. In a hot economy with high sensitivity (LM steep), crowding out dominates. This is why the same dollar of fiscal stimulus has wildly different effects in different macroeconomic environments — a fact often missed in political debates about stimulus.

16.heading: Worked Examples
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
📐 Worked Example 16.2 — Monetary policy at and away from the zero lower bound
Compare two cases. Case A: the economy is in a normal equilibrium at Y* and r = 4%. The Fed undertakes a monetary expansion that shifts LM rightward by an amount that would lower r by 1 percentage point. Case B: the economy is in a deep recession with Y well below Y* and r already at 0%. The Fed undertakes the same-sized LM shift. Trace and compare the output effects.
1
Case A — normal times: LM shift lowers r from 4% to 3%. This stimulates investment by I'(r) × ΔR per the IS curve. Y rises along the unshifted IS curve to a new higher equilibrium. Standard monetary stimulus works through the interest rate channel.
2
Case B — at the ZLB: the LM shift cannot push r below 0% because banks would prefer to hold paper cash. So r remains at 0%. Without a change in r, investment does not change. Without a change in investment, Y does not change. The monetary expansion has zero effect on output.
3

16.heading: Worked Examples
16.title: Chapter 16, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
16.body:
The economic intuition: in Case A, banks hold reserves only reluctantly because they earn nothing while loans earn 4%. Extra reserves get lent out, money multiplies through the banking system, interest rates fall. In Case B, banks already earn 0% on loans — extra reserves just sit on the central bank's books. The transmission mechanism is broken.
This is the formal IS-LM prediction of monetary impotence at the ZLB. Empirically the 2008-2015 episode produced a more nuanced result — quantitative easing affected long-term rates and asset prices even with short rates pinned at zero, so the effect was not literally zero but was much smaller than equivalent rate cuts in normal times would have been. The textbook IS-LM prediction was directionally correct: at the ZLB, monetary policy is much weaker. This is why economists pivoted so strongly to fiscal policy as the primary tool after 2008.

17.heading: Overview
17.title: Chapter 17, The IS-LM Model A two-curve framework that has been at the center of macroeconomic policy debates for nearly ninety years — what it gets right, where it broke in 2008, and how modern central banks have quietly replaced it without telling anyone On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve c
17.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — IS-LM in the Engine
The MacroNations engine uses the modern IS-MP convention rather than classical IS-LM: one sets the interest_rate_target directly (not the money supply), and the engine handles monetary mechanics. The IS-curve logic still applies: gov_spending_pct and tax_rate shift the IS curve via the 1.4× and −1.1× multipliers respectively. Crowding-out is partial in this engine: when one raises gov_spending_pct, the immediate GDP boost arrives via the multiplier, but inflation rises via the Phillips curve, which forces real interest rates higher and dampens future investment. Unlike textbook IS-LM, the engine does not have a separate money-market equilibrium — the LM curve is effectively flat at whatever rate one sets. The IS-MP framework from §16.7 maps better to the engine than classical IS-LM does.

17.heading: Insight
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Introductory treatments of monetary policy often present it as something close to a frictionless exercise: the central bank picks a money supply or an interest rate, the IS-LM diagram shows what happens to output and prices. End of story. Real monetary policy looks nothing like this. Central banks operate in a fog of uncertainty about where the economy actually is, debate fiercely among themselves about what to do, communicate carefully to avoid market disruption, weigh political pressures, and frequently get things wrong — sometimes catastrophically. Understanding monetary policy without understanding the institutional reality is like understanding war by reading the rulebook of chess.

17.heading: Insight
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
The 2022-2024 episode is the central case study of this chapter because it tested almost every theoretical proposition about how monetary policy works. The Fed entered with a relatively new framework (FAIT, adopted August 2020) that explicitly committed to running inflation hot. Then inflation surged, the framework became an obstacle to fighting it, and the Fed had to reverse course aggressively. The success of the 2023-24 disinflation — without a recession — was unexpected by most economists. Understanding why it worked, and whether it can be repeated, is the central question of monetary policy today.
— A.S.

17.heading: The Central Bank's Mandate
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📘 Principles Level — What is the central bank actually trying to achieve?
Every central bank operates under a mandate — a legal and political statement of what its monetary policy is supposed to achieve. The mandate determines what the central bank prioritizes when choices conflict — for example, when fighting inflation might cause unemployment to rise.
Central bank mandates vary across countries in ways that matter. The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate — established by the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977 — which requires the Fed to promote both "maximum employment" and "stable prices." The European Central Bank, by contrast, has a hierarchical mandate: price stability is the primary objective; supporting general economic policies is secondary, and only allowed when it does not conflict with price stability. The Bank of England, the Bank of Canada, and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand all have hierarchical mandates focused primarily on inflation. Most modern central banks have settled on some version of these two models.

17.heading: The Central Bank's Mandate
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
When economists talk about the Fed having a "dual mandate," they mean the 1977 statutory requirement to pursue both stable prices and maximum employment simultaneously. This sounds simple but creates genuine policy dilemmas. If unemployment is high and inflation is also high (as in 1979 or, briefly, in 2022), which problem should be addressed first? The Fed's answer has evolved over decades: in the late 1970s it tried to fight unemployment first and inflation took off; under Volcker (1979 onward) it fought inflation aggressively and accepted high unemployment; under Greenspan, Bernanke, Yellen, and the early Powell years it generally treated the two as complementary because inflation stayed low. The 2022-2024 cycle was the first major test of the dual mandate under genuinely conflicting conditions in 40 years.
⚙ A Numerical Inflation Target
\[ \pi^{*} = 2\% \]The target adopted by nearly every major central bank.

17.heading: The Central Bank's Mandate
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: The central bank's inflation target. In the U.S., this was made explicit by the Fed only in January 2012, when it announced a 2% target measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index. The ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, and Bank of Japan all have similar 2% targets. The Reserve Bank of Australia targets 2–3%. Why 2% and not 0%? Because measured inflation slightly overstates true inflation (quality improvements are hard to measure), and because a small positive target gives the central bank room to cut real rates in a recession without hitting the zero lower bound. The exact number is somewhat arbitrary, but the principle — anchored expectations around a publicly-known target — has been widely accepted since the 1990s.

17.heading: Who Decides? The FOMC and Its Counterparts
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📘 Principles Level — Decision-making bodies
Monetary policy decisions are not made by one person. In the U.S., they are made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — the Fed's policy-setting body. The FOMC has twelve voting members: the seven Governors of the Federal Reserve Board (including the Chair), the President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (permanent vote), and four of the other eleven regional Fed Bank Presidents (rotating votes). The Chair (currently Jerome Powell, whose term runs until May 2026) sets the agenda and speaks for the committee, but does not unilaterally decide.
The FOMC meets eight times per year on a published schedule. Each meeting produces a statement, a Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) four times a year including the famous "dot plot" showing each member's expected rate path, and a press conference by the Chair. Six weeks later, the meeting minutes are released. This is one of the most carefully orchestrated communication exercises in any government — every word is scrutinized by markets for shifts in tone.

17.heading: Who Decides? The FOMC and Its Counterparts
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: The European Central Bank's Governing Council operates similarly, with 25 voting members (six members of the Executive Board plus 19 national central bank governors, with rotating voting rights for some). The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee has nine voting members. The committee structure matters because it institutionalizes deliberation and slows down decision-making — a feature, not a bug, in environments where rash decisions can be very costly.

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📘 Principles Level — Three conventional tools
Before the 2008 crisis, central banks operated mostly with three conventional tools. After 2008, they had to invent several new ones (covered in §17.4). The three traditional tools are: open market operations, the discount rate, and reserve requirements.
The three conventional monetary policy tools
ToolWhat it isFrequency of use
Open market operations
The central bank buys or sells government bonds in the open market. Buying bonds injects reserves into the banking system and lowers the policy rate; selling bonds drains reserves and raises the rate. This is the primary tool for steering the federal funds rate day-to-day.
Continuous (daily, sometimes multiple times per day)
The discount rate
The interest rate the Fed charges banks that borrow directly from it (through the "discount window"). Banks turn to the discount window when they cannot borrow in the federal funds market. The Fed sets this rate slightly above the policy rate, so borrowing from the discount window carries a stigma — banks only use it when they have to.
Rare for most banks; spikes during crises (March 2020, March 2023 banking turmoil)
Reserve requirements

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
The fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves rather than lending out. Setting higher requirements forces banks to keep more cash on hand and reduces lending; lower requirements free banks to lend more. Historically a major tool in the 1950s-60s; gradually deemphasized as financial markets evolved.
Effectively zero. The Fed reduced reserve requirements to 0% in March 2020 and has not changed them since.

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "The Fed sets interest rates"
One will often hear journalists say the Fed "raised interest rates" by 25 basis points. Strictly speaking, the Fed does not directly set any interest rate. What it does is set a target range for the federal funds rate — the overnight rate at which banks lend to each other — and then use open market operations to keep the actual federal funds rate within that target range. All other interest rates in the economy (mortgages, business loans, Treasury yields, credit card rates, etc.) are set by private actors in private markets. They respond to the federal funds rate, but they are not set by the Fed.

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: This distinction matters because the Fed's control over the broader economy is indirect. It cannot make a 30-year mortgage rate fall by 25 basis points just by deciding so; it can only adjust the very-short-term rate and hope that the rest of the yield curve adjusts in roughly the way it wants. Sometimes the rest of the curve does not cooperate — like in 2022, when the Fed raised the federal funds rate aggressively but long-term Treasury yields lagged behind for months, frustrating the tightening campaign. The Fed sets a price for overnight reserves. Everything else is the market's response.

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
⚙ How a Rate Decision Reaches the Real Economy: Five Transmission Channels
1. Interest rate
The most direct channel. A rate cut reduces borrowing costs across the term structure. Households spend more on cars and houses; firms invest more in capital. The standard IS-LM transmission. Effective in normal times; impotent at the zero lower bound.
2. Exchange rate
Lower rates make domestic-currency assets less attractive to foreign investors, weakening the currency. A weaker currency raises exports and reduces imports, boosting net exports. Important for small open economies; modest for the U.S.
3. Asset prices
Lower rates raise asset prices: lower discount rates raise present values of future earnings, so stocks rise; mortgage rates fall, so house prices rise. Higher asset prices raise household wealth, which raises consumption. This channel became especially important in the QE era as long-rate manipulation became a primary Fed tool.
4. Credit

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
Lower rates improve banks' net interest margins and balance sheets, making them more willing to lend. Borrowers in turn find credit easier to obtain. This channel was crucial in the 2008 crisis when the credit channel collapsed even though the Fed had cut rates to zero.
5. Expectations
Perhaps the most important channel in modern monetary policy. The Fed's commitment to a future path of rates (forward guidance) and its credibility on inflation anchor expectations. If markets expect rates to stay low for years, long rates fall today. If markets expect the Fed will fight inflation aggressively, wage and price-setters moderate their expectations of future inflation today. Communication is policy.
Figure 17.1 Corridor and floor systems. When reserves are scarce, the overnight rate is set at the intersection with a steeply sloped demand curve, and small open-market operations move it. When reserves are ample, demand is flat at the rate paid on reserves, so the policy rate is set administratively and the size of the balance sheet becomes a separate instrument. The move from the first regime to the second is the main institutional change in central banking since 2008.

17.heading: The Conventional Toolkit
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: Figure 17.2 Why monetary policy is set on a forecast. A change in the policy rate reaches output with a lag of several quarters and inflation later still. A central bank that waits for inflation to arrive before acting is already late, and one that reacts to every month's data imparts noise to an economy that will feel the decision a year from now. This is the practical case both for forecasting and for the gradualism central banks display.

17.heading: The Unconventional Toolkit: What 2008 Forced the Fed to Invent
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📘 Principles Level — Beyond the policy rate
When the federal funds rate hit zero in December 2008 and stayed there for seven years, the Fed could not use its primary conventional tool any further. So it invented new ones. These unconventional tools — sometimes lumped together as "non-traditional monetary policy" — are now permanent features of the modern Fed toolkit. Three deserve careful attention.
⚙ Three Unconventional Tools
QE
Quantitative Easing (introduced in Chapter 12). The central bank buys long-term assets (Treasury bonds, mortgage-backed securities) directly from the market, expanding its balance sheet and pushing down long-term interest rates. Used in three rounds 2008-2014, growing the Fed balance sheet from $900B to $4.5T; then again in 2020-2022 expanding it from $4.3T to $9T. The effects are debated empirically: most studies find QE compresses long-term rates by 50-100 basis points and supports asset prices, but the boost to real output is smaller than conventional rate cuts of equivalent size.
FG

17.heading: The Unconventional Toolkit: What 2008 Forced the Fed to Invent
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
Forward Guidance (introduced in Chapter 16). The central bank communicates its intentions for future policy in order to influence today's long-term rates and expectations. Two forms: Delphic guidance describes the central bank's economic outlook ("we expect inflation to return to 2%"); Odyssean guidance commits the central bank to a specific future action ("we will not raise rates before 2024 regardless of conditions"). Odyssean guidance is more powerful but harder to credibly commit to.
QT
Quantitative Tightening — the reverse of QE. The central bank lets its bond holdings run off (mature without reinvestment) or actively sells them, shrinking its balance sheet. Used by the Fed from 2017-2019 (modest) and again from June 2022 onward (more aggressive, alongside rate hikes). Reduces the supply of reserves in the banking system, pushing up long-term rates and tightening financial conditions.

17.heading: The Unconventional Toolkit: What 2008 Forced the Fed to Invent
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
A fourth tool deserves a mention: yield curve control (YCC). Under YCC, the central bank does not just buy bonds; it commits to buy whatever quantity is needed to keep a specific long-term yield at a target level. The Bank of Japan adopted YCC in 2016 and used it until 2024. The Federal Reserve has discussed YCC in internal papers but has never implemented it; the Fed's preference for flexibility over hard commitments has kept it off the U.S. table. YCC is the most aggressive forward-guidance commitment available — it backs the promise with whatever balance-sheet expansion is required to enforce it.
Figure 17.3 What the Federal Reserve bought. Before 2008 the portfolio was almost entirely short-dated Treasury securities held to supply currency and a small quantity of reserves. The purchase programs added long-dated Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities, which is the operative point: by taking duration and mortgage risk onto its own balance sheet, the central bank influenced long rates and mortgage spreads directly once the short rate had reached its floor.

17.heading: Central Bank Independence
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why the Fed is not run by the President
One of the most consequential design choices in any country's monetary policy framework is the degree of central bank independence — how insulated the central bank is from short-term political pressure. The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 with substantial protections: the seven Governors serve fourteen-year staggered terms (so no single President can replace the entire board), the Chair serves a four-year renewable term (so the President can replace one person every four years), and the Fed's operating budget comes from its own portfolio earnings rather than congressional appropriations (so Congress cannot defund or starve it).

17.heading: Central Bank Independence
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: Why bother with independence? Because the political incentive is almost always to keep interest rates too low. Low rates make voters feel richer, raise asset prices, lower the cost of financing government debt, and boost short-term employment. Low rates also tend to generate inflation eventually — but the inflation comes after the next election. An elected official's incentive is to push rates down before each election, accept the inflation later, and let someone else clean up. The economic literature calls this the time-inconsistency problem in monetary policy: what is optimal in the long run (a credible commitment to low inflation) conflicts with what is optimal in the short run (looser policy that boosts employment temporarily). Independent central banks exist primarily to solve this problem.

17.heading: Central Bank Independence
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Independence under pressure
The empirical evidence on central bank independence is robust: countries with more independent central banks have lower inflation on average, and do not have systematically worse unemployment outcomes. This finding is one of the cleanest results in applied macroeconomics, replicated across dozens of studies and decades of data. It is why nearly every country has moved toward greater central bank independence since the 1980s — Germany's Bundesbank was the historical model, the Bank of England was made independent in 1997, the ECB was created with strong independence baked into the Maastricht Treaty.

17.heading: Central Bank Independence
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
That said, independence is never absolute, and political pressure on central banks has become a more visible issue in recent years. During his first term, President Trump publicly criticized Fed Chair Jerome Powell repeatedly for not cutting rates fast enough; in his second term, that pressure has intensified, with several public threats to fire Powell (the legal authority to do so is contested and untested). Other countries — Turkey under Erdoğan, Argentina under various administrations — have demonstrated what happens when central bank independence is genuinely undermined: inflation rises, the currency collapses, and economic credibility evaporates.
Whether the long-running consensus on central bank independence holds in the next decade is one of the most important open questions in macroeconomics. The Fed's success in the 2022-2024 disinflation — which required maintaining tight policy despite political pressure — was a strong vindication of the independence model. Whether that success can be repeated under more sustained political pressure remains to be seen.
— A.S.

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — A framework, an experiment, and a reversal
A monetary policy framework is the central bank's written statement of how it interprets its mandate and how it intends to respond to economic conditions. The Fed announced its first formal numerical inflation target (2%) in January 2012, after decades without a public target. It published a "Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy" that has been reviewed and revised twice — in 2020 and again in 2025.

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: The 2020 review concluded in August 2020 with one of the most consequential framework changes in Fed history: the adoption of Flexible Average Inflation Targeting (FAIT). Under FAIT, the Fed committed to allowing inflation to run modestly above 2% for some time following periods when inflation had run below 2%, so that average inflation over time would equal 2%. The motivation was honest: from 2012 to 2020, inflation had run persistently below 2% (averaging about 1.5%), the Fed had repeatedly failed to lift it to target, and Fed officials worried that low expected inflation was constraining policy effectiveness near the zero lower bound. FAIT was meant to anchor expectations higher by signaling that the Fed would not preemptively tighten as soon as inflation reached 2%.

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
The timing was unfortunate. The framework was adopted in August 2020 — six months into a pandemic that would unleash the largest fiscal stimulus in modern history and trigger an inflation surge unlike anything since the early 1980s. From August 2020 forward, every time inflation rose above 2%, the FAIT framework gave the Fed a reason to wait — inflation had been below target for years; some "make-up" was appropriate. Inflation rose to 7% by the end of 2021. The Fed continued purchasing assets (QE) until March 2022 and did not begin raising rates until March 2022, when inflation was already at 8.5%. The framework that was meant to anchor expectations higher when inflation was too low became an obstacle to fighting inflation when inflation was too high.
August 2025
Jackson Hole
Framework reversal
The End of FAIT — Powell's Jackson Hole Reversal

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: At the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in August 2025, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell announced that the Fed was abandoning Flexible Average Inflation Targeting and returning to plain Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) — the framework the Fed had used from 2012 to 2020. The reversal was substantively significant. Under FIT, the Fed treats inflation deviations symmetrically: 1% above target is treated as equally undesirable as 1% below target. There is no "make-up" requirement, and no commitment to let inflation run hot following periods of undershooting.

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: The motivation, as Fed staff papers have documented, was clear: FAIT had probably contributed to the post-2020 inflation surge by delaying the Fed's tightening response. A 2025 Dallas Fed working paper estimated that FAIT raised CPI inflation by about 1 percentage point over 2020-2022 compared to a counterfactual without FAIT. Other Fed officials concluded — somewhat more critically — that FAIT was simply too complicated to communicate effectively: markets and the public could never quite determine how the Fed would respond to varying conditions under an "average" framework, which is the opposite of what a framework is supposed to do. Brookings papers in 2024 (e.g., Eric Swanson) had concluded that FAIT was "a giant step backward in clarity and communication and accountability."

17.heading: The Fed's Framework: FAIT and Its 2025 Reversal
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: The 2025 framework change matters for two reasons. First, it explicitly acknowledges that the 2020 framework contributed to the 2021-22 inflation problem — a meaningful institutional learning. Second, it signals that the Fed expects to operate in an environment where inflation surprises in both directions are now plausible, not just persistently-too-low inflation. The post-2008 world of permanent disinflation worries has, at least for now, ended.

17.heading: The 2022-2024 Tightening Cycle: The Defining Episode
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
2022–2024
United States
The Powell tightening
Fastest Tightening in 40 Years — And the Soft Landing That Was not Supposed to Happen
By the end of 2021, U.S. inflation had reached 7% and was still accelerating. The federal funds rate was at 0–0.25%. The Fed had been buying $120 billion of assets per month for nearly two years. Real rates were deeply negative. By any standard measure, monetary policy was wildly too loose for the inflation environment. The Fed faced a genuine policy challenge — but it also faced its own credibility being at risk if it did not act decisively.
March 2022: First rate hike, 25 basis points. The Fed began tapering its asset purchases and signaled aggressive tightening ahead. Inflation that month: 8.5%.
May–June 2022: 50 and then 75 basis-point hikes, the first 75-bp move since 1994. Inflation peaked at 9.1% in June. The Fed sent unmistakable signals it would prioritize inflation over employment.
July through December 2022: Three more 75-bp hikes, then a 50-bp hike in December. By year-end, the federal funds rate target was 4.25–4.50%. Inflation had begun easing — CPI fell from 9.1% (June) to 6.5% (December).

17.heading: The 2022-2024 Tightening Cycle: The Defining Episode
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
2023: Smaller hikes (25 bp) continued through July, reaching 5.25–5.50%. The Fed then paused. Inflation fell from 6.5% (December 2022) to 3.4% (December 2023). Unemployment stayed near 3.7%. GDP grew 2.5% in real terms. This was not how the playbook said it should go.
2024: The Fed held rates steady until September, then cut by 50 bp. Inflation fell to under 3% by mid-year, then drifted back up modestly later. Unemployment crept up to 4.2% by year-end. Real GDP grew 2.8%.
What made the disinflation work without a recession? Several explanations have been offered, none completely satisfactory:
Supply normalization: much of the 2021-22 inflation was supply-side (Chapter 15's SRAS shift). As supply chains repaired, energy markets stabilized, and labor markets cooled from their record-tight state, SRAS shifted right, lowering prices without requiring lower demand.
Anchored expectations: despite the surge in actual inflation, long-run inflation expectations (measured by market and survey indicators) never moved meaningfully above 2.5%. The Fed's aggressive action reinforced credibility, preventing wage-price spirals.

17.heading: The 2022-2024 Tightening Cycle: The Defining Episode
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
Wealth and consumption resilience: households entered the tightening cycle with unusually strong balance sheets (savings from pandemic stimulus, low debt service costs from years of low rates), buffering them against rate hikes.
Labor market repair without unemployment: as discussed in Chapter 14, the Beveridge curve shifted favorably — vacancies fell from 12 million to 8 million without unemployment rising much, suggesting better matching efficiency rather than a demand-driven recession.
Whether these factors will repeat in the next inflation episode is genuinely uncertain. The 2022-2024 disinflation is the canonical case study for monetary policy in our generation, but it should not be taken as a recipe — it depended on conditions that may not recur.
Figure 17.4 The tightening cycle of 2022 to 2024. The policy rate rose by more than five percentage points in sixteen months, the fastest increase since the Volcker period, while measured inflation fell from above nine percent toward the target. The conventional forecast was that disinflation on this scale required a recession; unemployment instead remained below four percent throughout, which is the episode chapter 19 returns to.

17.heading: Rules vs. Discretion
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Should monetary policy follow a fixed rule?
One of the longest-running debates in monetary economics is whether central banks should follow a fixed rule (e.g., always set rates by the Taylor rule formula) or instead exercise discretion (judge each situation case-by-case). The case for rules: transparency, predictability, accountability, immunity to political pressure, anchored expectations. The case for discretion: ability to respond to novel circumstances, ability to use judgment about supply versus demand shocks, ability to handle non-economic emergencies (financial crises, pandemics) that no rule could anticipate.

17.heading: Rules vs. Discretion
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: Real central banks have settled on something in between: they communicate as if they follow a rule (the Fed's framework statement; the ECB's strategy statement; the published inflation targets), but they preserve substantial discretion in practice. The Fed has never officially committed to a Taylor rule even though its behavior since the 1980s is reasonably well-described by one. Milton Friedman's famous 1968 proposal of a fixed money-supply growth rule was never adopted by any major central bank; the closest implementation was Volcker's 1979-82 monetarist experiment, which was effective at breaking inflation but volatile in its impact on the real economy.

17.heading: Rules vs. Discretion
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
⚠ Why pure rules never quite work
Every fixed rule eventually encounters circumstances its designers did not anticipate. The classic Taylor rule prescribes a specific federal funds rate based on inflation and output gaps — but what should the rule say when rates hit zero? When there is a financial panic? When inflation is supply-driven? When markets are pricing in a war? The literature has answered each of these with rule modifications — augmented Taylor rules with ZLB caveats, financial stability adjustments, supply-shock buffers — but the proliferation of caveats undermines the original case for a rule, which was simplicity and clarity. Today's mainstream view: rules are useful as benchmarks, but central banks need flexibility to deviate when conditions warrant. The art is in deciding when.

17.heading: Rules vs. Discretion
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body: Figure 17.5 The Taylor principle. A rule of the form \(i = r^* + \pi + a(\pi - \pi^*) + b\,\tilde{y}\) with \(a > 0\) moves the nominal rate more than one-for-one with inflation, so the real rate rises when inflation rises. A response flatter than the 45-degree line lowers the real rate as inflation increases and is destabilising — the standard diagnosis of policy in the 1970s.

17.heading: Interactive: The Taylor Rule Calculator
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
🎛 Interactive — Taylor Rule
Set current inflation and the output gap; see the rule-prescribed policy rate
Current inflation (π): 2.5%
Output gap (% of potential): 0%
Inflation response \((\phi_{\pi })\): 1.5
Output response \((\phi_{Y})\): 0.5
What is being observed: the rule-prescribed real rate (the policy real interest rate the Taylor rule suggests) shown as the blue bar, and the implied nominal rate as the red bar. The gray dashed line marks the zero lower bound. Adjusting \(\phi_{\pi }\) below 1 violates the Taylor principle — watch what happens to the real rate when inflation rises in that case.

17.heading: Worked Examples
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📐 Worked Example 17.1 — Applying the Taylor rule to the 2022 inflation peak
In June 2022, U.S. CPI inflation was 9.1% (PCE measure: about 6.8%). The Fed's inflation target is 2% (PCE basis). The output gap was approximately +1.5% (output slightly above potential). Assume r* = 0.5% (neutral real rate) and use Taylor's original coefficients \((\phi_{\pi } = 1.5, \phi_{Y} = 0.5)\). (a) Compute the rule-prescribed real and nominal policy rate using the PCE measure. (b) Compare to the actual federal funds rate in June 2022, which was 1.50–1.75%. (c) Comment on what this comparison indicates about the Fed's stance in mid-2022.
1
(a) Taylor rule (real): \(r = r* + \phi_{\pi }(\pi - \pi *) + \phi_{Y}(Y - Y*)/Y\)* = 0.5% + 1.5×(6.8 − 2) + 0.5×1.5 = 0.5% + 7.2% + 0.75% = 8.45% real.
2
Nominal: nominal = real + expected inflation ≈ 8.45% + 6.8% = ~15.2% nominal (assuming expected inflation tracks current inflation, which is a simplification).
3
(b) Actual federal funds rate in June 2022: 1.50–1.75%. Gap between rule-prescribed and actual: ~13–14 percentage points. This is enormous — easily one of the largest deviations from the Taylor rule in modern Fed history.
4

17.heading: Worked Examples
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
(c) What it tells us: the Fed was running policy extraordinarily loose in mid-2022 relative to what a rule-based approach would have prescribed. Several factors explain this gap: (i) the FAIT framework explicitly authorized running inflation hot for some time; (ii) the Fed believed much of the 2021-22 inflation was supply-driven and would resolve on its own; (iii) the Fed places weight on smoothness — it does not want to raise rates abruptly in single moves of 5-10 percentage points. But the Taylor rule warning was real: by mid-2022, the Fed was very far behind the curve, and the eventual catch-up required 525 basis points of tightening in 18 months.
Lesson: the Taylor rule is a benchmark, not a literal policy prescription. Fed deviations from the rule are revealing — they indicate what the Fed's framework, beliefs about the economic environment, and political constraints are doing. The 2022 gap was the largest in 40 years, and it preceded the largest tightening cycle in 40 years. Rule deviations carry information.

17.heading: Worked Examples
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
📐 Worked Example 17.2 — Forward guidance and long rates
A central bank announces on January 1 that it will keep its policy rate at 1% for the next three years, regardless of economic conditions. Before the announcement, markets had been expecting the rate to gradually rise to 3% over the next three years. (a) What was the previously-expected average rate over the next three years? (b) What is the new expected average rate? (c) The current 3-year bond yield is approximately the average of expected short rates over three years. By how much should the 3-year yield change immediately after the announcement? (d) Why does this matter for the real economy?
1
(a) Old expected average: if rate rises from 1% to 3% linearly, average ≈ (1% + 3%) / 2 = 2%.
2
(b) New expected average: committed to 1% throughout, so average = 1%.
3
(c) Change in 3-year yield: falls by about 100 basis points (from 2% to 1%), since the 3-year yield reflects the expected average path of short rates.
4

17.heading: Worked Examples
17.title: Chapter 17, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
17.body:
(d) Why this matters: mortgage rates, corporate bond rates, and other long-term borrowing rates are anchored to the 3-, 5-, and 10-year Treasury yields. A 100-basis-point drop in 3-year yields translates almost immediately to lower mortgage rates and lower business borrowing costs. Households refinance and increase consumption; firms invest more; the economy gets stimulated today — even though the actual short rate has not moved.
This is the magic of credible forward guidance. The central bank does not have to do anything except announce a credible plan, and long-term rates fall today. The August 2011 Fed announcement that it would hold rates low "at least through mid-2013" was precisely this kind of move; 10-year Treasury yields fell about 30 basis points within hours. Communication is policy — but only if it is credible.

18.heading: Overview
18.title: Chapter 18, Monetary Policy How central banks actually conduct monetary policy in the real world — the institutional structure, the toolkit beyond the textbook diagram, the unprecedented 2022-2024 tightening cycle, and the dramatic August 2025 framework shift no other textbook has yet covered On Mar
18.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Monetary Policy in the Engine
In MacroNations, one directly sets interest_rate_target each round (range 0–20%, default 4.5%, neutral = 4.0%). The engine's monetary transmission is encoded in three equations: (1) GDP impact: each 1pp above neutral subtracts 0.5pp from gdp_growth — applied as a level effect, not a change effect, so sustained tight policy keeps dampening growth every round. (2) Inflation impact: each 1pp above neutral subtracts 0.4pp from inflation. (3) Exchange rate impact: each 1pp rate change moves the currency by 1.5% via UIP. There is no Taylor rule or reaction function — one sets the rate, the engine just applies the consequences. The Volcker-style scenario unfolds if one sets rate well above neutral and hold it: inflation falls steadily, unemployment rises via Okun, fin_health takes a hit, but Stability eventually recovers. The post-disinflation reset (rate back to 4%) restores GDP growth toward potential.
References
Bernanke, B. S. (2022). 21st century monetary policy: The Federal Reserve from the Great Inflation to COVID-19. W. W. Norton.

18.heading: Insight
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Fiscal policy is taught in textbooks as if it were a clean lever the government can pull whenever stabilization is needed. In practice, it is nothing of the sort. Fiscal policy is slow (months or years between identifying a problem and Congress responding); it is political (every dollar of spending has a constituency that does not want it cut, and every tax cut has a constituency that does not want it reversed); and it is targeted by interest groups rather than by economic logic. The textbook story of a benevolent technocrat adjusting G and T to optimize output gets the institutional reality almost exactly backwards.

18.heading: Insight
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
And yet — and this is the central tension of fiscal policy as a field — when fiscal policy works, it works enormously. The 2020-21 fiscal response prevented a depression-grade collapse. The 2009 ARRA, despite endless retrospective disputes, almost certainly prevented unemployment from peaking three or four percentage points higher than it did. Fiscal policy is most powerful when it is most necessary — at the zero lower bound, in deep recessions — and most controversial when it is least helpful — in mature recoveries when the budget can least afford it. The 2021 American Rescue Plan was, by most reasonable analysis, an example of the latter. The challenge for any student of macroeconomics is to develop the judgment to tell these cases apart.
— A.S.

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two main levers, two main directions
Fiscal policy has two main instruments: government spending (G) and taxes (T). Either can be raised or lowered. The combination defines the fiscal stance — whether policy is expansionary (raising aggregate demand) or contractionary (reducing it). Expansionary fiscal policy means either raising G, cutting T, or both. Contractionary fiscal policy is the reverse.
The two instruments have different economic properties. Government spending changes affect demand directly: every dollar the government spends shows up immediately as a dollar of GDP. Tax changes affect demand indirectly: lower taxes raise household disposable income, but households save some of that income rather than spending it all. The fraction they spend — the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), introduced briefly in Chapter 16 — determines how much of a tax cut actually feeds into aggregate demand.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Simple Multiplier
\[ \Delta Y = \Delta G \times \frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}} \]
ΔG
A change in government spending (positive = expansion).
MPC

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
Marginal propensity to consume — the fraction of an additional dollar of disposable income that households spend rather than save. In the U.S., aggregate MPC has been empirically estimated at about 0.5 to 0.7, varying with household income (poorer households have higher MPC since they are closer to subsistence; richer households save more of additional income).
1/(1−MPC)
The textbook "multiplier." With MPC = 0.7, this equals 1/0.3 ≈ 3.33. The idea: $1 of government spending generates $1 of direct demand, plus $0.70 spent by the recipient (who got it as income), plus $0.49 spent by the next recipient, plus $0.34 by the next, and so on — a geometric series summing to about $3.33.
This formula is the single most-taught equation in introductory macroeconomics. It also dramatically overstates real-world multipliers in most situations. The simple multiplier ignores: crowding out (Chapter 16), the response of monetary policy, leakages into imports, and the fact that MPC varies dramatically by household type and economic context. Empirical estimates of actual fiscal multipliers usually fall in the range of 0.5 to 2.5, almost always well below the simple formula's prediction.

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Tax Multiplier
\[ \Delta Y = -\,\Delta T \times \frac{\text{MPC}}{1 - \text{MPC}} \]
ΔT
A change in lump-sum taxes.
MPC/(1−MPC)
The tax multiplier. With MPC = 0.7, this is 0.7/0.3 ≈ 2.33. Notice this is smaller than the spending multiplier: a $1 tax cut only generates $0.70 of immediate spending (the rest is saved), so it has a smaller first-round effect than a $1 increase in government spending.
The textbook lesson: dollar-for-dollar, government spending is a more powerful stimulus than tax cuts. This is the textbook case for spending-based stimulus over tax-based stimulus in recessions. Empirical evidence is more mixed: tax cuts that are clearly permanent and targeted at high-MPC households (low-income, financially constrained) can rival spending multipliers, while government spending that is poorly designed or slowly implemented can underperform. Design matters as much as the choice between G and T.

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Treating the textbook multiplier as a number one can rely on
The simple multiplier formula 1/(1−MPC) is a useful starting point for thinking about fiscal policy, but it should never be quoted as if it were a literal estimate of what stimulus will deliver. The 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) was sized using a Romer-Bernstein assumption of a multiplier around 1.6. Subsequent retrospective studies have produced estimates ranging from 0.5 (small multiplier, mostly crowding out) to over 2.0 (large multiplier, deep slack absorbed), depending on assumptions and methodology. The honest scientific answer is that we do not know the multiplier to better than a factor of three.

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body: The multiplier varies systematically with macroeconomic conditions. Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012) showed that multipliers are roughly twice as large in recessions as in expansions — when resources are slack, fiscal stimulus has room to work; when the economy is at full capacity, it mostly crowds out private activity. Multipliers are also higher at the zero lower bound (no monetary tightening to offset fiscal expansion) than when the central bank is actively responding. Different contexts → different multipliers. Anyone who quotes a single multiplier number with confidence is selling the reader something.

18.heading: The Instruments of Fiscal Policy
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
Figure 18.1 Estimated fiscal multipliers by instrument. The spread is wide and systematic: transfers to households that will spend them, and purchases made when monetary policy cannot offset them, deliver more than a dollar of output per dollar spent, while tax reductions concentrated on households with low propensities to consume deliver well under one. Quoting a single multiplier for fiscal policy as such is therefore meaningless; the composition is the policy.
Figure 18.2 The multiplier process with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.6. Each round of spending becomes income, a fraction of which is spent again. The series converges to \(1/(1-\text{MPC})\) times the initial injection. Taxes, imports and any rise in the interest rate all leak from the circuit and reduce the multiplier below this textbook value.

18.heading: Automatic Stabilizers
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why fiscal policy partly runs on autopilot
Not all fiscal policy requires congressional action. A significant portion of the federal budget responds to economic conditions automatically — these are automatic stabilizers. When the economy enters a recession, tax revenues fall (because incomes fall, so income tax receipts fall; and because spending falls, so sales-tax receipts fall) while transfer payments rise (unemployment insurance claims rise, food assistance enrollment rises, Medicaid enrollment rises as people lose employer-sponsored insurance). The federal budget moves toward deficit automatically, providing demand support exactly when it is needed.
The opposite happens in booms: tax revenues rise as incomes and spending grow, transfers fall as unemployment drops, the budget moves toward surplus, and demand is automatically restrained. This counter-cyclical pattern happens with no legislation, no debate, no political decision — it is built into the structure of taxes and spending.

18.heading: Automatic Stabilizers
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
Automatic stabilizers are quantitatively important. Estimates from the IMF and CBO suggest that U.S. automatic stabilizers reduce business-cycle fluctuations by roughly 20-30%. The progressive income tax is the single largest stabilizer; unemployment insurance and means-tested transfers add meaningfully on top. Larger welfare states tend to have larger automatic stabilizers: in Sweden or Denmark, where transfers are larger and tax rates are higher, automatic stabilizers absorb a much greater share of cyclical shocks than in the U.S.
⚙ Discretionary vs. Automatic Fiscal Policy
Discretionary
Active legislative action — new spending bills, tax cuts, infrastructure programs. Slow, political, often miscalibrated. Examples: 2009 ARRA, 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, 2020-21 pandemic stimulus, 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Automatic

18.heading: Automatic Stabilizers
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body: Built-in responses of revenue and transfer programs to economic conditions. Fast (immediate), apolitical (no legislation needed), and well-targeted (the income tax falls hardest on those whose income falls hardest; transfers rise for those who actually need them). Most economists prefer larger automatic stabilizers over more aggressive discretionary policy, precisely because of the political dysfunction discretionary policy involves.

18.heading: Automatic Stabilizers
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — The case for boring fiscal policy
One underappreciated insight from macroeconomics: the boring parts of fiscal policy — the parts that no politician runs for office on — do most of the actual stabilization work. Unemployment insurance, food assistance, the progressive income tax, Medicaid eligibility expansions during downturns — these do not make headlines. They are not named after senators. They do not get covered with stimulus-package fanfare. They just quietly inject demand into the economy whenever joblessness rises, and quietly withdraw it whenever joblessness falls.

18.heading: Automatic Stabilizers
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
The interesting econometric debate about fiscal multipliers tends to focus on discretionary stimulus packages, because those are the ones we can identify in the data as a clear policy shock. But the bulk of fiscal stabilization is not seriously debatable — it follows directly from the structure of how taxes and transfers move with the cycle. If one wanted to improve U.S. counter-cyclical policy without doing anything controversial, the highest-value reforms would be expansions of automatic stabilizers (e.g., automatic UI extensions when unemployment rises above some threshold, similar to existing extended-benefit triggers but more generous). This is one of the very few macroeconomic reform areas where there is near-universal expert agreement and almost no political traction.
— A.S.

The deficit observed in a recession is therefore not by itself evidence of discretionary loosening, which is why the cyclically adjusted balance is the series used to judge the stance of policy.

18.heading: Crowding Out: The IS-LM Reminder
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why fiscal stimulus has interest-rate side effects
Chapter 16's IS-LM analysis showed that a fiscal expansion shifts the IS curve right, raising both output and the interest rate. The rise in r reduces private investment by the amount I'(r) — that is crowding out. When the central bank is actively setting rates (the modern IS-MP framework), the same logic applies: fiscal expansion pushes up demand for credit; the central bank, if it is responding to inflation pressure, raises rates to lean against the expansion; higher rates dampen private investment.
The size of crowding out depends critically on what the central bank is doing. If the central bank passively holds rates steady (an "accommodating" stance), there is no crowding out — fiscal stimulus reaches its full multiplier. If the central bank actively raises rates to offset fiscal stimulus, crowding out can be near 100% — the rate hike completely cancels the fiscal expansion. Most real cases fall somewhere in between.

18.heading: The Zero Lower Bound Exception
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📘 Principles Level — Why fiscal policy is uniquely powerful at the ZLB
From Chapter 16: when the policy interest rate is at the zero lower bound, monetary policy cannot ease further. The LM curve is effectively flat at r = 0. In this regime, fiscal expansion shifts IS right but the central bank cannot lean against it through rate hikes — and indeed, has every reason not to, since the economy is in a recession needing all available stimulus. Crowding out is essentially zero. The textbook multiplier comes closer to applying in full force.
This insight is the strongest argument in modern macroeconomics for aggressive fiscal policy in deep recessions. The 2008-2009 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic both produced ZLB conditions; in both cases, the standard policy advice was for large fiscal expansion. This is not a controversial view among professional macroeconomists — even those who are generally skeptical of fiscal stimulus tend to accept its power at the ZLB. The major disagreement is about how much stimulus, not whether.

When the policy rate is already at its floor and the central bank is not raising it, the rate does not move, no investment is displaced, and the full multiplier operates. This is the main reason estimates of the multiplier from normal times understate what fiscal policy achieved after 2008 and in 2020.

18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? 18.body:
2009
United States
ARRA
The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act — The Test Case for Modern Fiscal Stimulus
The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, signed by President Obama in February 2009, was an $831 billion package combining tax cuts, transfers to individuals, aid to state governments, and infrastructure spending. About one-third was tax cuts, one-third transfers, and one-third spending on goods and services. The Romer-Bernstein analysis used to justify the bill assumed an output multiplier of about 1.6.
The retrospective evidence on whether ARRA worked is one of the most studied questions in applied macroeconomics. The CBO's 2015 retrospective concluded that ARRA had output multipliers ranging from 0.5 (for tax cuts to high-income households) to 2.5 (for direct purchases and aid to state and local governments). A widely-cited study by Chodorow-Reich et al. (2012) using state-level variation in stimulus exposure found multipliers of about 2.0 for the most stimulus-intensive states. The honest summary: ARRA almost certainly worked — but probably less than its designers initially projected, and with a wide uncertainty band.

18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
The ARRA debate also surfaced a now-standard insight: the multiplier depends on how the stimulus is composed. Aid to state and local governments showed the largest multipliers, because states facing balanced-budget rules were cutting spending sharply, and federal aid offset those cuts dollar-for-dollar without leakage. Direct infrastructure spending also worked well but was constrained by "shovel-ready" requirements that turned out to be a misnomer — most infrastructure projects took years to plan and execute. Tax cuts to higher-income households showed the smallest multipliers because much of the tax cut was saved. Stimulus design matters enormously, and not all stimulus is created equal.

18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body: Across three major bills — the CARES Act (March 2020, $2.2 trillion), the December 2020 supplemental ($900 billion), and the American Rescue Plan (March 2021, $1.9 trillion) — the federal government deployed roughly $5 trillion in pandemic-era fiscal stimulus, equal to nearly 25% of GDP across the three packages. The CARES Act was widely seen, even by stimulus skeptics, as appropriately sized to a once-in-a-century pandemic shock that froze the economy nearly overnight. The December 2020 bill arrived as the recovery was already underway. The March 2021 American Rescue Plan landed when unemployment was already at 6% and falling, household savings were unusually high, and supply chains were already strained.

18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
By mid-2021, mainstream macroeconomists — including former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers in a much-discussed Washington Post column from February 2021 — were warning that the combined fiscal stimulus was substantially larger than the output gap and would likely produce inflation. By the end of 2021, CPI inflation had risen to 7%. Whether ARP caused that inflation, accelerated it, or merely coincided with it remains genuinely debated. A Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco study in 2022 estimated that ARP added 3 percentage points to inflation by the end of 2021. Other studies attribute more of the inflation surge to supply-side disruptions and less to fiscal stimulus.
The 2020-21 episode is the cleanest example in recent memory of fiscal policy being too aggressive: not because the early stimulus was wrong (it almost certainly was not), but because the late stimulus was sized to fight a worse recession than the one actually unfolding. This is a structural problem with discretionary fiscal policy: by the time legislation passes, the economy has often moved on, and the stimulus is calibrated to conditions that no longer exist.
