18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act — Fiscal Expansion at the Wrong Time
In July 2025, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), making permanent many of the temporary tax provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, expanding several deductions, and tightening eligibility for federal benefits including SNAP and Medicaid. NBER analyses estimate that OBBBA adds approximately 29 percentage points to the debt-to-GDP ratio over 30 years compared to the no-OBBBA baseline. The Congressional Budget Office's preliminary scoring shows OBBBA raising primary deficits by roughly $3-4 trillion over the next decade, on top of the $22 trillion deficit increase already projected.

18.heading: Three Case Studies
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
From a textbook fiscal-policy standpoint, the timing is striking. OBBBA is a major fiscal expansion enacted when (i) unemployment is below the natural rate, (ii) inflation is above the Fed's 2% target, (iii) interest rates are well above zero, and (iv) the debt-to-GDP ratio is approaching 100%. Every condition that makes fiscal expansion more defensible — slack, ZLB, low inflation, low debt — is absent. Every condition that makes fiscal expansion less defensible — full employment, inflation pressure, positive rates, high debt — is present.
None of this is to take a political position on the merits of the underlying policies; that is a question for voters. The point is purely analytical: OBBBA is an example of fiscal expansion driven by political logic rather than macroeconomic logic. It would have been textbook-appropriate in 2009 or 2020 and is textbook-questionable in 2025. The disconnect between when fiscal stimulus is most needed and when it is politically achievable is one of the deepest problems in the field.

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — When does borrowing become unsustainable?
The U.S. federal deficit averaged about 3.8% of GDP over the 50 years from 1975 to 2025. It exceeded 5% only six times in that span — during the deepest recession years (2009-2012) and the pandemic years (2020-2021). In every other year, deficits stayed in single digits and the debt-to-GDP ratio remained well below 80%. Then, starting around 2022, something changed: deficits failed to fall back to historical norms even as the economy returned to full employment. FY 2024 deficit: 6.4% of GDP. FY 2025 deficit: 5.9% of GDP. Both peacetime, full-employment years. Both at deficit levels previously associated only with deep crises.
The debt-to-GDP ratio passed 99% in FY 2025. CBO projections show it reaching roughly 120% by 2034 under the OBBBA-included baseline. If OBBBA's temporary provisions are made permanent — which is politically likely — debt reaches 183% of GDP by 2054 according to NBER analyses, and 199% if all temporary provisions become permanent. These are unprecedented levels for a peacetime economy.
⚙ Debt Dynamics — When Does Debt-to-GDP Stabilize?

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
\[ \Delta\!\left(\frac{D}{Y}\right) \approx (r - g)\,\frac{D}{Y} - \frac{\text{primary surplus}}{Y} \]
D/Y
Debt-to-GDP ratio.
r − g
Real interest rate minus real GDP growth rate. The single most important number in fiscal sustainability analysis. When r > g, debt-to-GDP grows automatically through compounding interest even with no primary deficit. When r < g, debt-to-GDP shrinks naturally as the economy grows faster than the debt.
Primary surplus
The budget balance EXCLUDING interest payments. This is what is left over from current revenues after paying for current spending. Required primary surplus for stability: (r − g) × (D/Y).
Example: if r = 4%, g = 2%, and D/Y = 100%, then to keep debt-to-GDP flat at 100%, the government needs a primary surplus of (4% − 2%) × 100% = 2% of GDP. The U.S. is currently running a primary deficit of about 4% of GDP. So debt-to-GDP is rising by about 6% per year mechanically: 2% from the r-g gap, plus 4% from the primary deficit. This is what "fiscal unsustainability" actually means: a path that, if unchanged, leads to ever-rising debt-to-GDP without limit.

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "The U.S. can never default, so deficits do not matter"
The argument: the U.S. borrows in its own currency, so it can never technically default on dollar-denominated debt — the Treasury can always pay by having the Fed print money. Therefore deficits never constrain anything. This argument confuses the question of legal default with the question of economic cost. The U.S. will not default on its bonds in nominal terms. But the costs of running large deficits indefinitely show up in three places:
Higher interest rates: more debt issuance raises the supply of bonds; absent matching increases in demand, prices fall and yields rise. Higher yields crowd out private investment, raise mortgage rates and business borrowing costs, and constrain future growth.
Higher inflation risk: at some level of debt, markets begin to suspect that future debt servicing will require either monetization (which is inflationary) or sharp fiscal adjustment. Even the perception of this can raise expected inflation and inflation risk premia.

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
Reduced fiscal space: every dollar going to interest payments is a dollar not available for defense, infrastructure, healthcare, or future stimulus. By FY 2024, the U.S. was spending over $1 trillion per year on interest payments alone — more than defense spending, more than Medicare. This is real money with real opportunity cost.
The U.S. does not face an imminent debt crisis. It does not even face one within ten years. But the trajectory matters. The question is not "will the U.S. default?" but "what is the cost of crowding out, higher interest rates, and reduced fiscal space, and is that cost worth what we are getting in return for the borrowing?" That is an actual policy question, not a manufactured one.

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why fiscal sustainability is hard to discuss honestly
Fiscal sustainability is one of the topics where economists struggle the most to be heard accurately by the public. Two opposing oversimplifications dominate. On one side: "America is bankrupt, the dollar will collapse, hyperinflation is coming." On the other side: "Deficits are fake, money is just numbers in a spreadsheet, the U.S. can borrow forever." Both views are wrong, and both views actively obscure the real question.

18.heading: Deficits, Debt, and the Sustainability Question
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
The honest analytical framework is the debt-dynamics equation above. A country can sustain very high debt-to-GDP ratios indefinitely if r − g stays favorable (Japan has done so at 250%+ debt-to-GDP for decades, because g has typically exceeded r in Japan). A country can find itself in crisis at modest debt-to-GDP ratios if r − g moves against it sharply (Italy faced crisis at debt-to-GDP around 130% when its r spiked in 2011-12). The U.S. position today is unprecedented: high and rising debt-to-GDP combined with rising r (because the Fed raised rates in 2022-23 and they have stayed elevated) and modest g. That is the combination that makes debt dynamics genuinely difficult, and it is why this generation of policymakers has a problem their predecessors did not face.
The practical lesson: do not take rhetorical shortcuts on either side of this debate. Whether U.S. fiscal policy is "sustainable" is a genuine question, and the answer depends on assumptions about future r, future g, and future political willingness to constrain spending or raise taxes. Reasonable economists can disagree about all three. What is not reasonable is dismissing the question.
— A.S.

18.heading: The Cyclically-Adjusted Budget Balance
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Separating discretionary policy from cyclical effects
One of the trickiest analytical problems in fiscal policy is distinguishing changes in the budget that are caused by policy choices from changes caused by the business cycle. The headline deficit moves with both. To isolate discretionary stance, economists use the cyclically-adjusted budget balance (also called the structural balance or full-employment balance): the budget balance that would prevail if the economy were operating at potential output.
The intuition: in a deep recession, revenues are low and transfers are high purely because the economy is weak, not because Congress is being expansionary. If one wants to measure how aggressive the government's fiscal stance actually is, one needs to strip out the cyclical part. The CBO and IMF both publish cyclically-adjusted budget balances regularly. This is the right measure for comparing fiscal stances across time or across countries.

18.heading: The Cyclically-Adjusted Budget Balance
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
By the cyclically-adjusted measure, the U.S. fiscal position is even more striking. The CBO's structural deficit estimate for FY 2025 is approximately 5% of GDP — meaning that even if the economy were perfectly at potential, the deficit would still be 5% of GDP. The structural component is almost entirely discretionary: tax cuts, spending growth, and the rising cost of mandatory programs (Social Security, Medicare, interest). This is fundamentally different from the 2009 deficit, which was largely cyclical (the structural component was much smaller, around 3% of GDP). The U.S. has moved from cyclical deficits to structural deficits, and that is a far harder problem to fix.
Figure 18.5 The actual deficit and the deficit adjusted for the cycle. A recession widens the deficit automatically, because receipts fall and transfer payments rise, before any decision is taken. Subtracting that component leaves the discretionary stance, which is the series to use when asking whether policy was expansionary. The two differ most precisely when the question matters most, which is in a deep downturn.

18.heading: Worked Examples
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📐 Worked Example 18.1 — Computing the Multiplier in Three Different Regimes
A government considers spending $400 billion of fiscal stimulus. Aggregate MPC is 0.6. Compute the effective multiplier and ΔY in three scenarios: (a) Economy at full employment, central bank actively tightening; (b) Economy in mild recession (output gap −3%), central bank holds rates steady; (c) Economy in deep recession (gap −7%), zero lower bound binding.
1
Naive textbook multiplier: 1/(1−0.6) = 2.5. This is the upper bound — what one would get with no crowding out and perfect transmission.
2
(a) Full employment + Fed tightening: the Fed responds to fiscal expansion by raising rates to neutralize inflation pressure. Empirical evidence suggests the effective multiplier in this regime is approximately 0.5. ΔY ≈ 0.5 × $400B = $200B. Most of the stimulus is crowded out.
3
(b) Mild recession, Fed accommodates: some slack exists; the Fed does not lean against the expansion. Empirical multiplier ≈ 1.2. ΔY ≈ 1.2 × $400B = $480B. Stimulus more than pays for itself in dollar terms.
4

18.heading: Worked Examples
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
(c) Deep recession at ZLB: abundant slack; no monetary tightening possible (LM is flat at zero). The multiplier approaches the textbook ceiling. Empirical multiplier ≈ 1.8 to 2.5. ΔY ≈ 2.0 × $400B = $800B. Stimulus achieves close to its theoretical maximum.
Same $400B of stimulus → $200B, $480B, or $800B of additional output depending on context. The variation is enormous. This is the empirical foundation for the modern view that fiscal stimulus should be aggressive in deep recessions at the ZLB but modest in normal times. The same policy is brilliant in one regime and wasteful in another. Knowing which regime one is in is the central skill of fiscal policy.

18.heading: Worked Examples
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
📐 Worked Example 18.2 — Debt Dynamics
A country has debt-to-GDP of 100%. Its real interest rate on debt is 3%, real GDP growth is 2%, and its current primary deficit is 3% of GDP. (a) Compute the change in debt-to-GDP this year. (b) What primary surplus would stabilize debt-to-GDP at 100%? (c) If the government wants to reduce debt-to-GDP to 60% over 25 years, what primary surplus is required (approximately)? (d) Comment on the political feasibility of this adjustment.
1
(a) Change this year: Δ(D/Y) ≈ (r − g) × (D/Y) − primary surplus/Y = (3% − 2%) × 100% − (−3%) = 1% + 3% = 4%. Debt-to-GDP rises from 100% to 104% in one year.
2
(b) Primary surplus to stabilize: need (r − g) × (D/Y) = 1% × 100% = 1% of GDP. So a +1% primary surplus stabilizes debt-to-GDP. Going from a 3% deficit to a 1% surplus is a 4 percentage-point swing.
3

18.heading: Worked Examples
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body:
(c) Reducing D/Y from 100% to 60% over 25 years: need to reduce D/Y by about 40 percentage points over 25 years = 1.6 percentage points per year. Annual change must be −1.6%. Solving: −1.6% = 1% × (D/Y average) − primary surplus. With average D/Y around 80%, primary surplus needed ≈ 0.8% + 1.6% = 2.4% of GDP. Roughly a 5.4 percentage-point swing from the current 3% deficit position.
4
(d) Political feasibility: a 5+ percentage-point swing in the primary balance is enormous. The largest sustained U.S. fiscal consolidations in the post-WWII era have been about 2-3 percentage points of GDP, achieved gradually over years. Achieving 5+ percentage points would require either large tax increases, large spending cuts, or both, sustained over a generation. Such consolidations are politically extraordinary, requiring rare cross-party consensus that has not existed in the U.S. since the late 1990s.

18.heading: Worked Examples
18.title: Chapter 18, Fiscal Policy How taxing and spending affect the economy — multipliers, automatic stabilizers, the politics of deficits, and the unprecedented question facing the U.S. in 2026: what does a 99% debt-to-GDP ratio at full employment actually mean? In October 2025, the United States closed t
18.body: This is what fiscal sustainability arithmetic looks like. Stabilizing debt-to-GDP at current levels requires modest, ongoing adjustment. Actually reducing debt-to-GDP requires far larger and more sustained adjustment. The U.S. is currently doing neither — its debt-to-GDP is rising, and projections show no realistic path back to historical norms. This is the structural fiscal challenge of our generation, and it cannot be solved by growth alone unless r − g shifts dramatically in our favor (which the post-2022 environment suggests is unlikely).

🎮 MacroNations Connection — Fiscal Policy in the Engine
MacroNations provides direct control over two fiscal levers: gov_spending_pct (range 10–60%, multiplier = 1.4) and tax_rate (range 5–60%, multiplier = −1.1). Note that the engine uses a single multiplier, not a regime-dependent one — there is no ZLB regime switch. If one wants larger fiscal effect, one needs a larger ΔG. The engine encodes the Laffer curve: tax above 40% has an efficiency drag (−0.008/pp), and below 12% an underfunding drag (−0.015/pp). The Reinhart-Rogoff debt drag activates at debt above 90% of GDP: each 10pp of excess subtracts 0.02pp from gdp_growth — small per round, but compounding. Debt is double-penalized in pillar scoring: Stability's debt_pts (60 pts, threshold 40%) plus Sustainability's sust_debt_pts (80 pts, threshold 30%). The cleanest fiscal strategy is moderate G, moderate T, balanced budget, debt under 60% — preserving fiscal space for crisis response options on crisis rounds.

19.heading: Insight
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
The Phillips curve is in some ways the most contested empirical relationship in macroeconomics. It has been pronounced defunct by serious economists at least four times in the past fifty years — in the 1970s when stagflation broke the simple version, in the late 1990s when low unemployment failed to produce expected inflation, in the 2010s when the post-GFC "missing deflation" puzzle emerged, and in 2023-24 when the immaculate disinflation seemed to bury the relationship entirely. And yet the Phillips curve keeps coming back, because the underlying economic intuition is sound: when labor markets are tighter than their long-run sustainable level, wage growth accelerates, firms pass costs through to prices, and inflation rises.

19.heading: Insight
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
What is actually happened over fifty years is not the death of the Phillips curve. It is the gradual realization that the curve is far more complicated than the simple downward-sloping line of 1958. The curve shifts with expectations. It is nonlinear — much steeper when labor markets are very tight than when they are slack. The slope depends on credibility of the central bank's inflation target. It has been "anchored" by inflation targeting frameworks since the 1990s. And during episodes like 2021-22, supply-side shocks can dominate the demand-side mechanism entirely. The honest summary: the Phillips curve is alive but heavily modified, and any policymaker who treats it as a simple trade-off they can exploit will get burned. The 2021-24 episode is just the latest reminder.
— A.S.

19.heading: The Original Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
📘 Principles Level — The 1958 relationship
In 1958 William Phillips, a New Zealand economist working at the London School of Economics, published a paper plotting the rate of change of money wages against the unemployment rate in the United Kingdom from 1861 to 1957. He found a strikingly clear negative relationship: when unemployment was high, wage inflation was low or even negative; when unemployment was low, wage inflation was high. The fit across nearly a century of data was tighter than most economic relationships ever achieve.
In 1960 Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow at MIT replicated the analysis for the United States, substituting price inflation for wage inflation. Their version became the textbook Phillips curve: a downward-sloping curve in (unemployment, inflation) space. The economic interpretation was natural — low unemployment means tight labor markets, which means workers can bargain for faster wage growth, which firms pass through to prices. The policy implication seemed equally natural: policymakers can buy lower unemployment at the cost of higher inflation, and vice versa. The Phillips curve looked like a menu of policy options.

19.heading: The Original Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Original Phillips Curve
\[ \pi = \alpha - \beta u \]
π
Inflation rate (originally wage inflation, later generalized to price inflation).
u
Unemployment rate.
α
A positive constant — the inflation rate that would prevail at u = 0%.
β
The slope of the Phillips curve — how much inflation falls for each 1pp rise in unemployment. In Samuelson-Solow's U.S. data of 1960, β was estimated at roughly 0.5 to 1.0.
The Samuelson-Solow policy interpretation: if one wants 4% inflation, one has to accept about 3% unemployment; if one wants 0% inflation, one has to accept about 7% unemployment. The curve was treated as a stable menu — a structural feature of the economy that policymakers could move along like a demand curve. This interpretation, as it turned out, was wrong. But to understand why, we have to first see what happened in the 1970s.

19.heading: The Original Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Figure 19.1 The relationship as it appeared in the 1960s. Each point is one year of American data; the fit is close enough that policy discussion of the period treated the curve as a menu from which an administration could choose. The reading was mistaken in a specific way: the relation holds only for a given state of inflation expectations, and choosing a point on it repeatedly is what causes expectations, and the curve, to move.

19.heading: The 1970s Breakdown: Stagflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
The simple Phillips curve worked beautifully through the 1960s. U.S. inflation rose from about 1% in 1961 to 4% by 1968 as unemployment fell from 7% to 3.5%. The Federal Reserve, taking the trade-off literally, ran an accommodating monetary policy that pushed unemployment down and accepted moderate inflation. Both rates of change tracked the Samuelson-Solow curve almost perfectly.
Then in the 1970s, something happened that the simple Phillips curve said could not happen. Inflation and unemployment both rose, simultaneously, for the better part of a decade. The 1973-75 episode saw U.S. CPI inflation hit 12% while unemployment reached 9%. The 1979-82 episode was worse: inflation peaked at 14.8% in 1980 while unemployment climbed past 10% by 1982. The phenomenon got a name — stagflation, the combination of stagnant growth and inflation. The Phillips curve appeared not just to have shifted but to have disappeared.
1968-1970
Friedman and Phelps
Theory before data
The Friedman-Phelps Critique — Predicted Stagflation Before It Happened

19.heading: The 1970s Breakdown: Stagflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: In December 1967, in his presidential address to the American Economic Association, Milton Friedman delivered what is now considered one of the most consequential macroeconomic papers of the 20th century. Friedman argued that the Phillips curve was fundamentally misconceived. Workers and firms care about real wages, not nominal wages. If inflation is expected to be 0%, then a nominal wage increase of 3% really is a 3% real raise. But if inflation is expected to be 5%, then the same nominal 3% increase is actually a 2% real cut. Workers will demand higher nominal wages to compensate for expected inflation. The Phillips curve must therefore shift with expectations.

19.heading: The 1970s Breakdown: Stagflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Edmund Phelps reached the same conclusion independently in 1968. Both predicted that if policymakers tried to keep unemployment permanently below its "natural rate" by accepting higher inflation, expectations would adjust upward, the Phillips curve would shift up, and eventually both unemployment and inflation would be higher than before. They predicted stagflation before it happened. When stagflation arrived in the 1970s, Friedman and Phelps were vindicated, and macroeconomics shifted permanently toward expectations-based modeling. Both won the Nobel Prize for this work (Friedman in 1976, Phelps in 2006).

19.heading: The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
\[ \pi = \pi^{e} - \beta\,(u - u^{*}) + \varepsilon \]
\(π^{e}\)
Expected inflation — what workers and firms expect inflation to be over the period when wages and prices are being set. The single most important addition to the simple Phillips curve.
u − u*
Unemployment gap — actual unemployment minus the natural rate u*. When unemployment is below the natural rate, inflation rises above expectations; above, inflation falls below expectations.
β
The slope coefficient. Smaller values mean a "flatter" curve — large changes in unemployment produce small changes in inflation. Empirical estimates have fallen from ~1.0 in the 1960s to as low as 0.1-0.2 in some post-2000 estimates.
supply_shock
A residual capturing supply-side disruptions — oil prices, supply chain disruptions, weather events — that move inflation independently of the unemployment gap.

19.heading: The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: The key insight: there is no permanent trade-off between unemployment and inflation. In the long run, expectations adjust to whatever actual inflation policymakers deliver, and the unemployment rate returns to its natural rate u*. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at u = u*. Policymakers can only push unemployment below u* in the short run, and they pay for it later with a persistent rise in expected inflation.

19.heading: The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Treating the natural rate as a constant
Textbooks often write u* as if it were a constant of nature. It is not. The natural rate of unemployment depends on labor market institutions, demographics, technology, and search frictions — all of which change over time. The U.S. natural rate is estimated to have peaked near 6.5% in the early 1980s (high union power, demographic bulge of inexperienced young workers, oil price shocks driving structural unemployment) and fallen to as low as 4.0% by 2025 (deunionization, aging workforce, online job matching). What looks like a 5.5% unemployment rate moving above the natural rate in 1985 might look like a 5.5% unemployment rate moving well above the natural rate in 2025.
This matters for policymakers because the "appropriate" unemployment rate at any moment depends on what u* is — and u* can only be estimated, never observed directly. The CBO publishes an estimate, the Fed has its own, and academic estimates vary by 1+ percentage point at any given time. Anyone who quotes a confident estimate of "the" natural rate without uncertainty bands is overstating what we know.

19.heading: The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Figure 19.2 The expectations-augmented Phillips curve, \(\pi = \pi^e - \alpha(u - u^*) + \varepsilon\). Each short-run curve is drawn for a given expected rate of inflation. Holding unemployment below \(u^*\) raises inflation, expectations adjust to the higher rate, and the short-run curve shifts up. In long-run equilibrium expectations are correct, unemployment returns to \(u^*\), and the relationship is vertical: there is no permanent trade-off to exploit.

19.heading: The Long-Run Phillips Curve is Vertical
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Why no permanent trade-off exists
The expectations-augmented Phillips curve has a striking long-run property. In long-run equilibrium, expected inflation equals actual inflation: \(\pi^{e} = \pi\). Substituting this back into the Phillips equation:
π = π − β × (u − u*)⟹ 0 = −β × (u − u*)⟹ u = u*
In long-run equilibrium, unemployment must equal the natural rate, regardless of what inflation is. This is the famous result that the long-run Phillips curve is vertical. The economy can be in long-run equilibrium with 2% inflation and 4% unemployment, or with 10% inflation and 4% unemployment, or with 0% inflation and 4% unemployment — but unemployment in each case is 4%. The only equilibrium that depends on policy is the inflation rate. The unemployment rate is determined by structural factors.

19.heading: The Long-Run Phillips Curve is Vertical
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
This is the central long-run lesson of post-1970 macroeconomics: monetary policy can choose the long-run inflation rate but not the long-run unemployment rate. There is no permanent trade-off. Attempts to push unemployment below u* succeed temporarily but only by raising expected inflation, which then has to be reversed at the cost of an above-u* recession. The 1979-82 Volcker disinflation was exactly this reverse — bringing inflation back down after the 1960s-70s attempted exploitation of the (illusory) long-run trade-off.
Figure 19.3 Why the long-run curve is vertical. Starting at A, an expansion buys lower unemployment at B only while inflation exceeds what wage-setters expected. Once expectations adjust, the short-run curve shifts up and the economy returns to the natural rate at C, with higher inflation and no employment gain. Repeating the attempt repeats the cycle at successively higher inflation, which is the 1970s in one diagram.

19.heading: The Sacrifice Ratio: What Disinflation Costs
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Sacrifice Ratio
\[ \text{sacrifice ratio} = \frac{\text{cumulative excess unemployment}}{\text{reduction in inflation}} \]
cumulative excess unemployment
The sum of unemployment-rate percentage points above the natural rate over the disinflation period. If unemployment is 2pp above u* for 3 years, cumulative excess = 6 percentage point-years.
reduction in inflation
The total percentage-point reduction in inflation achieved over the disinflation episode.
Empirical estimates of the sacrifice ratio: Lawrence Ball's 1994 meta-analysis estimated the U.S. sacrifice ratio at approximately 2.4 percentage point-years of excess unemployment per percentage point of inflation reduction. The Volcker disinflation (15% inflation in 1980 to 4% inflation in 1983, with cumulative unemployment gap of about 20 percentage point-years) produced a sacrifice ratio of about 2.0 — slightly below Ball's average. The 2022-24 disinflation was unusual: 9.1% inflation to 2.4% with cumulative excess unemployment of essentially zero — a sacrifice ratio close to zero, an outcome that no standard model would have predicted.
1979-1983
United States
Volcker Disinflation

19.heading: The Sacrifice Ratio: What Disinflation Costs
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
The Volcker Disinflation — The Textbook Sacrifice Ratio in Action
When Paul Volcker became Federal Reserve Chair in August 1979, U.S. inflation was running at 11.5%. By 1980 it had peaked at 14.8%. Volcker raised the federal funds rate from 11% to a peak of about 20% in late 1980 (with a second peak of 19.1% in June 1981) and held it at extraordinarily high levels for over two years. The result: inflation fell to about 4% by 1983. The cost: unemployment rose from 5.8% in 1979 to 10.8% in November 1982 — the highest unemployment rate since the Great Depression. Cumulative excess unemployment over the 1980-1983 disinflation was approximately 20 percentage point-years.

19.heading: The Sacrifice Ratio: What Disinflation Costs
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
This was textbook expectations-augmented Phillips curve behavior. To bring inflation down, expected inflation had to be brought down. Bringing expected inflation down required convincing workers and firms that the Fed would tolerate high unemployment indefinitely rather than back off the disinflation. The credibility cost — measured in lost output and elevated unemployment — was substantial: cumulative real GDP losses are estimated at about 6% of one year's GDP, or roughly $400 billion in 1980 dollars (~$1.5 trillion today). This was the model disinflation: painful, credible, and ultimately successful in shifting expectations.
Figure 19.4 A disinflation and its cost (schematic). Reducing inflation requires a period of unemployment above the natural rate; the sacrifice ratio is the cumulative excess unemployment, or lost output, per percentage point of inflation removed. The ratio is smaller when the policy is credible, because expectations fall without having to be forced down by slack.

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
Now we come to the puzzle that opened this chapter. Between June 2022 and December 2024, U.S. CPI inflation fell from 9.1% to 2.4% — a 6.7 percentage-point disinflation, exceeding even the Volcker reduction. Unemployment rose from 3.5% to 4.2%, a gap of less than 1 percentage point above most estimates of the natural rate. The cumulative excess unemployment over the disinflation period was approximately 1.5 percentage point-years, producing an implied sacrifice ratio of about 0.22 — roughly one-tenth of historical norms.
This outcome was widely predicted to be impossible. In February 2021, Larry Summers warned that the American Rescue Plan would produce "inflationary pressures of a kind we have not seen in a generation" and that disinflation would eventually require "extended unemployment of 6%+." When inflation peaked at 9.1% in mid-2022, almost every forecaster expected a recession would be needed to bring it back to target. The Federal Reserve itself, in its Summary of Economic Projections through 2023, repeatedly projected unemployment rising above 4.5% as a necessary condition for disinflation. None of these forecasts came true.

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
Four leading explanations for the 2022-2024 immaculate disinflation
ExplanationMechanism
1. Supply-side normalization
Most of the 2021-22 inflation was supply-side: global supply chain disruptions, energy price spikes, and labor force participation drops from COVID. As these normalized — supply chains repaired, energy prices fell, participation recovered — inflation fell mechanically with little role for demand-side mechanisms.
2. Anchored expectations
Long-run inflation expectations stayed remarkably stable throughout the inflation spike. Survey-based expectations (Michigan, NY Fed) rose modestly to 3% and quickly returned to 2.5-3%. Market-based expectations (5-year breakevens) similarly stayed anchored. This is the payoff of three decades of credible inflation targeting — the Fed's credibility prevented expectations from de-anchoring as they did in the 1970s.
3. Beveridge curve dynamics

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
Labor market tightness can be measured by vacancies (job openings) divided by unemployment. In 2022 this ratio was extraordinarily high — roughly 2 vacancies per unemployed worker, the highest in recorded history. The labor market cooled primarily through falling vacancies, not rising unemployment. This is the "soft landing" channel: tightness eased without workers being laid off.
4. Phillips curve nonlinearity
Recent Fed Board research (Smith, Timmermann, Wright 2024) shows the Phillips curve is steep when labor markets are very tight and flat when slack exists. So inflation surged in 2021-22 (steep portion) and fell rapidly in 2023-24 even with modest unemployment increases (still on steep portion). Once at the flatter portion, further inflation reduction would be slower.

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — What the immaculate disinflation actually proved
Three years after the fact, I think we can be reasonably confident about the lessons of the 2021-24 inflation cycle. First, the Phillips curve was never defunct — but it was heavily modified by anchored expectations. Without three decades of credible inflation targeting and the Fed's willingness to raise rates 525bp from 2022-23, the disinflation would not have happened. The "immaculate" part of the disinflation rests on the credibility built up over decades, not on the absence of Phillips-curve forces.
Second, most of the 2021-22 inflation really was supply-side, and once supply normalized, most of the inflation went away mechanically. The demand-side Phillips curve contribution was probably 2-3 percentage points of the 9% peak; the rest was supply. Third, the "soft landing" was partly the result of a labor market with considerable room to cool through vacancies rather than layoffs — an unusual structural condition that may not recur.

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
What the immaculate disinflation did not prove: it did not prove that the Phillips curve is gone, it did not prove that monetary policy is costless, and it did not prove that future inflation episodes will resolve so painlessly. Anyone arguing "we just disinflated without a recession, so the Phillips curve trade-off was always overstated" is overgeneralizing from one episode with unusual features. The next inflation cycle is unlikely to be as forgiving.
— A.S.

19.heading: The 2022-2024 Immaculate Disinflation
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Figure 19.5 Two disinflations of comparable size, drawn as paths. The Volcker episode moved far to the right before inflation fell: unemployment reached nearly ten percent. The 2022-2024 episode achieved a similar fall in inflation with unemployment barely above four percent. The standard explanations are that expectations were anchored this time and that much of the inflation came from supply disruptions that unwound on their own; the episode remains the most important open question in current macroeconomics.

19.heading: The Modern Phillips Curve: New Keynesian Form
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The New Keynesian Phillips Curve
\[ \pi_t = \beta\,E_t[\pi_{t+1}] + \kappa\,\tilde{y}_t + \varepsilon_t \]\(\tilde{y}_t\) is the output gap and \(E_t[\pi_{t+1}]\) is expected inflation.
\(π_{t}\)
Current inflation rate.
\(E_{t}\)\([\pi_{t+1}]\)
Forward-looking expected inflation — what agents at time t expect inflation to be in the next period. The "expectations" channel from Friedman-Phelps, but using forward-looking rather than adaptive expectations.
β
A discount factor close to 1.0 (typically 0.99 in calibrated models). Captures how much weight current inflation puts on future inflation expectations.
κ × output_gap
Real-side pressure on inflation — output above potential pushes inflation up, output below potential pulls it down. κ is small in modern estimates (often 0.05-0.15), capturing the "flatness" of the modern Phillips curve.
\(ε_{t}\)
A residual representing supply shocks, markup variation, and other inflation drivers not captured by the gap or expectations.

19.heading: The Modern Phillips Curve: New Keynesian Form
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Modern central banks operate with this form in mind. The Fed's policy framework, articulated through Federal Open Market Committee communications, explicitly references "longer-run inflation expectations remaining well anchored" as a precondition for using the Phillips channel for stabilization. If expectations are anchored, the Fed can let unemployment dip below u* temporarily without triggering inflation; if expectations are de-anchored, even modest tightness produces large inflation. This is why the early 2022 inflation pickup was treated as a five-alarm fire by FOMC participants — they were terrified the de-anchoring would happen, and ran a fast tightening cycle specifically to prevent it.

19.heading: Interactive: The Phillips Curve Simulator
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
🎛 Interactive — Phillips Curve Simulator
See how the Phillips curve behaves under different expectations regimes and slopes
Set the unemployment rate, expected inflation, and Phillips curve slope. Watch inflation respond to each — and compare the short-run vs long-run outcomes. The natural rate (u*) is shown as a vertical reference line.
Unemployment rate (%): 5.0%
Expected inflation \(\pi^{e}\) (%): 2.0%
Phillips slope β: 0.5
Natural rate u* (%): 4.5%
Reading the chart: The downward-sloping line is the short-run Phillips curve at the current expected inflation level. The vertical line is the long-run Phillips curve at the natural rate. Where one sits on the short-run curve depends on current unemployment; long-run equilibrium is always at u*. Notice how the 1960s β=1.0 setting makes the curve steep — a 1pp unemployment change moves inflation by 1pp. The 2022 β=0.2 setting makes it nearly flat — a 1pp change moves inflation by only 0.2pp.

19.heading: Worked Examples
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
📐 Worked Example 19.1 — Computing the Phillips Inflation
Suppose \(u* = 4.5\%, \beta = 0.4, \pi^{e} = 2.0\%\) (anchored). (a) Compute inflation if unemployment is 3.5%. (b) Compute inflation if unemployment is 6.5%. (c) What level of unemployment would produce zero inflation? (d) Now suppose \(\pi^{e}\) jumps to 5% after a year of running 3.5% unemployment. Recompute (a) at the higher expected inflation level. Interpret.
1
Use the formula: \(\pi = \pi^{e} - \beta \times (u - u*)\).
2
(a) u = 3.5%: π = 2.0 − 0.4 × (3.5 − 4.5) = 2.0 − 0.4 × (−1.0) = 2.0 + 0.4 = 2.4%. Below natural rate → inflation slightly above expected.
3
(b) u = 6.5%: π = 2.0 − 0.4 × (6.5 − 4.5) = 2.0 − 0.4 × 2.0 = 2.0 − 0.8 = 1.2%. Above natural rate → inflation below expected.
4
(c) Zero inflation: 0 = 2.0 − 0.4 × (u − 4.5). Solve: 0.4 × (u − 4.5) = 2.0, so u − 4.5 = 5.0, u = 9.5%. Would require unemployment 5pp above the natural rate — a very deep recession.
5

19.heading: Worked Examples
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
(d) De-anchored expectations: \(\pi^{e} = 5\%, u = 3.5\%\). π = 5.0 − 0.4 × (3.5 − 4.5) = 5.0 + 0.4 = 5.4%. Same unemployment gap but inflation is 3 percentage points higher. This is exactly what Friedman-Phelps predicted: trying to maintain below-natural unemployment shifts the curve up via expectations.
The lesson: the Phillips curve does not indicate "inflation given unemployment" in a context-free way. It indicates inflation given unemployment and expectations. If expectations are anchored at 2%, a tight labor market produces only mild inflation. If expectations are de-anchored at 5%, the same labor market produces serious inflation. Anchored expectations are the difference between a manageable inflation episode and a 1970s-style disaster.

19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body:
📐 Worked Example 19.2 — The Volcker Sacrifice Ratio
Use the expectations-augmented Phillips curve to compute approximately how long it would take to reduce inflation from 12% to 4% under the following: β = 0.5, u* = 6%, and unemployment held at 9%. Assume \(\pi^{e}\) adjusts slowly: \(\pi^{e}_{t+1}\) = \(0.7 \times \pi^{e}_{t}\) + \(0.3 \times \pi_{t}\) (adaptive expectations, weight 0.3 on actual). Compute the path year by year.
1
Year 1: \(\pi^{e} = 12\%\) (initial). π = 12 − 0.5 × (9 − 6) = 12 − 1.5 = 10.5%. Updated expectations: \(\pi^{e}_{2}\) = 0.7 × 12 + 0.3 × 10.5 = 8.4 + 3.15 = 11.55%.
2
Year 2: π = 11.55 − 1.5 = 10.05%. \(\pi^{e}_{3}\) = 0.7 × 11.55 + 0.3 × 10.05 = 8.085 + 3.015 = 11.10%.
3
Year 3: π = 11.10 − 1.5 = 9.6%. \(\pi^{e}_{4}\) ≈ 10.65%. The disinflation is happening slowly because adaptive expectations are stubborn.
4
By Year 8: Working through the algebra, π is approximately 4.5%. At the geometric rate of decay built in, it takes about 8 years to fully reach 4%.

19.heading: Worked Examples
19.title: Chapter 19, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
19.body: Cumulative unemployment cost: 8 years × 3pp excess unemployment = 24 percentage point-years of excess unemployment. Implied sacrifice ratio: 24 / 8 = 3.0 pp-years per pp of inflation reduction, close to Ball's empirical average of 2.4. The slowness comes from the adaptive expectations specification — workers and firms keep expecting yesterday's inflation, so disinflation has to "outwait" expectations. Under perfectly rational forward-looking expectations, the same disinflation could happen much faster if the Fed's commitment were perfectly credible.

20.heading: Overview
20.title: Chapter 20, The Phillips Curve The unemployment-inflation trade-off in its short-run, long-run, and expectations-augmented forms — plus an honest treatment of what the 2021-2024 episode taught macroeconomists about the curve's flatness, nonlinearity, and survivability In December 2024, the U.S. econ
20.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — The Phillips Curve in the Engine
The Phillips Curve is the engine's main GDP-vs-Stability tension. The engine's inflation equation: inflation = (0.5 × prev_inflation + 0.5 × 2.0) + 0.4 × output_gap + monetary_inf + cost_push + crisis + noise. Pushing gdp_growth above potential creates positive output_gap, which feeds inflation at slope 0.4 per pp. The 50% adaptive component means inflation persistence is real: if inflation rose this round, next round's expectations carry half of that increase forward — exactly the Friedman-Phelps mechanism but built into the engine directly. The 50% anchored-to-2% component represents the credibility benefit of inflation targeting. There is no separate "credibility" state variable that one can manipulate — anchoring is structural. The optimal long-run strategy: keep gdp_growth ≈ potential (zero output gap, no Phillips inflation pressure), and use supply-side levers (rd_investment, infrastructure, green_energy) to slowly raise potential — giving GDP room to grow without triggering inflation.
