20.heading: Insight
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Supply-side economics suffers from a definitional problem that makes empirical evaluation maddeningly difficult. If "supply-side" means tax cuts and deregulation have some positive growth effects, then it is uncontroversial — every reasonable economist agrees. Tax cuts raise after-tax returns to work, savings, and investment, which on the margin produces more of all three. Deregulation removes deadweight loss. These are real effects in real data. The controversy is about the magnitudes: are the growth effects large enough to offset the revenue loss? And the empirical answer to that question, across multiple major tax-cut episodes, is essentially no — the growth effects are real but modest, and the deficit increases are large and persistent.

20.heading: Insight
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
What makes the political debate frustrating is that proponents of supply-side cuts almost never lose the political argument by admitting this. They argue: "The growth effects are larger than CBO scores suggest." "The cuts will pay for themselves over a longer horizon." "The deficit increases are due to spending growth, not the tax cuts." Each of these arguments has some merit at some level, but none stands up to careful empirical scrutiny as a primary explanation. The honest empirical summary, from a politically neutral economic perspective, is that major U.S. tax cuts produce growth effects in the range of 0.1 to 0.5 percentage points of GDP per year over a decade — real but modest — at a cumulative deficit cost in the trillions. The 2025 OBBBA is unlikely to be an exception.
— A.S.

20.heading: The Laffer Curve
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
📘 Principles Level — The relationship between tax rates and revenue
The Laffer curve describes the empirical relationship between tax rates and tax revenue. At a tax rate of 0%, revenue is zero — no revenue is collected. At a tax rate of 100%, revenue is also zero — no one engages in taxable activity if all the gains are taken by government. Between these two extremes, revenue is positive. Somewhere along the curve, revenue peaks. That peak — the "Laffer point" — is the tax rate that maximizes government revenue. Above the peak, raising tax rates further reduces revenue, because the discouragement of economic activity outweighs the higher rate.

20.heading: The Laffer Curve
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
The Laffer curve is, in its basic form, completely uncontroversial. The controversy is about where the peak is. Laffer himself often suggested the peak was around 50% for the U.S. federal income tax. Most empirical estimates put it considerably higher: Saez and Piketty (2014) estimate the U.S. revenue-maximizing top marginal income tax rate at around 75-80%. Trabandt and Uhlig (2011) estimate U.S. labor income tax revenue maximizes around 65%. If the peak is at 65-80%, then U.S. tax rates have been well below the peak throughout the period in which Laffer arguments have been deployed politically.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Laffer Curve in Simplest Form
\[ R(\tau) = \tau \times Y(\tau), \qquad Y'(\tau) < 0 \]
τ
The tax rate (0 to 1).
Y(τ)
The taxable income base as a function of the tax rate. Higher tax rates reduce labor supply, savings, investment, and tax-compliance effort, so Y(τ) is a decreasing function of τ.
Revenue maximum
Differentiating: dRevenue/dτ = Y(τ) + τ × Y'(τ) = 0 at the peak. Solving: τ* = −Y/Y' = 1/|elasticity of base|. If the elasticity of the tax base with respect to (1−τ) is 0.25, then the Laffer point is at τ = 1/(1+0.25) = 80%.

20.heading: The Laffer Curve
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body: The empirical key: the Laffer point depends critically on the elasticity of taxable income (ETI). Most U.S. estimates put the ETI at roughly 0.2 to 0.4 — putting the Laffer point at 70-83%. For comparison, the current U.S. top federal marginal rate is 37% (40.8% with Medicare surcharge). The U.S. is on the rising portion of the Laffer curve, not the falling portion. Tax cuts therefore reduce revenue, not increase it. Even the most pro-supply-side empirical estimates by Trabandt-Uhlig and others put the U.S. firmly below the peak.

20.heading: The Laffer Curve
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Conflating "tax cuts produce growth" with "tax cuts pay for themselves"
These are two different claims. The first — tax cuts produce growth — is uncontroversial. The second — tax cuts pay for themselves — requires the additional claim that the economy is on the falling side of the Laffer curve, which the U.S. has not been on at any point in modern history. Supply-side advocates often slide from the first claim (true) to the second (false) without noting the difference.
A separate but related fallacy: "the 1980s saw tax cuts and revenue increases, so tax cuts must have paid for themselves." Tax revenue rises with the size of the economy regardless of tax cuts — what matters is whether revenue rose more or less than it would have without the cuts. Counterfactual analysis by Romer-Romer (2010), Mertens-Ravn (2012), and others consistently finds tax cuts reduce revenue relative to the counterfactual. The 1980s revenue growth happened despite, not because of, the Reagan cuts.

20.heading: The Laffer Curve
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body: Figure 20.1 The Laffer curve. Revenue is zero at a rate of zero and at a rate of one hundred percent , so somewhere between them lies a maximum. The proposition is not in dispute; the empirical question is where an economy sits. Estimates of the revenue-maximizing average rate for advanced economies lie well above prevailing rates, which implies that rate reductions in those economies lose revenue even after any behavioral response.

20.heading: Supply-Side Effects in Theory
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
Tax cuts can affect economic activity through three main channels — labor supply, savings/investment, and tax compliance. Each is real, but each has empirical limits that make the magnitudes much smaller than supply-side rhetoric usually implies.
The three supply-side channels: theory vs. empirical magnitudes
ChannelTheoretical mechanismEmpirical magnitude
Labor supply
Lower marginal tax rates raise after-tax wage, encouraging more labor supply (income effect) or less (substitution effect, depending on preferences). Net empirical effect is usually positive but small.
Compensated elasticity of labor supply ≈ 0.1 to 0.3 for primary earners; up to 0.6 for secondary earners. A 5pp tax cut might raise hours worked by ~1-2%.
Savings & investment
Lower taxes on capital income raise after-tax return on saving, incentivizing more saving. Lower corporate tax raises after-tax return on investment, incentivizing more investment.
Elasticity of saving with respect to after-tax return ≈ 0 to 0.3 (small to negligible in most estimates). Investment is more responsive: corporate tax cuts have measurable but modest effects on investment (~5-15% increase per 10pp cut in some studies).

20.heading: Supply-Side Effects in Theory
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
Tax compliance & reporting
Lower marginal rates reduce the gains from tax avoidance and evasion, increasing reported income relative to true income.
Elasticity of reported (vs. true) income ≈ 0.2 to 0.4 at the very top of the distribution. Substantial for the highest 1% of taxpayers, modest for everyone else.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Static vs. Dynamic Revenue Scoring
\[ \text{dynamic loss} = \text{static loss} \times (1 - \text{feedback ratio}) \]The static loss is the revenue change holding behavior fixed; the feedback ratio is the share recovered through the behavioral response.
Static scoring
CBO's traditional approach: compute revenue loss assuming behavior does not change. A 1pp tax cut on a $20 trillion income base produces a $200 billion static revenue loss.
Dynamic scoring
Newer CBO approach (post-2015): incorporates behavioral responses. The same 1pp tax cut might produce ~2% additional labor supply and investment, raising the income base, partially offsetting the revenue loss.
Feedback ratio

20.heading: Supply-Side Effects in Theory
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
The fraction of the static revenue loss recovered through behavioral effects. CBO's dynamic scores of the 2017 TCJA gave a feedback ratio of about 0.15-0.20 — supply-side effects offset 15-20% of the static revenue loss, not 100%. For OBBBA 2025, CBO's preliminary estimate is similar.
The empirical answer: dynamic supply-side feedback offsets some of the static revenue loss, but not most of it. For a major U.S. tax cut, expect supply-side effects to recover roughly 10-25% of the static loss, with 75-90% being net deficit increase. The math does not support the "pays for itself" claim.
Figure 20.2 The labor-market tax wedge. Income and payroll taxation drives a wedge between the cost of an hour to the employer and the amount the worker keeps, and hours fall from \(H^*\) to \(H_{\text{tax}}\). The size of the response is governed by labor supply and demand elasticities, which are the quantities supply-side arguments turn on and which are modest for prime-age men and larger for second earners.

20.heading: The 1981 Reagan Tax Cuts: Evidence from the Definitive Test
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
1981-1983
United States
Economic Recovery Tax Act
The Reagan Tax Cuts and the Empirical Verdict
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 cut U.S. federal income tax rates by approximately 25% across the board, reducing the top marginal rate from 70% to 50% (eventually to 28% by the end of the decade through subsequent legislation). The tax cuts were sold heavily on Laffer-curve grounds: tax revenue would grow faster, not slower, because of the supply-side response. The supply-side school predicted federal revenues would rise sharply.
What actually happened: federal revenue as a share of GDP fell from 19.4% in fiscal 1981 to 17.4% in fiscal 1984, a decline of 2 percentage points of GDP. The federal deficit, which had averaged 2.3% of GDP in the late 1970s, grew to 5.0% of GDP by 1983. The CBO retrospectively estimated that ERTA reduced federal revenue by about $200 billion in 1986 dollars (~$700 billion today) over its first five years. The supply-side response was positive — GDP did grow faster in 1983-89 than it would have without the cuts — but the growth response captured only a small fraction of the static revenue loss.

20.heading: The 1981 Reagan Tax Cuts: Evidence from the Definitive Test
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
Importantly, this was not a clean test: the 1981-82 recession (driven by Volcker disinflation) and the subsequent recovery confounded the analysis. Most retrospective studies, including Romer-Romer (2010) using a "narrative" identification approach, estimate the ERTA cuts produced GDP growth effects of roughly 0.4-0.6 percentage points per year over five years — substantial but well below what would be needed to recoup revenue. The 1981 cuts are the closest thing to a definitive test of supply-side claims, and they failed those claims, even using the most favorable empirical methods.
Figure 20.3 Federal receipts and outlays around the 1981 tax reductions. Receipts fell by roughly two points of output and did not recover to their previous share, while outlays continued at their earlier level, so the deficit widened and stayed wide. The episode is the cleanest test of the strong supply-side claim that reductions in marginal rates pay for themselves, and the claim failed it: the subsequent expansion was real but not large enough to replace the lost revenue.

20.heading: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
2017-2024
United States
TCJA
TCJA — The Most Carefully Studied Modern Tax Cut
The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was the largest U.S. tax cut since 1981. It cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%, doubled the standard deduction, capped the SALT deduction at $10,000, and modified individual tax brackets. CBO scored the static revenue loss at approximately $1.9 trillion over 10 years. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimated dynamic feedback would recover roughly $400 billion of that, leaving a net deficit increase of about $1.5 trillion — a feedback ratio of about 21%.

20.heading: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body: The post-passage empirical evidence has been substantial. Chodorow-Reich et al. (2024) using firm-level data find that the TCJA corporate tax cut increased investment by about 8-14% over the 2018-2022 period — a real and measurable effect. But the wage and labor supply effects were small: real wage growth in 2018-2019 was about 0.5pp faster than it would have been, attributable to the tax cut — modest. Reconciling the studies, the consensus is that TCJA raised GDP growth by roughly 0.1-0.3 percentage points per year, producing a cumulative GDP increase of perhaps 1-3% over 10 years. Static revenue loss of $1.9T, dynamic offset of perhaps $300-500B. Net deficit increase: approximately $1.5 trillion, matching CBO's scoring almost exactly.

20.heading: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
The TCJA debate is essentially settled in the empirical literature: the cuts produced measurable supply-side effects, but those effects offset only 15-25% of the static revenue loss. The cuts did not pay for themselves, and the persistent deficit consequences are now showing up in 2024-2025 debt-to-GDP ratios approaching 100%. The political rhetoric of "the cuts will pay for themselves" was empirically wrong, predictably wrong, and the post-cut evidence has been conclusive.
Figure 20.4 Business investment and share repurchases around the 2017 corporate tax reduction. Investment did rise, which is the effect the theory predicts, but by considerably less than the sponsors projected and by less than the increase in repurchases in the first year. The honest summary is that the measure had a real and positive effect on the capital stock that was too small to recover the revenue forgone.

20.heading: The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
2025
United States
OBBBA
OBBBA — Doubling Down at the Worst Time
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, made permanent many of the temporary TCJA provisions, expanded several deductions, and tightened eligibility for federal benefits including SNAP and Medicaid. The supply-side argument was similar to 1981 and 2017: lower marginal rates would stimulate so much additional activity that the cuts would substantially pay for themselves. CBO's score: static revenue loss of approximately $4 trillion over 10 years; dynamic offset of approximately $700 billion (feedback ratio of ~18%); net deficit increase of approximately $3.3 trillion. NBER analyses project OBBBA will add approximately 29 percentage points to the debt-to-GDP ratio over 30 years compared to the no-OBBBA baseline.

20.heading: The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
OBBBA's macroeconomic context distinguishes it from prior episodes. In 1981, the U.S. was emerging from a deep recession with debt-to-GDP near 30%. In 2017, the economy was at moderate slack with debt-to-GDP near 76%. In 2025, the economy was at full employment (unemployment 4.3%, near the natural rate), inflation slightly above target (2.7%), interest rates were elevated (4.0% federal funds), and debt-to-GDP had reached 99.8%. Every macroeconomic condition that made fiscal expansion more defensible in earlier episodes was absent in 2025. Yet the policy proceeded.
The supply-side claims around OBBBA face an additional empirical challenge: the U.S. corporate sector is now operating at much higher pre-tax profit shares than during prior tax-cut episodes, suggesting weaker investment elasticities at the margin. Some preliminary studies estimate the supply-side feedback ratio for OBBBA could be as low as 10-15% — even smaller than TCJA's. The likely outcome: substantial deficit increase, marginal growth boost, debt-to-GDP path that turns from "rising" to "rising faster," and a future round of fiscal consolidation made harder by another decade of accumulated debt.

20.heading: Deregulation as the Other Supply-Side Lever
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Deregulation effects in theory and practice
Supply-side economics encompasses not just tax cuts but deregulation — removing rules, requirements, and restrictions that impose costs on businesses. The economic case for deregulation is straightforward: if a regulation imposes costs that exceed its benefits, removing it raises net welfare. The challenge is that the benefits of regulation are often diffuse (better air quality benefiting millions), while the costs are concentrated (specific industries paying compliance costs), making cost-benefit analysis politically asymmetric.

20.heading: Deregulation as the Other Supply-Side Lever
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body: The empirical evidence on deregulation is mixed and context-dependent. Sectoral deregulation — like airline deregulation in 1978 or trucking deregulation in 1980 — has produced large welfare gains by lowering prices and increasing competition. Financial deregulation — like the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley repeal of Glass-Steagall — has produced more ambiguous welfare effects, with substantial gains in some areas (consumer credit access) and significant costs in others (contributing to the 2008 crisis). Environmental deregulation consistently produces gains in measured productivity at the cost of unpriced externalities like pollution.

20.heading: What Actually Works for Productivity Growth
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
Critics of supply-side economics sometimes overcorrect, dismissing the productivity-side of macroeconomic policy entirely. That is also wrong. There are policies that reliably raise long-run productivity growth — they are just mostly not tax cuts. The empirical literature on what raises productivity is much stronger than the literature on what tax cuts achieve.
Productivity-raising policies and their empirical track record
PolicyProductivity effectEvidence
Public R&D investmentLarge, persistentBloom et al. (2013): social returns to R&D are 3-4x the private return. Public R&D is generally complementary to private R&D, not crowding out.
Infrastructure investmentLarge in deficient casesAschauer (1989) and successor studies: 1% increase in public capital stock raises private productivity by ~0.4%. Diminishing returns once infrastructure is adequate.
Education (especially early-childhood)Very large, very long-tailedHeckman: early-childhood education programs return 7-13x their cost over 50 years. K-12 effects more modest but still positive.

20.heading: What Actually Works for Productivity Growth
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
Trade opennessLarge for closed economies, modest for openFrankel-Romer (1999): 1% increase in trade as % of GDP raises GDP per capita by 0.5-2.0%. Effect saturates as openness increases.
Immigration (skilled)SubstantialHunt-Gauthier-Loiselle (2010): a 1pp increase in college-graduate immigration raises patenting per capita by 9-18%.
Antitrust enforcementModest but consistentRecent literature (Khan, Crouzet et al.) suggests rising market power has reduced productivity growth; vigorous antitrust could reverse some of this.
Marginal tax cutsSmall to modestEstimates of 0.1-0.5pp growth boost per major tax cut, vs. trillions in revenue loss. Lowest productivity-per-dollar of policies listed here.

20.heading: What Actually Works for Productivity Growth

20.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — What "supply-side" should mean
If "supply-side economics" actually meant a coherent set of policies aimed at long-run productivity growth, it would focus on the policies that empirically work best per dollar of cost: public R&D, infrastructure, early-childhood education, skilled immigration, and antitrust enforcement. That is not what "supply-side economics" has come to mean in the political debate. Instead, it has become a label for tax cuts justified by supply-side rhetoric, with the actual productivity-raising policies often crowded out by the deficit consequences of the tax cuts.

20.heading: What Actually Works for Productivity Growth
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
The empirical case for "supply-side economics" in the productivity-raising sense is strong. The empirical case for "supply-side economics" in the tax-cuts-pay-for-themselves sense is weak. Conflating the two is one of the most damaging confusions in modern macroeconomic policy debate. If a candidate or policy advocate says they are for supply-side growth, ask which specific policies they mean. If the answer is "lower marginal tax rates," one has the answer. If the answer is "more R&D, infrastructure, and education investment," one has a different one. The empirics support the second.
— A.S.

20.heading: Worked Examples
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
📐 Worked Example 20.1 — Computing Where the Laffer Peak Is
An economy has an ETI of 0.4. Currently the marginal tax rate is 35%. (a) Compute the Laffer peak tax rate. (b) Is the economy above or below the peak? (c) Would raising the tax rate by 5pp increase or decrease revenue?
1
Use the Laffer peak formula: τ* = 1 / (1 + ETI).
2
(a) Peak: τ* = 1 / (1 + 0.4) = 1/1.4 = 0.714 ≈ 71%. The Laffer peak is at a 71% marginal rate.
3
(b) Below peak: 35% is well below the 71% peak. The economy is on the rising portion of the Laffer curve.
4
(c) Raising rate: at 35% (well below peak), raising the rate by 5pp to 40% would increase revenue. The supply-side response (less labor supply, more avoidance) would shrink the base, but not by enough to offset the higher rate.
The deeper insight: for the U.S., realistic ETI estimates (0.2-0.4) imply a Laffer peak in the range of 70-83%. The U.S. top federal rate has been below 50% for the past 40 years, and the broad average effective rate is much lower (~25%). The Laffer curve provides no support for the argument that U.S. tax cuts pay for themselves at current rates. Empirically, U.S. tax cuts always reduce revenue.

20.heading: Worked Examples
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body:
📐 Worked Example 20.2 — Dynamic Scoring a Tax Cut
A proposed tax cut would lose $2 trillion in static revenue over 10 years. The CBO estimates the tax cut will raise GDP by 1.5% over the decade through supply-side effects, generating roughly 18% of the static revenue back through induced economic activity. (a) Compute the dynamic revenue cost. (b) Compute the implied increase in real GDP. (c) Discuss why this falls far short of "paying for itself."
1
(a) Dynamic cost: static cost × (1 − feedback ratio) = $2 trillion × (1 − 0.18) = $2 trillion × 0.82 = $1.64 trillion.
2
(b) GDP boost: 1.5% × U.S. GDP ≈ 1.5% × $27 trillion = $405 billion cumulative additional GDP over the decade.
3
(c) Why not pay for itself: the cut loses $2T statically. It generates $405B in extra GDP. Even if every dollar of that extra GDP were taxed at a marginal rate of 20%, the recovered revenue would be only ~$80B. The CBO's 18% feedback ($360B) is generous. Even with optimistic dynamic-scoring assumptions, the cuts recover less than a fifth of the static cost.

20.heading: Worked Examples
20.title: Chapter 20, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
20.body: The math does not support the rhetoric. For tax cuts to pay for themselves, the feedback ratio would need to be close to 1.0 — essentially every dollar of static revenue loss would need to be recovered through induced economic activity. Empirically, the feedback ratio for major U.S. tax cuts has been roughly 0.15-0.25. The "pays for itself" claim is not just empirically wrong; it is wrong by an order of magnitude.

21.heading: Overview
21.title: Chapter 21, Supply-Side Economics Tax cuts, deregulation, the Laffer curve, and the empirical track record of "supply-side" policies — from the 1981 Reagan cuts through the 2017 TCJA to the 2025 OBBBA, with an honest look at what these policies actually do versus what they are claimed to do "Supply-
21.body:
🎮 MacroNations Connection — Supply-Side Levers in the Engine
Three supply-side levers feed productivity and potential GDP in the engine: rd_investment (largest coefficient: 0.12 × (rd − 2) per pp/round on potential, 0.048 on productivity), infrastructure (0.10 × (infra − 5) on potential, 0.025 on productivity), and green_energy (0.008 × (green − 30) on potential, smaller on productivity). The engine also implements the Laffer curve: tax_rate above 40% triggers an efficiency drag of −0.008pp per pp of excess, capturing deadweight loss above the revenue-maximizing point. Tax_rate below 12% triggers an underfunding drag of −0.015pp per pp of shortfall, capturing the cost of providing too few public goods. The optimum is somewhere in the 25-40% band. There is no separate "deregulation" lever — the engine uses regulation with optimum at 50%, treating both excessive and insufficient regulation as costly. The engine rewards patient, productivity-raising supply-side policies (R&D, infrastructure) over marginal-rate-cutting tax policies — consistent with the empirical literature.

21.heading: Insight
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
✦ Author's Commentary
Of all the macroeconomic topics covered in this book, debt and deficits is probably the one where the gap between public understanding and economic analysis is the widest. The public discussion is dominated by two opposing oversimplifications. One side says deficits do not matter because the U.S. can never default on dollar-denominated debt — economically true but politically misleading. The other side says deficits are inherently catastrophic and require immediate balanced budgets — economically wrong and historically refuted by countries that have run deficits productively for decades.

21.heading: Insight
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
The careful answer is in between, and it is not particularly partisan: deficits matter when they exceed what a country's growth can absorb, which depends on the interest rate relative to growth, the productivity of the spending being financed, and the durability of the institutional setup. Japan has run 8%+ deficits for 30 years and debt at 250% of GDP without crisis because growth has outpaced interest rates persistently. The U.S. ran 3-5% deficits productively for most of the post-WWII era because GDP grew faster than the debt. The current U.S. trajectory is different, and worse, because growth is no longer reliably above the interest rate — the (r − g) term has turned positive. That is the technical reason today's situation is harder than yesterday's, and why every honest fiscal projection shows debt-to-GDP rising without limit. The political question of what to do about it is genuinely hard. The analytical framework for thinking about it is not.
— A.S.

21.heading: Stocks vs. Flows: Debt Is Not Deficit
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
📘 Principles Level — Two different things
The first conceptual hurdle in fiscal analysis is distinguishing between debt and deficit. Deficit is a flow: it is the amount by which spending exceeds revenue in a single year. The U.S. federal deficit in fiscal year 2025 was approximately $1.8 trillion. Debt is a stock: it is the cumulative borrowing the government has done over its lifetime. U.S. federal debt held by the public at end-2025 was approximately $30 trillion. Debt this year equals debt last year plus this year's deficit (plus accrued interest, plus a few other adjustments).
This sounds basic, but the public debate often conflates the two. "We need to cut the debt" usually means cutting the deficit — which slows debt growth but does not reduce the debt level. To actually reduce the debt, one would need not just balanced budgets but surpluses. The U.S. last ran four consecutive years of surpluses in 1998-2001. Before that, one has to go back to the late 1940s.
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — The Government's Budget Constraint
\[ D_{t+1} = D_t\,(1 + r_t) - S_t \]\(S_t\) is the primary surplus: revenue less non-interest spending.
\(D_{t}\)
Outstanding debt at start of period t.

21.heading: Stocks vs. Flows: Debt Is Not Deficit
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
\(r_{t}\)
Interest rate paid on the debt in period t.
\(S_{t}\)
Primary surplus — tax revenue minus non-interest government spending. Note: this excludes interest payments. A negative primary surplus is a primary deficit.
Total deficit
= primary deficit + interest payments. When one reads "the U.S. deficit is $1.8T," that includes ~$1T of interest. The primary deficit is the $0.8T of spending in excess of revenue before interest.
Why the primary surplus matters: primary surplus is what the government has direct policy control over. Interest payments are largely determined by previous borrowing and current market rates. To stabilize debt, one does not need a balanced total budget — one needs a primary surplus large enough to offset (r − g) × D/Y. That is a much lower bar than "balance the budget."

21.heading: Stocks vs. Flows: Debt Is Not Deficit
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body: Figure 21.1 The distinction that most public commentary elides. The deficit is the amount borrowed during a year; the debt is everything still owed. The two are connected in both directions: this year's deficit adds to the stock, and interest on the stock is part of next year's flow. A government that halves its deficit is still adding to its debt, which is why headlines about deficit reduction say less than they appear to.

21.heading: The Debt-to-GDP Ratio and Its Dynamics
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Debt-to-GDP Dynamics
\[ \Delta\!\left(\frac{D}{Y}\right) \approx (r - g)\,\frac{D}{Y} - \frac{\text{primary surplus}}{Y} \]
Δ(D/Y)
Change in debt-to-GDP ratio. Positive = debt-to-GDP rising.
(r − g)
The single most important number in fiscal sustainability analysis. Real interest rate minus real GDP growth rate. When r > g, debt-to-GDP grows automatically through compound interest even with a balanced primary budget. When r < g, debt-to-GDP shrinks naturally even with modest primary deficits.
primary surplus/Y
Primary surplus as % of GDP. The policy lever.
Stability condition
D/Y is stable when (r − g) × (D/Y) = primary surplus/Y. If r > g and the country runs a primary deficit, D/Y rises monotonically — no convergence.

21.heading: The Debt-to-GDP Ratio and Its Dynamics
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
The (r − g) regime is everything: for most of the post-WWII period, U.S. real interest rates averaged below real GDP growth (g averaging ~3%, r averaging ~2%). This "(r − g) negative" regime meant debt-to-GDP fell automatically even with modest deficits — the post-1945 reduction from 113% to 35% by 1974 happened mostly through (r − g) dynamics, not through surpluses. Post-2008, real rates fell to near zero while growth slowed too, so (r − g) was close to zero. Post-2022, real rates rose substantially while growth stayed modest — (r − g) is now positive for the U.S. for the first time in a generation. This is the structural shift.
Figure 21.2 Debt dynamics with a zero primary balance. The ratio evolves according to \(\Delta d_t \approx (r - g)\,d_{t-1} - pb_t\). When the interest rate on the debt exceeds the growth rate of nominal output, the stock compounds faster than the economy and the ratio rises without any new borrowing; when growth exceeds the interest rate, the ratio falls on its own. The sign of \(r - g\), not the level of the debt, is what determines whether a given path is sustainable.

21.heading: The (r − g) Regime: Why Japan Is not a Crisis But Italy Sometimes Is
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — Confusing high debt with a crisis
Japan has debt-to-GDP of 250% and has not faced a sovereign debt crisis in 30 years. Italy at 130-140% has faced repeated crisis episodes (2011-12, 2018, 2022). The U.S. at 100% has yet to face a crisis. The level of debt does not determine crisis risk — the trajectory does. A country with debt at 250% and (r − g) negative is on a stable path; a country with debt at 70% and (r − g) strongly positive plus rising primary deficits is on an unstable path. What matters is whether the math implies convergence to a stable D/Y or divergence without bound.
Japan's stability rests on multiple favorable factors: low interest rates (BOJ rate at zero for two decades, then yield curve control), high domestic savings (90%+ of Japanese debt is held domestically, mostly by the central bank and pension funds), demographic decline (less competing demand for domestic capital), and aging-population deflationary pressure. The U.S. has fewer of these factors, which is why the same debt-to-GDP ratio implies more risk in the U.S. than in Japan. Mechanical comparison of debt-to-GDP across countries is misleading; one needs to look at the dynamics.

21.heading: The (r − g) Regime: Why Japan Is not a Crisis But Italy Sometimes Is
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body: Figure 21.3 The single most important fact about a debt position. When the interest rate on the debt is below the growth rate of the economy, the ratio of debt to output falls on its own even with a modest primary deficit, and when it is above, the ratio rises even with a balanced primary budget. Japan has lived below the line for thirty years with a debt ratio far above anything once thought survivable; the countries that met crises did so after moving above it.

21.heading: The Ricardian Equivalence Debate
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
📗 Intermediate Level — Do deficits crowd out private spending?
In 1974, Robert Barro published a paper arguing that government deficits do not matter for aggregate demand. His argument: when the government runs a deficit, rational forward-looking households realize that future taxes will be higher to pay off the debt. They save the entirety of the current tax cut (or government transfer) to pay future taxes. Net effect on consumption: zero. This is Ricardian equivalence (named after David Ricardo who first noted the idea in 1820, though he did not fully endorse it).
If Ricardian equivalence held strictly, fiscal policy would have no demand effects — every tax cut would be fully saved, every deficit would be exactly offset by private saving. Empirically, this is false. Tax cuts do raise consumption (just by less than the full amount), and deficits do affect interest rates and aggregate demand. But the Ricardian intuition captures something real: forward-looking households do adjust their saving when they anticipate future tax increases, and high-debt countries have more saving than otherwise comparable low-debt countries. The pure form is wrong; the directional insight is right.

21.heading: The Ricardian Equivalence Debate
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
1980s-1990s
Cross-country evidence
Imperfect Ricardian
Testing Ricardian Equivalence in the Data
Empirical tests of Ricardian equivalence have consistently found partial but incomplete offset. Studies from the 1980s-90s (Bernheim 1987, Seater 1993) found that approximately 30-50% of a deficit-financed tax cut shows up in additional private saving — meaningful, but far from the 100% Ricardian equivalence predicts. The 2008 financial crisis provided a quasi-natural experiment: countries that ran larger deficits saw private saving rise, but by less than 1-for-1 with public dissaving.

21.heading: The Ricardian Equivalence Debate
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body: The empirical literature suggests three reasons Ricardian equivalence fails in practice: (1) liquidity constraints: many households cannot actually save more even if they wanted to — they are already consuming all their income; (2) finite horizons: households discount future taxes more heavily than future income, especially across generations; (3) uncertainty: future tax burden is uncertain and depends on political outcomes. The honest summary: deficits do affect aggregate demand, but the effect is smaller than naive Keynesian models predict because some Ricardian offset exists. Typical estimates put fiscal multipliers somewhere in the 0.7-1.5 range — clearly positive, but not the 2.5+ of pure Keynesian multipliers.

21.heading: The Crowding-Out Channel
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
⚙ Equation Walkthrough — Crowding Out
\[ S^{\text{national}} = \underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{public}} = Y - C - G = I \]
Private saving
Disposable income minus consumption.
Government saving
Tax revenue minus government spending. Negative when government runs a deficit.
Crowding-out logic
When government dissaves (runs a deficit), national saving falls (unless Ricardian offset is complete). Less saving means less funds available for private investment at any given interest rate, so the interest rate rises to clear the market, and investment falls. The deficit "crowds out" private investment dollar for dollar (in pure form) or partially (in practice).

21.heading: The Crowding-Out Channel
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body: The empirical question: by how much does $1 of additional deficit reduce private investment? Empirical estimates range from $0.10 to $0.50 per dollar of deficit, depending on regime. In deep recessions with the zero lower bound binding, crowding out is near zero (the central bank does not tighten in response). In full-employment conditions like 2025, crowding out is substantial — perhaps $0.30-$0.50 per dollar of deficit. This is the mechanism through which sustained deficits eventually slow long-run growth.

21.heading: The U.S. Trajectory: 1945 to 2055
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — Why this time is structurally different
Three changes distinguish the 2020s+ U.S. fiscal trajectory from any prior period. First, (r − g) has turned positive for the first time sustained in 60+ years. The mechanical debt-stabilizing force of past decades is gone. Second, the structural primary deficit is large and growing — about 4% of GDP and projected to grow to 6%+ over coming decades. Past episodes of high debt-to-GDP (postwar) had primary surpluses running 2-4% of GDP, which combined with favorable (r − g) drove debt down quickly. Today's primary deficits run in the opposite direction. Third, demographic pressure on entitlements is just starting. Medicare and Social Security spending grow faster than GDP for the next 30 years no matter what; absent reform, they alone account for most of the projected debt-to-GDP rise.

21.heading: The U.S. Trajectory: 1945 to 2055
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
What is different from past warnings about debt is that the math now genuinely does not work. The 1980s "deficits matter" warnings turned out to be too pessimistic because (r − g) stayed favorable. The 2010s warnings turned out to be too pessimistic for the same reason plus the zero lower bound. The 2020s+ warnings about debt sustainability are based on changed underlying mechanics, not on the same old story being repeated. The trajectory is not just bad relative to history — it is bad relative to the parameters that made history work.
— A.S.

21.body: Figure 21.4 Federal debt held by the public since 1946. The ratio fell from above one hundred percent to under thirty without the government ever running large surpluses: nominal growth did the work, with the denominator rising faster than the numerator. The projected path reverses that arithmetic, because interest costs now rise with the stock and the primary deficit is structural rather than cyclical.

21.heading: How Sovereign Debt Crises Actually Happen
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
Despite the mechanical math of debt dynamics, sovereign debt crises do not follow a predictable schedule. Some countries cross 100% debt-to-GDP and never face crisis (Japan, Italy in non-crisis years). Others face crisis at 70% (Argentina 2001). The actual trigger is rarely the debt level itself — it is a loss of market confidence that pushes interest rates up sharply, making the debt instantly less sustainable. Understanding how crises happen is essential to understanding what risk the U.S. actually faces.
Mechanism of sovereign debt crises
PhaseWhat happens
1. Slow buildupDebt-to-GDP rises gradually over years as deficits exceed (g − r) × D/Y. Markets accept this — the country has fiscal space, growth continues, rates stay manageable.
2. Confidence shockSome event — a political crisis, a banking shock, a global rate rise, a missed payment — causes markets to reassess. The "Greek moment" of 2010 was this: revised deficit numbers revealed the situation was worse than thought.

21.heading: How Sovereign Debt Crises Actually Happen
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
3. Rate spiralRequired interest rate jumps as risk premia rise. Higher rates mean higher interest costs, which widen the deficit, which raises the debt, which raises the rate further. Greece's 10-year yield went from 6% in early 2010 to 30%+ by 2012.
4. Forced adjustmentThe country cannot service debt at the new rates. Options: default (Argentina 2001, Greece 2012), bailout (multiple Eurozone countries 2010-12), inflation-out (effectively a soft default through currency debasement), or aggressive austerity.

21.heading: How Sovereign Debt Crises Actually Happen
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
⚠ Common Pitfall — "The U.S. can never default"
The argument is technically right but practically misleading. The U.S. borrows in dollars and the Federal Reserve can always create dollars to pay debt. So technical nominal default is impossible. But this does not mean the U.S. can borrow without consequence:
Interest rates can rise sharply. The post-2022 rise in 10-year yields from 1.5% to 4.5%+ added roughly $400B/year to interest costs over 10 years. A further rise to 6% would add another $500B/year.
Inflation is a "soft default." If the Fed monetizes large deficits, inflation rises. Bondholders are repaid in dollars worth less than the dollars lent. The 1970s saw real returns on Treasury bonds of −2%/year for a decade — effective default by inflation.
Fiscal space erodes. Every dollar going to interest is a dollar not available for defense, infrastructure, R&D, or crisis response. By 2034 CBO projects interest payments will exceed defense + Medicare combined.

21.heading: How Sovereign Debt Crises Actually Happen
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
Reserve currency status is not permanent. The dollar's reserve role rests on confidence in U.S. fiscal management. A sustained loss of that confidence — even slowly — could erode the privilege the U.S. has been getting for 80 years.
The U.S. will not default in the technical sense. But "cannot default" carries considerable weight in arguments that pretend deficits do not matter. The real question is the cost of carrying high debt, and that cost is rising, not falling.

21.heading: What Reduces Debt-to-GDP
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
If a country wants to reduce its debt-to-GDP ratio, it has five options. None is easy, and several involve substantial trade-offs.
Five ways to reduce debt-to-GDP and their historical track records
ApproachHow it worksHistorical example
1. Growth (raise g)Faster GDP growth shrinks debt-to-GDP at any given debt level. Most painless option, but requires productivity gains.U.S. 1945-1974: growth at 3.5% drove debt-to-GDP from 113% to 35%.
2. Inflation (reduce real r)Higher inflation reduces the real value of nominal debt. Effectively a soft default on bondholders.U.S. 1970s: 7%+ inflation eroded real debt value.
3. Financial repressionGovernment compels banks/pensions to hold low-yield government debt, keeping r artificially low.U.S. 1945-1951 (Treasury-Fed Accord rates caps), Japan 1990s-present.
4. Austerity (raise primary surplus)Cut spending and/or raise taxes to run primary surpluses. Politically painful, often slow.Sweden 1993-2000 (consolidation), UK 2010-2015, Ireland 2008-2012.
5. Default (formal)Outright refusal to pay. Most damaging to future borrowing capacity. Rare for developed economies.Argentina 2001, Greece 2012 partial restructuring.

21.heading: What Reduces Debt-to-GDP
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
✦ Author's Commentary — The most likely U.S. path
If forced to predict, I think the most likely U.S. path through the 2030s-40s is some combination of options 1, 2, and 3: moderately faster growth from AI productivity gains, moderately higher inflation than the 2010s norm (3-3.5% rather than 1.5-2%), and gradually rising financial repression through Fed balance sheet operations that keep long-rates lower than they would otherwise be. This combination would not reduce debt-to-GDP, but it would slow its rise enough to avoid forced adjustment.
What is politically unlikely in the U.S. context: a sustained primary-surplus-driven consolidation. The 1990s budget surpluses required a unique political alignment (divided government, strong growth, fiscal consensus on deficit reduction from both parties). None of that exists today. Both U.S. political parties have abandoned fiscal consolidation as a priority. The most plausible outcome is therefore drift — debt-to-GDP rising for decades while the underlying mechanics gradually catch up with the political consensus.

21.heading: What Reduces Debt-to-GDP
21.title: Chapter 21, Government Debt & Deficits Why deficits matter, why they sometimes do not, how debt-to-GDP dynamics actually work, the Ricardian equivalence debate, the difference between sustainable and unsustainable trajectories, and the unprecedented post-2020 path the U.S. has chosen In December 202
21.body:
What is important to understand: this is not necessarily catastrophic. Japan has been doing essentially this since 1995 — debt-to-GDP at 250% with no crisis, modest growth, deflationary pressure, gradual erosion of fiscal space. The U.S. could find itself in a similar steady state at 150%+ debt-to-GDP within a generation. It just would not be a vigorous, growth-friendly outcome. It would be slow erosion of fiscal capacity and slow rise in financial fragility. Not a crash, but not a triumph either.
— A.S.
